The measure captures the difference between the average ESG concerns of public companies and those of the prototypical B Corp member within the industry context. Mean centered.

A count of the number of B Corp terms that appeared within the first three 'levels' of a company's website, i.e., any page on or within two clicks of the home page. The dictionary was developed by manually reviewing the B Lab website and includes references to the B Corporation certification as well as related distinguishing phrases such as 'The Change We Seek.' Data were collected by the CULTR text scraper, which started on each company's home page and followed all internal links. Results are based on data collected in late October and early November 2015.

A count of the number of B Corp images that appeared within the first three levels of a company's website. The library of images was created by manually reviewing all pages of the B Lab website and includes the Certified B Corporation logo, the B the Change logo, and the Declaration of Interdependence image. Data were captured by the CULTR image scraper, which followed all internal links from each company's home page.

A count of the number of Certified B Corporations within a focal organization's state. Observed as of December 2013, providing temporal separation from the dependent variables. Mean centered. Because this variable correlated .96 with regional public companies, its common variance with that control was partialed out and the residuals were used in the analysis.

A count of the number of Certified B Corporations within a focal organization's industry. Observed as of December 2013, providing clear temporal separation from the dependent variables. Mean centered.

Project managers were asked whether they utilized a 'project principles' document (principle) during their project; each response was coded 1 if the manager used a principle and 0 if not. For the models of knowledge use, the responses were combined into a four-category knowledge-use scale.
scale: 0/1; combined with template use into a 1-4 knowledge-use scale

description: Knowledge template use was measured by asking project managers whether they consulted a 'previous project completion report' (template), coding the response 1 if the manager used a template and 0 if not. For the models of knowledge use, the responses were combined into a four-category knowledge-use scale.
scale: 0/1; combined with principle use into a 1-4 knowledge-use scale

description: After the completion of each project, the Metrics and Evaluation Unit evaluated efficiency by measuring the degree to which the project met two key criteria and then rated the efficiency of each project as excellent, satisfactory, or unsatisfactory. In the sample, 11% of the projects were rated excellent, 69% were rated satisfactory, and 20% were rated unsatisfactory.

Customer responsiveness reflects the degree to which the customer's specific goals and objectives were met by the project, assessed after completion against project-specific criteria by the Metrics and Evaluation Unit through customer surveys and local sector or industry assessments. If the project exceeded its goal it received a rating of excellent, if it met its goal satisfactory, and if it did not perform to expectations unsatisfactory; in the sample 13% of projects were rated excellent, 62% satisfactory, and 25% unsatisfactory.

Project managers were surveyed on the extent to which they attended global and regional training sessions to help them in their project work. The question in the survey asked, 'To what extent did you attend a [companywide] training session related to your project?'

Experience within country was measured by the project manager's local language proficiency and tenure in the local country. The questions asked managers 'How many years have you worked in your current location?' and 'How well do you speak the local language? (1-not at all, 2-basic, 3-proficient, 4-fluent, 5-native).'
scale: language proficiency 1-5; local tenure in years

description: Industry experience was measured by the project manager's prior years of experience working in a related industry prior to joining the firm, the number of foreign languages spoken by the manager, and by counting the number of countries in which he or she had worked for longer than six months.

Geographic distance was coded as the log of the miles from headquarters to the project's country office. The average distance was 5,581 miles with a standard deviation of 2,755 miles and a maximum of 9,724 miles.

Institutional distance was measured by assessing cultural distance, which primarily involves normative and cognitive institutional distance. Using Kogut and Singh's (1988) cultural distance index formulation, the authors created a separate index from the deviation along all nine GLOBE indices, corrected for variation differences within each dimension, and used the average.

Distance from the knowledge source is measured by two project-level variables: geographic distance, the log of miles from headquarters to the project's country office, and institutional distance, a Kogut and Singh style index of cultural distance across the nine GLOBE dimensions.

An unobtrusive measure calculated from four behavioral indicators derived from quarterly earnings conference call transcripts, where low relative volubility indicates high CEO humility. The indicators are the sequence when the CEO made the first comment, the total number of times non-CEO executives spoke divided by the number of times the CEO spoke, the number of times the most frequently speaking non-CEO executive spoke divided by the number of times the CEO spoke, and the highest total number of words by a non-CEO executive divided by the total number of words by the CEO. Items two to four were log transformed, all four items were standardized, and their average generated quarterly humility scores; in hypothesis testing humility is measured using two-year moving averages of years t - 1 and t - 2.
time_window: two-year moving average (years t - 1 and t - 2)

description: A dummy variable that equals one if the firm has any CSIR incident in a year (year t), and zero otherwise. CSIR was operationalized as legal or regulatory violations resulting in conviction or settlement, such as pollution, accounting misstatements, unsafe products, employment discrimination, and contract violation. Two coders manually identified incidents from media reports, resolving discrepancies (Cohen's kappa = 0.841), and only incidents that occurred in the third or any subsequent year of a CEO's tenure were retained.
scale: dummy (1 = any CSIR incident in a year, 0 = otherwise)

description: The number of corrective actions within six months following the first news report of the CSIR incident. Corrective actions were searched in press releases from Business Wire and PR Newswire, with an initial list generated from content categories of Factiva's 'intelligent indexing' (process redesign, supply chain management, auditor, worker pay, workplace safety, welfare, and employee training/development) and verified by two coders (Cohen's kappa = 0.839). Verbal accounts such as apologies and executive replacements were excluded, and only press releases capturing actual actions were counted.
time_window: six months following the first news report of the incident

description: Measured as one if the total number of industry peer CSIR incidents was above the median level, and zero otherwise. Industry peer CSIR incidents refer to CSIR incidents reported in the past three years in a given (two-digit) industry, excluding the focal firms.
scale: dummy (1 = above the median level, 0 = otherwise)

description: The number of female and nonWhite members divided by the total number of TMT members, excluding CEOs. Top managers' information was collected from Execucomp, and race was inferred using the machine learning-based classifier developed by Chintalapati et al. (2018), which uses first and last names to predict race.

Ordinal measure of when a hospital began using TQM, coded 0 if the hospital began using TQM less than two years ago, 1 for more than two years ago but less than four years ago, and 2 for more than four years ago. Higher values therefore indicate earlier adoption. Used as the independent variable in the models predicting motivation for TQM adoption.

Survey item asking the CEO, on a scale of 1 to 7, how important 'improve productivity' was as a reason for the hospital's decision to implement CQI/TQM. The item was selected from an initial set of four economic-gain items after qualitative interviews and a survey of physicians indicated it was one of only two items that cleanly tapped economic issues, so it was retained as the indicator of economic gains.

Survey item asking the CEO, on a scale of 1 to 7, how important 'be perceived as a market leader' was as a reason for the hospital's decision to implement CQI/TQM. Interviews and the validation survey indicated that this item dealt with social rather than economic issues and reflected a focus on achieving gains.

Survey item asking the CEO, on a scale of 1 to 7, how important 'loss of market share' was as a reason for the hospital's decision to implement CQI/TQM. Because this item loaded on the predicted factor but also partially on the other factor, the authors regressed it on the two measures of social and economic gains and subtracted the predicted values from the actual values, leaving only its unique variation related to economic losses.

Survey item asking the CEO, on a scale of 1 to 7, how important the 'influence of the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations (JCAHO)' was as a reason for the hospital's decision to implement CQI/TQM. The authors took citing JCAHO influence as important to indicate a view of TQM adoption as a way to avoid social losses.

Measured with three indicators. The first is a survey item asking CEOs to indicate, on a scale from 1 to 10, the extent to which CQI/TQM philosophy, principles, and methods had been implemented throughout the hospital. The second covers implementation efforts related to management and personnel, using the percentage of senior managers and of full-time-equivalent personnel who had received formal quality improvement training. The third is the overall score on the use of TQM tools, calculated as the average number of tools used divided by the possible number of tools used, weighted by whether each tool was used by many, few, or no departments/teams.

variable_name: Entrant Partner / Incumbent Partner (entry collaboration dummies)
description: A set of partnership variables that record whether a business had formed at least one collaborative relationship by the end of its first full calendar year of participation in the industry. The variables distinguish entry relationships with other industry entrants from those with incumbents, and marketing relationships (used to market products) from R&D relationships (used to develop products).
time_window: by the end of the first full calendar year in the industry

description: Dummy variables that record whether a business formed at least one relationship in a given year, measured as Created Entrant Relationship (relationships with industry entrants) and Created Incumbent Relationship (relationships with industry incumbents), as well as Created Relationship for any relationship. In the post-entry sales growth equations the same entrant/incumbent and marketing/R&D partner dummies denote whether firms formed new relationships during observation years after the entry year.
time_window: given year after the entry year

description: Sales revenue that each business obtained during its first full calendar year in the industry, expressed in millions of dollars. Untransformed values are used in the sales level analyses, with log values used only in the sales growth analyses.
time_window: first full calendar year in the industry

description: Percentage change in sales for the 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year periods after entrants' first full year in the industry, computed as ln S2/S1, ln S3/S1, and ln S4/S1, where S1, S2, S3, and S4 are sales in years 1-4. The 3-year growth window is used to test the comparison between incumbent and entrant partners.
time_window: 1-, 2-, and 3-year windows after the first full year

description: Percentage change in sales measured as ln S_{t+1}/S_t for 1-year growth (t > 1), ln S_{t+2}/S_t for 2-year growth (t = 2, 4, ...), and ln S_{t+3}/S_t for 3-year growth (t = 3, 6, ...) after the first full year of participation, with the 2-year and 3-year models using non-overlapping business-year spells. The same 1-year percentage change in sales, lagged one year (ln S_{t-1}/S_{t-2}), serves as the sales growth independent variable in the collaboration formation equations.
time_window: 1-, 2-, and 3-year windows after the first full year; lagged one year in the collaboration formation analysis

description: Natural log of annual sales revenue in millions of dollars, lagged one year. The authors specify the log of sales because size is likely to have a nonlinear impact on collaboration, as the incentives to form links decline as business sales become particularly large.

Cumulative number of partnerships that a business created before a given record year, lagged one year and assigned a value of 0 if the business had no partnerships. The collaboration records report the cumulative number of interfirm agreements that each business created rather than the number of agreements active in each year.
time_window: cumulative through the year before the record year (t-1)

description: Positions on a core/periphery continuum were measured for all individuals with Borgatti and Everett's algorithm. The authors chose a continuous core/periphery model because they were interested in the continuum rather than in assigning people to either the core or the periphery. The algorithm attributes large values for pairs of nodes that are both high in coreness, middling values when one is high in coreness and the other is not, and low values when both are peripheral; positions were calculated in UCINET.

In the online survey, respondents were asked a yes or no question: 'Have you actively participated in other online communities NOT hosted by Propellerhead during the last three years?' Those who answered yes were asked to list in up to 10 free-text slots the names of other online communities not hosted by Propellerhead that they most actively spent time in. The communities mentioned were identified with Google and other search engines and content coded by type, and general social network communities such as Facebook were excluded. The number of communities listed by each respondent was used as the measurement for boundary-spanning activities, and the number was further subdivided into technical and artistic communities.
scale: count of communities listed, up to 10

description: Propellerhead and four experienced people in the community independently ranked the 280 survey respondents on a scale of 0, 1, or 2 for whether each had been innovative in the community in their view, and the judges then explained their evaluations by telephone. Judges were instructed: 'Please identify users in the community who have made innovative, new, and valuable contributions to the community. These could be mods/GUI, extras, and new applications. However, beta testers should not be nominated as delivering innovations.' Two composite scores of how innovative individuals were were developed by summing the judges' scores: one capturing whether people are ranked as innovative or not, and one measuring the degree to which they were considered innovative.
scale: 0, 1, or 2 per judge, summed across five judges

description: The number of physicians per capita within each hospital's SMSA market. The authors argue that hospitals operating in markets where physicians are scarce are more dependent on physicians as critical sources of patient referrals and revenues, so a comparatively lower supply of physicians indicates higher intraorganizational power of physicians.

variable_name: Percentage of physician representation on the board of directors
description: The total number of physicians on the board as a proportion of total board members. Representation on the board may provide physicians with an opportunity to influence how hospitals respond to regulatory and competitive pressures. The authors note that hospital boards are made up of multiple constituencies, so an increase in the physicians' percentage of board membership could come at the expense of these other groups rather than managers.

The total number of HMOs per capita within each hospital market, used to measure the intensity of market competition. The authors argue that as competitive pressures in the environment become a critical strategic contingency for a hospital, managers assume a more central and powerful role in determining how hospitals respond to these pressures.

variable_name: Percentage of management representation on the board of directors
description: The total number of hospital management board representatives as a proportion of total board members. The authors argue that management power is enhanced when hospital managers assume more formal authority through representation on the board of directors.

A dummy variable distinguishing for-profit hospitals from not-for-profit hospitals. The authors argue that the comparatively stronger focus on organizational performance and strategic adaptation in for-profit hospitals increases the power of managers, who are in a more central position to mediate between environmental changes and strategic responses.

The dependent variable is the percentage of services contracted by the hospital. The measure was developed from the CHFC distinction between services directly organized and staffed by the hospital and those provided on a contractual basis and staffed by the contractor: the total number of contracted services as a proportion of all services provided. The analysis is directed to 62 ancillary services designated by the CHFC, which show greater variation in availability and organization than basic hospital services.

The analysis is estimated separately for the pre-PPS period (1980-83) and the post-PPS period (1984-86), following the introduction of the PPS in 1983. A statistical procedure developed by Bloch and Kushin (1978) is used to test for significant differences in the regression parameters of the independent variables across the two periods.

A two-item scale measured on a seven-point scale (1 = disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Respondents were asked (1) if the existing knowledge base in the company for the internal development of the required competences was limited, and (2) if the barriers that could hinder the internal development of the required competences (patents, copyrights, complex learning, and development processes) were high. The variable was recoded to capture the transferability of the established firm-specific resources to the new segment, i.e., absence of limitations/barriers indicates high transferability.
time_window: time the decision was actually made

description: A three-item scale measured on a seven-point scale (1 = disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Respondents were asked if (1) integrating the new target segment activity effectively into daily operations will clearly set the firm apart from the competition, (2) gains from performing the new target segment activity (in terms of lower costs or superior quality for customers) were difficult to match by the firm's competitors, and (3) the synergies between the new target segment activity and the core activities of the firm are durable and sustainable.
time_window: time the decision was actually made

description: The dependent variable is nominally scaled with the expressions 'entry by internal development' (1) and 'collaborative entry' (0).
time_window: time the decision was actually made

description: A single-item measure on the seven-point scale, referring explicitly to the investment volume in the entry phase and not to the running costs in the implementation phase. Respondents were required to give an indication of whether the focal business segment could be characterized as being investment intensive in the entry phase.
time_window: time the decision was actually made

description: A three-item scale on the seven-point scale, based on Zaheer and Venkatraman (1995) and Zaheer, McEvily, and Perrone (1998). Before the items, respondents were reminded to think about the specific (selected or would-have-chosen) collaboration partner. Respondents assessed (1) if the (potential) collaboration partner had always been fair and considerate towards them in negotiations about the collaboration, (2) if they were certain—based on reputation and/or past experience—that the partner would be reliable and keep any promises made, and (3) if they were not worried that the partner might take advantage of their dependency and use modified contextual constraints to profit at their expense.
time_window: time the decision was actually made

description: A two-item scale on the seven-point scale, again asking respondents to think about the specific collaboration partner. Respondents assessed (1) how certain they were that the potential collaboration partner would possess the required technical and organizational competencies as well as the financial resources to jointly accomplish the activity successfully, and (2) to what extent they could correctly assess the quality of the required partner resources.
time_window: time the decision was actually made

description: CEOs listed up to ten of the most significant resource bases used in the businesses of their firm and up to ten of its most significant businesses, entered the proportion of total firm revenues obtained from each business, and indicated in which businesses each resource was used. Because the resources identified were significant resources, use in multiple businesses was a surrogate for economies of scope. From these data the author identified groups of resource-related businesses and computed an entropy measure of diversification that also controlled for differences in total diversification.

CEOs listed up to ten of the most significant client bases of their firm, listed up to ten of its most significant businesses, and indicated in a matrix which businesses sold goods or services to each client base. From these data the author identified groups of client-related businesses and computed an entropy measure of diversification that also controlled for differences in total diversification.

Two independent raters familiar with the literature on information economics categorized all services listed in the four-digit SIC classification into either the search or the experience category, with cases of disagreement resolved by reference to the services literature and discussion. The summary measure for each firm is the proportion of revenues obtained from search services; by the measure's construction, its complement measures the proportion of revenues obtained from experience services.

variable_name: industry- and risk-adjusted return on equity
description: Average ROE over the five years 1985-89, divided by an accounting-based measure of systematic risk defined as the ratio of the covariance of a firm's ROE with the ROE of a broad market portfolio to the variance of the market portfolio's ROE. The ratio was then adjusted by subtracting a weighted sum of the respective industry averages for each industry in which the firm participated, using the percentage of total revenues in each business as weights.
time_window: average ROE 1985-89; risk computed from 1965-84 data

description: The ratio of the market value of equity to its book value, computed as the average during 1987 from COMPUSTAT data. The average was adjusted by subtracting a weighted sum of the respective industry averages for each industry in which the firm participated, using the percentage of total revenues in each business as weights.

Obtained as the estimate of the intercept in a regression equation of firm returns on market returns, both computed in excess of the risk-free rate, using daily firm and stock market returns from the CRSP tapes for 1987. The risk-free rate was computed as the 12-month treasury bond rate for each month of 1987.

Accounting-based performance measure used alongside the stock-market-based measures in the hypothesis tests; the same as the industry- and risk-adjusted return on equity, and the measure for which the two hypotheses were not supported.

variable_name: NUMSUB (number of a firm's subsidiaries in a host country)
description: The number of an MNC's subsidiaries in a host country, hand collected by the authors. Changes in investment are measured in terms of the increase or decrease in the number of a firm's subsidiaries in a given host country, which the authors argue captures substantial changes in resource commitment. They argue it is better than a binary measure of subsidiary existence because it scales the strategic importance of countries and reflects the firm's perceived level of exogenous risk.

Log of one plus the number of people killed by terrorist activities in the host country, drawn from the International Terrorism Activity Database (ITERATE). The number of people killed is used to operationalize the severity of the disaster. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Log of one plus the number of people killed by natural disasters in the host country, drawn from the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT). EM-DAT covers nine types of natural disasters: drought, earthquake, extreme temperature, flood, landslide, volcanic eruption, wave/surge, wild fire, and windstorm. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Log of one plus the number of people killed by technological disasters in the host country, drawn from the Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT). EM-DAT covers three types of technological accidents: industrial, transportation, and miscellaneous. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Composite Worldwide Governance Indicator for the host country, scored between -2.5 and +2.5, where a higher score indicates a higher quality of the institutional environment for that indicator. The authors argue that a government's ability to formulate appropriate responses to crises and its willingness and ability to implement them, rather than financial resources alone, underlie government effectiveness. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Composite Worldwide Governance Indicator for the host country, scored between -2.5 and +2.5. The authors define regulatory quality as the ability of governments to formulate and implement sound policies and regulations, and note that regulations must be properly implemented and effectively enforced to be effective. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Composite Worldwide Governance Indicator for the host country, scored between -2.5 and +2.5. The authors define rule of law as the extent to which citizens abide by the rules of society, the ability to enforce contracts and property rights, and the degree to which the police and courts fairly and capably enforce the law. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Composite Worldwide Governance Indicator for the host country, scored between -2.5 and +2.5. The authors describe it as the degree to which individuals are able to express their views and demand action of those in power, through the courts, the ballot box, the media, or other institutional mechanisms, and to hold officials accountable for their actions. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Composite Worldwide Governance Indicator for the host country, scored between -2.5 and +2.5. The authors discuss political stability in terms of the absence of political instability, manifested in the form of coups d'etat, civil strife, threats to the peaceful transfer of power, expropriation of assets, unstable policies and regulations, or other forms of social and political turmoil, which managers cite as an important influence on foreign direct investment decisions. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Composite Worldwide Governance Indicator for the host country, scored between -2.5 and +2.5. The authors argue that corruption affects the quality of governance and the ability of the host country government to respond to major disasters, with victims of disasters in high-corruption countries finding it difficult to receive aid and assistance. The variable is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

Major disasters are measured as three host-country variables, each the log of one plus the number of people killed in the year: by terrorist activities, by natural disasters, and by technological disasters. Governance quality moderates each of them.

Dummy variable that measures whether a firm received a Y-program grant without the final score on record. The Y-program is a merit-based grant that allocates funds based on a firm's evaluation score ranking, so financing firms without scores contradicts the grant's official allocation policy; about 3.0% of the firms received grants without merit-ranking scores on record.

Dummy variable measuring whether a grant applicant and the Z-center are colocated in Country X's capital city, to proxy their physical proximity. It is the focal geographic variable in the logit models of irregular awards and is interacted with the indigenous innovation era, the venue of application, and state ownership.

Dummy variable measuring the Y-program's institutional context, assigned a value of one to 2007-2010 and zero to 2005-2006 to gauge if a grant allocation occurred during 'indigenous innovation'. The authors state that after the 2006 national innovation initiative the Z-center greatly secured its budget and administrative authority and the Finance Ministry's scrutiny and pressures diminished, so the variable indexes the era in which external inter-agency oversight was relaxed.

Dummy variable measuring whether a firm submits its application through a provincial STC that interacts with the Z-center on a routine basis. About 39.3% of applicants submitted their proposals through provincial STCs, which the authors treat as the only intermediaries with direct and routinized interaction with the central grant agency.

Dummy variable measuring whether a firm has state-affiliated equity owners such as the state-owned assets administration commission, public research institute, and government bureau and public organization. The information was hand-collected from grant proposals; about 10% of applicants have state-affiliated equity owners.

The amount of Y-program funding a firm receives, in US dollars (2007 values). The authors compare irregular and regular winners on this amount to test whether collusive rule-violation also brought larger funding; irregular winners received an extra 10,887 USD compared to regular winners, whose average grant size is 79,934 USD.

Firm valuation is the market value of the company's equity, operationalized as the product of its shares outstanding and the stock price per share. The authors argue this is a more accurate measurement of firm performance for small firms than other commonly used financial measurements (e.g., P/E ratio) because biotech start-ups are typically not profitable. Valuation data were collected primarily from CRSP and RECAP, and the market value is derived as the average of 12 end-of-month daily values for the corresponding year.
time_window: corresponding year (average of 12 end-of-month daily values)

description: Count of a small firm's alliances with large partners that were classified as exploitation or exploration alliances according to detailed alliance information acquired from either BioScan or RECAP. Alliances focused on upstream activities of the value chain such as drug discovery and development were coded as exploration alliances, using the perspective of the focal firm, i.e., the small firm. The count is taken within an alliance portfolio that includes all alliances announced between year t and t - 4.

Count of a small firm's alliances with large partners that were classified as exploitation alliances according to detailed alliance information from BioScan or RECAP. Alliances involving downstream activities of the value chain such as manufacturing and marketing were coded as exploitation alliances, using the perspective of the focal small firm. The count is taken within an alliance portfolio covering all alliances announced between year t and t - 4.

The number of the small firm's exploration alliances with large partners that involve equity ownership such as equity transfers or the creation of a new entity. Alliances were classified as exploration or exploitation from the perspective of the focal small firm and counted within the five-year moving alliance portfolio window. The authors used the absolute number of these alliances rather than a ratio in order to assess which alliance type was likely to generate greater valuation for small firms.

The number of the small firm's exploration alliances with large partners that are contractual agreements without any equity ownership changes. Exploration alliances are those focused on upstream activities of the value chain such as drug discovery and development, coded from the perspective of the focal small firm. Counts are taken within the five-year moving alliance portfolio window.

The number of the small firm's exploitation alliances with large partners that involve equity ownership such as equity transfers or the creation of a new entity. Exploitation alliances are those involving downstream activities of the value chain such as manufacturing and marketing, coded from the perspective of the focal small firm. Counts are taken within the five-year moving alliance portfolio window.

The number of the small firm's exploitation alliances with large partners that are contractual agreements without any equity ownership changes. Exploitation alliances are those involving downstream activities of the value chain such as manufacturing and marketing, coded from the perspective of the focal small firm. Counts are taken within the five-year moving alliance portfolio window.

Ego network density is used as the proxy for relational governance, calculated as the percentage of existing alliance ties within an ego's alliance portfolio divided by all possible ties. The authors constructed yearly alliance matrices within the biopharmaceutical industry from 1984 to 2006 using a five-year moving window, and identified 65,864 pairs of alliances from various data sources. Alliances with more than two firms were entered into the matrices as separate dyadic combinations of all firms within the alliance.

This variable identifies the instances when an inventor moved from a focal firm to an alter firm in the sample. A case of mobility was identified when a researcher was listed as inventor in patents granted to two different firms over the 1980-1995 period, following the procedure in the Appendix; the time of the mobility event is estimated as the year before the application year of the first alter firm's patent where the mobile employee appears as inventor. Outbound mobility was coded as one if at least one case of outbound mobility occurred in the five-year window preceding the year of observation; otherwise it was coded as zero. Ninety-nine of the 154 firms in the sample experienced an outbound mobility event.
time_window: five-year window preceding the year of observation

description: For each focal-alter dyad, this variable is a count of the number of times the focal firm cited the alter firm on patents granted with application dates on the year of observation. Each citation is treated as one instance of the focal firm's drawing on the knowledge of the cited firm. Cites is compiled from the NBER dataset.

When two firms are located in the same metropolitan statistical area (MSA) or same country (in the case of foreign firms), GeoProximity is coded as one, otherwise it is coded as zero. MSAs are those for 1993 as defined by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget. The location of the firm was obtained from the first page of the USPTO patents granted to the firm during the year of the observation; for firms reporting more than one location across their patent portfolios, the primary location is the site with the majority of the patents.

Daily stock returns were collected from CRSP within 250-day estimation windows [-800, -551] prior to the announcement dates of the divestitures in the sample. Normal returns were predicted from these firms' daily stock returns and the stock market's returns using the paper's Equation 1, whose rendering is unreadable in the text; the text states that alpha is the company's average stock market return during the estimation window, beta captures the correlation between the company's and the stock market's returns, and epsilon is a normally distributed error term. Abnormal returns were then calculated within 3-day event windows [-1, +1] surrounding the divestiture announcement dates by subtracting the expected returns obtained from this model from the actual returns achieved during this event window. The cumulative abnormal return is the cumulative sum of these abnormal returns over this three-day event window.
time_window: 3-day event window [-1, +1] surrounding the divestiture announcement date; 250-day estimation window [-800, -551]

description: Buy-and-hold returns that compound divesting firms' abnormal returns, defined as a divesting firm's return net of the stock market's return, over the months following the effective dates of their divestitures; the compounding formula is Equation 2, whose rendering is unreadable in the text. The text states that the term is company i's CMR from month t (the month of the effective date of a given divestiture) to month t + n, and that each term is company i's end-of-month abnormal stock market return in month t + j. CMRs were calculated in the 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, and 24 months following the effective date of each divestiture.
time_window: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, and 24 months following the divestiture effective date

description: Indicator that takes the value one if a matched divestiture belongs to Treatment Group 1 and zero if it belongs to the Control Group (manager-led). Treatment Group 1 includes all divestitures that are announced during a SharkWatch-identified successful campaign with a 'Breakup Company, Divest Assets/Divisions' demand, plus divestitures that were specified in the activist investor's demands but that were only announced after the campaign ended. TG1 consists of 115 divestitures undertaken by 28 firms between 2007 and 2015.

Indicator that takes the value one if a matched divestiture belongs to Treatment Group 2 and zero if it belongs to the Control Group (manager-led). Treatment Group 2 includes all TG1 divestitures plus all divestitures that are announced during a SharkWatch campaign with either a 'Breakup Company, Divest Assets/Divisions' or 'Seek Sale/Merger/Liquidation' demand, irrespective of the SharkWatch-identified outcome of the campaign. TG2 consists of 138 divestitures undertaken by 37 firms between 2007 and 2015.

Number of countries in which the venture sold its products, counted from secondary sources as a proxy for the geographic diversity of a firm's international operations. The count was cross-checked against at least two secondary sources for 59 companies and against managers' reports of the number of foreign countries to which their products were exported and of the number of countries, other than the US, in which the company's products were sold.

Average country R&D spending, computed as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP), used as an indicator of the technological vitality of a venture's international markets. The average was calculated by dividing the total of R&D ratios across the countries the new venture had entered by the number of these countries.

Number of cultural groups in a venture's markets, measured using Hofstede's classification of national cultures, which indicated 11 country groups. Each country a firm entered was assigned to a cultural group and the firm's score is the number of separate groups its markets fell into.

Entropy measure of the geographic diversity of foreign revenue, developed from data provided by managers on the percentage of their companies' international revenues earned outside the United States in Canada, Europe, Asia, Australia, Latin America, and Africa. The formula as printed (GD = 2S, where S was the percentage of a venture's sales in a given market, summed across the six regions) is difficult to read. The measure was validated against secondary data for 103 firms and interrater agreement between two managers on the entropy measure was high.

For each country in which a firm's products were sold, managers provided the number of different market segments their firms targeted. The total number of segments was divided by the number of countries a firm entered, and this average was used in the analyses.

Number of announcements of international start-up (greenfield) transactions, collected from Lexis-Nexis. The number of announcements of international transactions within each entry mode was used as the study's measure for that mode.

Number of announcements of international acquisition transactions, collected from Lexis-Nexis. The number of announcements of international transactions within each entry mode was used as the study's measure for that mode.

Number of announcements of international licensing agreements, collected from Lexis-Nexis. The number of announcements of international transactions within each entry mode was used as the study's measure for that mode.

Number of announcements of international export transactions, collected from Lexis-Nexis. The number of announcements of international transactions within each entry mode was used as the study's measure for that mode.

Managers' averaged responses to 19 items covering the technological activities from which firms learn in international operations. For each item managers indicated the extent to which their company had gained knowledge and new insights, or learned skills or capabilities, from its international business operations, where a score of 5 meant many different and varied skills and 1 meant only a few. Managers' responses were averaged and the resulting score was used as the measure; Cronbach's alpha was .78.

Measured as the average rating on the same 19 items used for breadth. Managers were asked to indicate how well their company had learned or mastered new skills in each area, where a score of 5 meant the company had thoroughly and completely mastered new skills and a score of 1 meant the company had been exposed to these skills at an elementary or basic level but had not mastered them yet; responses were averaged. Cronbach's alpha was .71.

Measured with the same 19 items. Managers were asked to indicate how fast their company was in learning and mastering new skills in the areas listed, and the responses were averaged. Cronbach's alpha was .72.

Seven items measured on a five-point scale (5 = widely used, 1 = never used), asking managers the extent to which their ventures used each activity to capture, interpret, synthesize, and integrate what they had learned from their international operations. When factor-analyzed with a varimax orthogonal rotation, one factor explaining 64.8 percent of the variance emerged; the sum of managers' responses to the seven items was averaged and used as the measure (alpha = .67).

Return on equity, measured by dividing net profits by equity as reported by trade publications and other secondary sources. Data were collected for, and averaged over, the period 1995-96 to represent a time period of two to three years after the data on the independent variables were collected, and the figures were adjusted for industry-specific averages.

Sales growth, measured as the difference between sales in two consecutive years divided by sales one year earlier, with the quotient multiplied by 100, as reported in the secondary sources. Data were collected for, and averaged over, the period 1995-96 and the figures were adjusted for industry-specific averages.

variable_name: International diversity and mode of entry
description: International expansion is measured by two sets of variables: international diversity (number of countries, technological, cultural and geographic diversity, number of foreign market segments) and mode of market entry (counts of start-ups, acquisitions, licensing agreements and export agreements).

Coded for the years after a client lead partner exited the firm, using the firm's personnel records on the entry and exit dates for all of the firm's lawyers; the authors verified that the client lead partners identified as exiting did not return in subsequent years. Because exits are not randomly assigned, the second-stage models use the predicted value of exit from a first stage in which exit is regressed on the instruments and all independent and control variables.

The total billable hours charged to each client in a given year, the sum of all partner and associate billings, which reflect a key internal shorthand for representing the relative performance of a given client account. Total client billable hours ranged from a minimum of less than 100 to a maximum of nearly 100,000 with a mean value of roughly 500 hours per year. The log of total client billable hours is used in the analysis to ensure a normal distribution of the dependent variable.

A count of the different departments (i.e., knowledge domains) represented in the team billing the client each year. All lawyers were assigned to exactly one of eight different departmental units based on their domains of legal expertise, including corporate transactions, litigation, tax, intellectual property, labor and employment, bankruptcy, and two other minor areas; those assignments were very stable over time.

A count of the different city office locations of the lawyers in each client knowledge network each year. There were four different possible office locations for the lawyers used in the analysis, all located in one of the top 10 largest U.S. metropolitan statistical areas, with very little movement between the locations over time.

For each lawyer in the knowledge network the authors generated an internal expert status score (eigenvector centrality of the lawyer in the firm's overall billings network in a given year) and an external expert status score (an indicator for whether a partner was awarded 'preeminent' (2), 'distinguished' (1), or neither (0) in the Martindale Hubbell peer review lawyer rating system for that year). The internal and external expert status indicators were standardized and averaged to create each lawyer's overall average expert knowledge score, and those indices were then averaged across all lawyers in the knowledge network for that year to create an expert knowledge index for each client knowledge network.

Two lawyers in a given knowledge network were considered tied if they both billed 10 or more hours together on common projects for clients other than the focal client in a given year (10 hours was the minimum threshold set by the firm to signify nontrivial involvement in a client matter). Those ties were used to calculate knowledge network cohesion following the standard network density formula, observed ties over possible ties, where possible ties is n(n-1)/2.

Network closure was measured as ego network constraint, following Burt (1992), who measured the continuum of configurations between structural holes and cohesion in terms of the absence or presence of constraint. The measure is based on name generator ego network data: respondents indicated, on a three-point scale (1, 'not at all'; 2, 'somewhat'; 3, 'very well'), how well two contacts knew each other, and relevant network contacts were included on the basis of two survey items on frequency of interaction over the last year (eight-point scale) and closeness (seven-point scale). Four measures of constraint were constructed for more or less inclusive specifications of agents' networks. The formula for constraint is printed only as an unreadable formula block in the text.
time_window: network survey administered during the first week of the executive program; interaction frequency over the last year

description: Degree of divergence of each change project from the institutionalized model of professionals' and organizations' role division, measured with two scales developed by Battilana (2011). The first scale uses four items capturing the extent to which the change challenged the dominance of doctors over other health care professionals in both the clinical and administrative domains; the second uses six items capturing the extent to which it challenged the dominance of hospitals over other types of organizations in both domains. Each of the ten items was assessed using a three-point rank-ordered scale. Two independent raters blind to the hypotheses coded the change project descriptions written by participants after three months of implementation (interrater reliability kappa = .90) and resolved discrepancies by consensus until they reached consensus. Scores on each scale correspond to the average of the items included in it, and change divergence is the unweighted average of the two scale scores.
scale: three-point rank-ordered scale for each of the ten items
time_window: project descriptions written three months after implementation

description: Three-item scale from the telephone survey administered one year after implementation. The first item asks, on a scale of 1-5, how far the change agent progressed toward completing the change project, where 1 is defining the project for the clinical strategists program and 5 is institutionalizing the implemented change as part of standard practice in the organization. The second item states that the change is now part of the standard operating practice of the organization, and the third that the change was not adopted in the organization; the third item was reverse-coded. The last two items were assessed using a five-point scale ranging from 1 ('strongly disagree') to 5 ('strongly agree'). Cronbach's alpha for the scale was .60.
scale: five-point scales for two items; 1-5 progress scale for the first item

description: A Herfindahl-Hirschman index calculated across six racial categories using student enrollment data by race from the CCD, which estimates the likelihood that any two randomly selected students in a school district will be from different racial groups. The authors also use racial entropy based on the same racial categories as an alternative and get consistent results.

Total revenue from local sources (property taxes, tuition, donations, and other income) for a given school district and year divided by the number of students enrolled in that district in the same year, based on the Common Core Data from the National Center for Education Statistics. All dollar amounts are adjusted to 2018 dollars using the consumer price index.

The total amount approved in a district's school tax referenda divided by the district's total enrollment in the year the bond was approved. The measure is constructed from official statements of bonds issued by school districts collected from the Electronic Municipal Market Access. It takes the value of zero when either no bond referenda were put forth or when they failed to pass.

One minus Theil's index of racial segregation across census tracts that overlap with the school district, calculated from tract-level racial composition data from IPUMS NHGIS using the R Segregation package. Overlaps between census tracts and school districts are identified using the geographic relation files provided by NCES EDGE; a school district overlaps with 8.4 census tracts on average.

Data from Opportunity Insights reporting social interactions at the level of Census ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, aggregated to the school district level using NCES EDGE. The data set captures friendship links between Facebook users and has been validated as a reliable proxy for real-world social connectedness within communities; it captures connectedness across different economic groups rather than specifically across racial groups.

One minus the weighted sum of the absolute differences between each racial group's vote share for the Republican candidate and the overall Republican candidate's vote share in the congressional district of the school district, using racial voting patterns from the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections constructed by Kuriwaki et al. (2024). It captures how similar members of different races in the community are in their political ideologies.

One minus Theil's index of racial segregation between schools of the same level within a district, calculated from the racial composition of schools within each school district in the CCD using the R Segregation package.

The proportion of female directors on the board, entered in the logistic model in logarithm form, measured as ln(1 1 female director ratio). A linear specification of Female Director Ratio is also estimated, and the two specifications are compared with a likelihood ratio test. The authors report that the maximum percentage of women on a board in the sample is 50% and that the mean percentage of female board directors is 14%.

Dummy variable that takes a value of '1' if the firm is subject to an enforcement action for violation of a regulation or fraud, and '0' otherwise. It is coded 1 for the 742 fraud firms and 0 for the 742 matched non-fraud control firms, which were matched on stock exchange location, industry type and firm size category.

variable_name: abnormal returns measured by market return
description: Abnormal share price returns around the announcement of fraud, obtained by first estimating the market model (share prices as a function of market returns) and then inferring abnormal returns using the fraud announcement as the event. Coefficients are reported for the 0-3 day, 0-10 day and 0-20 day event windows. The authors state that the results are robust to measuring benchmark returns with a control firm approach and with propensity score matching.
time_window: 0-3, 0-10 and 0-20 day event windows around the fraud announcement

description: Dummy variable with the value of '1' if the firm is in a female-dominated industry, and '0' otherwise. Industries were classified using the average percentage of female employees across each industry class in Australia between 2004 and 2012; an industry class holding more than 50% female employees was classified as female dominated, and the Australian industry sectors were then matched with Chinese sectors. Female-dominated sectors include food processing, clothing (textile, garment) manufacturing, medicine and biological product manufacturing, the retail clothing trade, food and beverage services, hotels, tourism, radio, film and television, and publishing.

Dummy variable that takes a value of '1' if the firm is led by a female chairperson, and '0' otherwise. It is included in the logistic model as an additional test of whether gender affects the likelihood of fraud.

Dummy variable that takes the value of '1' if the firm is led by a female general manager, and '0' otherwise. It is included in the logistic model as an additional test of whether gender affects the likelihood of fraud.

A relationship is multiplex if a single agency maintains multiple ties to the same client firm. The within-agency multiplex tie score for a given tie is calculated as the number of accounts the agency has with each client divided by the agency's total accounts, excluding the focal account tie. Given the skewed distribution of the measure, the natural log of the measure was taken and included in the main models.

A relationship is multiplex when the agency is tied to a client that has a tie to another agency in the same holding company as the focal agency. Because the number of other agencies to which a focal agency has ownership ties limits the number of potential across-agency ties for a given agency-client tie, the measure is normalized by the count of possible ties, where t is the count of account ties not including the focal account tie and n is the number of agencies in the advertising parent firm; the specification is given as an equation whose rendering is not readable in the text provided. The measure is described as multiplex tie density, and the natural log was taken and included in the main models.

Measured as the proportion of agency executives leaving the agency annually; 'departure' is the absence of an executive name listed by the agency in the previous year from the agency's REDBOOKS entry in the current year. The proportion of departures was calculated as the count of departures divided by the count of executives listed. The executive data were aggregated to the agency level because the data do not link executives to specific client accounts.
time_window: annual, current year compared with the previous year's listing

description: A dichotomous variable set to one if the agency-client tie dissolved in that year. A tie is coded as 'dissolved' the first year the advertising firm no longer lists the client account in its REDBOOKS record. If a tie did not dissolve in the observation period or if data were not available, the relationship was considered censored.

Constructed by counting the number of across-agency multiplex ties involving agencies in the same network (and therefore not allowed to compete) divided by the count of all across-agency multiplex ties surrounding the agency-client dyad. It captures the extent to which the agency-agency ties in across-agency multiplex relationships were competitive.

For each of the nine innovation objectives available in the 2006-2008 data, respondents rated importance on a 0 (not relevant) to 3 (high importance) Likert scale. Each objective was assigned a binary value of 1 if rated medium or high importance (2 or 3) and 0 if low importance or not relevant. The binary values were summed to construct the breadth variable.

For each of the nine innovation objectives available in the 2006-2008 data, respondents rated importance on a 0 (not relevant) to 3 (high importance) Likert scale. Each objective was assigned a binary value of 1 if rated medium or high importance (2 or 3) and 0 if low importance or not relevant. The binary values were summed to construct the breadth variable.

For each of the ten innovation objectives available in the 2008-2010 data, respondents rated importance on a 0 (not relevant) to 3 (high importance) Likert scale. Each objective was assigned a binary value of 1 if rated medium or high importance (2 or 3) and 0 if low importance or not relevant. The binary values were summed to construct the breadth variable.

The breadth of knowledge sources was constructed in the same manner as the breadth of innovation objectives. Ten sources had binary values assigned based on importance ratings and were summed to construct the variable. Thus, this variable can take a value from zero to 10.

The breadth of knowledge sources was constructed in the same manner as the breadth of innovation objectives. Ten sources had binary values assigned based on importance ratings and were summed to construct the variable. Thus, this variable can take a value from zero to 10.

The breadth of knowledge sources was constructed in the same manner as the breadth of innovation objectives. Ten sources had binary values assigned based on importance ratings and were summed to construct the variable. Thus, this variable can take a value from zero to 10.

Binary variable indicating whether the firm introduced any technological innovation (product as well as process). These innovations were new to the firm but may or may not have been new to the market.

Binary variable indicating whether the firm introduced any technological innovation (product as well as process). These innovations were new to the firm but may or may not have been new to the market.

Binary variable indicating whether the firm introduced any technological innovation (product as well as process). These innovations were new to the firm but may or may not have been new to the market.

variable_name: percent of product sales revenues from innovation
description: Variable measuring the percentage of firm revenues from the sale of technologically new products.

variable_name: percent of product sales revenues from innovation
description: Variable measuring the percentage of firm revenues from the sale of technologically new products.

variable_name: percent of product sales revenues from innovation
description: Variable measuring the percentage of firm revenues from the sale of technologically new products.

The authors manually recorded the total dollar amount of corporate philanthropy from the National Directory of Corporate Giving in the years that match the sample; odd-numbered directory years report data from the even-numbered years of the sample. The variable was log-transformed to reduce highly skewed values.
The CEO tenure of each corporation in the sample was obtained from Standard & Poor's ExecuComp database.

Degree centrality calculated from the network of shared directors among the boards of all public firms in 1997 and 2002. A board's 1997 value was also assigned to 1996, 1998, and 2000, and its 2002 value was assigned to 2002, 2004, and 2006.
time_window: 1997 and 2002, carried to adjacent sample years

description: The number of directors of each corporation in the sample, obtained from Catalyst publications.
The percentage of women among senior managers of each corporation, obtained from Catalyst publications.
The percentage of women among the corporation's directors, obtained from Catalyst publications.

Foundation assets recorded from the same directory used for the dependent variable. Approximately 70 percent of companies in the sample have foundations; for companies without a foundation, this variable was given the value of zero. The level of foundation assets was log-transformed because organizational structure does not increase linearly with size but increases marginally less as the organization grows.

A simple dummy variable, 1 if at least one team member has worked at a public firm in the industry, 0 otherwise; since the spawning variable is at the firm level, founding teams with at least one individual who worked at any point in his career at a publicly traded medical device or pharmaceutical/biotechnology firm are considered spawns. The authors note that founding team size was difficult to determine reliably and that they conducted their own research (interviews, LexisNexis, company Web site searches) to determine whether an individual was actually the entrepreneur.

Calculated by taking the difference in days between the first reported round of outside funding in VentureOne and the founding date for the company. In the regressions the dependent variable is the log of time to funding, so a negative sign indicates faster time to funding. The authors note that founding dates are reported to VentureOne by surveys and may not always be accurate, and that neither database has reliable data on individual or 'angel' investments that could have been made prior to the first round of venture capital funding.

variable_name: pre-money valuation at the last round of outside financing
description: The 'pre-money' valuation, or the valuation of the company as determined by investors at rounds of nonpublic financing, measured at the last observed round of financing. Since the number of rounds varies across firms, the authors look only at the last round and control for the round number and other important variables so that ventures are compared at the same round of funding; the dependent variable in the regressions is the log of the pre-money valuation. Valuations can be determined by identifying comparable companies in the industry, using a discounted cash flow model, or using the replacement value of assets.

Successful approval of a product by the Food and Drug Administration, from FDA data, used as a binary dependent variable for performance in a probit model, controlling for relevant observable characteristics. FDA approval is an important milestone for medical device firms and is critical to future rounds of financing. A hazard specification also analyzes time to product approval, allowing for censoring.

Dummy variable for those spawned firms that did cite their parent firm on their patents, with the remaining spawns coded as Spawn Simple. In the analysis the single spawn variable is replaced by Spawn Tech Inheritor and Spawn Simple; 12 of the 69 spawned firms are coded as Spawn Tech Inheritor and the rest as Spawn Simple.

For each spawn, the average citation rate is total citations to the parent divided by total citations made; for each spawned firm this is compared with a control patent portfolio matched on application year, IPC four-digit class and closest grant date. The average citation rate to the parent for the control patent portfolio represents, in the authors' words, the percentage of citations that would go to the parent firm if no parent-spawn link existed, and the difference between the spawn rate and the control rate cannot be shown to be different than zero.

Dummy variable for those spawned firms that did patent predominantly in one of their parent's top three patent classes, with the remaining spawns coded as Spawn Unrelated. To identify the parent's three primary classes the authors divide the parent firm's patent portfolio by International Patent Classification class and identify the three classes with the most patents. In the analysis the single spawn variable is replaced by Spawn Related and Spawn Unrelated; 23 of the 69 spawned firms are coded as Spawn Related.

Each nonresponsible firm's total usage (in pounds) of each toxic chemical involved in each accident, measured the year before the accident. Chemical usage was calculated by weighting the amount generated of that chemical by its level of toxicity, measured using the 'reportable quantities' (RQ) data required under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980. The final measure captures the degree to which a firm handles the chemicals involved in an accident, normalized by these chemicals' toxicity.

Cumulative abnormal returns of a nonresponsible firm following each accident, calculated following the standard methodology outlined in McWilliams and Siegel (1997). Each firm's intercept and systematic risk were estimated through ordinary least squares regression of its daily stock return on the value-weighted CRSP index over the period t = -250 to t = -50, where t = 0 was the day of the event. Daily abnormal returns were then summed over the event window (0, +4). The equations themselves are not legible in the available text.
time_window: event window (0, +4); estimation window t = -250 to t = -50

description: The total value (in US$ millions) of the fines administered by the EPA and levied on each toxic chemical, aggregated across all firms from all manufacturing industries, in the five years before the accident. For accidents in which more than one chemical was involved, the measure is the average total value across all chemicals involved in that accident.

The number of services offered by a given ILA representing the chemical involved in the accident, ranging from '0' (where no ILA existed) to '4' (for ILAs that provided all four services). The four services are: providing information about the risks of the toxic chemical; sharing technical reports, annual publications, and/or research findings about best practice with investors and all facilities dealing with the chemical; providing risk management services to all members; and providing support, training, and assistance to nonmembers in the event of an emergency. In accidents in which more than one chemical was involved, the measure is the average across all chemicals.

A facility-level dyad measure of input-portfolio similarity between the responsible facility and each nonresponsible facility, based on the distribution of emissions across all 347 regulated chemicals for each facility in the year before the accident; the values for chemicals involved in the accident are set at '0' in the vectors of both facilities. The measure varies between '0' and '1,' where '1' represents the greatest similarity between two facilities' distribution of toxic chemical emissions. Because a nonresponsible firm may have more than one facility, the final firm-level measure is the weighted average (weighted by facility size) across all of the firm's facilities. The exact formulas are not legible in the available text.

The distance (in thousands of miles) between the facility of the responsible firm where the accident took place and the facilities of the nonresponsible firms, calculated from latitude and longitude data on all regulated facilities. The final measure is the average distance (weighted by facility size) between each of the nonresponsible firm's facilities and the responsible facility; the sign of this final measure was reversed to capture proximity.

Measured by two subscales: three-item interpersonal interaction and five-item task-related interaction. Each item was measured by a seven-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (completely disagree) to 7 (completely agree); Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.93. Sample items include whether members of the top management team are ready to help each other complete jobs and meet deadlines (task-oriented interaction) and whether they enjoy cultivating personal connections with each other (interpersonal interaction). Individual responses were aggregated into firm-level data (ICC(1) = 0.35, ICC(2) = 0.60; mean rWG(J) = 0.92).

A four-item, seven-point Likert-type measure derived from D'Aveni (1994) (alpha = 0.92). Respondents indicated agreement on a scale from 1 (completely disagree) to 7 (completely agree) with statements such as 'My company operates in an industry where head-to-head rivalry is common' and 'My company operates in an industry where cause-and-effect relationships in the environment are often difficult to discern.' Because the responses of individual team members were aggregated into firm-level data, interrater reliabilities were assessed (ICC(1) = 0.43, ICC(2) = 0.67; mean rWG(J) = 0.95).

Action volume and action speed were each measured with three items, respectively, forming a six-item, seven-point Likert-type scale (alpha = 0.96) ranging from 1 (far fewer or far slower than direct competitors) to 7 (far more or far faster than direct competitors). The three types of actions used were market expansion, new product introductions, and new service offerings. The correlation coefficient between action volume and action speed is 0.84, and aggregation checks were acceptable (ICC(1) = 0.43, ICC(2) = 0.68).
scale: 1 (far fewer or far slower than direct competitors) to 7 (far more or far faster than direct competitors)

variable_name: Profit margin and return on equity (ROE)
description: Two financial performance measures obtained from China Credit Information Service. Profit margin is operating profit divided by operating revenue, and ROE is net profit divided by equity. To control for temporal fluctuations, the authors used three-year average profit margin and ROE subsequent to the survey.
time_window: three-year average subsequent to the survey

description: The 104 sample firms were classified into 40 industries based on the three-digit SIC code, with 25 industries containing at least three firms, and intraindustry variation in profit margin and ROE was related to the average perceived hypercompetition within an industry. In addition, for each firm the absolute difference in average performance between the focal 2004 to 2006 period and the 2007 to 2009 period was computed and correlated with the measure of hypercompetitive environment.
level: industry (intraindustry variation) and firm (volatility over time)

variable_name: Home country's stakeholder pressure on MNE's HQ
description: Measured as the sum of all controversies affecting each HQ averaged by their corresponding weight, which is provided by Sustainalytics. Appendix A provides more details on the 64 items used to measure this variable.

A subsidiary's realized CSR is regressed on its expected CSR inferred from the focal industry and various firm controls (commitment to ethics, performance, size, and R&D intensity), using a firm fixed-effect estimation, and the predicted value is compared with the reported value. A predicted CSR value larger than the realized CSR value is indicative of the transfer of CSiR practices to a focal subsidiary. The difference between predicted and realized subsidiary CSR is the proxy for the transfer of CSiR practices.

A subsidiary in which the HQ of a focal MNE held a stake between 5 and 10 percent and at least one HQ executive served on the subsidiary's board. The name of the owner of a subsidiary and the equity holding of entities and individuals owning a stake of 5 percent or more were recorded, and OSIRIS data were used to identify board interlocks.

The principal component of three previously normalized indexes. The first is the Fraser Institute's Index of Economic Freedom, which measures the degree to which labor-market regulations infringe on the economic freedom of employees and employers and was reversed so that higher scores represent stronger regulation. The second is the World Bank's Rule of Law Index. The third is the number of the 13 main international environmental treaties ratified up until the previous year. Cronbach's alpha was .85 for regulatory pressure in MNEs' home countries.
Measured as the number of NGOs at home. Data were gathered from the Yearbook of International Organizations.

The principal component of three previously normalized indexes: the Fraser Institute's Index of Economic Freedom (reversed so that higher scores represent stronger regulation), the World Bank's Rule of Law Index, and the number of the 13 main international environmental treaties ratified up until the previous year. Cronbach's alpha was .79 for regulatory pressure in subsidiaries' host countries.
Measured as the number of NGOs abroad. Data were gathered from the Yearbook of International Organizations.

Dummy variable taking a value of 1 when the team chooses to go for it on the fourth down and 0 otherwise. Not going for it is treated equally, regardless of whether the team chooses to punt the ball or to attempt a field goal conversion.

Spline variable capturing the difference in points between the focal team and the opposing team when the points of the opposing team exceed those of the focal team and 0 otherwise; values are negative, so a lower value indicates a larger shortfall. The model also includes a Valence indicator, taking a value of 1 when performance is above the aspiration level and 0 otherwise, which allows for discontinuity at the aspired level of performance.

Spline variable capturing the same difference in points between the focal team and the opposing team when the points of the focal team exceed those of the opposing team and 0 otherwise. The model also includes the Valence indicator, taking a value of 1 when performance is above the aspiration level and 0 otherwise.

Set of dummy variables for quarters 2, 3, and 4 (quarter 1 serves as a baseline), each taking the value of 1 if the play is in the respective quarter and 0 otherwise. The authors use quarter dummies instead of continuous time to facilitate the interpretation of the results and interact them with the independent variables to test Hypotheses 0, 1, and 2.

Reflects the position of the attacking team on the field, centered at the middle of the field such that value 0 represents being in the middle, values -49 and 49 represent being one yard from one's own end zone and one yard from the opponent's end zone. When the team is close to the opponent's end zone the magnitude of potential gains is high and the magnitude of potential losses is low, because scoring becomes easier on successive plays and a failure leaves the opponent far from the focal team's end zone.

variable_name: Yards to go for first down (log)
description: Number of yards needed to complete the 10-yard advance necessary for a first down. The fewer the yards left for a first down, the more likely the team is to succeed in its attempt, so the variable is an inverse indicator of the likelihood of a successful outcome. It is measured on a logarithmic scale because the increase in difficulty is concave rather than linear.

Measured in terms of six indicators capturing both the procedural and the human aspects of asset specificity. The procedural aspect was operationalized as three indicators capturing the extent to which the focal carrier's workflows and routines were customized; human asset specificity was measured in terms of the extent to which the skill levels of employees working on the focal carrier's business are specifically customized. All the indicators were measured on a seven-point scale from 'significantly customized' to 'relatively similar to other carriers'. The authors report a Cronbach alpha for this construct of 0.86.

Behavioral uncertainty was operationalized with two indicators regarding the uncertainty the agency perceives due to the pricing and the new product introduction actions of the focal carrier. The indicators ask the extent to which the respondent could predict changes in those factors in relation to the focal carrier for the next year, on seven-point scales anchored from 'relatively predictable' to 'relatively unpredictable'. The authors report a Cronbach alpha reliability for this construct that was marginal, but acceptable, at 0.61.

Reciprocal investments take the form of the extent of transaction-specific resources invested by the insurance carrier in the development of the relationship with the agency. They were measured using three indicators in terms of the agent's perception of the degree to which the focal carrier has invested resources in customized support to the agency, in developing personal relationships at the agency, and in providing training to agency staff. Each indicator was measured using a seven-point scale from 'invested hardly any resources' to 'invested considerable resources'; the authors report a Cronbach alpha of 0.77.

Consistent with Anderson and Narus (1990) and Heide and John (1990), the authors operationalized trust using three indicators tapping the extent of perceived trust between the focal carrier and the agency. Specifically, the construct includes the mutuality element of trust, as well as behavioral and 'process' dimensions of trust. Each indicator was measured on a seven-point scale from 'strongly agree' to 'strongly disagree'; the authors report the reliability of the trust construct was good, with a Cronbach alpha of 0.81.
