This transition was compared to the transition of a white man replacing a white man CEO and the transition of an occupational minority replacing an occupational minority CEO. There were 28 transitions where a traditional leader followed an occupational minority and only 4 transitions where an occupational minority leader followed an occupational minority.

An inventor's reach in the intra-firm inventor network is the sum of reciprocal geodesic distances to every other inventor in the network, where distance is the geodesic distance between the two inventors; inventors connected to other inventors through smaller path lengths have higher reach. The authors present the specification as a formula, but the formula block is not readable in the available text, so the exact equation cannot be recorded; only this prose description is available. The variable was computed with UCINET VI, yearly for all inventors, using the annual intra-firm inventor networks.
time_window: annual, using a moving three-year window of collaborations

description: Calculated with UCINET VI using Burt's (1992) efficiency measure, which calculates the ratio of nonredundant contacts to total contacts. The authors give the specification as a formula block that is not readable in the available text, so the exact equation cannot be recorded; they state that the measure yields a value ranging from 0 to 1, with higher values representing the spanning of a larger number of structural holes. The measure was computed for each inventor in each of the annual intra-firm networks created for each firm.
time_window: annual, using a moving three-year window of collaborations

description: For each inventor-year in which an inventor has patent application(s), the prior art citations in those patents to organizational knowledge are counted, organizational knowledge being indicated by the assignees on the cited patents; citations to the inventor's own knowledge are excluded. Organizational knowledge consists of all the patents assigned to the firm or its subsidiaries from 1975 up to the last year.

Computed as the number of unique technology classifications of an inventor's citations to organizational knowledge in a year, based on the prior art sections of the inventor's patents and excluding citations to the inventor's own knowledge.

Computed as the total number of unique locations on the inventor's prior art citations to the organization's patents in a year, based on the prior art sections of the inventor's patents and excluding citations to the inventor's own knowledge. The locations used are the locations of the inventors and not the assignee, and using latitude-longitude information nearby locations within 30 miles of each other were combined.

The dependent variable is the sum of the partners' unique patents cited by the patents filed by a focal firm in a specific month; if a focal firm files five patents that each cite five of the partner's patents, the value is 25. The cross-citation count excludes those partners' patents that the company had already cited prior to the beginning of the alliance. The default variable counts only newly cited patents, so only the first citation for every specific patent is incorporated, meaning that subsequent exploitation of technology that has already been exploited is not counted.
time_window: monthly spells over the first 48 months after alliance announcement

description: Duration from the beginning of the interorganizational relationship. Because the dependent variable is measured for monthly spells during the first four years from the formation of the alliance, the variable received values from 1 to 48.

Overlap of a focal company's patents with those of its partner in terms of patent classes, based on patents filed during the three years preceding the alliance. Patent counts were made in each patent subclass using International Patent Classification coding, and the patent count was weighted by the number of subclasses in each patent; a moving three-year window was used. The number of patents in patent classes for companies A and B was multiplied, summed over every patent class, and divided by the geometric mean of patent portfolio sizes. The index ranges from 0 (no overlap between patent classes) to 1 (perfect overlap of patent classes); the underlying formula is not readable in the text provided.
time_window: three-year window preceding each observation year

description: Herfindahl index representing the diversity versus focus of the firm's technological activities, based on its patenting in the three years preceding the alliance. The index is calculated from the share of patents in each patent class during the past three years. A maximum value of 1 represents a firm that has all of its patents filed in the same main patent class, and values approaching 0 represent a situation where every patent filed by the company is in a distinct patent class of its own; the underlying formula is not readable in the text provided.

Captures the inputs into the R&D process as a share of total sales, taken from the year in which the alliance was announced. The authors chose R&D intensity rather than total R&D spending because intensity is the measure most commonly used in prior research and because it better reflects the relative amount of resources available for knowledge creation and exploitation.

Six items reflecting the attributions of benevolence and credibility associated with trust, strongly influenced by the dyadic trust scale of Larzeleve and Huston (1980) and Crosby, Evans, and Cowles (1990) and focused on dyadic rather than generalized trust. Benevolence and credibility were combined into a single factor. Items were assessed on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Coefficient alpha in T1 was 0.94.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Five items drawn principally from John (1984) and Dwyer and Oh (1987) representing the behavioral elements on the part of the opportunistic party. The variable is operationalized as ex post behavior and reflects the agents' perceptions of the principal's opportunism. Items were assessed on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Coefficient alpha in T1 was 0.90.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Second-order construct operationalized in terms of norms of solidarity (four items), flexibility (four items), and mutuality (four items), with scale items taken from Kaufmann and Dant (1992). Items were assessed on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Individual reliabilities in T2 were 0.81 for solidarity, 0.85 for flexibility, and 0.89 for mutuality; the composite scale's coefficient alpha in T2 was 0.81.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

description: Five aspects of efficiency and productivity, namely sales growth, profit growth, overall profitability, labor productivity, and cash flow, using scale items from Lusch and Brown (1996). Responses were elicited in terms of performance relative to other similar agents of the principal, and were given on a five-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Subjective measures were used instead of standard financial measures because of the diversity in agents' main lines of business. Coefficient alpha in T3 was 0.91.
scale: five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)

variable_name: Startup's search in corporate partner's domains
description: The number of citations that a startup's successful patent applications up to the focal year make to each technological class in which its corporate partner searched previously, where the startup's citations in each class are weighted by the proportion of the corporate partner's citations that fall into that same class. The specification is given as a formula that was not extracted; the text states only its elements in prose, namely that cint is the number of citations the startup makes in technological class n up to year t, cjnt-1 is the number of citations the corporate partner made to that class in its previous patents until the previous year, and cjt-1 is the total number of citations in the corporate partner's patents. Greater values reflect greater search activity in technological domains relevant to the partner's search, and the natural logarithm of the value plus one is entered in the models.
scale: count (entered as natural logarithm plus one)
time_window: up to the focal year; the partner's citations until the previous year

description: Dummy variable set to 1 if the focal startup formed an investment relationship with an incumbent and to 0 otherwise. Counterfactual startups that did not form such a relationship are coded 0, and the interaction term CVC x Post captures the effect that Hypothesis 1 hypothesizes.

Dummy variable set to 1 for years after the year of formation of the investment relationship and to 0 for the year of investment and years preceding that event. For matching startups without a corporate investment relationship, the dummy is coded based on the year of formation of the corporate investment relationship of the observation for which the startup functions as a counterfactual.
time_window: years of the observation relative to the year of investment

description: The average patent originality score, as established by prior research, across all patents granted to a startup up to the focal year. The score measures the diversity of knowledge on which an innovation builds, so that innovations building on a wide range of fields, thereby breaking traditional molds, receive higher scores. The formula was not extracted; the text states only its elements in prose: citesn is the number of patents the focal patent cites in technological class n, citesm is the total number of patents the focal patent cites as prior art, and N is the total number of distinct technological classes, other than the class of the focal patent itself, observed among the focal patent's backward citations.
time_window: all patents granted to the startup up to the focal year

description: The count of the corporate partner's drugs that the Pharmacy Times listed among the 50 top-selling drugs in the year preceding the observation year.

Ratio of the monthly sales goal for wine to the monthly sales goal for spirits for each salesperson. Goals are set monthly by the sales supervisor within the firm's delegated goal setting process. In the experiment the ratio was shifted exogenously by adding 15% to the goal of one category and subtracting 15% from the goal of the other; a one-unit increase in the difference-in-treatment variable is equal to evaluating a change of (1 + 15%)/(1 - 15%) - 1 in the ratio of wine goals to spirit goals.

Ratio of a salesperson's monthly sales of wine to her monthly sales of spirits, measured in hectoliters. Sales are taken from the company's administrative records for the salespersons who participated in the experiment. The authors study this ratio rather than the level of sales to avoid income effects, following the model's prediction for the ratio of sales of two products.

Estimated separately for each sales supervisor as the degree to which the goal in period t responds to the ratio of sales to goal in period t-1. The estimation uses, for consistency, only wines and spirits as the product categories, controls for seasonality with time fixed effects and for unobserved heterogeneity at the joint salespersons and product type level with a dummy set, and is run on the periods before the experiment. The authors then use these estimates as the salesperson's expected ratcheting.
scale: ratchet coefficient ranging from 13% to 100% across supervisors, with a mean of 60%

description: Measured in months by subtracting the month in which each salesperson signed a formal labor contract with CCU from the month t. The variable is left-censored because the authors do not have information before July 2011. The authors also build a dummy taking the value of 1 for the first decile of tenure and 0 otherwise, and in the historical analysis they include ten dummies, one for each tenure decile observed in the data.
time_window: months since contract signature, measured each month of the data

description: Indicator of whether an actual citation occurred between the two patents of a pair. It is coded 1 for cited/citing patent pairs, in which the citing applicant is assumed to have been aware of the invention protected by the cited patent, and 0 for pairs in which the initially cited patent is matched with a randomly drawn nonciting patent. The likelihood of a citation between any two patents is modeled in a generalized probit regression framework.

variable_name: Minimal km distance between inventors on patent pairs (logs)
description: The geographic distance in kilometers between the inventors listed on the paired patents, based on the place of residence listed in the patent document. If more than one inventor is listed on a patent application, the distance between the two inventors on the separate applications that are closest to each other is used. The distance is entered in the regression as the log of the km distance between the inventors on paired patents.

A dummy variable indicating whether the paired cited and (non)citing patents are assigned to different IPC4 technology classes; in Table 3 it is described as 'Citation pairs share no IPC4 class (0/1)'. Pairs matched on the same IPC4 class are coded as technologically close.

A dummy variable indicating whether the two applicants listed on the paired patents were clients of the same patent law firm, i.e., whether the applicant of the citing patent was represented by a patent law firm that had also been contracted by the applicant of the cited patent. It indicates that the focal firm has access to knowledge that was incorporated in this law firm's repository.

Based on Miles and Snow's description, a nine-item scale was developed to measure the defender type; for each item an average for the firm was derived from the individual responses. An overall individual evaluation of the degree to which the firm conformed to the defender type was derived by taking the mean score across the nine items, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.69. An overall firm measure was derived by taking the average of the individual overall evaluations.
time_window: after the last set of decisions, at the end of the game

description: Derived in the same way as the defender measure, from seven items based on Miles and Snow's description of the prospector type, each rated on a 1 to 7 scale and averaged for the firm from the individual responses. Cronbach's alpha of the scale is 0.82.
time_window: after the last set of decisions, at the end of the game

description: Derived in the same way as the defender measure, from six items based on Miles and Snow's description of the analyzer type, each rated on a 1 to 7 scale and averaged for the firm from the individual responses. Cronbach's alpha of the scale is 0.60.
time_window: after the last set of decisions, at the end of the game

description: Derived in the same way as the defender measure, from three items based on Miles and Snow's description of the reactor type, each rated on a 1 to 7 scale and averaged for the firm from the individual responses. Cronbach's alpha of the scale is 0.67.
time_window: after the last set of decisions, at the end of the game

description: The entrepreneurial mode proved highly problematic: the authors report that the original description of the mode is internally inconsistent, with an alpha of -0.05 for the four items. It was therefore operationalized by taking the mean score of only two items (E1 and E2); the Pearson correlation between the two items is 0.35 (p=0.001). Firm values are averages of the individual responses.
time_window: after the last set of decisions, at the end of the game

description: Derived in the same way as the other strategy-making measures from four items describing the adaptive mode, each rated on a 1 to 7 scale and averaged for the firm from the individual responses. Cronbach's alpha of the measure is 0.41.
time_window: after the last set of decisions, at the end of the game

description: Derived in the same way as the other strategy-making measures from four items describing the planning mode, each rated on a 1 to 7 scale and averaged for the firm from the individual responses. Cronbach's alpha of the measure is 0.93.
time_window: after the last set of decisions, at the end of the game

description: Each of the seven strategy and strategy-making measures for the 18 firms was first normalized. Based on the normalized values, firms were defined as high-defender/high-planning, as high-prospector/high-entrepreneurial, or as low-reactor/low-adaptive; no firm was defined as high-analyzer/high-planning and entrepreneurial. All in all, seven firms exhibited strategy/strategy-making fit and 11 did not.

Retail market share at the end of the game, one of the two market share indicators of firm performance. The authors report that it is positively correlated with stock price. For the Fisher exact tests a cut-off point was designated for the measure so that each firm was classified as a high or low performance firm.

Accumulated sales over the last 6 months of the game, one of the two market share indicators of firm performance. The authors note a modest positive correlation with retail market share and a negative correlation with gross profit as a percentage of sales. A cut-off point was designated so that each firm was classified as a high or low performance firm for the Fisher exact tests.

variable_name: Gross profit as percentage of sales (GPP)
description: Gross profit as a percentage of sales, one of the five profit indicators of firm performance. The authors report that it was not significantly correlated with any of the strategic or strategy-making variables and was not significantly associated with strategic fit.

Profit as a percentage of sales, one of the five profit indicators of firm performance. Most of the profit indicators are reported to be highly correlated among themselves, while the market and profit indicators are not correlated. A cut-off point was designated so that each firm was classified as a high or low performance firm in the Fisher exact tests.

Owners' equity, one of the five profit indicators of firm performance. The authors report that the defender measure was only marginally positively correlated with this indicator. For the Fisher exact tests a cut-off point was designated to classify each firm as a high or low performance firm.

Return on assets, one of the five profit indicators of firm performance. It is reported among the profit indicators that are highly correlated among themselves and uncorrelated with the market indicators. A cut-off point was designated so that each firm was classified as a high or low performance firm in the Fisher exact tests.

Stock price in currency units, one of the five profit indicators of firm performance. The authors note a positive correlation between retail market share and stock price. A cut-off point was designated so that each firm was classified as a high or low performance firm for the Fisher exact tests.

variable_name: Order of entry (first mover vs follower)
description: In the copycat follower and non-copycat follower conditions, participants were first told that Firm A was launched in 2015 and was the first to provide the service, and Firm B entered the market with the same business model in 2016. A 'no order' baseline condition presented the identical two firms without the order of entry information, and a further 'one firm' condition presented a single entrant. The presentation order was counterbalanced.

variable_name: Extent of similarity (copycat follower vs non-copycat follower)
description: In the 'copycat follower' condition, the follower firm appears very similar to the first mover in both its substantive and cosmetic features; firms were introduced via screenshots of simulated websites that showed a high level of similarity in their design, such as the use of color and the layout, although they were not identical. In the 'non-copycat follower' condition, the follower was similar to the first mover in terms of substantive features but showed no evidence of cosmetic similarities, and the two firms were presented in a plain-text format.

variable_name: Follower entry timing (early follower vs late follower)
description: The information about the industry and the firms was identical across conditions, except that Firm B was described as entering in 2016 in the early follower condition and in 2019 in the late follower condition. In the late follower conditions the story of the industry's struggle to attain normative and sociopolitical legitimacy pertained only to Firm A, whereas in the early follower conditions it implicitly pertained to both firms.

Participants were informed about a 'year of crisis' along several dimensions of concern and were asked for their opinion about what would most concern them; they were then informed about the effort that Firm A (in the 'no legitimation work' condition) or both Firm A and Firm B (in the 'legitimation work' condition) undertook to ameliorate these concerns. This involved undertaking significant lobbying efforts, mobilizing physicians relations teams to address doctors' skepticism, and recruiting software engineers who demanded high compensation given the risks of joining an unproven startup to address data security. In the 'no legitimation work' condition the second mover entered at the juncture at which the industry's efforts had gained traction. The manipulation check asked how much effort each firm was perceived to have put in establishing this industry.

Participants were again presented with the set of firm overviews and asked to state their agreement with several statements evaluating the firm, with the order randomized. In addition to 'this service provider is authentic', the statements included '… sincere', 'genuine', 'committed to helping people who need healthcare', 'trustworthy', and 'competent'. The analyses use the within-individual difference in authenticity ratings between Firm A and Firm B.

In the 'authenticity study,' participants were asked to rate their perceptions of authenticity as well as the related perceptual variables included in Study 1 for each firm, after reporting their willingness to use each firm. The analysis compares the within-individual difference between Firm A and Firm B across the early follower and late follower conditions.

Participants were asked to rate their perceptions of authenticity as well as the related perceptual variables included in previous studies. The analysis compares the authenticity perception contrast across the legitimation work and no legitimation work conditions.

variable_name: Willingness to use / willingness to recommend
description: Audience preference was measured in two different ways. As a direct measure, study participants were asked (seven-point Likert scale) how interested they would be in using each firm's service (willingness to use); an alternative, third-order version asked how likely they would be to recommend each firm (willingness to recommend). The hypothesis tests compare within-subject ratings on Firm A versus Firm B, and the relative discount on the follower is the within-individual difference Firm A minus Firm B.

Participants were asked their willingness to use each firm; the preference measure is the within-individual difference between willingness to use Firm A and willingness to use Firm B. This difference was compared across the early follower and late follower conditions in the authenticity study.

variable_name: Willingness to use / willingness to recommend
description: Participants were asked the same questions about their relative preferences for each firm as before, and were additionally asked to briefly explain their preference or indifference in their ratings of the two firms. The hypothesis tests compare the within-individual difference in willingness to use (and willingness to recommend) Firm A versus Firm B across the legitimation work and no legitimation work conditions.

variable_name: Perceived legitimacy of the new organizational form
description: Our measure of legitimacy derived from a series of items that asked participants' perception of this new organizational form: how they perceive 'app-based on-demand doctors' to be 'reliable,' 'valid,' 'worrisome,' 'inspires confidence,' 'deceptive,' or 'sensible.' These six items, measured on a seven-point scale (1: 'not at all,' 7: 'very much so'), were presented in random order and averaged to construct the measure of legitimacy, in which answers to the two negative statements were reverse coded (Cronbach's alpha ≈ 0.87).
scale: seven-point scale (1: 'not at all,' 7: 'very much so')

description: In the 'legitimacy study,' participants were asked to rate the legitimacy of each firm, using the same six items from Study 1. The analysis compares the within-sub-study difference in the legitimacy rating with the within-sub-study difference in the authenticity rating, and separately compares the legitimacy rating for the first entrant with that of the follower.

Coded using the longitudinal data set made available by Berry et al. (2010), which is based on well-established conventions in political science and improves on alternative measures based on party control or representation by incorporating information on the ideological orientations of elected politicians and by accounting for the relative power that the majority party wields in the state legislative chambers. Higher values reflect state policymakers who were highly conservative and therefore opposed to the practice, lower values cases where policymakers collectively leaned liberal.

variable_name: Prior adoptions by proximal corporations (corporate adoptions, same state)
description: Captures the adoption decisions of major for-profit corporations (i.e., Fortune 500 companies) headquartered in the same state where a given university is situated. Data were compiled by triangulating information obtained from Human Rights Campaign, companies' human resources policies, press releases, and media coverage.

variable_name: Prior adoptions by peer universities (peer adoptions, intercollegiate conference)
description: Counts prior adoptions by peer schools that are part of the same intercollegiate athletic conferences (e.g., Big 10 or Pacific 12) as the focal school, an approach that approximates how organizations conceptualize institutional equivalence in the higher-public-education sector.

The year of adoption was modeled for each university; the year is the appropriate temporal unit because universities, like corporations, change employee benefits on a once-per-year schedule. Codes were compiled from university press releases, newspaper articles, and Human Rights Campaign, and in a few uncertain cases from the human resource departments of the universities' central administration. A total of 139 adoptions were observed in the sample.

variable_name: Market-based justifications for domestic partner benefits adoptions
description: Coded by reading universities' press releases, public announcements, and media reports. Instances where universities cited 'being the best employer' or 'attracting and retaining talent' (or similar market-based phrasing) as reasons were coded as one; instances where they offered 'ending discrimination' or 'ensuring equal rights' (or similar equity-based phrasing) were coded as zero; instances involving mixed justifications were assigned a score of 0.50. Justifications could be identified for 91 of the 139 adoptions.

Responses on a 1 to 5 scale to the question of the extent to which a business activity is important to the success of the department were obtained for each department from departmental members and from those IS personnel who interacted with the department. Mean responses were calculated from both an IS and a departmental member perspective, and the difference between the IS perspective and the corresponding departmental perspective was obtained for each business activity. These differences were aggregated across the business activities loading on the primary activities factor. The closer the aggregate is to zero, the greater the convergence for a department.
time_window: Measured at time periods 1 and 5; time period 5 used in the causal analyses

description: Departmental members and the IS personnel who interacted with the department rated on a 1 to 5 scale the extent to which each business activity is important to the success of the department. Mean IS and departmental responses were differenced for each activity, and the differences were aggregated across the activities loading on the indirect support activities factor. The closer the aggregate is to zero, the greater the convergence for a department.
time_window: Measured at time periods 1 and 5; time period 5 used in the causal analyses

variable_name: IT to Support Primary Activities T5
description: Departmental members and interacting IS personnel rated on a 1 to 5 scale the extent of the potential use of computer based information systems for accomplishing each business activity in the department. Mean IS and departmental responses were differenced for each activity, and the differences were aggregated across the activities loading on the primary activities factor. The closer the aggregate is to zero, the greater the convergence for a department.
time_window: Measured at time periods 1 and 5; time period 5 used in the causal analyses

variable_name: IT to Support Indirect Activities T5
description: Departmental members and interacting IS personnel rated on a 1 to 5 scale the extent of the potential use of computer based information systems for accomplishing each business activity in the department. Mean IS and departmental responses were differenced for each activity, and the differences were aggregated across the activities loading on the indirect support activities factor. The closer the aggregate is to zero, the greater the convergence for a department.
time_window: Measured at time periods 1 and 5; time period 5 used in the causal analyses

description: A weighted average of communication richness was calculated for each department using the channel richness weights obtained from Zmud, Lind, and Young (1989). These richness weights were multiplied by the number of times each type of communication channel was used by the department's IS respondents in communication with a department's members, summed across the scores for all 14 channels for each department, and then divided by the total number of communication events recorded for a department. This produced a standardized communication richness measure for each department for each time period.
time_window: Five data collection periods; the analyses use averages of time periods 2 through 5

description: The communication log data resulted in a measure of the total number of communication events for each of the 48 departments. For each department, the aggregate communication measure was divided by the number of IS respondents who reported contact with the department, producing a standardized communication frequency measure. Standardizing the frequency measure in this way controlled for the fact that the number of IS personnel interacting with a department varied across departments.
time_window: Five data collection periods; the analyses use averages of time periods 2 through 5

description: Five vice-presidents in Division A and six vice-presidents in Division B evaluated the information technology innovativeness of each department. They responded to the item asking the degree to which each department generates new ideas for using computer based information systems, on a 1 to 5 scale from far below average to far above average. Averaging the expert evaluations for a department produced an innovativeness score for each department; the measure was collected during time periods 1 and 5.

U.S. box office information reported by the contemporary trade journals Boxoffice (for the period 1932-36) and Boxoffice Barometer (for 1937-41), which surveyed first-run movie theater operators across the United States weekly. Theater operators evaluated a movie's box office performance as a percentage of the expected box office performance of an average movie. The measure is continuous and always positive, with an average box office return being rated as 100 percent. Missing data required estimation of performance values for 16 movies from information from the Motion Picture Herald.
scale: percentage of the expected box office performance of an average movie (100 percent = average box office return)

description: Number of repeated dyadic relationships between key project contributors during the four years after project completion. The measure captures 12 dyadic relationships: producer-director, producer-first lead actor, producer-second lead actor, director-first lead actor, director-second lead actor, producer-cinematographer, director-cinematographer, producer-art director, director-art director, producer-editor, director-editor, and first lead actor-second lead actor. Screenwriters were excluded because their main contribution occurs during preproduction. The authors picked a four-year time window after the start of movie production and confirmed robustness for two-, three- and five-year windows.
time_window: four years after the start of movie production

description: Number of repeated dyadic relationships between key project contributors in future color movie projects during the four years after project completion. It was constructed as a similar future collaboration measure that only captured repeated collaborations in future color movies.
time_window: four years after the start of movie production

variable_name: Future collaborations governed by a different studio (periods 1 to 4)
description: Number of repeated dyadic relationships between key project contributors in future movie projects governed by a different studio during the four years after project completion. It was constructed as a similar future collaboration measure restricted to future projects governed by a different studio.
time_window: four years after the start of movie production

description: Number of prior dyadic relationships between key project contributors during the same and four preceding years, using the same coding rules as the future collaboration measure. Prior collaborations occurring in the same year and each of the four years preceding a focal movie project were examined.
time_window: same year and four preceding years

description: Number of prior dyadic relationships between key project contributors during the same and two preceding years. It was created, together with the periods -5 to -3 variable, through a simple and intuitive split-group approach to test the impact of more recent collaboration; both variables capture prior collaborations for three-year periods.
time_window: same year and two preceding years

description: Number of prior dyadic relationships between key project contributors during three to five preceding years. It was created, together with the periods -2 to 0 variable, through a simple and intuitive split-group approach to test the impact of more recent collaboration; both variables capture prior collaborations for three-year periods.

Movie project employing color technology, identified using the American Film Institute Catalog and dummy-coded 1 for color. It identifies whether a focal project and a later project are of the same type, since color movies introduced a new project type requiring substantial adjustments of interdependent tasks.

Movie project governed by a studio without substantial permanent production sites and theater chain ownership, coded 1 for United Artists, minor studios, and independent production companies. Nonintegrated studios did not enjoy long-term contractual control over project participants and could not bar them from joining future projects at other studios, whereas integrated studios did; the coding therefore indicates the open (low-control) side of the asymmetry.

We measured the M&A experience of the acquirer as the count of all M&As that the firm completed during the 10 years preceding the focal M&A. We then subtracted the target's M&A experience, measured likewise, from the acquirer's M&A experience to measure the difference in experience between the parties. This variable takes positive values if the acquirer's experience exceeds that of the target and negative values if the target's experience exceeds that of the acquirer.

The absolute amount of value, in U.S. dollars, obtained by the acquirer upon announcement, calculated by multiplying the acquirer's pre-announcement market value (number of shares on day -11 times share price on day -11) by the cumulative abnormal returns to the acquirer during the event window. Cumulative abnormal returns were calculated using the market model with a 250-day estimation window and a 21-day event window centered on the event date. The authors use absolute dollar amounts rather than percentage returns because acquirers and targets may differ considerably in size.
time_window: 21-day event window [-10, +10] around the announcement; 250-day estimation window

description: The absolute amount of value, in U.S. dollars, obtained by the target upon announcement, calculated in the same way as the acquirer's amount using the target's pre-announcement market value and the target's cumulative abnormal returns during the event window. Cumulative abnormal returns were calculated using the market model with a 250-day estimation window and a 21-day event window centered on the event date. The authors use the absolute amount obtained by the target rather than a ratio of both parties' returns because at least one party often has negative returns, which makes a ratio uninterpretable.
time_window: 21-day event window [-10, +10] around the announcement; 250-day estimation window

description: We measured the target's product-market scope as the number of four-digit SIC codes in which it operated at the time of the acquisition. This variable is commonly used in studies of the effects of product-market scope in M&As.
time_window: at the time of the acquisition

description: We measured whether the deal was friendly or not using a dummy variable coded 1 if the deal was reported as friendly in SDC, and 0 otherwise. This measure has frequently been used in M&A studies.

variable_name: Structural power: founder's CEO or chairman status
description: Categorical variable combining executive and board influence: 0 represents founders who were neither CEO nor chairperson, 1 represents founders who were CEO or chair of the board at IPO but did not hold both roles together, and 2 represents founder-CEOs who also chaired the board.

variable_name: Ownership power: founder's ownership relative to the ownership of the largest shareholder
description: A founder's ownership relative to the ownership of the largest shareholder at IPO, consistent with Attig, El Ghoul, and Guedhami (2009). Derived from the firms' IPO prospectuses, typically in the 'Directors and other interests' or 'Significant shareholdings' subsections.

variable_name: Expertise power: founder is the inventor or main developer
description: Dummy coded 1 when the focal founder was the inventor or the main developer of his or her venture's product, and 0 otherwise. The information was found in the IPO prospectuses, typically in the introduction, the R&D section, or the founder's resume.

variable_name: Expertise power: founder's experience in related industries
description: Number of years the founder worked in an industry related to the focal IPO firm before founding his or her firm. Experience was considered relevant if gained in the same Industry Classification Benchmark super sector as the focal IPO venture (19 super sectors in total). Captured from resumes reported in the IPO prospectuses and corroborated with company websites and social media.

variable_name: Prestige power: founder's directorships in other businesses
description: Number of directorships in other firms during the five years before the IPO, a figure reported in IPO prospectuses and visible to investment audiences.

variable_name: Prestige power: news mentioning the founder before IPO
description: Number of news items mentioning a founder together with his or her company from company founding until the IPO, obtained from the Nexis U.K. database, which includes coverage in national and regional newspapers. Approximately 10% of the pieces were randomly inspected and the coverage was found to be overwhelmingly positive, so total media coverage was used. Used in log form in the models.
time_window: from company founding until the IPO

description: Index calculated by standardizing and adding the six proxy measures of power, used to compare the effect size of power on different exit routes. In these models a variable capturing the average market value of the founders' holding shares was also included.

variable_name: Power at IPO condition (high vs low)
description: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions, high or low power at the time of IPO, and presented with a scenario (vignette) portraying them as a cofounder of a venture that had just achieved an IPO. The power dimensions were merged into a single description, the equivalent of a power index, to create the two conditions.

After reading the scenario, participants indicated the likelihood that they would exit the described firm with a full exit, a managerial partial exit, or a financial partial exit using a 7-point scale (1 = very low likelihood to 7 = very high likelihood).

After reading the scenario, participants indicated the likelihood that they would exit the described firm with a managerial partial exit using a 7-point scale (1 = very low likelihood to 7 = very high likelihood).

After reading the scenario, participants indicated the likelihood that they would exit the described firm with a financial partial exit using a 7-point scale (1 = very low likelihood to 7 = very high likelihood).

variable_name: Power at IPO condition (high vs low)
description: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two power conditions, using the same high- and low-power scenarios as in the first experiment.

Participants indicated the likelihood that they would exit the described firm with a full exit, a managerial partial exit, or a financial partial exit using the same 7-point scales as in the previous experiment.
Participants indicated the likelihood that they would exit the described firm with a managerial partial exit using the same 7-point scale as in the previous experiment.
Participants indicated the likelihood that they would exit the described firm with a financial partial exit using the same 7-point scale as in the previous experiment.

A 7-item scale selected from Spector's (1975) item list for organizational frustration, with items chosen for face validity for founders at the time of IPO and answered on a 6-point scale (-3 = disagree completely to +3 = agree completely). The scale was found to be reliable with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.86.

Productive efficiency is estimated with Data Envelopment Analysis: linear programming converts multiple input and output measures into a single measure of relative efficiency for each observation against a piecewise linear industry best practice frontier constructed from the observations in the sample. The productive efficiency of a firm in a specific year is computed by comparing it to all other firms in the same year, using an input-oriented measure that seeks to reduce the input quantities without changing the output quantities. Different firms are allowed to have different returns to scale so the productive efficiency measure is devoid of the scale effects. Inputs are labor cost, plant value, production expenses, transmission expenses, distribution expenses, sales, administrative and general expenses, and electricity purchased from other sources; outputs are quantities of low-voltage sales (residential and commercial), high-voltage sales (industrial, interchanges out, and wheeling delivered), and sales for resale to other utilities in megawatt hours.
time_window: each year from 1998 to 2001, computed within the year

description: DEREGULATION represents the stages of deregulation of each state for each year from 1998 to 2001, coded 0 (no activity), 1 (commission or legislative investigation ongoing), 2 (legislation orders pending), 3 (comprehensive regulatory order issued), and 4 (restructuring legislation enacted). Because firms may operate in several states subject to different levels of deregulation, the weighting of DEREGULATION is based on the percentage of the electricity sold by each utility in each state.

PROP GEN represents the proportion of electricity sold that is generated by the utility. Because a nonlinear relationship is hypothesized, the variable is entered as a quadratic term in the regression, its square being PROP GEN2. PROP GEN is de-meaned, so its values range from -0.5 (100 percent retail purchased) to 0.5 (100 percent generation).

Firm-level technological relatedness built from NBER patent cross-citations: citing and cited patents are assigned to industries based on the operating 4-digit SIC of the patent owners, and a 5-year rolling sum of total cross-citations between each industry pair is computed. The firm's TRD is obtained by averaging cross-citations between the industries in which the firm operates and then taking the natural logarithm of the value obtained; the formal expression is not legible in the text provided. It can only be calculated for diversified firms, those reporting sales in more than one SIC4 industry in a year.
time_window: year t, using patents granted between years t and t-4 (5-year rolling window)

description: Intercept (alpha) from the time-series regression of a portfolio's monthly excess return on the market risk premium and on size, value and momentum factors (Carhart four-factor model). Portfolio 0 contains all diversified firms exhibiting a zero TRD value on December 31 of year t-1 and portfolios 1-5 are quintiles of the stocks of firms with a positive TRD value; both equal-weighted and value-weighted portfolio returns are estimated. Alpha represents the abnormal monthly return realized by the portfolio after accounting for its exposure to the four sources of risk.
time_window: monthly returns between 1981 and 2007; portfolios formed on TRD as of December 31 of year t-1

description: Firm-level technological relatedness built from NBER patent cross-citations: citing and cited patents are assigned to industries based on the operating 4-digit SIC of the patent owners, and a 5-year rolling sum of total cross-citations between each industry pair is computed. The firm's TRD is obtained by averaging cross-citations between the industries in which the firm operates and then taking the natural logarithm of the value obtained; the formal expression is not legible in the text provided. It can only be calculated for diversified firms, those reporting sales in more than one SIC4 industry in a year.
time_window: year t, using patents granted between years t and t-4 (5-year rolling window)

description: Individual firm-level three-year alpha estimated with the same four-factor framework used in the portfolio analysis, using three years of monthly data. Between 1981 and 2007 there are up to nine estimation periods for each firm, starting with the 1981-1983 period and ending with 2005-2007. The raw alpha obtained from the individual regressions is used as the dependent variable.

Inverse of the ownership percentage by transient investors, following Hirshleifer et al. (2018) and using the transient investor classification of Bushee (1998). It is one minus the percentage of outstanding shares held by transient investors.
Average monthly number of sell-side analysts' earnings-per-share (EPS) forecasts for the current fiscal year.

Average cosine similarity between the text of patents granted to the firm and the rest of the patents granted by the USPTO in the previous 5 years, based on patent text data from Arts et al. (2021). It is measured as the average cosine similarity of patents granted to the firm over a 3-year rolling window from the focal year.
time_window: 3-year rolling window from the focal year

description: Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 starting from 2002, the year of the earliest release of patent application information under the American Inventors Protection Act.

Average time lag in months between patent application and publication for the period 1996-2000, estimated at the SIC4 sector level and aggregated at the firm level by computing an average based on segment sales. All firm-level variation comes from the segment sales averaging because the granting delay is estimated at the SIC4 level.
level: firm-year (sector-level lag aggregated by segment sales)

description: Each of the three business units was identified as pursuing one of Miles and Snow's three viable strategies. The identification was based on an analysis of the unit's products, market position, strategic goals and actual performance, using information obtained from the marketing director of each business unit; two corporate staff members independently categorized the units from Miles and Snow's descriptions and were in perfect agreement with the authors' classification.

variable_name: level of conflict between marketing and R&D
description: A three-item five-point scale asking respondents how frequently they disagree with personnel from R&D over (1) the goals and priorities of the business unit, (2) the specific ways work is done or services are provided between the departments, and (3) the specific terms of the relationship between marketing and R&D. Coefficient alpha for the measure was 0.83.

variable_name: formalization of the relationship with R&D
description: A four-item five-point scale asking respondents to judge the extent to which their relationship with R&D (1) was explicitly verbalized, (2) was written down in detail, (3) used standard operating procedures such as rules, policies and forms, and (4) followed formal communication channels. Coefficient alpha for the measure was 0.79.
One item of the conflict resolution measure asking respondents to indicate on a five-point scale how frequently conflicts are resolved by ignoring or avoiding the issue.
One item of the conflict resolution measure asking respondents to indicate on a five-point scale how frequently conflicts are resolved by smoothing over the issue.
One item of the conflict resolution measure asking respondents to indicate on a five-point scale how frequently conflicts are resolved by working out a compromise between the parties involved.

One item of the conflict resolution measure asking respondents to indicate on a five-point scale how frequently conflicts are resolved by passing the conflict to higher-level managers or authorities for resolution.
A single-item scale measuring the respondent's attitude toward how well conflicts are resolved, answered on a five-point scale ranging from very poorly to very well.
scale: five-point scale from very poorly to very well

variable_name: perceived effectiveness of marketing's relationship with R&D
description: Six five-point items exploring the respondent's perceptions concerning the overall effectiveness of the relationship, the extent to which the relationship is satisfying and productive, and the extent to which each side carries out its responsibilities. Coefficient alpha for the measure was 0.87.

Dummy variable set equal to '1' if a deal was completed and '0' otherwise, based on the status SDC reports for each attempted transaction. In this sample 73% of the deals were successfully completed and 27% failed to close, and the average duration to close a successful deal was about 129 days.

Dummy equal to one if the acquirer's immediate or ultimate owner was any level of the Chinese government. SDC ownership classifications were refined with CSMAR data for public companies and, where CSMAR did not cover a firm, ownership was collected directly from the firm's annual reports. To identify the ultimate owner the entire ownership structure was sometimes traced, counting ownership held directly and indirectly through pyramidal structures; if total state ownership was greater than the ownership share of any other individual entity the firm was considered an SOE. For publicly listed companies classified as SOEs, state ownership was in all cases greater than 15%.

An Opaqueness index created by a principal component analysis of the three transparency measures Public acquirer, Foreign-listed acquirer, and Big4, used as the main opaqueness measure. The three opaqueness (reversely coded) measures are highly correlated, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.56 to 0.81; Cronbach's alpha is 0.86 and all three measures load strongly on the first principal component, which explains 78.4% of all the variations. Opaqueness is negatively correlated with deal completion and positively correlated with SOE acquirer.
Equal to one if the acquirer was listed on any stock exchange.

Equal to one if the acquirer was listed on a stock exchange outside its home country (in this case rather than on the Shanghai or Shenzhen exchange). The foreign exchanges represented in the sample were all from developed economies and mainly those in the United States, Hong Kong, Singapore, and the United Kingdom.
Equal to one if an acquirer's auditing firm was PwC, Deloitte, EY, or KPMG (and before 2002, Arthur Andersen) and zero otherwise.

Three indicators derived from Petit and Bollaert (2012) and validated by the authors were used: has a grandiose sense of self; overestimates his/her abilities; considers him/herself as highly qualified. Three raters with doctorates in clinical psychology, blind to the study's purpose, rated each CEO after watching videos edited to 2.5 minutes in length and stripped of identifiers, using a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree). Ratings of the sampled new CEOs were reliable (alpha = .91) with significant intraclass correlations across raters, and all factor loadings were > 0.77.
scale: 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree)
time_window: videos dated prior to but within 1 year of the new CEO's appointment

description: Return on assets, taken from Compustat, used as a measure of organizational performance, the most common conceptualization of a more precarious situation. Measured over the 2 years preceding a CEO change.
Total shareholder returns, computed via Compustat with monthly reinvestment of dividends and stated as a percentage. Measured over the 2 years preceding a CEO change.

Following Dess and Beard (1984), industry sales categorized by the 4-digit SIC are regressed on the fiscal year over a 10-year period preceding the year of the announcement of the new CEO's hiring. The coefficient for each industry in the sample is extracted and divided by the mean value from the same period.
time_window: 10-year period preceding the year of the announcement of the new CEO's hiring

description: Following Dess and Beard (1984), the standard errors of the industry coefficients obtained from regressing industry sales categorized by 4-digit SIC on the fiscal year over the 10-year period preceding the year of the announcement of the new CEO's hiring.
time_window: 10-year period preceding the year of the announcement of the new CEO's hiring

description: Captured using Gentry et al.'s (2021) CEO turnover and dismissal dataset, coded 1 if a prior CEO was dismissed (codes 3 and 4) and 0 if not (codes 1, 2, 5, 6, and 7).

Log(Number of total departures + 1), constructed at the origin airport-carrier-year level for the total number of departures performed. The authors argue that an increase in flight departures leads to a boost in local employment, making it an appropriate measure of pork. The number of available seats and the number of passengers transported are used as additional dependent variables.
scale: log count (log of number of departures plus one)

description: Log(Number of departures to DC airports + 1), where the DC airports are Washington Dulles International (IAD), Reagan National (DCA), and Baltimore/Washington International (BWI). Constructed at the origin airport-carrier-year level for the number of nonstop departures to the DC area, which members of Congress frequently use for travel from and to their home districts, making it an appropriate measure of perk. Seats and passengers to DC are used as additional dependent variables.
scale: log count (log of number of departures plus one)

description: Log(# of total departures from the Transportation Committee chair's district + 1) in the same year that the bill is introduced to the House.
scale: log count (log of number of departures plus one)

description: Log(# of departures to DC from the Transportation Committee chair's district + 1), measured in the same year that the focal bill is introduced to the House.
scale: log count (log of number of departures plus one)

description: Dummy variable indicating whether a focal aviation bill is passed in the House of Representatives. The authors also use Report, a dummy indicating whether a bill is reported by the Transportation Committee to the full chamber, as a dependent variable. Higher values indicate less policy inaction.
Dummy variable indicating whether a focal bill is reported by the Transportation Committee to the full House floor. Higher values indicate less policy inaction.

Dichotomous treatment variable equal to one if the origin airport of an airport-carrier-year observation is located in the home district of the current House Transportation Committee chair, and zero otherwise. Airports were overlaid on a congressional district map to find those inside the chairs' district boundaries; chair identity comes from committee assignment records.

A multi-item scale measuring the degree to which suppliers had 'invested' or 'participated' in any of a series of knowledge acquisition programs listed, associated with the acquisition of team-based capabilities. The programs inventoried from literature searches and interviews with managers are total quality management, new machine set up techniques, kaizen, and lot size optimization techniques. Items were answered on a five-point Likert scale where 1 represents 'not at all' and 5 'to a large degree'.
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = to a large degree)

description: A multi-item scale measuring the degree to which suppliers had 'invested' or 'participated' in any of the above-listed knowledge acquisition programs where 'this' buyer had 'direct participation.' 'Direct participation' was defined as this buyer having taught, or consulted (e.g., buyer's personnel teach supplier's personnel), or co-participated (e.g., teams from both companies join efforts in a given training program). Items were measured on a five-point Likert scale where 1 represents 'not at all' and 5 'to a large degree.'
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = to a large degree)

description: A multi-item scale identifying the degree to which the supplier has invested in new or modified existing capabilities and physical assets primarily to serve the unique needs of 'this' customer. Items were based on previous work by Artz and Brush (2000), which captured dimensions related not only to physical assets, but also to personnel and routines that were specialized to the focal partner. Items were answered on a five-point Likert scale where 1 represents 'not at all' and 5 'to a large degree.'
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = to a large degree)
time_window: past three years of the relationship

description: A measure of the degree to which partners rely on social commitments of collaboration as gauged by their efforts to share information, assist each other, and promote fair sharing of cost savings and benefits arising out of joint efforts. The first two survey items were adapted from Heide and John (1992), Noordewier et al. (1990) and Artz and Brush (2000); the third was adapted from Ring and Van de Ven (1992). Items were answered on a five-point Likert scale where 1 represents 'not at all' and 5 'to a large degree.'
scale: five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 5 = to a large degree)

description: Measured with two dimensions: the number of inventory turns necessary to support 12 months of sales, and the percentage of goods delivered on time. For redeployable performance the authors used the respondent's input for the performance the supplier achieved with an 'average' customer, defined as a customer representative of the supplier's average performance. The two performance dimensions were factored together because construct validity analysis suggested they measure the same underlying construct, that is, production performance.
level: supplier firm (performance with an average customer)

description: Computed by subtracting the performance a supplier obtained with an 'average' customer from that it obtained with 'this' customer, on each of two dimensions (inventory turns and percentage of goods delivered on time). For example, where the inventory necessary to support sales to 'this' customer turned 18 times a year and the inventory for average customers turned 11, relational inventory performance was 7 turns. The two performance dimensions were factored together.

Five-trading-day cumulative abnormal return for the U.S. parent firm, formed by summing daily abnormal returns over the event window from t=-2 to t=+2, where t=0 corresponds to the event date. Daily abnormal returns are the difference between the firm's actual return and the return predicted by a market model estimated over the period t=-250 to t=-50. Daily returns for each U.S. parent firm and for the value-weighted market portfolio (including all distributions and excluding ADRs) were obtained from CRSP.
time_window: 5 trading days (t=-2 to +2); estimation period t=-250 to t=-50

description: Percentage of stock held by U.S. parent firm i's officers and directors. Data on inside ownership were obtained from the Compact Disclosure CD-ROM package for the quarter closest to the internalization event. The variable enters the cross-sectional regression as a continuous percentage.
scale: percentage (0.04 to 42.0 percent in the sample)
time_window: quarter closest to the internalization event

description: Income before extraordinary items plus depreciation and amortization less capital expenditures, which is then scaled by dividing by the parent firm's market value on the event date. Financial data were obtained from Compustat for the year prior to the internalization event and market value data from CRSP. In the regression the free cash flow and leverage means were subtracted from the direct effects prior to forming the multiplicative term.
time_window: year prior to the internalization event; market value on the event date

description: Total liabilities divided by total assets for U.S. parent firm i. The data were obtained from Compustat for the year prior to the internalization event. The mean of leverage was subtracted from the direct effect prior to forming the interaction term with free cash flow.
time_window: year prior to the internalization event

description: Coded as one if the targeted firm positively responded to the stakeholder demands within 5 years of initiation and zero otherwise; if there were multiple actions within this window they were all coded as a one if the firm responded. Coding drew on articles referencing the stakeholder action, searched by company and stakeholder group names; for civil suits saliency was coded according to the final disposition of the suit (e.g., the nature of the settlement). Two research assistants independently coded saliency and their coding was correlated at 95.21 percent.

Stakeholder group assets divided by targeted firm assets, both measured at the time an action was initiated. The stakeholder resource base is proxied by the total financial assets of the stakeholder group (for asset managers such as pension funds or individuals, the total amount of investments they control); the firm's resource base is its total assets. The ratio is used because numerator and denominator are in the same units.
time_window: at the time an action was initiated

description: Coding of the relative degree to which a stakeholder group is viewed as a legitimate arbiter of environmental issues, based on public opinion surveys that rank stakeholder group types and appear fairly stable over time. The scale runs from one for holding institutions, two for religiously affiliated groups, three for activist individuals, four for non-environmental NGOs, and five for environmental NGOs.

Coding of the degree to which the environmental issue raised by a stakeholder request is well accepted and well defined, based on public opinion studies covering 1996-2004. The scale runs from one for global warming, two for GMOs, three for habitat destruction, four for pollution, and five for recycling; the authors note the ordering is relatively subjective and that polling phrasings differ.

Binary coding of the immediacy of the request: demands for cessation or changes in current action are coded as one and demands for pledges to future action (or inaction) are coded as zero. The authors illustrate with a boycott requesting that BP pledge not to drill in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in the future, which was coded as zero.

Self-perceived distance between the problem solvers were attempting to solve and the solvers' own field of expertise. It is based on the answer to the survey question 'Is the particular challenge you attempted to solve: 1-inside your field of expertise, 4-at the boundary of your field of expertise, 7-outside your field of expertise?', with respondents choosing any value between 1 and 7. The higher the score, the greater the perceived distance between the solvers' field of expertise and the problem field, capturing a sense of technical marginality between the solver and the field of the problem.

Gender of the solver, coded 1 if the name was determined to be female and 0 if the name was male. It was derived by using IBM's Global Name Analytics program to identify gender from the full names of solvers, using a gender propensity score of 51% or higher to assign gender, and cross-verified against survey-reported gender (mismatch of 2.6% was corrected). The same variable is used in both stages of the model.

Binary dependent variable of the second stage, developed using data available from the IC database on whether a solver had won a prize or not for their submission. The variable was given a value of 1 if the solver had won, and 0 otherwise. Solvers that submitted solutions to more than one problem were included on the basis of their most recent submission, and solvers that had won at least once on the basis of their most recent winning submission.

Binary dependent variable of the first stage of the model, capturing the IC solver's decision to exert effort and submit a solution for evaluation upon getting the details of a problem. The unit of analysis is the solver who has downloaded at least one problem statement, and the variable takes a value of 1 when a solution was submitted and 0 otherwise. Solvers that submitted solutions to more than one problem were included on the basis of their most recent submission.

For the dependent variable, a new product was defined as one showing change in design characteristics. A robot was defined as new if one or more of its design characteristics differed from those of a firm's previous robots. Robots' design characteristics include load capacity, number of axes, power source, repeatability, sensors, speed, weight, and application areas. An existing product design introduced into a new geographical area does not qualify as a new product.

Search age variables were measured as the ages of the patents that were cited in a given firm's yearly patents, defining the latter as the patents the firm applied for in a given year. The age of a cited patent was the time elapsed since its issue. Internal search consists of citations to the firm's own patents, and the variable was the average age of such self-citations in a firm-year.

Search age variables were measured as the ages of the patents cited in a given firm's yearly patents, with the age of a cited patent being the time elapsed since its issue. A patent was defined as competitor knowledge if it belonged to any of the other 130 robotics companies in the sample. Average competitor search age was the average age of citations to competitor patents in a firm-year.

Search age variables were measured as the ages of the patents cited in a given firm's yearly patents, with the age of a cited patent being the time elapsed since its issue. External search age was the average age of cited patents that were not self- or competitor citations per firm year.

Every patent includes a unique solution to a technical problem, so the sum of external patents a firm cited in a year was used to measure the quantity of its external problem-solving (search) efforts in that year. A patent cited multiple times in a firm-year was counted only once.

This variable, representing the diversity in the ages of the internal knowledge elements a firm searches, was measured as the variance (cf. Sørensen, 2000) in internal search age for each firm yearly.
This variable stands for the diversity in the ages of the competitor knowledge a firm uses in its search. It was measured as the variance in competitor search age in each firm-year.
Capturing the diversity in the ages of the external knowledge used in search, this variable was measured as the variance in external search age in each firm-year.

variable_name: Executive to interlocking director employment ties
description: A count at the executive level reflecting the total number of interlocking directors on the focal firm's board to which the executive had a prior employment tie, ranging from '0' to some positive integer. It is the basis for the executive-level models, and about 7% of executives in any given year had a prior employment tie to at least one interlocking director.

variable_name: Executive to interlocking director employment tie
description: Coded '1' in each executive-director dyad where an executive and a given director had worked at a common prior employer at the same time in the past, and '0' otherwise. It was constructed by comparing the full employment histories of every executive and interlocking director in each firm during each year of the study and comparing the years worked for the common employer.

Coded '1' if the individual left the focal firm in t and became an executive of another public or private firm in t + 1, and '0' otherwise. Exits were identified using the Execucomp leftco variable for approximately 30% of sampled executives and, for the remaining executives, the exit date was determined from full employment histories in BoardEx; of 8,864 turnover events, 3,443 involved movement to another executive position in an outside firm.

Coded '1' if the executive left the focal firm and was listed as an executive in a firm that shared an interlock with the focal firm through a member of the focal firm's board in t + 1, and '0' otherwise; there were 208 movements to interlocking firms in the panel. Movements to outside firms that were not interlocked through a member of the focal firm's board were captured in a separate competing-risk variable.

variable_name: Movement to the director's interlocking firm
description: An alternative binary measure at the executive-director dyad level, created as a more direct test of executive movement to a specific director's interlocking firm. It was used in the dyad-level selection models, where movement to a noninterlocking firm also served as a competing risk.

Takes the value '1' when the director is either the independent chairperson of the board or the lead independent director, and '0' otherwise. It was assessed by examining the director's annual title in the focal firm.
Coded '1' when the director held the position of CEO at the interlocking firm and '0' otherwise. This variable was also assessed using the director's annual title, but in the interlocking firm.

Direct control exercised by institutional stockholders was measured as the proportion of institutional investors' shares in the company. Data on institutional stock ownership were collected from Standard and Poor's Stock Guide and Moody's Handbook of Common Stocks. The variable was recorded in the period just prior to the adoption of the antitakeover provision of interest, or at the time of censoring for censored observations.
time_window: period just prior to the adoption of the antitakeover provision of interest (time of censoring for censored observations)

description: The proportion of shares held by the CEO and all executive directors was used as the measure of stock ownership. These data were obtained from company proxy statements. A squared term of managerial stockholding was included to capture the curvilinear effect.
time_window: period just prior to the adoption of the antitakeover provision of interest (time of censoring for censored observations)

description: Information on the year and date of adoption were obtained from the Investor Responsibility Research Center's publication Corporate Takeover Defenses, and the month of adoption was approximated by using the date on the proxy statement in which the provisions were proposed. Three event histories were constructed: the adoption of all six provisions, provisions which require stockholder approval, and provisions which do not require stockholder approval. A firm's history was constructed as a sequence of amendment periods (spells), defined in months and separated by adoption of any antitakeover provision, with periods continuing until the study period ended (December 1988) and those cases coded as right-censored. The poison pill history was treated as a non-repeatable event, with duration time the number of months between January 1984 and the month of adoption.

Board composition, the relative mix of insiders and outsiders on the board, was measured as the proportion of outsiders on the board. Current and retired executives of the organization, and current or retired executives of one of its subsidiaries, were classified as insiders. Board composition data were obtained from company proxy statements.
time_window: period just prior to the adoption of the antitakeover provision of interest (time of censoring for censored observations)

description: Loyalty of outside board members was measured by their tenure on the board relative to that of the CEO. If the average tenure of outside members on the board was greater than that of the CEO, loyalty was coded 0, else 1. Tenure data for all directors and CEOs were collected from company proxy statements and COMPUSTAT-PC+.
time_window: period just prior to the adoption of the antitakeover provision of interest (time of censoring for censored observations)

description: The proportion of company shares held by outside board members was used as a measure of outsiders' stock ownership. Tenure and ownership data for all directors and CEOs were collected from company proxy statements and COMPUSTAT-PC+, and outsider director data were aggregated and averaged respectively.
time_window: period just prior to the adoption of the antitakeover provision of interest (time of censoring for censored observations)

description: Board leadership is a binary variable indicating unitary leadership (coded 0) or dual leadership (coded 1). Data were collected from company proxy statements.
time_window: period just prior to the adoption of the antitakeover provision of interest (time of censoring for censored observations)

variable_name: Board characteristics (composition, outsiders' loyalty, outsiders' shareholding, board leadership)
description: Board characteristics were measured as a set of board attributes: the proportion of outsiders on the board (composition), outsiders' loyalty (coded 0 if the average tenure of outside members exceeds the CEO's tenure, else 1), the proportion of company shares held by outside board members, and board leadership (unitary coded 0, dual coded 1). Data come from company proxy statements and COMPUSTAT-PC+. Each attribute enters the hazard models of antitakeover adoption separately, recorded in the period just prior to adoption or at censoring.
scale: set of proportions and binary indicators
time_window: period just prior to adoption or censoring, 1984-1988

description: Factor score for the first context factor. The factor reflects the relation of the project to the affected groups: the priority groups placed on the project, their level of concern and awareness about the project, and value conflicts surrounding the project (a negative association), together with how well participants thought they understood the causation of the problem and how well they actually understood what caused the problem. It was constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The underlying coded items posed choices from one to five, with one generally meaning low and five high.

Factor score for the second context factor, constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor is strongly associated with the experience, skill, and adequacy of numbers of planning staff. The underlying coded items posed choices from one to five, with one generally meaning low and five high.

Factor score for the third context factor, constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor reflects the level of technology perceived to be needed, the level actually needed, and the extent to which the technology differed from current technology. In the equations explaining outcomes the authors refer to this factor as Technical Change.

Factor score for the fourth context factor, constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor reflects how adequate the lead organization judged the staff and calendar time available.

Factor score for the fifth context factor, constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor associates positively with the potential impact on the organizational structures of affected groups, whether the lead organization was required to undertake the project, and the level of conflict over values, and negatively with the stability of the political environment.

Factor score for the sixth context factor, constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor reflects strongly economic and political environmental stability and somewhat past success.
