Factor score for the seventh context factor, constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor reflects the existence and stability of coalitions among affected organizations prior to the change effort.

Factor score for the eighth context factor, constructed from the coded context items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor associates positively with the power of the lead organization and the adequacy of the money available, and negatively with the potential impact on resources.

Factor score for the first process factor, constructed from the coded process items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor associates strongly with internal and external communication, the extent of search for solutions, and the number of groups involved in searching for solutions.

Factor score for the second process factor, constructed from the coded process items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor associates positively with the length of time the project took relative to expectations and the use of forcing as a conflict resolution technique, and negatively with the use of problem-solving as a conflict resolution technique.

Factor score for the third process factor, constructed from the coded process items with the highest loadings on the factor. The factor associates heavily with the number of groups involved in identifying problems and solutions, the use of compromise as a conflict resolution strategy, and turnover in the lead organization.

Factor score for the first outcome factor, which accounted for 59 percent of the total variance in the outcome variables. The factor associates heavily with overall goal achievement, satisfaction with the outcome, enhanced future problem-solving capacity, few deviations from success criteria, and little change from project-as-approved to the project-as-implemented.

Factor score for the second outcome factor, which accounted for 16 percent of the variance in the outcome variables. The factor associates positively with learning and negatively with deviation from the success criteria of others.

A self-report measure based on a 54-item seven-point Likert scale eliciting responses on environmental actions in eight categories of industry environmental impact; the categories were based on the author's exploratory research, on the CERES principles, and on the environmental strategy literature. Multiple responses from a company were averaged to represent the company as a whole, and the composite covers actions ranging from regulatory compliance and common industry practices to voluntary actions. To externally validate the measure, a panel of three long-standing industry experts rated the 99 responding companies on a one-to-seven scale of the extent to which their environmental actions went beyond conformance, and the correlation between the panel scores and the single composite self-report score was .79.
scale: seven-point Likert scale (self-report); one-to-seven panel rating

description: Three self-report items adapted from Jackson and Dutton (1988), intended to measure managerial interpretations of environmental issues for the three issue attributes of negative or positive emotional associations, loss or gain considerations, and a sense of controllability or uncontrollability. The items were coded so that higher values indicate threat interpretations, so inverse relationships were tested in the structural model. Multiple responses from a company were averaged to represent the company as a whole.

variable_name: Issue legitimation as an integral aspect of corporate identity
description: Two self-report items adapted from Miles (1987) asking respondents about the extent to which they perceived their companies as environmental leaders and the extent to which they considered the reduction of environmental impact as central to their companies' identities. Information from corporate annual and environmental reports was used to externally validate the measure for the 69 responding firms for which such reports were available: mentions of environmental elements in the mission statement, the chairperson's letter to shareholders, and the summary report of the previous year's operations were coded on a seven-point scale for frequency and emphasis. The correlation between the self-report measure and the archival measure was .69.

Two self-report items adapted from Nohria and Gulati (1995) to reflect the task and resource slack available at the discretion of managers to manage the business and natural environment interface. Because discretionary slack is highly perceptual, no suitable data were available for external validation of this measure. Multiple responses from a company were averaged to represent the company as a whole.

variable_name: Integration of environmental criteria into employee performance evaluation systems
description: Two items adapted from Miles (1987) asked managers to report on the extent to which environmental indicators had been included in reward and planning systems, and a third item was added to reflect the extent to which environmental criteria were balanced with economic performance criteria. As with the issue legitimation measure, the annual and environmental reports of 69 companies were analyzed for mentions of such reward systems, with frequency and degree of emphasis coded on a seven-point scale; the correlation between the self-report measure and the archival measure was .73.

A nine-item scale measuring the degree to which standards and procedures are imposed top-down and performance is evaluated via superiors' observation of subordinates' behavior. A principal components factor analysis with varimax rotation produced three stable factors representing input, behavior and output control; for behavior control, three items measuring feedback did not consistently discriminate between the three factors and were dropped, and the remaining six items were used. Data on this dependent variable came from the presidents. Responses across executives within a firm indicated interrater agreement.

A twelve-item scale measuring the degree to which performance evaluation and rewards are based on the results achieved. Data on this dependent variable came from the presidents, and interrater reliabilities indicated agreement across executives within each firm.

A seven-item scale measuring the degree of emphasis placed on rigorous staffing procedures and the opportunity provided for subordinate training and development. To distinguish the construct of input control from clan control and socialization, only formal selection and training practices were assessed. Data on this dependent variable came from the presidents.

A six-item Likert scale measuring the extent to which the relationship between subordinates' actions and outcomes can be predicted and observed. The measure was adapted from Ouchi and Maguire (1975), Ouchi (1978), and Thompson (1967), and was collected from vice presidents. Its coefficient alpha was somewhat lower than the conventional .70 level, but interrater reliabilities indicated agreement across executives within a firm.

variable_name: Crystallization of standards of desirable performance
description: A five-item scale measuring the extent to which executives have reliable and valid indexes of desirable performance. The measure was adapted from Ouchi and Maguire (1975), Ouchi (1978), and Thompson (1967), and was collected from vice presidents.

An eleven-item Likert scale adapted from Hambrick (1983) and Snow and Hrebiniak (1980). It positions firms along a continuum ranging from 1 to 7 on which low values represent narrow, stable strategic postures and high values represent broad, varied postures. The data were collected from vice presidents.
scale: 1 to 7. Direction: higher = more prospector (defender to prospector scale)

description: An instrument designed by Van De Ven, Delbecq, and Koenig (1976) to measure Thompson's (1967) three types of work flow integration (independent, sequential, and reciprocal). The three configurations represent increasing levels of technological interdependence. The data were collected from vice presidents.

Firm size was defined as number of full time employees; Standard & Poor's 1986 Directory of Corporate Affiliations provided the data. Following the arguments of Child (1974) and Kimberly (1976) that there is a curvilinear relationship between size and structural complexity, a natural logarithmic transformation of the data was used.

CEOs were asked to consider their personal relationships with outside board members and to indicate (1) how many they considered to be acquaintances but not friends and (2) how many they considered to be friends. Excluding mere acquaintances allowed a more precise measure of perceived friendship. The number of perceived friends was then divided by the total number of outside board members.

variable_name: Portion of board appointed after CEO
description: The portion of a board appointed after a CEO was calculated as the number of outside directors appointed during a CEO's tenure divided by the total number of outside board members. Board composition data were obtained from proxies and director registers.

Board monitoring was assessed with a multi-item scale in the CEO survey. Items asked the extent to which the board monitors top management strategic decision making, formally evaluates the CEO's performance, and defers to the CEO's judgment on final strategic decisions. Possible responses were 1, "minimally"; 2; 3, "moderately"; 4; and 5, "very much so." Items were factor-analyzed with the iterated principal factors method, the monitoring items loaded on a separate factor from the advice items with loadings greater than .5 on one factor and less than .2 on the other, and Cronbach's alpha was .92; factors were estimated using the Bartlett method.

Advice and counsel interactions were assessed with a multi-item scale in the CEO survey. Items asked the extent to which the CEO solicits board assistance in the formulation of corporate strategy, how often directors provided advice and counsel in discussions outside of board or committee meetings, and the extent to which outside directors are a "sounding board" on strategic issues. Possible responses were 1, "minimally"; 2; 3, "moderately"; 4; and 5, "very much so." The items loaded on a separate factor from the monitoring items, and Cronbach's alpha was .88.

CEO ownership was measured as the number of common shares owned by the CEO divided by the total amount of common stock outstanding. This definition captures the extent to which an agency problem exists by measuring the extent to which ownership and control are separated. Data were obtained from proxy statements.

Long-term incentive plan compensation indicated the extent to which CEO compensation was contingent upon the achievement of specific performance goals. It was calculated as the total value of long-term incentive grants made in the year prior to the survey date divided by total compensation in that year.
time_window: year prior to the survey date

description: Return on equity, an accounting-based measure of firm performance, was adjusted for industry differences by subtracting the average value for the firm's primary industry. Performance was measured two years after the survey date.
time_window: two years after the survey date

description: The market-to-book value of equity, a market-based measure, gauges a firm's effectiveness in creating value for shareholders by comparing its market value with the cost of capital contributed by shareholders. The measure was adjusted for industry differences by subtracting the average value for the firm's primary industry and was measured two years after the survey date.
time_window: two years after the survey date

description: Coded as 1 if three criteria are met at the time of a CEO succession: the firm announced a confounding event within +/- 1 day of the CEO succession announcement; the confounding event was completely under the control of the firm; and the confounding event was not intended to clarify and was not causally related to the CEO succession. Two coders read all confounding releases and agreed that 14 releases were intended to clarify or were causally related to the succession, so those successions were not coded as strategic noise. Successions confounded by events not entirely under the firm's control, such as acquisitions or lawsuits, were excluded from all analyses. This left 120 CEO successions, or 20 percent of the sample, coded as strategic noise.
time_window: +/- 1 day around the CEO succession announcement

description: Calculated as the number of years of tenure for the outgoing CEO. The variable was lagged one year in all analyses.

Computed as the log of the difference between the CEO's total direct compensation (tdc1 in Execucomp) and the average total direct compensation of the other listed executives. In a few firms the difference was actually negative; because the measure was logged, negative differences were set to 1. The variable was lagged one year in all analyses.
level: firm (CEO relative to other listed executives)

description: A measure of compounded market returns consisting of a firm's yearly stock returns, assuming reinvestment of dividends, computed as (Pricebeg - Priceend + Dividends)/Pricebeg. The measure was lagged one year in all analyses.

Five indicators of a CEO's firm-level discretion measured over the five years preceding a firm's CEO succession (for instance, 1994-1998 for a 1999 succession): market growth (average annual percentage change in firm sales), demand instability (standard deviation of the annual change in firm sales), research and development intensity (R&D/sales), advertising intensity (advertising/sales), and capital intensity (net value of property, plant, and equipment divided by the number of employees, multiplied by -1). Standardization and summation of these five measures provided an overall measure of firm discretion.
time_window: five years preceding the CEO succession

description: A dummy variable that takes a value of 1 if the newly appointed CEO had previously served as a CEO and 0 otherwise. It was constructed by reading the press release announcing the appointment, searching Execucomp for executive work histories when a biography was not included, and searching Zoominfo.com for executive work histories; if no information was found indicating prior service as a CEO, the individual was coded as 0.

Measured at the time the individual was announced as the new CEO. The information was obtained from Execucomp; for missing values the press release announcing the CEO succession was searched and Internet searches were performed.
time_window: at the time of the CEO announcement

description: Built from the Fortune Most-Admired (FMA) rankings and the Wall Street Journal/Harris Interactive Corporate Reputation (WSJ) list, which were combined because Fortune listed only the top 10 firms in an industry in 1998 and only the top 20 firms between 1999 and 2004. The authors counted the number of times a firm appeared on either list for the five years preceding the sample; 27 of the 143 outside CEO successions involved people hired from firms that appeared on either list in the five years preceding the CEO succession.
scale: count of appearances on either list
time_window: five years preceding the CEO succession

description: A count variable that tallied the cumulative number of years the founder had prior work experience with a product market, geographic market, or resource. It was constructed from the resumes of the founder and founding team together with company information from The Airline Encyclopedia, and is linked to the dependent variable in that each of the seven product markets, nine geographic markets, and seven aircraft classes receives its own value.

Measured by tallying the number of previous jobs that the founder held where he or she had experience with these strategy elements, capturing knowledge acquired by experiencing an element in different organizations. It is linked to the corresponding choice alternative.

A count variable that tallied the time elapsed in years since the founder had work experience with these strategy elements. This variable was then transformed using a power function; the formula is not readable in the text provided.

A count variable that tallied the number of product markets, geographic markets, or resources in which the founder had prior work experience. In the analysis it was entered together with a squared term.

A binary variable set to 1 if the founder and any of the team members had a shared work experience with a product market, geographic market, or resource, otherwise set to 0. It is a team-level variable linked to the corresponding choice alternative.

A binary variable set to 1 if any of the team members had a unique work experience that the founder lacked, otherwise set to 0. It is a team-level variable linked to the corresponding choice alternative.

Binary dependent variable set to 1 if that product market element was selected and 0 otherwise, taken from the operating plans concerning the new carrier contained in the DOT applications; seven distinct product markets were identified. This construction of the dependent variable is characteristic of a conditional logit model.

Binary dependent variable set to 1 if that geographic market element was selected and 0 otherwise, taken from the operating plans concerning the new carrier contained in the DOT applications; nine distinct geographic markets were identified.

Binary dependent variable set to 1 if that class of aircraft was selected and 0 otherwise, with aircraft representing a physical resource; seven distinct classes of aircraft were identified. Aircraft characteristics from the aviation support tables were used to cluster aircraft into categories.

Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 when the firm seeks to undertake one or more divestitures in its host country dyadic partner in a particular year, and 0 otherwise. The divesting modes covered are those that do not require the firm to sell the unit on a stock exchange: leveraged buyout, liquidation, restructuring, privatization, split-off, and sell-off, as per Thomson One's definition of divestiture and bankruptcy acquisition. Divestitures from within the firm's home country are excluded because the authors are interested in cross-border divestitures.

Dummy variable that takes the value of 1 in the year immediately before a firm registers a claim with ICSID against its host country dyadic partner, and in any subsequent year where the claim is still ongoing. Because claims are typically lodged after a dispute has already begun, the authors cross-referenced legal documents and press releases and found that the median point at which disputes begin is two years before a claim is registered, so a firm is coded as being in the 'shadow' of the dispute from the year prior to registration until the year of its conclusion. A firm is only coded as being in the shadow of the dispute if the dispute involves firm-specific policy behavior.
time_window: from the year prior to claim registration until the year of the dispute's conclusion

variable_name: Dispute Against Another Country in Host's Region
description: Constructed in the same manner as Dispute Against Host, except that it takes the value of 1 when the firm is in the shadow of a dispute against another country in the same geopolitical region as its host country dyadic partner. Only disputes that arise due to firm-specific policy behavior are counted. Regions are categorized so that their constituent countries display geographic proximity and broad similarities in political systems and structures, culture, and economics, using a slightly amended version of Hadenius and Teorell's politico-geographic classification of world regions.
time_window: from the year prior to claim registration until the year of the dispute's conclusion

variable_name: Total Disputes Against Host Involving Other Firms (log)
description: The sum of the number of disputes involving firm-specific policy behavior that other firms are involved in with the host country in the dyad, using the same measurement approach as for the other dispute variables to identify the presence of a dispute. Because the variable is heavily skewed and the marginal impact of each additional dispute is expected to diminish as the number of disputes increases, the log of the total disputes against the host country is employed.

variable_name: Reduced barriers to entry, growth, and exit
description: Applicants were coded as treated with reduced barriers to entry if the country of their operations experienced a reduction in the total number of procedures or in the time (in days) required to commence formal operations, including pre-registration, registration, and post-registration procedures. Applicants were coded as treated with reduced barriers to growth if the country increased the ease of obtaining credit from banks and other financial institutions, and with reduced barriers to exit if the country implemented reforms that increased the ease of resolving insolvency, liquidating assets, and recovering the initial investment capital through bankruptcy proceedings. Treatment status was coded based on regulatory changes in an applicant's country of operations in 2017.

Applicants ranked the potential benefits typically associated with entrepreneurial accelerators in terms of how important they are to the venture's development and success. Respondents ranked these benefits on a 1-7 Likert scale, in order of increased importance, and the rankings were reverse-coded so that 1 was the least important and 7 the most important. Separate components captured perceived benefits for network development (e.g., with potential partners and customers), for business skills development, and for securing direct venture funding (e.g., grants or investments).
A dichotomous measure equal to one if an applicant succeeded at being admitted to the accelerator program of choice, and zero otherwise.

variable_name: Average log Revenue, log Employees, and log Patents of selected applicants
description: The quality of selected applicants into each accelerator in each application cycle was measured as the average log Revenue, log Employees, and log Patents for selected applicants.

Log (Revenue + 1) measured the average monthly revenue (in US$) for each applicant at the time of applying to an accelerator, natural log-adjusted to correct for skew. Log (Employees + 1) measured the number of full-time and part-time employees of the start-up at the time of applying, natural log-adjusted for skew. Log (Patents + 1) measured the log of the count of patents related to inventions that the start-up owned or filed to protect at the time of applying.
The count of the total number of applicants per accelerator, computed by summing the total number of applicants to each accelerator per year.

Applicant heterogeneity was constructed by calculating the proportion of previously admitted applicants to the same accelerator that had the same industry/operating focus and stage of development as the applicant. This proportion was scaled to a 0-100 applicant fit score f for each applicant, with 100 denoting the best fit with the accelerator's revealed preferences based on its previously admitted applicants. The applicant heterogeneity measure for each accelerator in an application cycle was then constructed as H equals 100 minus mean f, with 100 denoting high heterogeneity and 0 denoting low heterogeneity.
Measured the combined education of members of the founding team listed on the application, using the sum of individuals' levels of education.
Measured the total number of years of prior work experience of members of the founding team listed on the application, using the sum of founders' years of previous work experience.
A dichotomous variable coded for whether any of the members of the founding team of each start-up applicant were women.

For each firm, the multivariate response is the three-dimensional binary response vector Y' = (PAC contributions, inside lobbyists, outside lobbyists). Each binary variable was set equal to 0 for a firm with no such political activity and set equal to 1 when the activity was present. The ALR model simultaneously estimates the probability of each response and the pairwise log-odds ratios among the responses, which capture the association or combination of tactics.

A binary variable set equal to 0 for a firm with no PAC contributions and set equal to 1 when PAC contributions had been made. The underlying measure is PAC contributions to all congressional candidates in the 1991-92 and 1993-94 elections.

A binary variable set equal to 0 for a firm with no inside lobbyists and set equal to 1 when the firm had inside lobbyists. The underlying measure is the average number of staff members in each firm's Washington office from 1991 to 1994.

A binary variable set equal to 0 for a firm with no outside lobbyists and set equal to 1 when the firm had outside lobbyists. The underlying measure is the average number of outside lobbyists and political consultants retained by each firm from 1991 to 1994.
For each industry, the four-firm concentration ratio, as published in a table, Concentration Ratios in Manufacturing, in the 1992 Census of Manufactures.

For each political activity, the proportions of a firm's competitors within its three-digit SIC code that used PACs, inside lobbying, and outside lobbying during the years 1991-94. The measure indicates for a target firm how many of its rivals engaged in each of the political activities.
For each industry, the percentage of its workforce that was represented by unions, as measured by Curme, Hirsch, and McPherson (1990).

A dummy variable coded 1 (0 otherwise) if a congressional caucus represented an industry during the years 1991-94. The source of this information was the Washington Information Directory (from CQ Press).
The logarithm of a firm's sales, averaged over 1991-94, calculated from COMPUSTAT data.

Free cash flow, averaged over 1991-94, calculated as net income minus income taxes minus gross interest expense on long-term debt minus dividends paid on preferred stock minus dividends paid on common stock.

The log of the dollar amount of Department of Defense Primary Contracts and Department of Defense Research and Development Contracts, divided by firm's total sales, averaged over 1991-94. Sources of these data were two U.S. Department of Defense publications.

Computed as the multiplicative interaction between the alignment scale and the adaptability scale, reflecting the authors' argument that these two capacities are nonsubstitutable and interdependent. Both component scales were rated by senior and middle management respondents and aggregated to the business-unit level. This variable is the authors' measure of contextual ambidexterity.

Senior and middle managers indicated the degree to which they agreed with three statements about the management systems in their organization; scores are means calculated across items after aggregation to the business unit. All items used seven-point Likert-style responses. Two items are worded negatively and were reversed. The items loaded on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 1.75 accounting for 58 percent of the variance, and internal reliability was .73.

Senior and middle management respondents indicated the degree to which they agreed with three statements about the management systems in their organization; scores are means calculated across items after aggregation to the business unit. All items used seven-point Likert-style responses. The items loaded on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 2.29 accounting for 76 percent of the variance, and internal reliability was .80.

Created as the multiplicative interaction of the performance management context variable and the social context variable, reflecting the argument that these should be considered holistically and are nonsubstitutable. This variable constitutes the authors' measure of organizational context. The two component scales were rated by line management and nonmanagement respondents and aggregated to the business-unit level.

Line management and nonmanagement respondents indicated the extent to which systems encouraged people at their level to set challenging/aggressive goals, issue creative challenges to their people instead of narrowly defining tasks, be more focused on getting their job done well than on getting promoted, make a point of stretching their people, reward or punish based on rigorous measurement of business performance against goals, hold people accountable for their performance, and use their appraisal feedback to improve their performance. Scores are means calculated across the seven items after aggregation to the business unit. All items used seven-point Likert-style responses; the items loaded on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 3.77 accounting for 54 percent of the variance, and internal reliability was .89.

Line management and nonmanagement respondents indicated the extent to which systems encouraged people at their level to devote considerable effort to developing their subordinates, give everyone sufficient authority to do their jobs well, push decisions down to the lowest appropriate level, give ready access to information that others need, work hard to develop the capabilities needed to execute the overall strategy/vision, base decisions on facts and analysis rather than politics, treat failure in a good effort as a learning opportunity, be willing and able to take prudent risks, and set realistic goals. Scores are means calculated across the nine items after aggregation to the business unit. All items used seven-point Likert-style responses; the items loaded on a single factor with an eigenvalue of 4.36 accounting for 55 percent of the variance, and internal reliability was .93.

Senior and middle management respondents reflected on performance over the last five years and indicated the degree to which they agreed that the business unit is achieving its full potential, that people at their level are satisfied with the level of business-unit performance, that the business unit does a good job of satisfying its customers, and that it gives them the opportunity and encouragement to do the best work they are capable of. Scores are means calculated across items after aggregation to the business unit, and all items used seven-point Likert-style responses. Principal component analysis produced a single factor with an eigenvalue of 2.56 accounting for 65 percent of the variance, and internal reliability was .80.

A binary variable operationalized with a proxy stemming from the database that measures confidentiality of an idea. From interviews with program management the authors learned that ideas marked as confidential are of strategic value to the company and consequently tend to be ranked as more important by Enco; ideas classified as confidential are considered the most radical because they typically deal with breakthrough technology. The importance of confidential ideas is reflected in the policy that users of the idea database have no access to detailed descriptions of such ideas.

The main dependent variable, a binary variable coded one if an idea generator worked with a team to develop the next idea. It is measured for the idea generator's second idea, the point at which the decision to work with a team or alone is observed.

A binary variable indicating whether an idea generator worked with a team to develop the prior idea. The authors also used it as an additional control variable in models predicting team idea development and to split the sample into idea generators with and without experience in prior team idea development.
A binary variable indicating that a prior idea passed the second stage of the screening process.

A binary variable coded as one when an idea passes the second stage of the screening process, that is, when the idea is selected after the second panel. Passing the second screening panel meant that a serious amount of resources was then allocated to further the execution of an idea, and at this stage an idea turns into a more formal project.

A dummy equal to 1 if there is a forthcoming election in the target country within one year after the acquisition announcement, and 0 otherwise, capturing heightened political uncertainty right before elections. The date, timing (snap or regular), and result of each election for the 43 countries are hand-collected; the primary source is the World Bank's 2012 DPI, supplemented with data from other institutions and web resources. Deals announced in countries with a noncompetitive electoral system (DPI item 'EIEC' below 7) and deals announced during snap elections are removed from the sample.
time_window: one year after the acquisition announcement

description: The target's cumulative abnormal dollar returns minus the acquirer's cumulative abnormal dollar returns over 7 days around the acquisition announcement, all scaled by the sum of the acquirer and target market values in US dollars 50 trading days prior to the announcement. Cumulative abnormal dollar returns are obtained by first estimating each firm's abnormal percentage returns over the 7-day window with a two-factor model using the equity market index for its country and the MSCI World index, then multiplying abnormal percentage returns by the firm's market value of equity on the previous day, and summing the daily dollar returns over the 7 days. A higher value means the target captures a larger share of the acquisition gains relative to the acquirer.
time_window: 7 days around the acquisition announcement; market values 50 trading days prior to the announcement; estimation window Days -280 through -30

description: Abnormal profit r it is the return on sales (ROS) for firm i in period t minus the industry average ROS. Return on sales is the firm's income relative to its revenues as reported in the ICC Form M annual reports. In the persistence model the lagged value of abnormal ROS is the key regressor, and the analysis of persistence is run on the subsample of superior performing firms (abnormal profits greater than zero).

The persistence rate is the coefficient on the lagged dependent variable in a first order autoregressive model of abnormal ROS, estimated separately for each cohort and defined as the percentage of total abnormal profits in any period before t that remain in period t. A value greater than zero and less than 1 suggests persistence of abnormal profits, a value less than zero and greater than (-1) indicates convergence, and a positive rate small in magnitude means the advantage is more transient. Persistence rates of the Entrant and Incumbent cohorts are compared with a modified Wald statistic.

Firms are classified into three cohorts: Incumbents (firms that entered before the institutional change and continue to compete in the new environment), All entrants (all firms that started up in the industry after the institutional change) and Early entrants (the set of firms that entered the trucking industry during the first four years following the change, 1981-1984). The persistence model is estimated separately for each cohort, and the Entrant and Incumbent cohorts are then compared.
time_window: entry years 1981-1984 define the Early entrant cohort

description: An indicator variable set to 1 in weeks 9 through 18, the period of greatest ambiguity, and 0 otherwise. The onset of heightened ambiguity was placed at week 9, when the CEO released the first of several communications providing details of the new organizational structure, and it ended at week 18, by which time all changes to the organizational structure had been made, key positions filled, and departing employees exited.

A time-varying indicator variable set to 1 when the two members of a dyad belonged to the same department, and 0 otherwise. It was used to identify network contacts with a strong formal component to the relationship.

A two-step measure built from the roster of email distribution lists. First, a time-varying count in week t of the lists shared by i and j, divided by the sum of the lists i belonged to and the lists j belonged to, a measure that could range from 0 for dyads with no shared lists to 0.5 for dyads with fully overlapping lists. Second, an indicator variable set to 1 for dyads that were above the mean in a given week on this shared-affiliation measure.
scale: indicator derived from a measure ranging 0 to 0.5

description: An indicator variable set to 1 for dyads that did not have a significant formal tie, did not have a strong semiformal tie, and nevertheless had contact with one another in weeks 1, 2, or 3. Because weeks 1-3 were used to define it, those weeks were excluded from all analyses in which the variable was used.

A time-varying count of one-to-one messages sent in a given week from focal actor i to a colleague j, where j was also an extended leadership team member. Mass emails and communications sent to distribution lists were eliminated, and messages that appeared to be sent automatically, for example those containing 'Out of Office' in the subject line, were identified and removed. The test of Hypothesis 1 uses this count for dyads that had a formal tie and no, or a limited, semiformal component.

A time-varying count of one-to-one messages sent in a given week from focal actor i to a colleague j, where j was also an extended leadership team member, with mass emails, distribution-list messages, and automatically sent messages removed. The test of Hypothesis 2 uses this count for dyads that had a significant semiformal component and no, or a limited, formal component.

A time-varying count of one-to-one messages sent in a given week from focal actor i to a colleague j, where j was also an extended leadership team member, with mass emails, distribution-list messages, and automatically sent messages removed. The test of Hypothesis 3 uses this count for dyads defined as informal ties, so weeks 1-3 are excluded.

Calculated by taking the fractionalization index of the subgroups within Islam, i.e., one minus the Herfindahl index of religious group shares. The World Religion Dataset identifies seven branches within Islam: Sunni, Shia, Ibadhi, Nation of Islam, Alawite, Ahmadiyya, and other.

Calculated by taking the fractionalization index of the subgroups within Islam, i.e., one minus the Herfindahl index of religious group shares. The World Religion Dataset identifies seven branches within Islam: Sunni, Shia, Ibadhi, Nation of Islam, Alawite, Ahmadiyya, and other.

variable_name: Founding rates of Islamic investment funds
description: Number of newly started Islamic investment funds per country year. Used to measure the entrepreneurial supply of Islamic investment funds in a country; the authors follow previous studies on new venture creations to model the founding of Islamic investment funds as the number of newly started funds per country year.

variable_name: Assets managed by Islamic investment funds
description: Logged assets under management. The measure captures the amount of pooled savings from investors, and as Islamic investing is still highly domestic, it proxies for the demand for Islamic investment funds in a given country. The original value of assets under management was highly skewed, so the authors applied a natural log transformation.

Average level of business freedom, trade freedom, property rights, and investment freedom from the Heritage Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom. The authors exclude other economic freedom indicators such as fiscal freedom and government size, consistent with conceptualizations of market logic and avoiding confounding with the state logic measure.

Average level of business freedom, trade freedom, property rights, and investment freedom from the Heritage Foundation's Index of Economic Freedom. The authors exclude other economic freedom indicators such as fiscal freedom and government size, consistent with conceptualizations of market logic and avoiding confounding with the state logic measure.
Percentage of government expenditure in GDP, obtained from the World Bank. The share of government expenditure in an economy is a measure of the state's influence.
Percentage of government expenditure in GDP, obtained from the World Bank. The share of government expenditure in an economy is a measure of the state's influence.

The authors adopt nine items in the BEEPS questionnaire asking whether government officials requested informal payments or gifts for electricity, water, telecommunications, compulsory certification, permits, tax inspections, construction permits, import licenses, and operation licenses for the last two years. They sum the instances of bribery requests from the nine items and build a variable of the frequency, which can range from zero to nine. Because each bribery request may accompany repeated and frequent interactions between government officials and firms, the increase in bribery requests represents the increase in bribery relationships.

The variable Firm sales growth rate was constructed by calculating the ratio of last year's sales over the sales of three years ago, with sales amounts obtained from two BEEPS questions. The firm sales growth rate is highly skewed, so the variable was log-transformed. It is used as the dependent variable because sales growth is the most imminent and critical goal for firms and a performance measure necessary for survival.
time_window: last year's sales over the sales of three years ago

description: A dummy variable that takes the value of one if the firm introduced new products or services and invested in research and development, and zero otherwise. The condition of research and development investment was included to refine New product to represent 'new products or services with significant features' because the concept of new products or services was overly broad in the BEEPS data. Two BEEPS items are used: whether the firm had introduced new products in the last three years and whether the firm had invested in research and development.

Measured with an item in the BEEPS questionnaire asking about the likelihood of corruption: whether it is always, usually, frequently, sometimes, seldom or never true that it is common for firms in the respondent's line of business to have to pay some irregular 'additional payments or gifts' to get things done with regard to customs, taxes, licenses, regulations, services, etc. The response to this question is used because the item is in line with the concept of the pervasiveness of corruption. The variable has values from 1 (not pervasive) to 6 (strongly pervasive).

Indicators of governance provided by WGI are used to measure the quality of governance for the sample countries. WGI provides six dimensions of governance indexes as estimated values with ranges from approximately -2.5 (weak) to 2.5 (strong). Quality of governance is measured using the average of those six indicators by country and year.

A four-item, five-point scale assessing respondents' perceptions of the rate of product obsolescence, the rate of technological change, their ability to forecast consumer tastes, and the extent of R&D in their industries. The items were derived from environmental perception scales used by Covin and Slevin (1989). The alpha coefficient for the scale was .73.
scale: four items on a five-point scale

description: Respondents were asked to circle the number of times their firm had used technology alliances for process research and development and for product research and development, on a scale ranging from 0 to over 5. From this question three measures were created: technology alliance use-product R&D, technology alliance use-process R&D, and technology alliance use-general. Each of these variables was coded dichotomously (0 = not used, 1 = used one or more times), and the general variable was coded 1 if the firm used technology alliances for either product or process R&D.

The respondent for each firm was asked whether his or her firm pursued equity investments either from other small-to-medium-sized companies or from large firms in its alliance formation. The variable was coded dichotomously (0 = no, 1 = yes). Separate models were estimated for the product R&D, process R&D, and general technology alliance samples.
level: firm (within the subsample that used technology alliances)

description: Hofstede's (1980) index of uncertainty avoidance, used for the country in which each SME is located. Hofstede standardized each measure to range from approximately 0 to 100. Mexico exhibits a high degree of uncertainty avoidance, whereas Sweden has a high tolerance for uncertainty, with Norway, Australia, and Indonesia falling between these two extremes.

Hofstede's (1980) index of masculinity, used for the country in which each SME is located. Hofstede standardized each measure to range from approximately 0 to 100. Mexico and Australia are the most masculine of the countries in the sample, whereas the Swedish and Norwegian cultures are the most feminine.

Hofstede's (1980) index of individualism, used for the country in which each SME is located. Hofstede standardized each measure to range from approximately 0 to 100. Australia exhibits a high level of individualism, Mexico and Indonesia are toward the collectivism end of the spectrum, and Sweden and Norway are slightly less individualistic than Australia.

Business descriptions from the Description of Business section (Item 1) of firms' 10-K filings were converted into 768-dimensional numerical vectors using the pretrained Sentence Transformer model all-mpnet-base-v2. Cosine similarity was then used to quantify the degree of similarity between each pair of vectorized business descriptions. For each focal firm the authors calculated the cosine similarity between its vector and that of all exemplar firms in its industry and used the highest cosine similarity, i.e., the similarity with the nearest exemplar, as the measure. A firm was classified as an exemplar if a composite score, formed by summing the normalized values of analyst coverage and analyst recommendations, exceeded one standard deviation above the average of all other firms within the same primary industry in a given year.
time_window: year t (explanatory variable, with dependent variables at t+1)

description: The number of analysts who actively follow a specific firm in a given year. To determine whether an analyst follows a firm, the authors identified analysts who issued fiscal year-end earnings forecasts for the firm. In cases where no analysts issued an earnings forecast for a particular firm in a given year, the coverage was assumed to be zero.
time_window: year t+1 (dependent variable, one-year lag from predictors)

description: Consensus recommendation data available in IBES's Recommendations Summary database. IBES standardized analyst recommendations into five discrete categories, ranging from 'strong buy' to 'strong sell,' with each category assigned a numerical value between one and five. The authors reverse-coded these numerical assignments, associating higher numerical recommendation values with more positive investment recommendations, so that a recommendation value of five indicates a strong buy in their coding scheme.
time_window: year t+1 (dependent variable, one-year lag from predictors)

description: The average document vector for each industry by year was computed by taking the average of the vectorized business descriptions of all firms within the industry for that year. The similarity between each firm's document vector and its primary industry's average vector for the same year was then calculated using cosine similarity; this measure is referred to as firm typicality. Category coherence is the average typicality of all firms within an industry in a given year, so that high category coherence indicates greater similarity among firms within the industry and low coherence indicates greater diversity and deviation from the industry average.

Using the average vector for each industry per year, the authors assessed the cosine similarity between each focal industry and all other industries within the same broader sector (2-digit NAICS code) and year. The resulting similarity measures for each industry and year were averaged to calculate category distinctiveness, and the resulting variable was multiplied by -1 so that higher values indicate greater category distinctiveness and reduced similarity with neighboring categories within the sector.

The authors used the firm typicality variable, computed as the cosine similarity between a firm's document vector and its primary industry's average vector for the same year, and identified the typicality value for the most similar exemplar to the focal firm each year.

Operationalized as the focal index proposed by Ziedonis (2007), which captures the degree of correspondence between the firm's core technologies and the licensed technology. It is computed as the citation-weighted sum of the licensor's patents applied for within six years of the date the license agreement became effective and belonging to the same primary patent class as the licensed technology, divided by the sum of all citation-weighted patents issued to the licensor applied for by that date. The index ranges between 0 and 1, where 1 indicates that the technology is a core technology and that there is complete correspondence between the primary patent class of the licensed technology and the licensor's technologies. The printed formula was not readable in the payload and was not reconstructed.
time_window: patents applied for within six years of the date of the license agreement

description: The same Ziedonis (2007) index described for the licensor, calculated separately for the licensee: the citation-weighted sum of the licensee's patents applied for within six years of the license agreement date that belong to the same primary patent class as the licensed technology, divided by the sum of all citation-weighted patents issued to the licensee applied for by that date. It ranges between 0 and 1, where 1 indicates that the technology is a core technology of the licensee. The printed formula was not readable in the payload and was not reconstructed.
time_window: patents applied for within six years of the date of the license agreement

description: Computed using the age of the backward citations in the licensed patents: the average age in months of all the backward citations in each patent, based on the date of application of the backward citation and the date of the focal patent application. The rationale is that the more recent the knowledge used to create a new technology, the greater the related uncertainty; the authors therefore invert the variable by multiplying the average age of the backward citations in the focal patent by (-1).
scale: months (average age of backward citations, inverted)

description: A dummy for whether or not the contract attached to the transfer of a technology includes a grant-back clause. The authors scrutinized the contracts for indications of a grant-back clause; some contracts refer explicitly to a grant-back clause, others indicate that the licensor has the rights to any improvements to the licensed technology by the licensee, and both descriptions are interpreted as expressing contractual agreement to a grant-back clause. The variable takes the value 0 for a licensed technology without the grant-back clause and 1 for a licensed technology with the grant-back clause.
level: licensing contract attached to a licensed technology

description: Dummy variable denoting that at least one member of the founding team had a direct business or social relationship with a venture investor prior to the founding of the firm. It does not necessarily indicate a pre-established tie to the specific investor who funded the venture. The variable was coded 1 only when a second information source confirmed that the relationship existed prior to the time of firm founding; in the modal case the two sources were interviews with a company founder and the TLO archives.

Dummy variable denoting whether at least one member of the founding team had a business or social tie to a third party who had a direct tie with a venture capitalist or angel investor prior to the founding of the firm. As in the case of direct ties, documentation from at least two information sources was required to code this variable in the affirmative. Ties created by TLO officers are excluded because they are likely invariant across firms in the sample.

The modelled event is the first occurrence of financing from a VC firm; the waiting time clock in the firm event histories turns on at the time of incorporation. The hazard of receiving venture financing is estimated in a separate set of regressions from the IPO and failure models and is specified with the piecewise-exponential functional form. Although data on angel financings are available, the regressions are limited to the first occurrence of financing from a VC firm.

variable_name: cumulative amount of venture financing received
description: An annually updated, cumulative total of the amount of venture financing received by each firm, included in the models of IPO and failure. The authors state that they include it reflecting their expectation that firms with more funding are able to quickly progress through the development process and are more likely to IPO.

The modelled event is an initial sale of securities on the public equity markets. IPO and failure are treated as competing risks and are modelled with the approach discussed in Kalbfleisch and Prentice (1980); these events are terminal in the sense that the occurrence of either obviates the possibility that the other transition will take place within the observation window. All firms are observed from the time of incorporation until a performance outcome is recorded or until right censoring at the end of calendar 1996.

The modelled event is firm failure, estimated as a competing risk with the IPO so that an organization exits the risk set after experiencing either event. The waiting time clock turns on at the time of incorporation and firms are observed until an event is recorded or until the observation is right censored at the end of calendar 1996. Twenty-two acquired firms were handled by censoring their event histories at the time of the deal.
Dummy variable coded 1 if at least one member of the founding team had previous experience in the new firm's industry.
Dummy variable coded 1 if at least one member of the founding team had previously launched a new company.
The number of MIT patents that were licensed to the new venture at founding; many of the firms in the sample license more than one MIT-assigned patent.
Indicates whether the new venture has an exclusive right to use MIT technology in a particular field of use.

variable_name: highest university rank of an inventor
description: The highest university rank achieved by any member of the team of inventors that created the technology licensed by the firm, used as a proxy for the status and depth of knowledge of the MIT inventors on whose knowledge the venture is based. The variable is coded student = 0, research associate = 1, assistant professor = 2, untenured associate = 3, tenured associate = 4, full professor = 5, department chair or research center director = 6, and institute professor = 7.

variable_name: size of industry, year of founding
description: The total value of shipments in the industry each organization enters, measured in the year that the new venture is founded and obtained from the Census of Manufacturers. The variable is measured in the year of founding and is not updated over time.

The Levin et al. (1987) measure of patent effectiveness, obtained from a survey of R&D managers, which gauges the extent to which patents are perceived to be successful at protecting intellectual property. It is used to capture the heterogeneity across industries in the strength of intellectual property protection afforded by patents.

Derived from the annual prestige ranking published by Vault.com, which surveys professionals in the industry and asks them to rate the prestige of the firms that they are familiar with (excluding the firm where they work) on a scale of 1-10; the average of the scores is calculated and firms are ranked from 1 (the most prestigious) to 50 (least prestigious). The ranks were reversed by calculating the difference between each rank and 50, so that increases in the status variable correspond to increases in organizational status. Because of the high persistence of status, each firm is assigned a single measure across all years in the sample, measured as the highest ranking that the bank achieved between 2001 and 2009.
scale: reversed rank (difference between the rank and 50)

description: Respondents' self-reports of their approximate annual earnings in their first year in each of the job spells that they reported. Because of the skewed nature of the pay variable, the authors use natural logarithms. Jobs outside the United States were dropped because reported pay may be in a currency other than U.S. dollars, and observations with missing pay data were excluded.
time_window: first year in each job spell

description: The survey asked respondents about their title within each job that they held, and these titles were coded to create a consistent rank across the various jobs; interviews suggested that the progression of job ranks was often similar across investment banks. Because the data consist of post-MBA jobs, the lowest rank graduates are hired into is the associate-level position, assigned a numerical value of 1, with 9 for senior executives, giving a variable that ranges from 1 (low) to 8 (high) in the final sample. Coding was tailored for some of the largest banks using a survey of current students about the titles in their former employers, and the hierarchy was validated by regressing pay on rank.

Measure of how far workers have advanced in their careers, interacted with employer status in the pay models. The authors report that when post-MBA experience equals 0 the estimated effect of one unit of status on log pay is negative and insignificant, and that pay rises more quickly in high status firms as experience increases.

A Deep Neural Net classifier produces a continuous percentage score from 0 to 1 indicating the model's confidence that the CEO is deceptive on the earnings call, based on the similarity of the speaker's linguistic patterns to those of known fraudulent individuals; lower scores imply honesty, higher ones suggest potential deception. Twenty-two linguistic features were processed through two hidden layers with 22 nodes each. The algorithm was trained on transcripts of firms charged in SEC AAERs describing fraudulent misconduct, matched with firms with no evidence of detected deception, and then applied to the study transcripts, none of which were used to train or evaluate the algorithm.
A running average of the CEO's deception score throughout their tenure. The measure reflects the CEO's average deception score prior to the conference call of interest and ranges between 0 and 1.
time_window: CEO's tenure prior to the focal conference call

description: Coded 1 for analysts recognized by Institutional Investor as a top analyst in a given year, regardless of region, and 0 otherwise. Institutional Investor conducts an annual worldwide survey of money managers to assess the best analysts in each region (America, Europe, Asia, and Latin America) and publishes its list of top analysts by region.

Analyst recommendations scored from 1 (Strong Sell) to 5 (Strong Buy). Recommendations were collected 3 days after each conference call, a window where the bulk of revisions typically occur. A recommendation was considered inactive and removed from the model if it had not been updated within the preceding 24 months.

A dummy variable (1/0) that identifies family firms. Firms were classified as family controlled when a family holds more than 50% of the shares of the firm and at least two board members share the same last name. In cases in which ownership data were missing, firms were identified as family firms when family board members comprised 20% or more of the board.

A composite index adapted from Le Breton-Miller et al. (2011) to the private firm context, measured as the sum of three ratios: (1) the annual investment in capital equipment and research and development expressed as a percentage of fixed assets; (2) the inverse of the dividend payout ratio (1 minus total dividends as a percentage of earnings); and (3) risk tolerance, the coefficient of variation of a firm's earnings before interest, taxes, depreciations, and amortizations. All variables were standardized and summed to create a composite index of financial stewardship.

Total labor-related expenses in a given firm-year divided by the total number of hours worked in the same firm-year. Total labor-related expenses include salaries and other costs insofar as they are part of an employment contract, such as direct social benefits, social insurance contributions, and bonuses granted as part of an employment contract. Compensation was measured in euros and corrected for inflation because Belgian compensation is tied to overall inflation, using the GDP deflator for 1996 in all models.

The total net costs (in thousands of euros) a firm spends on training during a given year divided by the total number of employees (measured as full-time equivalents). The social balance sheets report the net training costs payable by the employer, that is, the salaries and social contributions for employees in training, as well as education and registration fees, costs for teaching materials, and transportation costs, less subsidies from local and federal governments and/or European Union financial support. Off-site training excludes initiatives directly related to the task and workplace of the employee, such as coaching, training through rotation, and in-house workshops.
The number of employees (full-time equivalents) who were dismissed by the firm during a given firm-year divided by the number of employees (full-time equivalents) at the start of that firm-year.
The number of employees (full-time equivalents) who voluntarily left the firm during a given firm-year divided by the number of employees (full-time equivalents) at the start of that firm-year.

Value added for the year divided by the average number of employees (full-time equivalents) during that year. Value added is the firm's total revenue minus its costs of nonlabor inputs. The variable was log transformed to correct for its skewed distribution. The authors prefer this measure to the ratio of firm sales to number of employees because the latter does not control for potential increases in nonlabor costs that may accompany revenue generation.

Specified as (value added - wages - salaries)/(value of sales) for 1996, and hence highly associated with the firm's gross margin. The authors state that the PCM represents the proportional difference between output price per unit and the marginal cost of producing an additional unit, so that a high value reflects the firm's ability to elevate price above costs and/or lessen average costs. PCM was used because appropriate data to compute rate of return measures such as return on investment or return on assets were not available.

variable_name: strategy type variables (dummy and effects coding)
description: For each of the three generic strategy dimensions the authors identify the highest, middle, and lowest thirds of the observed values within each plant's respective 4-digit industry, giving 27 possible strategy combinations. Using dummy and effects coding schemes they define 11 variables to examine the performance outcomes of 12 distinct strategy types: three pure strategies, seven hybrid strategies, and the 'stuck-in-the-middle' group, with the remaining combinations forming the 'no strategy' reference group. In dummy coding each coefficient contrasts the group with the 'no strategy' reference group; in effects coding the contrast is between the group and the remaining groups.
scale: categorical (low, medium, high on each of three dimensions)
time_window: 1995 (all strategy measures specified as 1-year lags prior to 1996)

variable_name: number of generic dimensions distinctively emphasized
description: Not entered as a separate continuous variable; it is represented by the classification of hybrid strategy types according to how many generic dimensions they emphasize distinctively: three (COST + ADV + TECH), two (COST + ADV, COST + TECH, ADV + TECH), or one with average or low emphasis on the others (COST + OTHER, ADV + OTHER, TECH + OTHER).

The low cost dimension is approximated using a measure of employee productivity, i.e., value added per employee; high values of this measure signify success in cost efficiency and hence a realized low cost position. Within each plant's 4-digit industry, the highest, middle, and lowest thirds of the observed values define high, medium, and low scores on the dimension.

The marketing differentiation dimension is gauged using advertising intensity, i.e., the ratio of advertising expenditures to revenues. The highest, middle, and lowest thirds of the observed values within the plant's 4-digit industry define high, medium, and low scores on this dimension.

The technology differentiation dimension is expressed using technology intensity, i.e., the ratio of investment in new equipment to revenues. The highest, middle, and lowest thirds of the observed values within the plant's 4-digit industry define high, medium, and low scores on this dimension.

Concentration, measuring the number and size distribution of firms in each industry, was gauged by the well-known Herfindahl index based on the domestic sales of industry incumbents, i.e., excluding exports. Industry-level data are computed at the 4-digit SIC level.

Entry barriers were represented using four measures: product differentiation, measured as the industry-wide advertising intensity (ratio of total industry advertising to industry total shipments); cost efficiency, measured as industry value added per total number of employees; capital intensity, operationalized as the industry capital over sales ratio, with fuel and electricity expenditures used as a proxy for capital because capital figures were not available; and technology intensity, gauged using industry-wide investment in new equipment as a proportion of revenues.

Industry growth was operationalized in terms of industry sales, specified as the rate of increase in total industry shipments between 1995 and 1996; the authors note that this variable also reflects general macroeconomic conditions.

The price-cost margin lagged one year (1995), included in the extended model as a proxy for firm resources and capabilities and for variables omitted from the model. Within the partial adjustment interpretation, its coefficient implies an adjustment coefficient a of 1 minus 0.698, indicating that Greek firms' profitability adjusted by 30 percent to its targeted level from 1995 to 1996.

The board's cumulative experience with any CEO hiring decision, averaged across directors. A director's experience with CEO hiring is mapped on individual boards and carried forward to the focal CEO succession to a date immediately before the focal CEO's start date. For example, if a CEO's effective start date was December 15, all of the board's prior CEO succession experiences up to November 30 are used.
scale: count of prior CEO hiring experiences per director, averaged over the board
time_window: month prior to the effective CEO succession date

description: The estimation technique predicts annual firm performance in return on assets (ROA) using several contextual variables, including the year, industry performance, the firm's condition when the CEO took over, and the firm's market-to-book value ratio. The unexplained variance in ROA becomes the dependent variable in a new regression with fixed-effect variables for individual CEOs, where the regression coefficients indicate each CEO's distinct impact on firm performance after controlling for other factors. CEO performance scores are calculated based on a CEO's full tenure.

variable_name: experience with hiring after an involuntary transition / experience with hiring after a voluntary transition
description: A director was coded as having experience with CEO selection after a dismissal if they had previously served on a board where they had hired a new CEO after the prior CEO departed involuntarily. The board's average cumulative experience with CEO selection is calculated in both contexts, following an involuntary turnover and following a voluntary departure, using the classification of voluntary and involuntary departures from the CEO Dismissal Dataset and excluding cases involving mergers or interim CEOs. These variables reflect the same underlying experience measure used in H1, disaggregated by transition type and modeled separately. A second test interacts the nature of the current CEO's departure (voluntary or involuntary) with the board's context-specific hiring experience.
scale: count of context-specific prior CEO hiring experiences, averaged over the board
time_window: month prior to the effective CEO succession date

variable_name: firm-level strategic similarity / industry strategic similarity
description: Using the measure of strategic distinctiveness by Crossland et al. (2014), the measure is, for each director, the difference between the strategic distinctiveness of the director's other board seats and the strategic distinctiveness of the focal firm, reverse coded to ease interpretation and averaged first over the director and then over the board. Industry-level similarity looks at a director's experience at other boards in industries with levels of managerial discretion similar to those of the focal firm; the difference between the focal firm's industry similarity and the director's other board seats is averaged first across directors and then across the board. Each similarity variable is multiplied by cumulative experience with hiring to create an interaction term.
time_window: month prior to the effective CEO succession date

description: A Herfindahl measure of the breadth of strategic attention across 13 categories of strategic issue, based on the proportion of words or phrases associated with each strategic issue in a quarterly earnings call, adjusted for the size of the relevant strategy issue dictionary. The authors subtract the typical Herfindahl measure from 1 so that larger values are equivalent to a greater breadth of strategic attention. Counts of the words associated with each strategic issue were produced with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count software from the prepared statements by the top management team and executives' responses to analyst questions; any text pertaining to analysts' questions and commentary was excluded. To convert the variable from a quarterly to an annual measure, the authors calculated the mean value over a fiscal year, which represents strategic breadth.
time_window: quarterly calls 2008-2015, averaged over a fiscal year

description: Firms' return on assets (ROA) from Compustat, winsorized at the 1% level, used as the dependent variable. The authors report that the winsorized dependent variable ROA is continuous and normally distributed, which is why OLS regression is used.

Estimated at the industry level (four-digit GICS code) as the five-year revenue growth of an industry, estimated through a regression of annual revenues versus year, divided by the mean five-year value of revenues for firms within the relevant industry over the same time period. It is not lagged, to reflect current market conditions.

The rolling five-year average ROA for all firms in each industry, estimated at the four-digit GICS code level, providing an indication of the average profitability of the available opportunities within an industry at a point in time. It is not lagged, to reflect current market conditions.

The one-year lagged value of a firm's ROA, used to assess the firm's recent effectiveness in converting currently available opportunities into robust performance. The authors argue that managers can observe their firms' prior performance more readily than they can directly compare their firms' capabilities with external opportunities.

Firm annual revenues divided by average current assets in each relevant year, lagged one year. The authors use it because it is readily observable by managers and indicates the efficiency of a firm's usage of its current assets such as cash.

Trait positive affect was measured with the highly reliable and valid 11-item Well-Being Scale from the Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire, converted from a true-or-false format to a 7-point Likert-type scale. The scale mean was 5.48 and the Cronbach alpha reliability was .87.

variable_name: Mean level trait PA of the TMT
description: Group-level trait positive affect was calculated as the average of the team members' trait PA scores, including the CEO. The mean was 5.51 (s.d. = .37).

Following Tsui and O'Reilly (1989), each top management team member's relational demography score, his or her affective dissimilarity from the rest of the senior management team, was computed with the Euclidean distance formula, which compares the respondent's own score on dispositional affect with each of the other top management team members' scores. The printed formula in the text is garbled in this version of the paper. The mean trait PA relational demography score for the entire top management team, including the CEO, was 1.01.

Group-level affective diversity was measured with the standard deviation of the top management team's trait PA instead of the often used coefficient of variation, because trait PA was measured on an interval rather than a ratio scale.

variable_name: Difference between CEO and individual team members' PA
description: Each CEO's trait PA relational demography score was used separately as the predictor variable for affective diversity when examining the CEO's participative decision-making style, that is, the CEO's affective dissimilarity from the other team members. The mean trait PA relational demography score for the CEOs was .94.

Team members answered three questions on how satisfied they were with (1) the way they were treated by other members of the top management team, (2) the way they were treated by the CEO, and (3) the interpersonal relations between top management team members. Each item was rated from 1 (very dissatisfied) through 7 (very satisfied); the scale is the mean of the three items (mean 5.55, Cronbach alpha .73).

Team members answered two questions: (1) 'I feel I have a great deal of influence on the CEO regarding decisions within my area of responsibility' and (2) 'I feel I have a great deal of influence on decisions made by the top management team.' Items were assessed on a scale of 1 (Strongly Disagree) through 7 (Strongly Agree); the mean was 5.86 and the Cronbach alpha was .70.

Measured with Jehn's (1995) conflict scale using three items asking about differences of opinions in the top management team, team disagreement about work being done, and the general degree of task conflict in the top management team. For each company the mean of the senior managers' perceptions was used as the group-level score (mean 3.54, Cronbach alpha .73).

Measured through a four-item scale that asked about personality clashes in the top management team, degree of anger, degree of friction, and the general amount of emotional conflict in the top management team. The mean of each team's emotional conflict score was used as the group-level score (mean 3.42, Cronbach alpha .93).

A seven-item scale combining two scales. The first consisted of four items, two of them reverse coded, and the second consisted of three statements. Items were scored from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree); the team mean was used (mean 5.26, Cronbach alpha .82).

variable_name: CEO participative vs. autocratic decision-making style
description: Top management team members rated the degree of participativeness of their CEO when dealing with 17 organizational issues, using a 5-point response scale adapted from Heller (1971) that runs from 1 (CEO makes the decision alone without a detailed explanation to the TMT) to 5 (the CEO delegates the decision-making responsibility to the top management team). The five responses were recoded using the weighted scale 0, 1, 5, 8, and 10 as recommended by Vroom and Yetton (1973), the mean of the weighted 17 items was calculated for each senior manager's assessment (Cronbach alpha .90), and the ratings were aggregated across each group's top management team members to form a group-level score for each CEO (mean 5.90, s.d. 1.18 on a 1-10 scale).

Information on financial performance for the public companies in the sample was obtained from the COMPUSTAT industrial file and the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP). The variable used to measure financial performance was the logged annual market-adjusted return, averaged across each year that the entire top management team (including the CEO) worked together; market-adjusted returns are the company's stock returns minus the return on a value-weighted market index.
time_window: averaged across each year the entire top management team worked together

description: Each CEO's liberal versus conservative political preferences, measured by a validated index of the CEO's political contributions to the two major political parties (Democratic and Republican). Following Chin, Hambrick, and Trevin'o (2013), the index combines four indicators of political liberalism: (1) proportion of the number of donations to the Democratic Party to the number of donations to both parties, (2) proportion of the amount of donations to the Democratic Party to the amount of donations to both parties, (3) proportion of the number of years the individual donated to the Democratic Party to the number of years he or she donated to either party, and (4) proportion of the number of unique recipients of the Democratic Party to the total number of unique political donation recipients of both parties (Cronbach's alpha = .96). Donations during the prior ten years were used to code liberalism for the focal year, and the four indicators were averaged into a composite index ranging from 0 (high conservatism) to 1 (high liberalism).
time_window: prior ten years, coded for the focal year

description: A measure of CEO conservatism created by subtracting the liberalism score from one, so that lower scores indicate liberalism. It was created to make interpreting the results on downsizing easier and is used in the models predicting downsizing.
scale: 0 to 1; lower values imply CEO liberalism
time_window: prior ten years, coded for the focal year

description: Firms' CSR profiles compiled by KLD. Following Hillman and Keim (2001), KLD binary items from five CSR categories were included: community relations, employee relations, diversity, product quality, and natural environment.
