A net score for each category was created by aggregating the summed strengths minus the summed concerns, and the standardized scores of each of the five categories were averaged to compute an annual composite CSR score for each firm.

Firms' downsizing activities identified with a triangulated approach. Using Compustat, the authors computed the net percentage difference in employees between two successive years; for all firm-years with a net decline in total employee count, they manually searched media articles and company press releases in Factiva for announcements of personnel reductions, carefully reading articles to exclude job reductions that were byproducts of other intended strategies such as mergers and acquisitions, strategic alliances, and spinoffs. This yielded 214 stand-alone downsizing events, and because the variable was significantly skewed the authors added 1 to all observations and took the natural log.

CEO narcissism measured by the video-metric approach, which is rooted in the ''thin slice'' psychological measurement approach. Six student raters trained in psychology and allied disciplines and blind to the study's hypotheses rated the videos; each video was rated by three raters using a version of the Narcissistic Personality Inventory (NPI-16) adapted for third-party ratings. Videos created for other purposes were collected from publicly available sources and edited to exclude identifying information such as company name, logo, and banners, and a minimum duration of 2.5 minutes was specified; the multistep procedure yielded usable videos for 302 CEOs. The measure exhibited high inter-item reliability (alpha = .87) and interrater convergence, and temporal stability was assessed for a randomly selected subsample of 30 CEOs rated on an additional video.

CEO extraversion measured by the video-metric approach. Three raters independently rated each CEO on a 12-item adjectives-based scale of extraversion adapted from the Gough Adjective Checklist, which captures the extraversion dimension of the established NEO-PI-R personality inventory (e.g., jolly, sociable, active). The measure exhibited high inter-item reliability (alpha = .90) and interrater convergence, and temporal stability was assessed for a randomly selected subsample of 30 CEOs rated on an additional video.

A six-item scale developed by the authors because an appropriate scale for structural differentiation was not available. It taps into the extent that organizations segment their organizational system into spatially dispersed units, each of which tends to develop a particular attribute in relation to its relevant environmental requirements, and captures aspects of differences across units such as different mindsets, time orientations, functions, and product/market domains. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.78.

Measured with a two-step approach. Executive directors first provided information on the level of exploratory and exploitative innovation, and ambidexterity was then measured by adding exploratory and exploitative innovation. The additive model was chosen after Edwards's (1994) procedure showed it was superior to the subtractive model and to the multiplicative model, with no significant loss of information compared with the unconstrained model.

A four-item measure adapted from Collins and Clark (2003). It refers to the extent to which senior management team incentives, such as bonuses and profit sharing, were tied to overall firm performance. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.76.

A four-item measure adapted from prior studies (O'Reilly et al. 1989, Smith et al. 1994). It captures the attraction to senior management members, satisfaction, and social interaction among team members. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.73.

A five-item scale based on Hage and Aiken (1967) and Gupta and Govindarajan (2000). It captures the extent to which firms use cross-functional boundary-spanning integration mechanisms, such as cross-functional teams, projects, and liaison personnel. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.72.

A four-item scale adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993). It refers to the extent to which employees were networked to various levels of the hierarchy in their organization. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.74.

A four-item scale adapted from Jansen et al. (2006) that captures the extent to which organizations depart from existing knowledge and pursue radical innovations for emerging customers or markets. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.86.

A four-item scale adapted from Jansen et al. (2006) that captures the extent to which organizations build on existing knowledge and pursue incremental innovations that meet the needs of existing customers. Cronbach's alpha for the scale is 0.70.

Firm-level measure of inventor collaborativeness using inventor data from a firm's patents, measured as the average number of coinventors recorded in a firm's patents in any given year. The measure captures the extent to which the firm's innovation projects, on average, involve larger numbers of collaborators. The dependent variable is naturally logged to yield a log-log model so that coefficients can be interpreted as percentage point changes.

Time-varying state-level treatment indicator defined by the firm's headquarters location. NCA equals one for observations two or more years after NCA enforceability was strengthened, and zero otherwise (for all firms). The two-year lag follows Younge et al. (2015) and is consistent with exploratory event study analyses of the time taken for firms' collaboration behavior to change.
level: firm-year (state-level treatment assigned by headquarters location)
time_window: two or more years after the legal change

description: Time-varying state-level treatment indicator: IDD equals one for firms two or more years after the inevitable disclosure doctrine was applicable in their state, following IDD adoption by their courts, and zero otherwise. Its coefficient reflects the impacts of mobility barriers created by IDD on collaborativeness in firms' innovation.
level: firm-year (state-level treatment assigned by headquarters location)
time_window: two or more years after the legal change

description: Uses Sorenson et al.'s (2006) operationalization of complexity in patented inventions. The complexity measure captures the extent of complexity (or interdependency) 'K' between the knowledge components of any patented invention, proxied by four-digit international patent subclasses, by measuring the number of such components involved in a given patent and then scaling down by the frequency with which those components appear with others in all patents. For the firm-level regression analyses the authors construct an aggregate measure by averaging the complexity of patents applied for in the prior five years. The printed formulas for the ease of recombination, patent complexity and firm knowledge complexity were not readable in the extracted text.

Community income inequality was operationalized as the community's Gini index, gathered from the yearly data collected through the American Community Survey. A Gini value of 0 means that all households have equal income, and a value of 1 means that only one household has all of the income while all others have none. Higher Gini index values are indicative of greater levels of inequality. Theoretically the Gini index is calculated as the deviation between the Lorenz curve and a perfectly equal income distribution, but the Census Bureau relies on the Gini calculation developed by Dasgupta, Sen, and Starrett (1973); the formula printed in the paper is unreadable in this record.

Calculated as the Herfindahl index of the revenues of a community's welfare nonprofits, using the 'total nonprofit revenues' data point from the NCCS dataset to compute market shares. The index takes into account not only the number of welfare nonprofits but also their relative size in relation to their sector. Because the Herfindahl index decreases with the number of nonprofits, the authors reversed the variable to show density instead of concentration. Welfare nonprofits were identified as human-service organizations through NTEE codes and matched to their MSA by zip code.
time_window: lagged with respect to the dependent variable

description: Relying on the NTEE classification, the authors sampled all nonprofits whose primary activity was recreational and whose recipients could typically be identified as elite; when no clear elite orientation was identifiable, they excluded all nonprofits that might have a welfare orientation. After identifying the elite nonprofits, they applied the same procedure used for welfare nonprofit density and calculated an inverse Herfindahl index for elite nonprofits.
time_window: lagged with respect to the dependent variable

description: Calculated as the total number of enforcement actions (e.g., fines) taken by the Employee Benefits Security Administration against firms that failed to comply with labor laws, within the boundaries of the MSA, per 1000 firms operating in the MSA. Enforcement actions approximate the government's ability to identify and sanction companies that failed to comply with labor laws, most commonly relating to welfare benefit issues such as employer obligations, health benefits, and employee retirement income security.

The measure gathered data on direct actions undertaken by the government regarding income: supplements to social security, cash or equivalents given to people in conditions of poverty, and food stamps. The final measure was calculated as the total number of households receiving at least one of these direct benefits divided by the number of households below the poverty line. Because the measure describes weak government policies, it was reversed.

Calculated as the ratio of workers covered by a union contract to the total MSA workforce. Collected from Hirsch and Macpherson (2003), who compiled MSA unionization information based on the Current Population Survey and provide a yearly update of these statistics.

Calculated as the percentage of firms in the community belonging to the finance and insurance sector (North American Industry Classification System code 52). This measure includes all establishments engaged in either conducting financial transactions or facilitating those transactions, such as banks, financial brokers, investment funds, and insurance underwriters.

Calculated as the Blau index of the proportions of seven racial groups in the community: Hispanic, white, black or African-American, Asian, native Hawaiian, two or more races, and other race. An index closer to 0 indicates lower diversity, and the maximum occurs when the members of a community are evenly distributed among races. Because racial diversity has been shown to have a direct impact on inequality, this variable was also included as a control.

Calculated as the Blau index of the proportions of individuals across national-origin categories, spanning 30 nationalities. An index closer to 0 indicates lower diversity, and the maximum occurs when the members of a community are evenly distributed among the categories.

Following Di Giuli and Kostovetsky (2014), a dummy variable that equals 1 if the majority of people in the community had voted Republican in the previous presidential election. Data were obtained from David Leip's Atlas of U.S. Presidential Elections; because these data are available at the county level, the county-level number of votes was aggregated at the MSA level using the census delimitation file.

Binary outcome that takes the value of 1 if the focal new entrant bakery chooses a given available location, and 0 otherwise. The risk set is defined as locations (addresses) left empty by prior bakeries and not yet occupied, excluding locations that had been vacant for more than four years; it changes every year as locations are chosen or become vacant. The unit of analysis is the entrant-by-location dyad.

Coded in relation to whether the focal entrant was an unaffiliated bakery (value of 1) or an affiliated bakery (value of 0, Modernist entrant). Affiliation was established by matching the Chamber of Trade and Craft data, through common identification codes (SIRET), to lists of bakeries that were contractually part of each national affiliation group, provided by the groups' regional commercial directors for the observation period.

Dichotomous variable coded as 1 when the prior occupant of a location was a traditionalist, and 0 if it was a modernist. It captures location secondhand imprinting by the collective identity of the previous occupant of the location.

Distance between each location in the risk set and its nearest traditionalist competitor, obtained with Stata's geonear command from the longitude/latitude coordinates of bakery addresses and calculated at t-1. Distances were negated to capture geographic proximity, so higher values indicate locations closer to the nearest traditionalist bakery.

Distance between each location in the risk set and its nearest modernist competitor, obtained with Stata's geonear command from the longitude/latitude coordinates of bakery addresses and calculated at t-1. Distances were negated to capture geographic proximity, so higher values indicate locations closer to the nearest modernist bakery.

Geographic proximity to the nearest incumbent of the same collective identity as the entrant: Traditionalist proximity for traditionalist entrants and Modernist proximity for modernist entrants, each computed as the negated distance at t-1 between a location in the risk set and the nearest incumbent of that identity.

Dummy variable equal to one for agent-managed firms and zero for ventures that are managed by the entrepreneur himself or herself. A firm is owner managed when the CEO is also the owner; firms where the CEO is not an owner are designated as agent managed. The variable is measured in the firm's year of entry, that is, its first year of positive revenues.

Dummy variable set equal to 1 for industry-regions where the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) is below 0.15. The HHI is calculated for each industry within a focal region using firm revenues, with industries defined at the two-digit industry classification level and the total population of entrepreneurial firms (domestic and foreign owned) used in its construction. An increase in HHI implies a decrease in competition.

Continuous variable based on revenue growth in the industry over the five-year period preceding firm entry. The authors calculate the mean value of firm-level revenue growth for all entrepreneurial firms in the focal firm's industry-region over the period t-5 to t-1. The variable is evaluated at the industry-region-year level.

The standard deviation of operating return on assets (OROA) over the window t-5 to t-1 calculated for each firm and averaged across firms in the focal industry and region. Although evaluated at the industry-region level, the authors note it is a measure of firm-specific variability of returns.

Variable equal to one minus the general unemployment rate in the local region, that is, the regional employment rate. An increase in this variable implies greater outside employment options for potential agents or, equivalently, a decrease in the supply of available agents. It is not industry specific and is evaluated at the region-year level.

Indicator variable for foreign firms, entered alone and in interaction with the variables featured in the hypotheses in the pooled models of foreign and domestic firms. Foreign entrepreneurial firms are those with individual owners who are foreign nationals; new subsidiaries of multinationals and other established foreign firms are excluded.
A logged count of the number of domestic entrepreneurial firms in the region at time t-1. The variable is not industry specific and is evaluated at the region-year level.
A logged count of entrepreneurial firms in the region coming from the same home country as the focal firm, constructed as the analogue of the Domestic Density variable for foreign firms.

Firm profitability measured as operating return on assets (OROA). The authors compare the profitability of foreign versus domestic and owner-managed versus agent-managed entrepreneurial firms over the first three years of operation, controlling for other relevant observables.

Total direct compensation is the total amount of compensation paid to the CEO in a given year, including salary, bonuses, other annual compensation, the total value of restricted stock grants, the total value of stock options granted (using Black-Scholes), long-term incentive payouts, and all other miscellaneous forms of compensation. The authors use the natural logarithm of the total amount of compensation to reduce skewness and avoid biases from extreme outliers.
scale: natural logarithm of total direct compensation

description: Equal to one if a CEO won an award in the current year, and zero otherwise. One of two sets of binary variables created to distinguish between awarded and director CEOs.
Equal to one if a CEO won at least one award in the past four years, and zero otherwise; the postaward variables do not include the award year.
time_window: past four years, excluding the award year

description: Equal to one if a CEO was on the board of directors of a CEO who won an award in the current year, and zero otherwise. Director CEOs are identified from the board members of firms with an award-winning CEO at the time of the award, restricted to board directors who are simultaneously CEOs of S&P 1500 companies.
Equal to one if a CEO was on the board of directors of a CEO who won at least one award in the last four years, and zero otherwise; the postaward variables do not include the award year.
time_window: last four years, excluding the award year

description: Coded one if the number of articles published by the Wall Street Journal in the current year exceeds the number of articles published in the last year, and zero otherwise; interacted with Awarded CEO (postaward period). The results are robust to using continuous moderating variables.
time_window: current year compared with the last year

description: Coded one if the number of analysts covering the firm in the current year exceeds the number of analysts covering the firm in the last year, and zero otherwise; interacted with Awarded CEO (postaward period).
time_window: current year compared with the last year

description: Coded one if the firm's stock performance in the current year is higher than expected using a market-adjusted benchmark approach, and zero otherwise; the market's performance proxies for the expected firm performance in the respective year. Interacted with Awarded CEO (postaward period).

Dummy variable indicating an external successor (1 = external successor, 0 = internal successor). External successors are defined as CEOs who had 2 or fewer years of tenure in the firm upon becoming CEO. The sample contains 35 external successors, 11.5 per cent of the sample. This is the single successor dummy variable used in regression #1, which tests Hypothesis 1.

Dummy variable indicating an external successor from outside the industry (1 = external successor outside of industry, 0 otherwise). The classification is based on whether the CEO had prior work experience in at least one of the 3-digit SIC code industries in which the hiring firm had revenues in the year prior to the CEO's first year on the job, and within 5 years of moving to the firm. The sample contains 16 outside-of-industry external successors. In the regression the omitted category is internal successors, and the test of Hypothesis 2 is the difference between these two external successor coefficients.

Dummy variable indicating an external successor from within the industry (1 = external successor within industry, 0 otherwise). A within-industry successor had prior work experience in at least one of the 3-digit SIC code industries of the hiring firm, and within 5 years of moving to the firm. The sample contains 19 within-industry external successors. This dummy appears in the regression together with EXTGENERIC, with internal successors as the omitted category.

The natural logarithm of salary plus bonus reported in Forbes, in real dollars (in thousands of dollars), adjusted for inflation using the Consumer Price Index. The authors use second-year salary and bonus to measure 'initial' cash compensation, because first-year pay is not comparable across CEOs: for an external successor the first fiscal year covers only the months the CEO held the job, and for an internal successor the first-year figure includes pay in the previous job.
scale: natural logarithm of real salary plus bonus in thousands of dollars
time_window: second year of the CEO's tenure

description: An ordered categorical variable built from a media-based measure of CEO hubris. Articles mentioning the CEO in major publications were cumulated from the first year the CEO was in office through year t-1, and the counts of 'confident' terms and 'conservatism' terms appearing within ten words of the CEO's name were used to construct the continuous measure. CEO Hubris takes the value of 1 for CEOs in the top quintile of the CEO Hubris Continuous variable, -1 for the bottom quintile, and 0 for the remaining CEOs.
time_window: cumulated from the first year the CEO was in office through year t-1

description: Created by summing the number of strengths across five KLD dimensions: community, diversity, employee relations, environment, and product, measured at year t. Each of the five dimensions involves different categories of strengths and concerns, within which KLD assigns a 1 or 0 to items according to whether or not a firm meets certain criteria. All strength items are considered consistent with acting socially responsible.

The total number of concerns across the five KLD dimensions (community, diversity, employee relations, environment, and product), indicating the extent of a firm's participation in socially irresponsible activities. All concerns items are considered consistent with acting socially irresponsible.
Measured by the natural logarithm of firms' total assets at year t-1.

Measured by firms' cash holding scaled by firms' market capitalization at year t-1. Firms with more cash on hand have less need to raise funds externally, which suggests that they are less limited by resources.

Measured at the industry level (two-digit SIC code) by the industry median of the analyst forecast dispersion, i.e., the standard deviation of analyst earnings per share forecasts scaled by share price, at year t-1.

Measured by the natural logarithm of one minus the four-firm concentration ratio divided by the four-firm concentration ratio at year t-1. The four-firm concentration ratio was calculated by dividing the combined sales of the four largest firms (based on sales) in an industry by the total sales of that industry.

Respondents evaluated the extent to which their firm was successful in changing each particular knowledge set so as to make it more suitable to achieve a set of primary objectives. They used a 5-point Likert-type scale where 1 = unsuccessful, 5 = successful, with 0 = not applicable. Success of knowledge set change was determined by aggregating across the set of five items used to evaluate progress in making the knowledge set suitable for the new free market economy. All five items loaded onto a single factor with a Cronbach alpha measure of 0.828.
scale: 5-point Likert-type scale, 1 = unsuccessful, 5 = successful, 0 = not applicable

description: Firms were asked the extent to which their decision to undertake change reflected different institutional pressures. Respondents rated each reason on a 1-5 scale where 1 = not an important reason and 5 = very important reason for change. The socialist institutional measure is an arithmetic average of the ratings provided on these reasons; the four-item measure had a Cronbach alpha of 0.70.
scale: 1-5 scale, 1 = not an important reason, 5 = very important reason for change

description: Managers indicated the extent to which their decision to undertake change reflected improving product or service quality, improving productivity, and reducing costs, rated on a 1-5 scale where 1 = not an important reason and 5 = very important reason for change. Because these reasons reflect the pressures of a free-market economy, the scale was reverse coded so that high ratings indicate a high level of socialist market imprinting. The overall score is the simple arithmetic mean of the reverse-coded ratings for the three items; the measure had a Cronbach alpha of 0.71.
scale: 1-5 scale, 1 = not an important reason, 5 = very important reason for change, reverse coded

description: Two categories of search are distinguished: local search is defined as a search within formerly socialist countries (Lithuania, Russia, Poland) and distant search is defined as a search in traditionally free-market economies (Western Europe, Canada, United States). The country of origin of the assisting firm was used to determine search location. The variable is coded such that 0 = local search (within former socialist economies) and 1 = distant search (historically free-market economies); if a firm did not utilize outside assistance but implemented the change using only internal knowledge, this was coded as local search.

Each analyst's last forecast before the end of the fiscal year was used to calculate the 'consensus' of the EPS forecasts, the average of security analysts' forecasts of the firm's EPS. The size of the performance gap relative to analyst forecast was calculated as the absolute value of (actual EPS minus EPS forecast) divided by EPS forecast. The absolute value corrects for sign-switching when the forecast is negative, and the variable was mean-centered in the analysis. It is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

The analyst coverage each firm received was measured using the number of analysts who issued earnings forecasts for it during the year. A higher value of this measure indicates a higher level of analyst coverage. The variable was mean-centered in the analysis and is lagged one year relative to the dependent variable.

R&D intensity was measured as the percentage of firm R&D expenses over sales during each fiscal year. About 25 percent of observations had missing values in R&D expenses, which were replaced with zero on the assumption that these firms invested very little (less than 10% of SG&A) in R&D.

Degree of career specialization is captured with a Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) calculated from a staffer's cumulative years of experience across functional job categories. Staffer job titles from LegiStorm are classified into five functional job categories (legislative staff, political management staff, communications staff, office management staff, and constituency service staff) using the categorization scheme of Crosson, Furnas, and LaPira (2018). Specialist and Generalist dummy variables are created by median-splitting the sample by HHI, with Specialist equal to 1 for above-median specialization and Generalist equal to 1 for below-median specialization. Specialist displacement and Generalist displacement are then created through the interactions of the treatment variable, Job displacement, with the Specialist and Generalist dummies.
time_window: cumulative experience through election year t

description: Dummy variable set to 1 if a staffer is employed as a congressional staffer in the year after an election (i.e., t+1) and 0 otherwise. It captures the staffer's ability to secure work within the congressional staffing industry, or inversely the likelihood of exiting congressional staffing after displacement.

Dummy variable equal to 1 when a staffer loses their job because the politician they work for loses a reelection bid and 0 otherwise; staffers are considered displaced only if the data show their employment was terminated between the election loss in November and the end of the term. Displacement is set to 1 (0) when the member has a negative (positive) margin of victory and the margin of victory is within the bandwidth range specified in a given model. Margin of victory, the forcing variable of the regression discontinuity design, is the difference in vote share between the member and the second-best opponent when the member wins and the difference in vote share between the member and the election winner when the member loses.

Count of jobs at year t+1 that are categorized in the same functional job category as the focal staffer at the election year t, using the functional classifications developed by Crosson, Furnas, and LaPira (2018). The variable captures the thickness or market demand for a particular functional work area.
time_window: t+1 counts relative to election year t

description: A dummy variable coded 'one' to indicate an abandonment decision when the company failed to provide guidance for at least three out of the four consecutive quarters following the adoption period; firms were then removed from the risk set of QEG abandonment. A QEG adoption event was identified as the first guidance provision among at least three consecutive guidance events within a four-quarter period. Multiple abandonment histories were allowed.

The level of analyst coverage breadth was measured by tallying the number of financial analysts that followed the focal company, considered zero when no analyst covered the firm in I/B/E/S for a given quarter. The measure was adjusted by the two-digit SIC industry: the authors describe it as an industry mean deviated score, the difference between the number of analysts following the focal company and the industry mean, divided by the measure's industry standard deviation for the quarter. The text does not clearly state the sign of the deviation.

The average of the years of overlap between the focal firm CEO's tenure and the years that each individual analyst covers the firm. The authors first coded the start and end year of the focal firm CEO tenure and then identified the overlap with the start and end dates of the individual analysts' focal firm coverage. The measure was standardized as the industry mean deviated score for the respective quarter.

The authors aggregated individual sample companies' nonprovision of QEG for a respective quarter, coding nonprovision dichotomously as 'one.' They then calculated the mean within the focal firm's corresponding industry reference group over the previous four quarters. The measure includes nonprovision of QEG by companies that had never adopted QEG.

variable_name: Sanction Against QEG Abandonment, Industry Peers
description: The authors first assigned a dichotomous variable coded 'one' to each company that abandoned QEG for the respective quarter. They then created a continuous variable capturing the decrease in the number of analysts following the focal company compared with the prior four quarters. They computed the product of these two measures and aggregated its mean at the focal firm's industry for every quarter.

A dummy variable coded 'one' when the company's actual quarterly earnings failed to reach the consensus analyst forecast in the given quarter. The consensus forecast was the average of all quarterly earnings forecasts provided by the analysts who cover the firm. The authors also examined the degree of negative earnings surprise as a continuous variable.

Number of full-time equivalents (employees) at the corporate level providing information and support for pollution prevention, measured from surveyed responses of corporate managers of environmental affairs. The survey first defined pollution prevention, asked whether anyone at corporate headquarters ever promoted pollution prevention practices within the company and in what year this activity began, and then asked respondents to specify the number of full-time equivalents who worked to promote pollution prevention in each year since promotional activities began. The Cronbach alpha among the responses to the list of common mechanisms and the number of FTEs is 0.87.
time_window: each year since promotional activities began

description: Total count of pollution-reducing product or process modifications in a given year as indicated in the Source Reduction Activity (SRA) fields of the Toxic Release Inventory. 'Process Modifications' (elements W51, W52, W53, W54, W55, W58) and 'Product Modifications' (elements W81, W82, W83, W89) are a subset of those practices.
Percent of all facilities within a given four-digit SIC code that have adopted pollution prevention practices in a given time period.

Cumulative number of negative environmental events experienced by a firm, including hazardous material spills tracked through the U.S. EPA's Accidental Release Information Program, completed environmental lawsuits filed against a firm as reported on the Docket Database of the U.S. EPA, fines and violations accessed under both the Clean Water Act and RCRA, and the number of a firm's facilities investigated for inclusion on the National Priority List under CERCLA.

Dummy variable used as a proxy for the existence of quality management practices, where '1' indicates that the facility is ISO 9001 certified for that year. Certification data were gathered from the ISO 9000 Registered Company Directory of North America.

Degree to which corporate environmental managers report that headquarters provides explicit rewards (or punishment) for adoption of (or failure to adopt) pollution prevention practices. Measured using a seven-item scale where zero indicates that PP practice adoption is rewarded 'not at all' and six indicates PP practice adoption is rewarded 'very much.' Respondents were asked a series of questions concerning various compensatory activities before being asked to indicate the overall level for each year from 1990 to 1998; Cronbach's alpha for these questions is 0.92.

Perceptual multi-item measure, developed on the basis of Gatignon and Xuereb (1997) and Song and colleagues' (2005) work, of a firm's ability to use various technologies. Senior managers evaluated their firm's capabilities compared with major competitors in acquiring technology information, identifying new technology opportunities, responding to technology changes, mastering state-of-the-art technologies, and developing a series of innovations constantly. The measure was validated in a confirmatory measurement model; the paper reports that its composite reliability and average variance extracted are adequate.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = much worse; 7 = much better)

description: Perceptual multi-item measure built from Sanchez's (1995) theoretical work on the flexible allocation and coordination of resources in response to changing environments. Senior managers indicated the extent to which the firm's strategy emphasizes flexible allocation and reconfiguration of resources and product strategies, including flexible allocation of marketing and production resources, flexibility of product design, reconfiguring chains of resources, and redeploying organizational resources. The authors report satisfactory reliability and validity for the scale.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree)

description: Multi-item scale adapted from Atuahene-Gima (2005), rated by middle managers, reflecting the extent to which the firm uses existing knowledge and technologies in its new product development. Items cover exploiting mature technologies that improve the productivity of current innovation operations, searching for solutions near to existing solutions, upgrading skills in product development processes in which the firm already has rich experience, and strengthening knowledge and skills to improve the efficiency of existing innovation activities. The authors report that these measures possess adequate reliability and validity.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = very low; 7 = very high)

description: Multi-item scale adapted from Atuahene-Gima (2005), rated by middle managers, reflecting the extent to which the firm explores new knowledge and technologies in its new product development. Items cover acquiring manufacturing technologies and skills entirely new to the firm, learning product development skills and processes entirely new to the industry, acquiring entirely new managerial and organizational skills important for innovation, learning totally new skills in funding new technology and training R&D personnel, and strengthening innovation skills in areas where the firm has no prior experience. The authors report that these measures possess adequate reliability and validity.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = very low; 7 = very high)

description: Time-varying dichotomous indicator equal to 1 for all observation years after a woman had a child, and 0 otherwise, constructed from data on women's biological children. As an alternative measure the authors use a time-varying count of children coded 1 for one child, 2 for two children, and 3 for three or more children, with consistent results.

variable_name: Earnings gap between a mother and equivalent nonmothers in the firm
description: For a given mother in a given year, the average wage difference between her wage and the wages of observationally equivalent nonmothers in the same firm and same one-digit occupation, based on case-control matching. Each mother is matched with nonmothers in the same firm and occupation on years of labor market experience (plus or minus 2 years), tenure at the firm (plus or minus 1 year), years of education (plus or minus 1 year), and percentage of regular work hours (plus or minus 3%).

variable_name: Earnings growth gap between a mother and equivalent nonmothers in the firm
description: The average wage-growth difference between a mother and observationally equivalent nonmothers in the same firm and same occupation in a given year, using the same matching criteria as the earnings-gap measure. Earnings growth is computed from the previous year to the current year, and the measure compares how it differs between mothers and matched nonmothers in the same firm.
time_window: annual, growth from previous to current year

variable_name: Consecutive years not receiving a raise of 3% or more
description: The number of consecutive years in which a woman has not received a raise of 3% or more since becoming a mother. A 3% raise is used as a reasonable cutoff because average inflation in Sweden fluctuates between 1.5% and 3%, and a 2% cutoff yields similar results; a raise smaller than 3% proxies stagnated earnings growth in paid work.

Coded as 1 if an individual enters entrepreneurship from paid employment, where entry includes the transition to self-employment and the founding of a new organization, and as 0 otherwise. Alternative events, such as the transition from wage employment to unemployment, are treated as censored.

variable_name: Transition from wage employment to new-venture founding
description: Dummy variable set to 1 if individuals exited wage employment to launch an incorporated organization, and 0 if they stayed in wage employment; transitions to unemployment or to self-employment in an unincorporated business are treated as censored. Incorporation is the key proxy for new-business founding because incorporated businesses in the Swedish data tend to be employer firms, whereas unincorporated businesses are mostly sole proprietors running home-based businesses without employees.

variable_name: Transition from wage employment to self-employment
description: Coded as 1 if individuals exited wage employment to become self-employed in an unincorporated business, and as 0 if they remained in wage employment. Alternative events, such as the transition from wage employment to unemployment or founding an incorporated business, are treated as censored.

Dummy variable coded 1 for managerial positions and 0 otherwise, constructed from the standard occupation codes of each individual, where occupation codes with 1 as the first digit indicate managerial positions.
The annual average earnings within each occupation in the sample, with occupation defined at the two-digit level. A three-digit occupational level was used as a robustness check with similar results.

Respondents evaluated five phases of human resource planning and were asked to indicate the phases used in their process, and three human resource planning categories were formed: Category 1, no formal human resource planning; Category 2, partial or incomplete human resource planning; and Category 3, fully integrated human resource planning. A firm that did not meet all of the requirements for a category was assigned to the next lower category. Because of the disproportionately small number of firms classified as Category 3, that group was combined with Category 2 for the analyses.

Six performance measures were used, each calculated over the 5-year period 1976-80. Four represent traditional measures of financial performance: sales growth (average annual percentage growth over a 5-year period), earnings growth (average annual percentage growth over a 5-year period), earnings/sales ratio (average annual earnings as a percentage of sales over a 5-year period), and earnings/total assets (average annual earnings as a percentage of total assets over a 5-year period). Two further measures assess the impact of human resources on organization performance: earnings/employees and assets/employees (average annual earnings per employee and average annual assets per employee over a 5-year period). For the second hypothesis each performance variable is measured for pre- and post-human resource planning 5-year periods.
time_window: 5-year period (1976-80); also 5-year pre- and post-human resource planning periods

description: CSR is measured from six dimensions of KLD data: community, diversity, employee relations, environment, human rights, and product quality ratings. Because the study focuses on proactive engagement, CSR is captured with the 'strengths' measure. Because the number of individual strengths within each dimension changed over time, the strengths score across all six dimensions is divided by the sum of the maximum possible strengths score across these six dimensions for each firm-year, and the scaled strengths are then summed to obtain CSR engagement.

Content analysis of the letters to shareholders using the software Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC). The built-in LIWC dictionaries are used to calculate the value of CEO PA based on the percentage of positive words within each letter. The measure is lagged by 1 year relative to the outcome and standardized.

Content analysis of the letters to shareholders using the software Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC). The built-in LIWC dictionaries are used to calculate the value of CEO NA based on the percentage of negative words within each letter. The measure is lagged by 1 year relative to the outcome and standardized.

Measured as the number of individuals with whom the CEO is connected via employment, education, or other activities (such as connections through social clubs or professional associations) in the BoardEx universe. Two individuals are connected through employment if they previously had positions at the same employer within the same period. The natural log of one plus this social connection number is used as the measure.

When an industrial firm in the sample made a diversifying entry into an industry between 1980 and 1982 and maintained its presence there at least until 1986, the entrant business is deemed to have survived. The variable was assigned a value of 0 if the parent firm exited from the entered industry between 1982 and 1986, and 1 if it stayed in.
Sales Gain was measured as (Sales in 1986/Sales in 1982). Because the growth criterion is only applicable for surviving entrant businesses, it was used only for entries that survived as of 1986.

Advertising expenditures per unit of sales in the entered industry during the period preceding entry, computed as an expense-to-sales ratio as reported in the Federal Trade Commission's Line of Business (FTC-ALB) data.
time_window: the period preceding entry (FTC-ALB data for 1974-77)

description: R&D expenditures per unit of sales in the entered industry during the period preceding entry, computed as an expense-to-sales ratio as reported in the Federal Trade Commission's Line of Business (FTC-ALB) data.
time_window: the period preceding entry (FTC-ALB data for 1974-77)

description: Selling and distribution expenses per unit of sales in the entered industry during the period preceding entry, computed as an expense-to-sales ratio as reported in the Federal Trade Commission's Line of Business (FTC-ALB) data.
time_window: the period preceding entry (FTC-ALB data for 1974-77)

description: Capital intensity was obtained by multiplying minimum efficient scale (MES) by the cost disadvantage ratio (CDR) as suggested by Caves, Khalizadeh-Shirazi, and Porter (1975), i.e. CAPI = MES x CDR. MES is measured as the median plant size in the industry, whereas CDR is obtained by dividing sales per employee for the plants in the third quartile (PQ3) by sales per employee for plants in the first quartile (PQ1). These data were derived from Trinet.

Scale of Entry was taken to be dollar sales during 1982, as reported in Trinet. It is used both as an independent variable and, in interaction with seller concentration, as a moderator of the concentration-performance relationship.

Seller Concentration was measured as the sum of the market shares of the four largest firms in the destination industry as of 1980. The data for this variable were obtained from Census of Manufactures.

Relatedness between the entrant business and the rest of the businesses of the parent firm, computed using a modified version of the concentric diversification index: Product Relatedness = sum over l of (Pkl x dil), where Pkl is the percentage of firm k's sales that are in industry l and dil is a weight depending on the distance between the entered industry i and the other industries l in which the parent has operations. The weight is 2 if i and l are within the same 3-digit SIC, 1 if i and l are within the same 2-digit SIC, and 0 if i and l are in different 2-digit SIC industries. The data were obtained from Trinet.

Acquisitive entrants were identified by noting the change in ownership between 1980 and 1982 of relevant plants and locations in Trinet. Entries corresponding to plants or locations that did not exist in the 1980 Trinet files were deemed de novo. The mode of entry defines the two subsamples on which the analyses are run separately.

Each of the four industries was classified according to Thompson's typology, drawing on the organizations' descriptions of their work, annual reports supplied by firms in each industry, four-digit Standard Industrial Classification codes, and judgments made by four business school professors familiar with Thompson's typology, each of whom independently categorized the industries into exactly the same categories. The U.S. Postal Service and the freight transport firms were classified as long-linked, the eight public accounting firms as mediating, and the consulting firms as intensive. Technological intensity, or the extent to which members have technical training based on systematic knowledge of a profession and adhere to professional norms, was used as an additional indicator, measured with the percentage of employees with college education and with graduate training in each industry.

The growth rate in each of the four industries was defined as (1) the percent change in revenues and (2) the percent change in number of employees. These statistics were compiled for each industry for the five years prior to the collection of data on culture; among the four industries the average increase in revenues and in employees was lowest for the post office and highest for the consulting industry, and the ordering of the two indicators was consistent with the technology classification.
time_window: five years prior to the culture data collection

description: Factor score on the innovation dimension of organizational culture. Respondents familiar with their firm's culture sorted the 54 OCP value statements into nine categories ranging from most characteristic to most uncharacteristic of the firm's culture, with 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 9, 6, 4, and 2 statements allowed per category. Individual profiles were averaged item by item into a firm profile, and a principal component analysis with varimax rotation of the entire item set produced seven interpretable factors, with 38 of the 54 items loading above .30 on one of them. For each firm, item factor scores averaged across raters were used in the analyses of variance and planned comparisons.

Factor score on the stability dimension of organizational culture, obtained from the same 54-item OCP Q-sort in which respondents sorted the value statements into nine categories (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 9, 6, 4, and 2 statements per category). Individual profiles were averaged item by item into a firm profile and factor-analyzed with a principal component analysis and varimax rotation; item factor scores averaged across raters were used for each firm in the analyses of variance and planned comparisons.

Factor score on the people orientation dimension of organizational culture, obtained from the 54-item OCP Q-sort in which respondents sorted value statements into nine categories (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 9, 6, 4, and 2 statements per category). Individual profiles were averaged item by item into a firm profile, and a principal component analysis with varimax rotation produced seven interpretable factors; item factor scores averaged across raters were used for each firm.

Factor score on the outcome orientation dimension of organizational culture, obtained from the 54-item OCP Q-sort in which respondents sorted value statements into nine categories (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 9, 6, 4, and 2 statements per category). Individual profiles were averaged item by item into a firm profile, and a principal component analysis with varimax rotation produced seven interpretable factors; item factor scores averaged across raters were used for each firm.

Factor score on the detail orientation dimension of organizational culture, obtained from the 54-item OCP Q-sort in which respondents sorted value statements into nine categories (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 9, 6, 4, and 2 statements per category). Individual profiles were averaged item by item into a firm profile, and a principal component analysis with varimax rotation produced seven interpretable factors; item factor scores averaged across raters were used for each firm.

Factor score on the team (collaborative) orientation dimension of organizational culture, obtained from the 54-item OCP Q-sort in which respondents sorted value statements into nine categories (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 9, 6, 4, and 2 statements per category). Individual profiles were averaged item by item into a firm profile, and a principal component analysis with varimax rotation produced seven interpretable factors; item factor scores averaged across raters were used for each firm.

Factor score on the easygoingness dimension of organizational culture, obtained from the 54-item OCP Q-sort in which respondents sorted value statements into nine categories (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 9, 6, 4, and 2 statements per category). Individual profiles were averaged item by item into a firm profile, and a principal component analysis with varimax rotation produced seven interpretable factors; item factor scores averaged across raters were used for each firm.

Dummy variable indicating whether a newly hired individual has worked at an advocacy group in the year t - 1, that is, before being hired by an innovative firm. Advocacy groups are identified from the industry statistical classification code NACE (Rev. 1) 91. Organizations classified as advocacy groups cover religious organizations, foundations, voluntary health organizations, human rights organizations, environment, conservation and wildlife organizations, civic and social organizations, and business, professional, labor, political and similar organizations.

Gross annual income earned by the newly hired employees in the year t in which they are hired. The natural logarithm is taken to account for skewness of the data. The variable is the dependent variable in augmented Mincer-type income regressions estimated with coarsened exact matching weights.

The hiring firm's R&D intensity, measured as the number of employees in R&D divided by the total number of employees, relative to the average R&D intensity of the firm's two-digit industry in Denmark in t - 1. Increasing values indicate that a firm is relatively leading and closer to the technological frontier.

Dummy variable taking the value 1 if the individual worked in an occupation that involved stakeholder interaction at the previous employer in t - 1. Because there is no validated measure, experts rated the likelihood that two-digit occupation codes include social tasks, and occupations with at least an above average likelihood were used: health professionals (DISCO 22); teaching professionals (23); legal, social and cultural professionals (26); health associate professionals (32); sales and service associate professionals (33); and legal, social, cultural and related associate professionals (34). The reference group is occupations with mainly administrative or technical tasks.
Dummy variable based on the DISCO codes that takes the value 1 if the individual was a member of the top management team of the previous employer in t - 1.

Star analyst is an indicator variable that takes the value of '1' if the analyst appears in any of the various teams listed by Institutional Investor that year. The magazine conducts an annual worldwide survey of money managers at large investment and hedge funds asking them to rate each analyst, and the analyst with the highest score is placed on a 'first team' within his/her industry.

Our measure of CEO reputation (Star CEO) was a count of the number of times that a CEO had won awards from Forbes, BusinessWeek, Chief Executive Management, Industry Week, Institutional Investor, or Worth magazine over the prior five years. We captured our measures starting in 1991 so that every year in our sample had five years of preceding information.

Following Pfarrer, Pollock, and Rindova (2010), firm reputation was operationalized using the rankings of Fortune magazine's 'Most Admired Companies' and the Wall Street Journal / Harris Interactive list of 'Corporate Reputation'. Corporate reputation was operationalized as a dichotomous variable taking the value of '1' if the firm appeared on either of these lists in the year prior to the ratings change.
time_window: year prior to the ratings change

description: We measure the stock market's reaction to these ratings changes using the abnormal returns to a firm's stock on the day of a downgrade/upgrade using the market model. This measure captures the CAR on a [0,1] window surrounding the event.

Binary event measure coded 1 for firm-years whose structural change ratio exceeds a 0.30 cut-off. The ratio is computed by coding all top managerial titles on a horizontal dimension (business area, geography, functions, customers, technology) and a vertical dimension (up to four levels, with Chairman, CEO, President and COO coded General Managers), calculating the proportion of each group of codes on titles coded, and then summing the absolute differences in proportions of each group of codes between two consecutive years. Interview and documentary sources (annual reports, organization charts, media coverage) were used to establish the 0.30 threshold.
time_window: change between consecutive years, with lags up to t-5 in the models

description: Continuous count of reconfigurations in a particular year, following Karim's (2006) approach: addition of new units (internal development or acquisition), recombination of units as mergers, recombination of units as transfers, split of units to form a new stand-alone unit, and unit deletion (closure or divestment). Counted from annual reports, SEC 10-Ks and press announcements from the Lexis-Nexis database.
time_window: count in year t, with lags up to t-5 in the models

description: Ratio of the market value of equity (including common and preferred stock) plus the book value of total debt, over the book value of total assets. Tobin's Q is calculated at the end of the fiscal year of a restructuring or reconfiguration.
time_window: end of the fiscal year of a restructuring or reconfiguration

description: Ratio of the sum of net income and interests divided by total assets.
time_window: fiscal year, with lags up to five years in the models

description: Dess and Beard's industry-based measure of dynamism: the standard error of the rate of change of annual industry sales. Because the average primary industry accounts for 70 percent of firm sales in the sample, dynamism facing each firm is estimated on the basis of the primary industry it competed in.
time_window: annual, with lags up to t-5 in the models

description: For each task, the authors code whether or not the task belongs to a project whose project manager operates from a different unit than the worker, each unit of FAST being located in a different city. The variable is equal to one if the geographic location of the worker performing the task for a given project is different from the geographic location of the manager of that project, and zero otherwise.

The log of the total number of hours it takes a worker to complete a focal task. It is computed from daily records: at the end of each day, workers report how they divided their workday among various assigned tasks. The authors state that the time it takes to process a given task is the main metric used by managers in the unit to track workers' performance, and that it captures both worker speed and quality.

The count of the number of subtasks that have been assigned to the same worker within a project. The authors state that when a manager is concerned that a worker may struggle in executing a technically complex task, the manager usually decomposes the task into smaller subtasks, whereas for simple tasks such partitioning is not necessary.

A dichotomous variable that takes the value of one if there are both programming and analysis tasks involved in the focal project (i.e., at least a programmer and an analyst involved), and zero otherwise. The variable can also take the value of zero when there is only one worker involved in the project.

For each focal task, the total amount of tasks that have been solved by other workers present in the location of the focal worker up to the moment in which the focal task is assigned. The measure captures the cumulated total experience acquired by others in the worker's location at the moment of the assignment of the task. The authors also control for the total number of workers present in the unit at the moment of the assignment of the focal task.
time_window: up to the moment in which the focal task is assigned

description: The number of team members who are working in the same project and are collocated with the focal worker divided by the total number of the focal project team members. The authors control for the total number of focal project team members so that the proportion takes into account the extent to which the team is collocated with the focal worker. The variable takes the value of zero for all single-worker projects.

The total number of tasks performed in the past by the focal worker under the supervision of the focal manager prior to the assignment of the focal task. The authors describe it as essentially a measure of manager-worker familiarity.
time_window: prior to the assignment of the focal task

description: The total number of projects in which the manager has managed other workers than the focal one prior to the assignment of the focal task. The authors describe it as essentially a measure of breadth of experience.
time_window: prior to the assignment of the focal task

description: Adapted from Narver and Slater (1990). Single informant: responses obtained from senior marketing managers, who are most knowledgeable about the extent to which their firms promote MO culture. Covers customer orientation, competitor orientation, and interfunctional coordination.

Adapted from Jaworski and Kohli (1993). Because MO behavior emphasizes organizationwide coordination, middle managers from different functional units are used as multiple informants and their individual scores are aggregated to the firm mean. Covers intelligence generation, intelligence dissemination, and responsiveness.
level: unit-level responses aggregated to the firm

description: Scale adapted from Wood, Chonko, and Hunt (1986). Individual responses of frontline workers are aggregated to attain an appropriate firm-level indicator. Five items cover salary level, the importance the supervisor places on the employee, opportunity for promotion, fairness of supervisor treatment, and sense of job accomplishment.
level: individual responses aggregated to the firm

description: Following Zeithaml (1988), product quality is measured with three items that assess the degree to which a firm's products or services meet customer needs. Senior marketing managers serve as the single informant because they are the most knowledgeable about this assessment.

Borrowing from Awamleh and Gardner (1999), the measure includes five items that assess the envisioning and energizing qualities of firm leaders. Because senior personnel managers have more interactions with firm leaders, they serve as the single informant.

Firm performance is measured with an objective indicator, return on assets (ROA). To establish the causal link of the model, information about ROA was collected one year after the survey from the statistical databank supplied by the State Statistical Bureau.

Firm risk taking is proxied by R&D expenditures in millions of U.S. dollars divided by sales, with all data collected from Compustat. Because the raw R&D intensity variable had a relatively high average and standard deviation, the authors only focused on firms with R&D intensity less than or equal to 1.0 and removed a total of 202 firm-year observations from the sample. The dependent variable corresponds to the years 1993 to 2006.
scale: ratio of R&D expenditures in millions of U.S. dollars to sales

description: Return on assets is the accounting-based proxy for firm performance. Two alternate aspiration levels were used: the focal firm's own prior performance (historical aspiration level) and the median profitability of companies within each industry at the four-digit SIC level (social aspiration level). Actual firm performance was measured at year t-1 and each aspiration level was proxied at year t-2, and performance feedback was computed as the difference between the firm's actual performance and the aspiration level. An indicator for poorly performing firms equals 1 if the firm's previous performance drops below either the historical or social aspiration level.
scale: indicator (1 = performance below the historical or social aspiration level)
time_window: performance at t-1, aspiration at t-2

description: One minus the indicator for poorly performing firms is associated with well-performing firms whose performance met or rose above the historical or social aspiration level. Positive attainment discrepancy is the amount by which the firm's prior performance rises above the aspiration level, computed from the difference between actual firm performance and the historical or social aspiration level.
scale: difference between actual performance and the aspiration level
time_window: performance at t-1, aspiration at t-2

description: Values of CEO stock option grants are measured as the Black-Scholes valuation for stock options granted to the CEO in the fiscal year, based on data from ExecuComp, for each year from 1992 to 2005 inclusive. The authors place emphasis on at-the-money stock option grants and use the traditional Black and Scholes (1973) option value because this is a common method for evaluating stock options.

Values of outside director stock option grants are measured by multiplying the number of stock options granted to each director in the fiscal year with the Black-Scholes option value. Each outside director is awarded an annual option grant to buy an equal number of company shares, so the variable captures the average value of stock options per outside director.
A binary variable coded 1 if an actual resource exchange (transfer of players under contract) occurs between two teams and 0 otherwise.
A binary variable coded as 1 if both teams in a pair belong to the same NBA conference (Eastern or Western) and 0 otherwise.
Count of prior exchange ties between the two general managers (GMs) in the dyad, regardless of their current team affiliation, winsorized at the 95th percentile.
A binary variable coded as 1 if a player is traded together with other players to another team and 0 if the player is traded alone.

Calculated as the absolute average points margin difference in regular season games between two teams over the last three seasons. Higher levels of rivalry are represented by smaller margin differences.

The measure compares the comments made by discursive partners prior to entrepreneurs' responses with the entrepreneurs' responses within the same comment thread; where an entrepreneur responds multiple times, each response is compared to the discursive partner comments made after the previous response and before the current one. Word embeddings are trained with Word2Vec over the corpus of comments, each word vector is weighted by its TF-IDF score, and the mean vector across words is computed for the discursive partners' comments and for the entrepreneur's response; discourse broadening is the cosine distance between these mean vectors, weighted by the diversity of meaning among words in the entrepreneur's response. The pairwise values are averaged across all comment threads for a product during its first week of launch, and cases with values above 1 were excluded.
scale: cosine distance, values from 0 to 1 after excluding values above 1

description: The total number of upvotes a product receives within the first week of its launch. Upvotes are treated as expressions of support from silent audiences because 99.97% of upvotes come from individuals who were not direct discursive partners of the entrepreneurs at the time of voting, and upvotes from individuals who commented on the product during the same week were excluded.

variable_name: similarity between discursive partners and silent audiences
description: The cosine similarity between the mean TF-IDF-weighted Word2Vec vectors of the potential base of silent audiences and those of the entrepreneur's discursive partners for each product. The silent audience base is the users who were already following the entrepreneur by the end of the launch week, excluding users who began following after upvoting and excluding discursive partners who commented; their interpretative lenses are inferred from their comments on any Product Hunt launches in the three months prior to the focal product launch. Discursive partners' lenses are inferred from their comments in the threads where they interacted with the entrepreneur, following the same approach, and higher cosine similarity values indicate greater alignment between the two groups' interpretative lenses.
time_window: three months prior to the focal product launch for silent audience comments; launch week for identifying the audience base

description: A binary variable that captures whether a listing's category affiliation in the current period differs from its category affiliation in the previous period. Hosts are required to assign their listing to one of 47 predefined categories and may change it at any time, so a listing was never classified into more than one category. The repeated web-scraping surveys tracked each listing's affiliated category in every period; with six half-year periods, each listing has up to five potential opportunities to switch categories.
time_window: current period compared with previous period (six-month intervals)

description: Counts the number of negative customer reviews a listing received during a given period. Time-stamped review-level data from Inside Airbnb were collected for all sample listings, yielding 2,262,300 individual reviews, from which reviews automatically posted by Airbnb due to host-initiated cancellations were removed. Sentiment analysis using a fine-tuned version of DistilBERT trained on Version 2 of the Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST-2) classified reviews as positive or negative, classifying 3.5% of all online reviews as negative; because reviews are time-stamped, each negative review was matched retrospectively to the observation period in which it appeared.
time_window: matched to the same six-month observation period

description: Captures the degree of diversity in terms of category members' features, where low levels indicate that most listings closely align with a clear set of prototypical features. In the Airbnb context the authors focus on listings' set of provided amenities, of which hosts indicate whether their listing includes any of 54 pre-defined amenity types. Using time-sensitive amenity data, each category's prototypical amenity profile was inferred by calculating, for each amenity, the average share of listings in a category that offered it in a given period, yielding a 54-dimensional vector of amenity probabilities per category-period; category heterogeneity was then captured by a formula that is not readable in the provided text. The variable was mean-centered to align the sample's medium level with zero.

The inverse of the distance between the previously chosen category and each alternative in the choice set. Inter-category distance was calculated as the cosine distance between categories' probability vectors of features, where each element represents the probability of a given amenity in a category, summed across all 54 amenities; the formula for the distance is only partially readable in the text.

A binary indicator of whether a given category was chosen at a category-switching event, constructed in a dyadic database where each observation reflects a potential choice. All listing periods in which a category switch occurred were paired with all categories other than the one the listing originated from; the main analyses use a reduced choice set of five alternative categories selected for each listing based on the highest feature similarity (cosine similarity between the listing's vector of offered amenities and the category's average amenity profile) in addition to the one actually chosen.
Placeholder not used; see m_category_choice.

Term frequency of integrity-related words in the CEO's speech in the free-form question and answer sections of quarterly earnings conference calls. The dictionary contains 226 words derived from the machine-learning-supported dictionary of Li et al. (2021) and refined by the authors to capture the personal value of integrity at the CEO level. Only Q&A sections in which the respective CEO speaks at least 200 words are considered. The final scores are averaged over a 3-year window going back from the focal year using all available transcripts for the respective 3-year window.
time_window: 3-year window going back from the focal year

description: Term frequency of integrity-related words in the CEO's speech in the free-form question and answer sections of quarterly earnings conference calls, based on the same 226-word dictionary refined for the CEO level. Only Q&A sections in which the respective CEO speaks at least 200 words are considered. Scores are averaged over a 3-year window going back from the focal year.
time_window: 3-year window going back from the focal year

description: Composite measure of a firm's M&A activity in a given firm-year. It combines the number of M&As (M&A Number) and the natural logarithm of M&A transaction volume (M&A Volume). Both measures are standardized and aggregated into the composite measure of M&A Activity.
Binary variable based on the SDC categorization of deals. It equals 1 for cross-border deals and 0 for domestic deals.

Relative markup on top of the target's market valuation that the acquirer pays to gain access to the target's resource base. It represents a combination of the SDC price premium and the component premium using a period of 42 days, according to Officer (2003).

Absolute value of cumulative abnormal returns (CARs) from 2 days before to 2 days after the deal announcement, calculated with the event study methodology of Brown and Warner (1985) and interpreted as the amplitude of performance extremeness.
time_window: 2 days before to 2 days after the deal announcement

description: Natural logarithm of the number of days between the announcement and the closure of the deal.

A Herfindahl-style measure of the degree of concentration in cross-border collaborations with MNC i's inventors in country j in year t. xk is the number of cross-border collaborations involving inventor k and m denotes the total number of inventors belonging to MNC i and located in country j. The value of the measure ranges from 1/m to 1, with higher values indicating cross-border collaborations concentrated around fewer inventors. The equation as printed is unreadable in the extracted text.

The number of patents invented by the inventors of MNC i located in country j during year t + 1. A patent is assigned to a year based on the date when the firm filed its patent application, and patents are aggregated by MNC-host country based on the inventors' addresses.

Measured using effective size, capturing the extent to which a focal country serves as a broker connecting otherwise unconnected countries in the multinational co-inventor network. The cross-country network is constructed from MNC co-inventor data, where each node is a country and each tie indicates cross-border co-invention activity between inventors in different countries; the effective size of each host country's ego network is computed for each MNC. k indexes countries directly connected to j, q represents third-party countries also connected to j, pjq is the proportion of j's ties invested in alter q, and mkq is the marginal strength of k's connection to q. The equation as printed is unreadable in the extracted text.

An averaged distance-weighted reach measure that considers the number of inventors reachable by network path from a given inventor and the path length involved. m is the number of MNC i's inventors in the within-country network of country j and dpq is the minimum (geodesic) distance from a focal inventor p to inventor q. The variable ranges from 0 to m - 1, with higher scores indicating a greater reach. The equation as printed is unreadable in the extracted text.

The ratio of the actual number of local co-inventing ties to the total possible number in the context of country j of MNC i at time t. Possible ties refers to the number of potential ties, m(m - 1)/2, based on the total number of inventors m in country j. The equation as printed is unreadable in the extracted text.

The firm-level change of the fractional count of distinct types of formal R&D alliance partners over time. The count (y) ranges from 0 to 7 and is converted to a fractional variablerestricted to the interval [0,1].

variable_name: Above historical aspiration / Below historical aspiration
description: Calculated using a firm's price-cost margin (PCM) compared to exponentially weighted moving averages of historical performance (alpha = 0.7).

variable_name: Above social aspiration / Below social aspiration
description: Calculated as price-cost margin (PCM) relative to the performance of peers in the same two-digit sector and size class.
Binary variable: 1 for survey wave 2011 covering the financial crisis period 2008-2010; 0 otherwise.

The economic upturn is the complement of the downturn indicator: survey years outside the 2008-2010 Great Recession (all other waves from 1999 to 2020) are coded as upturn, and the 2011 wave covering the downturn is coded as not upturn. It is the same binary variable as economic downturn, read the other way.
Equals 1 if a startup completed the full accelerator program and 0 otherwise.

A composite score created based on a factor analysis using three team-level variables: Formal Education, Senior Management Experience, and Entrepreneurship Experience. The score was standardized to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Founding teams were also grouped into Low, Intermediate, and High subgroups based on whether their PEK scores were one standard deviation below the mean, within one standard deviation of the mean, or one standard deviation above the mean.

A startup's revenue during the calendar year following selection into the accelerator program. The measure is highly skewed, so a constant value of 1 is added and a natural-log transformation is taken.
time_window: calendar year following selection into the accelerator program (t + 1)

description: The number of full-time-equivalent employees of a startup during the calendar year following selection into the accelerator program. Part-time employees are excluded. A constant value of 1 is added and a natural-log transformation is taken.
time_window: calendar year following selection into the accelerator program (t + 1)

description: The equity financing a startup raised during the calendar year following selection into the accelerator program. A constant value of 1 is added and a natural-log transformation is taken.
time_window: calendar year following selection into the accelerator program (t + 1)

description: A binary indicator of whether the program has a structured curriculum, constructed from survey data collected from program managers. Program managers were asked: 'Does this program have a structured curriculum that is distributed to participants in written or electronic form?'

A binary indicator of whether the program has an explicit sector focus, constructed from survey data collected from program managers. Program managers were asked: 'Does this program have an explicit sector focus?'

The dependent variable is a theater-specific instantaneous rate of closing between the year the theater's focal county acquired TV coverage and 1962. The theater is the unit at risk, with duration measured as the time a theater has been open either since the first year its county received TV broadcast coverage or its founding year, whichever is later. Variation in the timing of closing is represented by a semi-parametric piecewise exponential function with the duration scale broken at 1, 3, and 9 years.

Measured as the proportion of TV shows with movie genres in a given year, lagged by one year. A genre was coded as a movie genre if it existed in feature films released between 1933 and 1944. Each show's grade of membership in movie genres divides the count of movie genres a show is based on by its total number of genres; these grades of membership are summed over all shows broadcast in a year and divided by the density of all shows to obtain a proportion.

A county-year measure of how much more closely TV shows reflect public discourse than movies do.
