Worker-reported stress from the app-based employee survey, measured on a 1–5 Likert scale. Stress-related items are reverse-coded such that a score of five reflects the lowest level of stress, and average scores are aggregated to the worker-month level.

Survey items covering workers' own sales forecasts and confidence in those forecasts, collected through the firm's workforce management app from June 2019 through January 2020. The authors examine treatment effects on these forecasts across forecast horizons.

Number of days of attendance in a month, one of the four individual labor supply and performance measures. The authors use attendance and productivity measures to test whether the treatments changed workers' labor supply under the career concerns channel.

Monthly compensation, which the authors describe as a measure of overall performance. The compensation scheme includes piece rates, task bonuses, and sales commissions; individual sales are calculated as the sum of pre-paid card and service package sales, and customer pick counts a task when the client selects the same spa worker for future visits.
Log of monthly store revenue, measured at the store-month level from January through December 2019 and used in the difference-in-differences estimation with store and month fixed effects.

App-based survey questions including overall satisfaction, trust, sense of belonging, whether an employee would recommend the company as a place to work, and willingness to stay. All items are measured on a 1–5 Likert scale, with higher values indicating greater satisfaction, and average scores are aggregated to the worker-month level.

App-based survey questions capturing employee-reported levels of managerial care, problem-solving skills, willingness to seek help from managers, ease of requesting leave, and perceived fairness. Items are measured on a 1–5 Likert scale, with higher values indicating more favorable evaluations of managers, and average scores are aggregated to the worker-month level.

In Samples 1 and 2, investment motive was manipulated by instructing participants to assume the role of an equity investor whose primary objective was to achieve financial returns (economic motive) or the role of an impact investor not seeking financial return who evaluates ideas by their alignment with personal values (non-economic motive). In Sample 3, motive was measured with two 7-point items capturing economic and non-economic motives; participants who equally endorsed both were excluded and the remaining participants were categorized into a dominant motivation using a binary indicator.
scale: binary indicator (0 = economic motive, 1 = non-economic motive); contributing items on 7-point scales

description: Investment motive was not experimentally manipulated in Study 2; participants' motive was measured with the two questions used to classify economically and non-economically motivated investors. Participants who endorsed economic and non-economic motives equally were excluded, and the remaining participants were operationalized with a binary indicator reflecting their dominant motivation.
scale: binary indicator (0 = economic motive, 1 = non-economic motive)

description: Investment motive was experimentally induced by altering the content of the prescribed investor role to emphasize either an economic or a non-economic investment logic. As a manipulation check, participants in the economic condition reported a stronger economic motive and a weaker non-economic motive than participants in the non-economic condition.

Five items adapted from prior construal level manipulations and operationalizations. The foundational item asked: 'When making investment decisions, to what extent do you focus on feasibility (how aspects) or desirability (why aspects)?'. The next two items captured feasibility and desirability concerns separately, and the final two items adapted 'how' versus 'why' distinctions from prior construal level manipulations; the items capture participants' dominant construal orientation rather than constituting a standardized scale.
scale: 7-point scales; foundational item anchored 1 = 'entirely feasibility-focused' to 7 = 'entirely desirability-focused'

description: The same five-item measure used in Study 1 (Samples 1 and 2) was used to capture default construal level in Study 3.

Participants were randomly assigned to a high- or low-construal framing condition presented as a pitch slide describing quantum key distribution (QKD) technology, with all other elements held constant. In the high-construal ('why') condition the pitch emphasized long-term benefits and broad impacts through purpose and societal relevance, future value, conceptual language, and symbolic or value-based resonance. In the low-construal ('how') condition the pitch emphasized technical details and operational specifics through operational detail, step-by-step processes, technical language, and tangible functionality.

The same experimental procedure as in Study 2 was used to manipulate construal frame, varying the content of the description of the technology under consideration, but the focal technology was changed from QKD to a portable solar-powered cooler to enhance generalizability. After random assignment to an economic or non-economic motive, participants were randomly assigned to a high- or low-construal framing of the technology presented as a pitch slide.

A single-item indicator of participants' immediate emotional experience, measured among economically motivated investors by asking: 'To what extent did you feel hopeful after reading about QKD technology?'. The item was intended to capture the state-level experience of feeling hopeful, the phenomenological core of hope as conceptualized in hope theory.

A single-item indicator measured among non-economically motivated investors by asking: 'To what extent did you feel amazement after reading about QKD technology?'. The authors focused on amazement because awe is theorized as an emotional response to stimuli perceived as extraordinary and amazement has been identified as a core component of that emotional state.

Participants were asked: 'Would you be willing to invest in the development of QKD technology?' and 'How likely would you be to support the development of QKD technology with a monetary contribution?'. The average of the two items was used as the measure.

A five-item scale that included the single-item measure used in Study 2 ('I feel hopeful about this technology') plus four additional items adapted from prior work on state hope. The items capture the two core components of hope theory: perceived confidence that the technology can succeed (agency) and the perception that viable, workable paths exist for achieving that success (pathways). Responses were averaged to form a composite measure.

A five-item scale capturing participants' experience of amazement and perceived vastness in response to the technology, including the single-item measure used in Study 2 ('I feel amazed when thinking about this technology') plus four additional items adapted from prior research on awe. The items assess feelings of amazement, perceived vastness, and the sense that the technology transcends current understanding, and were averaged to form a composite measure.

Study 3 employed the same measure of willingness to invest used in Study 2, the average of two items asking about willingness to invest in and to support with a monetary contribution the technology under consideration.

Binary outcome representing announced decisions to retire the coal generator ahead of schedule, identified from records supplied by the Sierra Club. These records included the announcements of 570 retirement decisions. Generators left the dataset after an announcement.

The number of jobs attributed to the coal generator divided by the total number of jobs in the county. Coal plant employment came from FERC Form 1 for 215 of 500 plants; missing values were predicted with an OLS model regressing employment on the plant's number of generators, nameplate size, capacity factor, and generation totals by fuel type. Each generator's share of plant employment was calculated by multiplying plant employment by the percentage of the plant's capacity belonging to the generator; county-year employment totals came from BLS data.

The number of jobs attributed to the coal generator divided by the estimated total number of utility jobs. Total utility workforce was estimated by expanding FERC data on coal, natural gas and nuclear plants and adding BLS industry averages of employees per establishment for other plant types. The larger the proportion, the more the organization's workforce would be affected by a closure.

Cumulative count of local news articles that machine-learning classification indicated as movement criticism of the focal plant, generated by generator-month, logged to correct for skewness and lagged by 1 month. The corpus covered 416 newspapers within 100 miles of each generator; a Multinomial Naïve Bayes classifier trained on 335 manually coded articles and a 2,905-word feature set achieved 85% accuracy on a holdout set of 60 articles.

Indicator variable demarcating a for-profit firm, as opposed to a government or cooperative utility. In the U.S. electric utility context, cooperatives are typically nonprofit organizations and government utilities include municipal, state, and federal entities.
Dummy indicator for whether the state had a consumer advocate to represent consumers in rate cases; the data were provided by Guy Holburn.

Logged capacity in megawatts of new solar generators built by utilities that also had coal-fired generators. Using capacity means the measure includes information about the investment size. Twenty-one new solar generators were observed over the period.
The newspaper-based campaign activity measure, aggregated to the utility-state-year level; independent variables in the solar models were lagged 2 years.

The number of net metering customers at the utility-state-year level, as reported by the EIA, logged to correct for skewness. With more prosumers, there should be greater pressure on utilities to make exploratory investments in the solar technology favored by these disaffected customers.

Binary variable coded 1 if a high-ranking military officer (colonel or above) or their close relative (sibling or spouse) was part of the airline's founding senior management team, advisory board, or a major investor, and 0 otherwise. It was coded with archival information from the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, following Hiatt et al. (2018). In the instrumental variable analysis the instrumented value of this variable is used.

Binary variable indicating whether an airline has logistics support, shared use of military airports/airfields/bases, operational partnerships such as aircraft leasing arrangements, route transactions, military personnel employment, or collaborative training programs (1 = partnership present, 0 = absent). Two research assistants and one coauthor independently coded the variable from Davies (1984), achieving 97% initial agreement.

A keyword-based classification of whether the airline's name carries explicit military connotations, looking for terms historically associated with military aviation such as militar, naval, and aeronáutica, as well as naming structures that resemble formal military units, such as numbered groups or squadrons. Airline names were checked for partial and case-insensitive matches to capture explicit military references even in compound names or abbreviations.

Measured by the establishment of new international routes by airlines based on Davies (1984), excluding non-operational ones such as those that were experimental or proposed but not implemented. Coded 1 if the focal airline established an international route in a country in a given year, and 0 otherwise. Two research assistants and one co-author independently coded the variable, achieving an agreement rate of above 95%.

variable_name: Transition from military to civilian air traffic control
description: Coded 1 if the transition from military to civilian air traffic control had already happened and 0 if not. The timing was determined by searching legal documents, government websites of the countries, and Civil Air Navigation Services Organization records.
Coded 1 if the observation is after a domestic military coup occurred and 0 otherwise, taken from the Coups Agency and Mechanisms database and the Colpus dataset.

Number of BLM protests in the CBSA where the firm is headquartered that were reported to have included violence, per one million CBSA population. The variable is captured in a four-week moving window so that firms had time to debate, develop and announce a response; protest events with three or fewer participants are excluded. Violence is defined as reports of any property damage or injuries to police officers caused by the protests; injuries to BLM protesters and police arrests of protesters are excluded.
time_window: four-week moving window (weeks t-4 through t-1)

description: Number of incidents of non-BLM protests with reported violence that occurred in the firm's headquarters CBSA between January 2017 and April 2020, divided by CBSA population (per one million). The measure is time-invariant across the observation window and is scaled per capita to enable comparisons across communities of different sizes.

Number of police shootings of Black Americans per one million Black residents in a CBSA minus the number of police shootings per one million for other racial or ethnic groups within the same CBSA. The measure is time-invariant and captures all police shooting events from January 2015 to April 2020, prior to the murder of George Floyd.
scale: difference in police shootings per one million residents

description: Dummy variable equal to 1 if the firm announced any diversity action intended to benefit Black Americans and/or undefined racial minorities in the focal week, and 0 otherwise. Actions were hand-coded from press releases and media articles; announcements using related terms such as ''racial diversity'' and ''people of color'' were counted. Reports on diversity or CSR ratings, actions to settle lawsuits or conciliation agreements, and appointments of minority directors and executives were excluded.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the firm publicly endorsed the BLM movement in its announcement of corporate diversity actions, and 0 otherwise, collected from press releases and media articles. An announcement counted as an endorsement when the firm explicitly expressed ''Black lives matter'', when it opposed movements counter to BLM, or when it suggested its actions were prompted by the death of George Floyd.

Six items assessed the intensity and direction of efforts expended in knowledge acquisition. Items were measured on a seven-point disagree/agree scale and were partially based on existing items regarding absorptive capacity and market orientation. The scale was reliable (alpha = .79).
scale: seven-point disagree/agree scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Three items measured assimilation and gauged the extent to which units were able to analyze and understand new external knowledge. Items were measured on a seven-point disagree/agree scale; the scale was reliable (alpha = .76).
scale: seven-point disagree/agree scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Six items measured transformation and assessed the extent to which units were able to facilitate recognizing opportunities and consequences of new external knowledge for existing operations, structures, and strategies. Items were measured on a seven-point disagree/agree scale; the scale was reliable (alpha = .72).
scale: seven-point disagree/agree scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Six items tapped into the extent to which units were able to exploit new external knowledge; the scale gauged the ability of units to incorporate new external knowledge into their operations. Items were measured on a seven-point disagree/agree scale; the scale was reliable (alpha = .71).
scale: seven-point disagree/agree scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Managers were asked to indicate the extent to which their unit used liaison personnel, temporary task forces, and permanent teams to coordinate activities. The final measure was a weighted average of the three items, ranging from 1 for liaison personnel to 3 for permanent teams. The scale was not subjected to confirmatory factor analysis because of its weighted structure.
scale: weights from 1 (liaison personnel) to 3 (permanent teams); reported mean 4.39, s.d. 1.18

description: Participation was measured with the construct of participation in decision making from previous research. The scale was reliable (alpha = .79).
Job rotation was measured with two items that tapped the extent to which employees were rotated between different functions within and between subunits. The scale was reliable (alpha = .77).
Formalization was measured with a five-item scale from Deshpande and Zaltman (1982). The scale was reliable (alpha = .73).

Routinization tapped the extent to which tasks within units were invariable, uniform, or predictable. Withey et al.'s (1983) exceptions scale, which is based on Perrow's (1967) work on unit technology, was the measure of routinization. The scale was reliable (alpha = .73).

Connectedness was measured with a four-item scale (Jaworski & Kohli, 1993). Connectedness measured the extent to which individuals in organizational units were networked to various levels of the hierarchy. The scale was reliable (alpha = .74).

Two categorizations of Van Maanen and Schein's model (collective versus individual and serial versus disjunctive tactics) were used. Because the authors were interested in the overall effect of socialization tactics, they constructed a measure for socialization tactics by averaging the scores of collective socialization tactics and serial socialization tactics.

The number of financial analysts who upgraded their stock recommendation of the focal firm following the new CEO's first strategic announcement, as a percentage of the total number of analysts who actively covered the company (i.e., made or revised stock recommendations following the strategic action announcement). Upgrades serve as the numerator and total analysts actively making recommendations—upgrades, holds, and downgrades—standardize it, so the measure gauges the net change in how analysts evaluated the new information. The authors identified each analyst's first evaluative report within a month of the strategic action date.
time_window: first analyst report within a month of the strategic action announcement

description: Counts the number of days between the CEO's appointment date and the announcement of the first strategic action. The appointment date was taken from ExecuComp and the CEO succession database and verified against RavenPack; the first strategic action was identified by scouring informational releases for new product or market expansions, acquisitions, strategic alliances, capacity changes to the firm, and large-scale divestitures or spinoffs. The final version of the variable is calculated as the natural log of new CEO strategic action speed, because the raw values are lognormally distributed with skewness in the right tail.
time_window: from CEO appointment date to first strategic action announcement

description: A binary variable taking a value of "1" if the previous CEO was involuntarily dismissed and "0" if not. The authors consulted the codes delineated by Gentry and colleagues (2021), categorizing the variable as CEO dismissal when the CEO stepped down for reasons related to job performance, including immediate termination, termination after a transition period, or termination for behavioral or policy-related problems.

Assumes the value of "1" when the incoming focal new CEO was hired from outside the organization and "0" if they worked for the company within the previous two years or were an heir apparent. Insider or outsider status was identified by consulting employment records in ExecuComp and determining whether the focal new CEO was previously at the same firm.

Captures the median overall stock recommendation across all the analysts covering the firm at the time of the CEO succession. Analysts' discrete stock recommendations in the form of "strong buy, buy, hold, sell, and strong sell" are coded numerically as "5" to "1", respectively, and the variable reflects the median of these numerically coded stock recommendations across the analysts actively assigned to the firm.
time_window: at the time of the CEO succession

description: A binary variable that takes the value of "1" if the new CEO's first strategic announcement did not exist in the firm's competitive repertoire over the course of the prior year, and "0" if the firm had previously employed that type of activity. The strategic action is compared against the firm's repertoire in the prior year, which the authors argue constitutes a meaningful temporal period to produce strategic complexity.

Standardized unanticipated earnings; the SUE score measures the number of standard deviations the reported earnings deviate from the I/B/E/S deviation mean estimates for a firm for the reporting period, computed as (actual EPS - deviation mean) / standard deviation of deviation. A positive SUE score represents positive earnings deviations and a negative SUE score represents negative earnings deviations.

Investor reactions to earnings events are captured by computing the firm's cumulative abnormal returns, the sum of the abnormal returns to a firm on each day of the observation window; abnormal returns are the difference between observed market returns and the theoretically expected market returns derived from the Fama and French (1993) three-factor model. The event window runs from one day before the earnings announcement to one day after (t-1 to t+1), and the baseline normal period is 250 trading days starting 295 trading days and ending 45 days before the earnings disclosure. Values range from negative to positive, with positive CARs representing positive investor reactions.
time_window: event window t-1 to t+1; baseline 250 trading days ending 45 days before the earnings disclosure

description: Measured in the year prior to the earnings deviation by content analyzing the language used in the annual CEO letter to shareholders, using the regulatory focus dictionary used by prior researchers together with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software to determine the number of promotion-focused words per 1,000 words in the shareholder letter. The dictionary is empirically validated and includes 27 promotion words.
time_window: t-1 (year prior to the earnings deviation)

description: Measured in the year prior to the earnings deviation by content analyzing the language used in the annual CEO letter to shareholders, using the regulatory focus dictionary used by prior researchers together with Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software to determine the number of prevention-focused words per 1,000 words in the shareholder letter. The dictionary is empirically validated and includes 25 prevention words.
time_window: t-1 (year prior to the earnings deviation)

description: For each work, the cosine distance between its feature vector and the feature vector of each of the pieces in the 19th-century corpus was computed, and the average of these 2,000 cosine distances represents the distance of the focal work from the corpus. The distance varies between 0 and 1, wherein the greater this distance for the focal work, the more distinct it is. The aggregate distinctiveness from prior competitors for an artist in a year is the average of the cosine distances of all the works they created in that year; if an artist did not have any work in a given year, the work they created in the most recent year before the given year was used. Feature vectors were extracted with a convolutional neural network applied to each artwork image.

The peers comprised the focal artist's alters in the exhibition network in a given year, and the reference group for each focal artist is a moving one-year window of all their alters' work created one year before a given year. The measure is the average of the cosine distances of a focal work from those in the reference group, and the artist-level value for a year is the average of the cosine distance values of all the artist's works created in that year. If an artist did not have any work in a given year, the work they created in the most recent year before the given year was used.
time_window: One-year window of alters' work before the focal year

description: For each year, the cosine distance of all of a focal artist's works created that year from each of the artist's own works created five to 15 years before was computed; for example, for works created in 1914 the reference group was all their works created in 1899-1909. The five-year lag is to allow an artist's own recent work to have had enough time on the market to constitute a meaningful reference group in audiences' minds. The distinctiveness for each focal painting is the average of the cosine distances of a focal work from those in the reference group, and the artist-year value is the average of these values for all works the artist created in that year.
time_window: Reference window of the artist's own works five to 15 years before the focal year

description: A count of the number of exhibition opportunities afforded to each artist for each year between 1905 and 1916. Data on exhibition opportunities were gathered from the DoME collection, which catalogs exhibitions of modern art paintings and drawings by European artists.

The geographic breadth of exhibition opportunities, computed as the count of the number of unique cities where an artist's exhibitions took place. It is an alternative dependent variable to the exhibition count, taken from the same DoME exhibition records.

Two artists were considered connected in the peer network if they were included in the same exhibition, as represented in DoME, and a cumulative time-varying network based on the artists' coexhibitions in Europe for 1905-1916 was constructed. Peer-network status was based on eigenvector centrality and calculated as the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix resulting from the exhibition network. A squared term of peer network status is also entered in the models.
time_window: Cumulative from 1905 to the focal year

description: Each of an artist's exhibitions in previous years entered the calculation, weighted by the exhibition venue's status at the time of that exhibition. The venue's status in every year is its eigenvector centrality in the valued venue by venue network, where two venues are connected according to how many times in prior years both presented the same artist.
time_window: Exhibitions in previous years, weighted by venue status at the time of the exhibition

description: Latent construct indicated by two observed variables: expected volume fluctuations and uncertain volume estimates. Sales managers answered questions about the level of volume uncertainty on a Likert-type scale of 1 to 5. The reliability of the construct was .59.

Latent construct initially indicated by two observed variables: changes in specifications and technological improvements. Product engineering managers reported the frequency of expected specification changes and the probability of future technological improvements on a Likert-type scale of 1 to 5. The two indicators correlated .93, so the second measure was dropped from further analysis and the construct was carried by the first indicator.

Latent construct indicated by three observed variables: difference in manufacturing process, difference in scale of operations, and the natural logarithm of the division's estimate of the annual savings to make a component. The purchasing manager judged supplier advantages in operations and manufacturing on a Likert-type scale of 1 to 5. The reliability of the construct was .68.
scale: 1 to 5 Likert-type for the judgment items; natural logarithm for annual savings to make

description: Latent construct indicated by three observed variables: competitiveness of quotes, number of suppliers, and supplier proprietary technology. The component purchasing manager answered the questions on a Likert-type scale of 1 to 5. The construct was reverse scaled in the estimated model. Its reliability was .70.

Latent construct indicated by two observed variables: buyer tools and equipment and buyer manufacturing technology. Manufacturing engineering provided information about the division's experience in producing each component and rated it on a Likert-type scale of 1 to 5. The reliability of the construct was .66.

The observed outcome variable of the model, the actual governance mode chosen for each component after the committee's evaluation. Decisions were coded 0 for make and 1 for buy. It was the only construct indicated by a single observed variable.

A four-item scale derived from the Yale Survey on innovation, in which technology managers answered Likert-style questions about their line of business and their answers were averaged across respondents in each line of business. The first item is 'patents to prevent competitors from duplicating the process' and the second is 'patents to secure royalty income', both responses to the question about capturing and protecting the advantages of new or improved production processes; the third and fourth items are the same but asked about new or improved products. All items were weighted equally and measured on a seven-point scale from 1 (not at all effective) to 7 (very effective); the scale had a Cronbach's alpha of 0.78. Line-of-business mean scores were matched to patents by mapping each patent's six-digit primary patent classification to a SIC code with the USPTO concordance and then to the Levin et al. (1987) SIC concordance; where the patent's SIC code was more aggregated, the effectiveness scores were averaged across all corresponding lines of business.
level: line of business, matched to patent
time_window: Yale Survey measures matched to patents issued 1980-1996

description: Annual spells were constructed that begin when a patent is issued and end when a patent is first licensed. The variable was coded 1 if the TLO records revealed that a patent was first licensed in that year, 0 otherwise, and patents that were not licensed during the observation period were treated as censored. Of the 1,397 inventions in the sample, 51.3% were licensed.

TLO records were examined to identify the entity that licensed each of the 717 licensed patents. The licensees were coded 'noninventor' if the entity was a firm that was not founded by any of the inventors listed on the patent, and the authors predict the probability of license to noninventors. The authors note that license to inventors and license to noninventors are not inverse operationalizations because some patents were licensed by both inventors and noninventors.

An indicator of licenses taken by firms founded by one of the inventors on the patent, entering the termination and first-sale models as a main effect and interacted with patent effectiveness. The authors also note that in unreported regressions they examine the probability that the licensee will be a firm founded by one of the inventors, with qualitatively the same results. Firm founding rather than consulting or advisory board membership is used because it represents the construct of entrepreneurship and captures equity ownership.

Annual spells were constructed that begin when a patent is first licensed and end when the license agreement's coverage for a patent is terminated. The variable was coded 1 if TLO records revealed that the license agreement coverage for a patent was terminated in that year, 0 otherwise, and licensed patents that were not terminated during the observation period were treated as censored. Of the 966 patent-licensing efforts in the sample, 33.4% were terminated.

Annual spells were constructed that begin when a patent was licensed and end when a product or process using the licensed patent first generated revenues through sale to another company. The variable was coded 1 if the TLO records revealed that a first sale occurred in that year, 0 otherwise, and a patent was treated as censored if a product or process using it did not achieve a first sale during the observation period. Of the 966 patent-licensing efforts in the sample, 20.4% were embodied in products or processes that reached a first sale.

The dollar value of the nonequity royalty payments made to MIT from sales of products that employed licensed patents through 1997, for the 167 inventions that had been commercialized by noninventors; option fees, patent maintenance fees, sublicense revenues, and one-time fees are not included. The variable was constructed from the TLO records of its royalty receipts, and because the royalty receipts are highly skewed the log of the royalty figure is predicted.

The overall U.S. News & World Report graduate school ranking (1991-1998), a measure of the relative status ordering of different institutions as perceived by university presidents, deans, and admissions directors. U.S. News & World Report distributes questionnaires asking respondents to evaluate the prestige of other schools by placing them into four quartiles; four points were given for each vote in the top quartile, three for the second, two for the third, and one for the last category. Universities were then placed in order of their scores and ranked against one another, and because some years were reported in ranks and others on a scale, the scores were converted to ranks to make all years consistent.

variable_name: Annual count of new technology licensing and option agreements
description: The annual count of new technology licensing and option agreements established by the university. These data are provided by AUTM through their surveys of university technology licensing offices.

The Pearson correlation between evaluations performed by corporate and subsidiary managers for each of the 29 different knowledge dimensions across all firms. Significance against the null hypothesis that the correlation is at or above a benchmark level is assessed with computer simulations of samples drawn from a population with the given correlation.

The absolute difference between the evaluation of a capability dimension of a specific subsidiary by subsidiary managers and the evaluation by corporate managers. It is an integer variable restricted to be at least zero, with a maximum of six on the seven-point scale.

One corporate manager at each firm responded to the statement: "There is strong agreement among managers on how to define the indicator [X]," for each capability dimension X, using a seven-point Likert scale ranging from "I strongly disagree" to "I strongly agree."

One corporate manager at each firm responded to the statement: "It is easy to evaluate a subsidiary's expertise in [X]," for each capability dimension X, using a seven-point Likert scale ranging from "I strongly disagree" to "I strongly agree."

One corporate manager at each firm responded to the statement: "It is easy to describe, document and teach the capabilities required being skilled at [X]," for each capability dimension X, using a seven-point Likert scale ranging from "I strongly disagree" to "I strongly agree." Higher values denote more articulable, i.e. less tacit, capabilities.

Corporate managers responded to the statement: "The capabilities of [subsidiary x] are well understood by us," using a seven-point Likert scale ranging from "I strongly disagree" to "I strongly agree."
Subsidiary and corporate managers were asked for the number of years that they have spent in marketing in any firm.

On a frequency scale where 1 = daily and 7 = yearly or even less frequently, subsidiary managers indicated how often they communicated with corporate managers face to face and by other means, i.e., not face to face, to discuss operations. The communication items were reverse-coded so that a higher number is associated with more frequent communication.

A two-item scale based on Ghoshal's (1986) scales for the strategic importance and competitive intensity of the markets in which each subsidiary operates. Corporate managers assessed each market "in terms of strategic importance for [the firm]" on a seven-point Likert scale from "not important" to "extremely important," and "in terms of presence of key global competitors" on a seven-point Likert scale from "no presence" to "strong presence." The correlation between the two dimensions was 0.52.

Both corporate and subsidiary respondents assessed the profitability of subsidiaries on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from "much below average" to "much above average" with "average" as the midpoint. Subsidiary respondents evaluated the "operating profit" of their own subsidiary; corporate respondents evaluated each subsidiary on the same scale.
scale: 7-point Likert (much below average to much above average)

description: Subsidiary managers were asked for the year in which their unit was established; the age of the subsidiary is the number of years from the starting year to 1997 (when the survey was distributed).

Kogut and Singh's (1988) estimation of the Euclidean distance from the subsidiary country to the multinational companies' home country, i.e., Sweden, using Hofstede's (1991) four dimensions of national culture.

Subsidiary managers marked on a scale ranging from 1 to 7 whether they agreed that their firm's strategy was best characterized as "A high level of responsiveness to national markets where local, functional units typically enjoy a high degree of autonomy" or "a tightly integrated chain of subsidiaries that covers several geographical markets with internationally standardized output."

The dependent variable is the transition rate between active units and their failure. The length of time is calculated by subtracting the founding date (or acquisition date by the current owner) from the exit date or from December 31, 1999 if the unit is still open for business. Units were considered failures only if they had closed down; franchisor-affiliated units that became unaffiliated or vice versa were not considered failures.

For each unit, the owner's congenital experience is a summation across all time periods between the owner's first unit and the unit's founding, counting units affiliated with the owner at each time period and dividing by a discount factor. Local experience includes only the owner's existing units within the closest 25 units from unit i. The square root discount factor is used in the reported regressions.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year spell; experience discounted to the unit's founding

description: For each unit, the owner's congenital experience is a summation across all time periods between the owner's first unit and the unit's founding, counting units affiliated with the owner at each time period and dividing by a discount factor. Distant experience includes only the owner's existing units outside the closest 25 units but within Texas. The square root discount factor is used in the reported regressions.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year spell; experience discounted to the unit's founding

variable_name: Same Franchisor/Other Owners' Local Congenital Experience
description: For each franchisee-affiliated unit, separate levels of congenital experience are calculated for the owner of that unit and for its franchisor. The Same Franchisor/Other Owners' Congenital Experience variables include experience gained at the units of other franchisees affiliated with the same franchisor and at company-owned units of that franchisor. For a unit company owned by a franchisor, the variables include experience gained only at the units of franchisees affiliated with the same franchisor. Local experience includes only units within the closest 25 units from unit i.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year spell; experience discounted to the unit's founding

variable_name: Same Franchisor/Other Owners' Distant Congenital Experience
description: For each franchisee-affiliated unit, separate levels of congenital experience are calculated for the owner of that unit and for its franchisor. The Same Franchisor/Other Owners' Congenital Experience variables include experience gained at the units of other franchisees affiliated with the same franchisor and at company-owned units of that franchisor. For a unit company owned by a franchisor, the variables include experience gained only at the units of franchisees affiliated with the same franchisor. Distant experience includes only units outside the closest 25 units but within Texas.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year spell; experience discounted to the unit's founding

The length of time is calculated by subtracting the founding date (or acquisition date by the current owner) from the exit date or from December 31, 1999 if the unit is still open for business. Units were considered failures only if they had closed down; franchisor-affiliated units that became unaffiliated or vice versa were not considered failures.

Local experience includes only the owner's existing units within the closest 25 units from unit i. The square root discount factor is used in the reported regressions.

Distant experience includes only the owner's existing units outside the closest 25 units but within Texas. The square root discount factor is used in the reported regressions.
time_window: measured at the beginning of each one-year spell; experience discounted to the unit's founding

description: Waste prevention is the weighted average of a firm's facility-level scores (RW_it) based on the percentage of total production that each facility represents for the company. The facility score is the standardized negative residual from an OLS regression of log waste generation on facility size (quadratic) within each 4-digit SIC code and year, with the sign changed so that positive scores indicate more waste prevention.

The ratio of the material treated onsite (e.g., treated, burned, or recycled) to the total waste generated is calculated for each facility; the average and standard deviation of these ratios are computed for each SIC code in each year and a deviation is calculated for each facility. These deviations are then summed to form a firm measure of onsite management (waste treatment).

Waste transfer measures the percentage of waste that is processed offsite and is calculated in the same way as onsite waste treatment: facility deviations from the SIC-year average ratio are computed and then summed to form a firm measure.

Waste generation is calculated as the sum of predicted waste generation (W*) across all facilities owned by a firm, i.e., the best guess for how much waste the company would have generated if it were an average performer for its size in its industry.

A firm-level variable created by taking the natural log of the total toxicity-weighted emissions across all of a firm's facilities. Releases of the 246 "core" toxic chemicals consistently reported in the U.S. EPA's Toxic Release Inventory are summed, with each chemical weighted by its toxicity using the Reportable Quantities (RQ) list in the CERCLA statute.

ROA is a standard accounting measure of financial performance found commonly in strategy research, calculated by dividing earnings before interest by average total firm assets. The sample is smaller for ROA than for Tobin's q, primarily because of missing data on firm income levels, and 29 observations where ROA was more than five standard deviations away from the mean were eliminated.

Calculated by dividing the sum of firm equity value, book value of long-term debt, and net current liabilities by total assets. The authors use this simplified measure rather than the more complicated measure proposed by Lindenberg and Ross because past research found little qualitative difference.

Profitability per labor unit, in thousands of 1958 Israeli Lira: the market value of agricultural output minus direct expenses for agriculture, divided by units of labor used for agriculture (in thousands of days). Measured for each kibbutz in each year.

For kibbutz i in year T, an accumulation over the life of kibbutz i of the labor units employed by the other kibbutzim that were members of its federation, summed to the year preceding the observation. The kibbutz's own experience is not included.
time_window: cumulative since 1954 to the year preceding the observation

description: For kibbutz i in year T, an accumulation over the life of kibbutz i of the labor units employed by the other kibbutzim that were not members of its federation, summed to the year preceding the observation.
time_window: cumulative since 1954 to the year preceding the observation

description: The cumulative labor units used by the kibbutz in its history since 1954 to the year preceding the observation. A squared term, (Own Experience)2, was also included in the models in case competency traps caused profitability to decrease at high levels of a kibbutz's own experience.
time_window: cumulative since 1954 to the year preceding the observation

description: The total number of a university's equity interests divided by the number of the university's active licenses for 1998. Active licenses are the cumulative number of licenses that had not terminated by the end of 1998. The total number of equity deals is from the authors' survey, verified against the AUTM survey; the number of active licenses is from the 1998 AUTM survey. The share is a fraction truncated at zero and bounded by one, and it is used as the dependent variable in a lower-bound TOBIT model with the number of 1998 licensing agreements as an analytic weight.

Three measures of the university's own technology-transfer experience: the age of the technology transfer office; the cumulative number of executed licenses (1991-1998), which is also entered as a squared term; and the log of the cumulative amount of industrial research support received (1991-1998). These data are from the annual AUTM surveys, verified and augmented by the authors' survey and institutional data from the National Science Foundation's CASPAR database.

variable_name: Expectation that TTO will be self supporting
description: A dummy variable constructed from the authors' survey data, equal to 1 if the expectation is that the technology-transfer office will be self-supporting, and 0 otherwise. Roughly half (47%) of the respondent offices in the survey had expectations of being self-supporting.

Dummy variables for the university's technology transfer performance relative to its cohort. Institutions were grouped into four cohorts based on status as a public or private institution and the presence or absence of a medical school. The cohort variable of licensing income relative to R&D expenditures was calculated as total annual licensing revenues from 1991-1998 relative to the university's total research budget; institutions more than one standard deviation above the category average are classified as leading their cohort and institutions more than one standard deviation below the category mean as lagging their cohort.

The target for sales of certificates of deposit, stated in US dollars, set for each retail unit each quarter. These values represent the aspiration level of the ith retail unit at time t and constitute the dependent variable.
Measured as the sales target for the same unit in the previous period; the aspiration level of the ith retail unit in the period (t-1).

The difference between performance and aspiration level in the previous period, where performance is defined as the actual volume of sales of certificates of deposit achieved by the ith unit in the previous period.

Computed by subtracting the median performance divided by assets under management among all units at time t-1 from the performance divided by assets under management of the ith unit at time t-1. A negative value indicates that the focal unit's performance divided by assets under management fell below the median among all other retail units in the business; a positive or zero value indicates it exceeded or equaled the median.

Computed by subtracting the median performance divided by assets under management among only those units in the focal unit's administrative area at time t-1 from the performance divided by assets under management of the ith unit at time t-1. A negative value indicates that the focal unit fell below the median among other retail units in its administrative area; a positive or zero value indicates it exceeded or equaled that median.

variable_name: real exchange rate of the home currency
description: The trend of the real exchange rate of the U.S. dollar (home currency) with respect to the appropriate foreign currency, associated with each of the seven alternatives for changing or keeping the production mode. A negative coefficient indicates a trend toward appreciation of the home currency and a positive coefficient a trend toward depreciation. In the multinomial logit this real exchange rate variable is used to explain the probability of each mode choice.

Each subsidiary is classified as a WOS if the parent company owned more than 50% of its equity, and as a JV if the parent owned less than 50%. Seven different choice alternatives were recorded for the change (or keeping) of the production mode between the beginning and the end of a period: two for switching from a WOS to either a JV or EXP, two for the respective switches between JV and WOS and EXP, and three in case the subsidiary kept the same mode of operations. If the subsidiary had the same mode at the beginning and the end of the period it was assumed not to have changed its mode, if it had withdrawn from a country it was recorded as a switch to the EXP mode, and a change was recorded as occurring some time during the period.

The real exchange rate with respect to its mean for the entire period, entered in the reduced-form regression in logarithmic form and interacted with the volatility of the real exchange rate and with the switchover cost. The authors calculate the real exchange rate of the home currency so that an increase indicates an appreciation of the home currency with respect to the foreign currency.

variable_name: volatility of the real exchange rate (ve)
description: The volatility of the real exchange rate, entered in the reduced-form equation in logarithmic form and interacted with the real exchange rate. The paper does not describe in prose how this volatility is constructed.
The switchover cost, entered in the reduced-form equation in logarithmic form and interacted with the real exchange rate. The paper does not describe in prose how the switchover cost is measured.

variable_name: growth rate of net outflow of WOS (dep)
description: The dependent variable of the reduced-form equation when the dependent variable is WOS: the growth rate of net outflow of investment in wholly owned subsidiaries, all regressors being in logarithmic form. It is estimated by ordinary least squares and by a fixed effects model on a panel organized by the country in which the subsidiaries operate and by 2-digit SIC industry.

variable_name: growth rate of net outflow of JV (dep)
description: The dependent variable of the reduced-form equation when the dependent variable is JV: the growth rate of net outflow of investment in joint ventures, all regressors being in logarithmic form. It is estimated by ordinary least squares and by a fixed effects model on a panel organized by the country in which the subsidiaries operate and by 2-digit SIC industry.

For the 54 components, design experts identified the types and criticality of design dependencies between all components, which were mapped into a design interface matrix. The off-diagonal entries of the matrix are marked with either a W or an S to indicate the existence of a weak or strong design interface between two components, and 569 nonzero design interfaces were documented.
scale: categorical (W, S, or no design interface)

description: Key members of design teams were surveyed about the peak frequency and criticality of their technical interactions, and a six-point scale combining frequency and criticality yields a single metric called interaction intensity. The binary variable of interest is the presence or absence of significant information exchange, defined as those technical interactions that were relevant during the design phase due to their criticality and/or frequency and captured by a nonzero interaction intensity; 680 nonzero technical team interactions were identified, of which 423 were between the component teams.
scale: six-point scale for interaction intensity; binary for significant information exchange

description: The design interface matrix and the team interaction matrix are overlaid, because each of the 54 components is assigned one-to-one to a design team, to obtain the alignment matrix. Its cells record aligned presence of interface and interaction, aligned absence of interface and interaction, unmatched design interfaces (marked W or S), and unmatched team interactions (marked O); 90% of the cells show aligned presence or absence and the unexpected cases accounted for 10% of the cells.
level: dyad of component and design team

variable_name: unmatched design interface cells (W and S)
description: Cells of the alignment matrix in which a design interface exists between two components but no significant team interaction is reported between the corresponding teams are coded as unmatched design interfaces, marked W for a weak interface and S for a strong interface. In the study these were 220 unmatched design interfaces, 39% of the 569 design interfaces.
level: dyad of component and design team

description: Cells of the alignment matrix in which teams report significant technical interaction although no design interface is identified between the components they design are coded as unmatched team interactions, marked O. In the study these were 74 unmatched team interactions, 17% of the 423 team interactions.
level: dyad of component and design team

description: The strength of a design interface is the sum, over the five dependency types, of the level of criticality of each dependency of component i on component j, where criticality is scored on a five-point scale from −2 to +2. The resulting indicator variable trichotomizes the criticality of design interfaces: NULL = 0 when the design interface strength is 0, WEAK = 1 when it is greater than 0 and up to 4, and STRONG = 2 when it is greater than 4; 319 weak and 250 strong interfaces were determined.

Structural variable capturing whether tie ij is across boundaries, that is, whether the two design teams belong to different groups of teams and the two components belong to different systems. It is entered in the models to capture the clustering effects due to organizational and system boundaries embedded in both the design interface and the team interaction matrices.

Structural variable capturing whether tie ij is between modular systems. Six of the eight systems into which the engine was decomposed were identified as modular systems and the other two, the mechanical components system and the externals and controls system, were recognized as integrative systems.

Network statistic capturing configurations in which two design teams have other intermediary teams through which they can indirectly communicate, entered in the logit p* models as the ρ221 parameter and, within boundaries, as WITHINρ221. A significantly positive parameter indicates a stronger propensity for indirect team interaction configurations to be present.

Network statistic capturing configurations in which two components share interfaces with a common component, entered in the logit p* models as the ρ112 parameter and, within boundaries, as WITHINρ112. A significantly negative WITHINρ112 parameter indicates that indirect design interface configurations are much less likely to occur within boundaries than across boundaries.

variable_name: SITMISF, NO TECH-CLIM, NO STRAT-CLIM, NO MANA-CLIM, NO ENVI-CLIM, NO STRA-ENVI, NO STRA-TECH, NO MANA-ENVI, NO MANA-STRA, NO MANA-TECH, NO TECH-ENVI
description: SITMISF equals 1 if any situational misfit is present, 0 otherwise. The ten NO-* variables each equal 1 if a situational misfit is present in any dimension but not in the named dimension (technology-climate, strategy-climate, management-climate, environment-climate, strategy-environment, strategy-technology, management-environment, management-strategy, management-technology, technology-environment), 0 otherwise; a missing value is treated as a fit. The dummy variables aggregate particular types of extreme situational misfits rather than distinguishing among the individual misfit statements within a group.

variable_name: CONTMISF, NO CONF, NO FORM, NO COMP, NO CENT
description: CONTMISF equals 1 if any contingency misfit is present, 0 otherwise. NO CONF, NO FORM, NO COMP, and NO CENT each equal 1 if a contingency misfit is present but not a misﬁt related to conﬁguration, formalization, organizational complexity, and centralization respectively, 0 otherwise. As with the situational variables, missing values are treated as a fit, making the measure and tests conservative.

MISFIT equals 1 if any misﬁt is present, 0 otherwise; NO SIT equals 1 if only contingency misfit is present, 0 otherwise; and NO CONT equals 1 if only situational misfit is present, 0 otherwise. These dummies are used in the combined model to compare firms with both kinds of misfits against firms with only one kind or none.

ROA97 = (PROFIT97/ASSETS97)*100%, the dependent variable of all three regression models. Financial data for 1996 and 1997 were collected from public sources as they became available in 1998, 1999, and 2000.

ROA96 = (PROFIT96/ASSETS96)*100%, included among the regressors as the lagged dependent variable to account for historical factors that cause current differences in the dependent variable and to instrumentalize against bias from omitted control variables. The authors expected its coefficient to be positive to represent inertia.

The number of new product introductions for firm i in period t. A new product is defined as any new, unique brand-CPU combination, because manufacturers generally incur significant expenses associated with the production and launch of each brand model. The data contain 1,070 new product introductions with a per-firm range of 2 to 136 new products. Both current and one-year lagged introductions are used in the models.
time_window: annual, current year and one-year lag

description: Return on assets, a measure of firm profit rate used as a dependent measure. The authors use ROA as opposed to ROE because they wish to focus on operating returns, which depend on the total resources (i.e., assets) that the firm has deployed; the main measure is based on operating income, with a net-income-based measure used as a check.

Persistence is captured by the autoregressive pattern of performance, i.e., the coefficient on lagged performance in the dynamic model. The authors also allow the autoregressive coefficient to vary with firm product introductions to test whether persistence depends on new product introductions.
Growth of firm size as reflected in asset growth, used as a dependent measure alongside return on assets. Sales growth is used as an additional size measure in a sensitivity analysis.

A categorical variable based on the exploration index. The authors identified the total number of alliances formed by a firm each year, located all partners, and checked whether each partner had a prior relation (old partner) or no prior relation (new partner) with the firm; a value of 1 or 0 on the index indicates only new or only old partners respectively, while a value between 0 and 1 indicates a mixed number of new and old partners. Firms with the exploration/exploitation index ranging from 0.2 to 0.8 were categorized as having an ambidextrous formation of alliances in that year, whereas those with an index less than 0.2 or greater than 0.8 were categorized as having a focused formation in either exploitation or exploration.

Net sales over current assets in year t. The authors state that this ratio captures the amount of resources being produced and exchanged as well as the amount of total resources a firm has, and that it has been adopted in other ambidexterity research.

Measured using a firm's physical resources, namely current assets lagged by one year, to facilitate pattern comparison with the simulation model. The authors note a correlation of 0.73 between this measure and the number of firm employees and argue that current assets give information about the available resources of each firm in the sample.

The volatility of net sales of all firms in a four-digit SIC industry, following Bergh and Lawless (1998). Larger values of volatility indicate greater environmental uncertainty. Data for four-digit industry sales were collected from the U.S. Census Bureau: The Annual Survey of Manufacturers.

The observation year of the study, which in the empirical data run from 1988 to 1995. Unlike the simulation model, the authors note that the year when alliance activities originated in an industry is unknown in the empirical setting.

A categorical variable based on the simulation experimental design: firms are assigned experimental conditions of pure exploratory, pure exploitative, or ambidextrous alliance formation, and alliance ambidexterity equals 1 when an ambidextrous approach is used and 0 otherwise. For ambidextrous alliance relationships the simulation forces each firm to search for its next potential partner in an alternating fashion, one based on familiar/strong ties and the next based on new/weak ties.

A measure comparable to the empirical one, defined as the net resource exchanged and accumulated by the firm, which is the total resource exchanged and accumulated in that new year minus the initial output resources and divided by the initial output resources. The authors double-checked autocorrelation between last year's and current year's resources and found a value at 0.5, which they consider reasonable.

Measured as the total initial resources, including both input and output resources, held by the firm in the previous year. This measure was chosen to reduce conceptual overlap with the simulation measure of firm performance.
Set as an experimental parameter: each firm in the industry network faces an environmental volatility rate around 0.003 or 0.04 in each experiment, representing lower and higher uncertainty.

The observation year in the simulation, running from 1 to 30, since the alliance formation dynamic was modeled over a 30-simulation-year period. This allows exploration of network dynamics, which the authors state is not possible empirically.
A weighted degree centrality of the firm based on tie strength in year t, used to capture the firm's centrality in the network.

The authors first identified a firm's alliance partners and then counted how often any two of its alliance partners are not directly connected. This measures the number of structural holes that have been filled by the firm.

The cumulative traffic measure of all former months up to month t. The traffic measure is a weighted average of the number of products delivered of the different product types multiplied by a standard rate for each product type; the standard rates are a relative indication of the time spent for different products and were unchanged during the years of the study.

The total costs of region i in month t divided by the traffic measure of region i in month t. Total costs include the costs of delivery and sorting of the mail and the costs made in the service center and customer center, and are deflated by the consumer price index.
The percentage of total hours worked by employees with a temporary contract in region i and month t. The contract length of these temporary employees runs from a few weeks to a maximum of six months.

The percentage of total hours worked in overtime in region i and month t, used as an indicator of strained capacity; when capacity is strained, regions use more overtime. Capacity is influenced by seasonality, with strained capacity around Christmas and New Year and abundant capacity in the summer.

An inverted Herfindahl index of product diversity: one minus the sum over the seven product types of the squared share of each product type in the total number of mail items delivered in region i and month t. The measure weights the number of different product types by the volume of each product type; its theoretical range is 1 to 7.

The percentage of letters delivered on time at the right address in region i and month t, measured by an external agent that sends test letters and registers on-time delivery. The measure mainly captures variation in mistakes made in the delivery and distributing processes and not variation in the speed of delivery.

Equation (1) is adapted by computing region-specific learning rates, so that the learning coefficient is allowed to differ between the 27 regions. The average learning rate reported for the sample is the learning coefficient of Equation (1).

variable_name: Total years produced; Production leader; Numbers 1 or 2 producer; Years of parent production; Parent no. 1; Secondary parent no. 1
description: For the spinoff-rate model, firm quality in year t is measured by the total number of years the firm produced automobiles and two 1-0 dummies, one equal to 1 if the firm had been among the production leaders of the industry in year t or the preceding 5 years, and one equal to 1 if it had been the number one or two producer in year t or the preceding 5 years. For the performance of the parents of spinoffs, four variables were constructed: the total years the parents produced automobiles, a 1-0 dummy equal to 1 if the parent was ranked among the production leaders in the entry year of the spinoff or the preceding 5 years, a 1-0 dummy equal to 1 if the parent was the number one producer in that period, and a comparable dummy for the secondary parent.
time_window: year t and the preceding 5 years; for parents, the spinoff's entry year and the preceding 5 years

variable_name: Years of production of automobiles / annual hazard of exit
description: Performance is measured by the total years a firm produced automobiles and analyzed as the annual firm hazard of exit in a Gompertz specification in which background variables enter the proportional term. Firms that exited by being acquired are treated as censored exits.
time_window: age of the firm from entry through exit, 1895-1966

variable_name: Number of spinoffs (one, two, or three)
description: The dependent variable of the ordered logit is the number of spinoffs a firm had in each year t, coded as one, two, or three spinoffs, with thresholds for one, two, and three spinoffs estimated. Each firm's history is broken into annual intervals from the year before its date of entry (or 1899 if it entered earlier) through 1924, and the observations of all firms are pooled.
scale: count of spinoffs in a year (1, 2, or 3)
time_window: annual intervals from the year before entry (or 1899) through 1924

description: A 1-0 dummy equal to 1 for spinoffs, firms in which at least one founder had worked for or founded an automobile firm in Smith's list; the parent is the prior firm where the principal automobile founder of the spinoff worked, with a secondary parent designated when a prior employer to the parent could be identified. In the hazard models the spinoff dummy and a dummy for spinoffs located in the Detroit area are included, with inexperienced firms as the omitted reference category.

variable_name: Experienced firms; experienced entrepreneurs; inexperienced firms
description: Three 1-0 dummies equal to 1, respectively, for experienced firms, experienced entrepreneurs, and spinoffs, with inexperienced firms the omitted reference category. Separate 1-0 dummies are also included for experienced firms and experienced entrepreneurs with backgrounds in the carriage and wagon, bicycle, and engine industries.

A 1-0 dummy equal to 1 for firms located in the Detroit area in year t, where the Detroit area comprises Detroit plus named Michigan locations within approximately 100 miles of Detroit. A second 1-0 dummy equal to 1 for Detroit-area firms in years after 1916 is also included in the spinoff-rate model.
time_window: year t; separately for years after 1916

variable_name: Spinoffs located within 100 miles of their parents
description: The location of each spinoff is compared with the location of its parent: of the 145 spinoffs, 110 located within 100 miles of their parents, and 50 of the 61 spinoffs whose parents were located in the Detroit area also located there. The measure is reported as counts rather than as an estimated model.

variable_name: Years of production if producer; Years of production squared if producer
description: For producers, the number of years of production of automobiles through year t and its square are included as explanatory variables in the ordered logit. The estimates imply that the probability of a spinoff rises until age 14 and then declines.
time_window: years of production through year t

variable_name: Acquired by auto firm; Acquired by non-auto firm
description: Two 1-0 dummies equal to 1 for firms that were acquired by another auto firm between years t-2 and t+1, and for firms acquired by non-auto firms in the same window, based on listings of ownership changes in Smith (1968); acquisitions are allowed to affect the spinoff rate 1 year before they occur.

The dependent variable equals 1 if there is a citation between the potentially citing and the cited patent, and 0 otherwise. Because citations between random patents are extremely rare, a choice-based sample is used: all actual citations in the population are included (each matched with five control pairs from the same technology classes) and observations are weighted by the number of population elements they represent, following the WESML estimator.

Indicator variable that is 1 if the citing and cited patents originate from inventors located in the same region, and 0 otherwise. A patent's geographic region is taken as one of the 337 Metropolitan Statistical Areas or Primary Metropolitan Statistical Areas in the United States, as determined by the first inventor's address; patents with a non-U.S. address, and about 20% of U.S.-based patents without a usable patent-area mapping, were dropped.

Indicator variable that is 1 if the citing and cited patents are owned by the same parent firm, and 0 otherwise. Patent ownership was resolved with a parent-subsidiary match using corporate directories and Compustat identifiers from Jaffe and Trajtenberg (2002), and because only the first assignee is known, all inventors of a patent were assumed to have the same employer.

All observations with a nonzero social distance are classified into five mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories based on whether the social distance is 1, 2, 3, any finite value greater than 3, or infinity, captured by indicator variables past collaboration, common collaborator, collaborators with ties, indirect social link, and no social link (the reference group). Ties are inferred from coinventing on patents, an observed collaboration is assumed to mark the beginning of a persistent tie, and the graph for year t includes all inventors who patented between 1975 and t.
time_window: collaborations from 1975 onward; graphs built separately for each year 1986-1995

description: Respondents reported the number of members of the founding team who had previously started a new firm. A dummy variable captures whether the founding team possessed prior entrepreneurial experience (1) or not (0).

In a multistage question, respondents were asked to indicate whether, prior to first market entry, they had considered commercializing their technological resources (respectively, competences or know-how) in market domains completely different from the market entered. Respondents who had indicated that they had considered alternative markets were then asked to report the number of alternatives considered. The variable takes only nonnegative integer values and consists of zeros and ones to a significant degree; it is used in logarithmic form in the performance models.
A dummy variable capturing the consideration of alternative market opportunities prior to the first entry; it indicates whether the new firm considered more than one market opportunity.

Annual sales revenues (in euros) achieved by the new venture in Year 1 and in Year 2 after the initial market entry were used as dependent variables. Following Fox (1991), logarithmic transformations (natural logarithms) were utilized for the positively skewed sales variables. The collaboration partner's data set provided monthly revenue data, which were totaled to obtain the yearly revenue figures used in the analysis.
time_window: Year 1 and Year 2 after initial market entry

description: Mode of entry is captured by a dummy variable which takes a value of one if the Japanese parent made an acquisition and zero if it established a greenfield plant. A positive sign for a regression coefficient means that the variable increases the probability of acquisition.

Research and development expenditures as a percentage of the Japanese parent's domestic sales for the year preceding entry. Taken from the parent's report to Japan's Ministry of Finance (Yukashoken Hokokusho); when not available there, the Japan Company Handbook was used.

The number of years between a given entry and the establishment of the parent's first U.S. manufacturing subsidiary. The authors assume that the parent's level of experience of the U.S. market is proportional to the number of years it has operated in the U.S.
time_window: at the time entry was made

description: A dummy variable equal to one if any one of the products produced by the affiliate matched those produced by the parent, and to zero otherwise. Because the construct is the extent to which the entry is a diversification, a value of one on COMMON denotes the absence of diversification.

A Herfindahl-Hirschman type index of the degree of product diversification of the Japanese parent, computed from the sales breakdown of the parent the year before entry as published in the Japan Company Handbook. The formula proposed by Wernerfelt and Montgomery (1986) was used to handle sales lumped into an others category.

The ratio of media advertising expenditures to sales of the Japanese parent as listed in the company's Yukashoken Hokokusho. When advertising expenditure data was not available from this source, the authors turned to Toyo Keizai (1991).

Each year's Relative Value Index is calculated from OECD data using Khoury's (1980) formula: RVI = change in dollar value of yen / (U.S. stock price index / Japanese stock price index). The RVI is high when acquisitions of U.S. firms are relatively cheap for Japanese investors.

The absolute value of GROWTH's deviation from its sample mean divided by its standard deviation, where GROWTH is the average annual growth rate of shipments of the four-digit U.S. industry in the 5 years before entry. GROWTHDEV is high when the growth rate of the target U.S. industry is either very fast or very slow.

The average annual growth rate of shipments of the four-digit U.S. industry in the 5 years before entry, taken from the U.S. Department of Commerce, U.S. Industrial Outlook. Average industry growth rate was used for the few observations with multiple SIC's.

A dummy variable taking the value of 1 if the Japanese investor is a follower and if its U.S. subsidiary is active in an industry characterized by loose oligopoly, and zero otherwise. The first Japanese parent to enter a given four-digit SIC U.S. industry was called a leader and all subsequent entrants followers; loose oligopoly occurs in Japan when the Herfindahl-Hirschman index is between 1000 and 1800 or the 3-firm concentration ratio is between 50 and 70 percent.

The Herfindahl-Hirschman index for the 50 largest companies for each four-digit SIC U.S. industry (1982), as published in the 1982 Census of Manufactures. The arithmetic average of the concentration ratio was used for subsidiaries active in multiple SIC's.

A variable created to describe the combined impact of concentration and growth rate in the target industry: GROWCON takes the value of the concentration ratio when demand growth in the target industry is negative, and zero otherwise.

The ratio of the Japanese investor's average annual rate of growth of domestic employment over its rate of growth of domestic sales, both over the five-year period preceding entry. A high PSALG means that employment grew faster than sales, i.e., that the firm has excess labor personnel resources.
The ratio of the employment of the subsidiary over that of the parent.
A firm's financial leverage is measured by the ratio of its long term debt to its market value, as reported in its Yukashoken Hokokusho, following Palepu (1986) and Chatterjee (1990).

For each hotel, the variable is set equal to the (discounted) number of room-years the hotel had accumulated between the time the hotel was founded and the current year, scaled by 10^-6. The amount of operating experience accumulated by an organization in a year is measured by the number of rooms the hotel has available. To test for the U-shaped effect, organizational experience is modeled as a quadratic by including both organizational experience and organizational experience squared. Values are updated annually in the multiple-spell formulation.
time_window: accumulated from founding to the year before the current year

description: The instantaneous rate of failure r(t), estimated as a loglinear function of an age constant and the covariates in a piecewise exponential model, where each hotel's history is broken down into one-year spells in which the hotel is at risk of failing and each spell is right-censored unless the hotel fails.

For each hotel, set equal to the Manhattan hotel population's cumulative (discounted) operating experience between the current year and the time the hotel was founded, scaled by 10^-6. The mass of the population in a year is measured as the total number of rooms in all hotels.
time_window: from the focal hotel's founding to the year before the current year

description: For each hotel, set equal to the Manhattan hotel population's cumulative (discounted) mass of organizations alive in the year before founding, scaled by 10^-6. Only other organizations alive in the year prior to founding are included, since organizations that died earlier cannot be observed directly by the new organization.
time_window: from the population's founding to the year before the focal organization's founding
