The count of algorithmic skills in the firm-year-occupation cell, where occupations are Standard Occupational Classification six-digit occupations. The natural logarithm of this count is used in the regressions, with the count of total skills reported by workers in that cell entered alongside it.

Domain knowledge-intensive occupations are identified in the workforce data as those ranked highly in terms of the sum of the importance and level of domain knowledge required for the occupation, using the O*NET Knowledge Table. These occupational groups are used, together with high decision-making requirements, to construct the decentralization measure.

The importance of decision making for an occupation, retrieved from the O*NET database, which provides this measure on a scale of one through seven for each six-digit occupation. It is entered as an indicator of the importance of decision making for the occupation.

An indicator of whether the skill is related to a "no-code" technology, used as a proxy for whether the skill is easier to learn. These tools comprise a small fraction of all technical skills. Technologies are identified as being in this category using GPT-4-based labeling.

At the firm-occupation level, algorithmic skill measures are constructed as the fraction of workers with algorithmic skills (%ALG) in occupation groups that are highest in both their domain knowledge and decision-making requirements. For organization i in year t, φALG is computed as (%ALG minus the mean of %ALG) divided by the standard deviation of %ALG; firms in which employees in these occupations have more algorithmic skills have larger φALG values.

A proxy measure of the firm's investment in algorithms, computed as the quantity of relevant algorithmic skills in the firm's IT workforce in a given year, entered in logs. The rationale is that human capital is the largest component of a firm's digitization investment and that much of that software stack is open source, leaving no documented investment trail.

A measure of the firm's aggregate IT investment, computed as the quantity of relevant skills in the firms' IT workforce in a given year and entered in logs. It follows prior work in which proxy investment measures are constructed as quantities or intensities of skills relevant to the technological domain.

Total market value is computed as the value of equity at the end of the fiscal year plus the value of preferred stock plus total debt, which represents the total worth of a firm as assessed by the financial markets. The variable is used in logs in the market value regressions.

Risk tolerance is the reciprocal (1/c) of the risk-aversion coefficient c of the exponential utility function u(x) = -e^(-cx), estimated for each firm's exploration and production business unit in each year. The firm's annual domestic and foreign exploration budget allocations are interpreted as the certainty equivalent (buying price) of each lottery category, and the certainty equivalent is set equal to the expected value of the outcome distribution minus one-half c times the variance. The probability of success is estimated as the mean of the firm's actual success rates for the previous three years, and reserves per successful project as the mean reserve addition per successful project over the entire ten year period. The implied c is solved from the resulting equation for each of the eight year study periods.

RTR is a normalized measure of risk taking that controls for firm size, equal to the observed risk tolerance of firm i in period t divided by the predicted risk tolerance of that firm as a function of its size (SMCF) for the same period. An RTR value greater than 1.0 implies a stronger propensity to take risk than firms of equivalent size within the sample, and a value less than 1.0 implies a weaker propensity to take risk than firms of equivalent size.

variable_name: Standardized Measure of Discounted Future Net Cash Flows (SMCF)
description: The SMCF represents a measure of the value of the firm's oil and gas reserves, calculated by subtracting future production and development costs and income taxes from future cash inflows from production and then discounting by 10% for the timing of estimated cash flows. The measure is the same whether full cost or successful efforts accounting is used, and it is a required computation for 10-K filings. It serves as the measure of firm size and of the financial strength of the exploration business unit.

Ex post return is measured in terms of return on total exploration and production assets, with income defined as earnings before interest but after taxes. The RTR and the return measure are lagged one year, for example 1983 RTR against 1984 ROA. The same return measure is used both as the dependent variable in the nonlinear regression on RTR and as the basis of the ANOVA across risk tolerance categories.
time_window: Annual with a one-year lag between RTR and ROA

description: Variance of after-tax E&P asset returns is the ex post risk measure of interest, computed on a risk tolerance category (group) basis rather than a firm-level basis from data pooled across firms and time periods. For each RTR category, variance of ROA was computed as the arithmetic mean of the individually squared deviations of each observed value from the RTR category mean. Confidence interval estimates for each category were then calculated using a chi-square statistic.

Ordinal risk is an alternative ex post risk measure that directly addresses the issue of gains and losses and establishes risk in a strategic context. The competing oil companies are ranked against each other annually on the basis of return on E&P assets; favorable events are those that yield an improvement in rank and unfavorable events are those that result in a loss of rank. The component of ordinal risk used here is defined in terms of a loss in strategic position along the dimension of return on E&P assets, an entropy-based measure concerned with a firm's relative position within the system.
level: firm (assigned to a risk tolerance category)

description: The premium paid for the target company was calculated as the percentage difference between the final price per target share paid by the acquiring firm and the target's stock price four weeks before the offer announcement. Premiums are generally calculated two to eight weeks before the announcement date to avoid the distortion caused by typical increases in the target's stock price due to information leaks. Data were obtained from the SDC Merger and Corporate Transaction Database.
time_window: four weeks before the offer announcement

description: A proxy measure obtained from the I/B/E/S database: the coefficient of variation, i.e., the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean, of the analysts' projected target EPS estimates for the year the acquisition occurred, using estimates as of December of the year before the acquisition. The variance of estimates reflects the dispersion of opinion among analysts about the future performance of a company.
time_window: estimates as of December of the year before the acquisition

description: A variable representing the average premium paid by those firms on whose boards the inside and outside directors of the acquiring firm sat, during the three years before the date of the acquiring firm's transaction. Both inside and outside directors were used. Interlock data were obtained from proxy statements and premium data from the SDC database.
time_window: three years before the acquiring firm's transaction

description: For the investment banking firm used by an acquiror, a variable reflecting the average premium paid on all transactions involving that investment banking firm during the prior three years. If multiple investment bankers were used, these premiums were averaged.
A variable reflecting the average premium paid during the prior three years on all transactions involving investment banking firms not used by the acquiror.

variable_name: number of investment banking firms used by the acquiror
description: A count variable reflecting the number of investment banking firms used by the acquiror on each transaction, ranging from zero to four. The investment banking firms used by the acquirors and targets for each transaction were obtained from the SDC database.

variable_name: failure (exit from the Form M population)
description: A carrier is categorized as failed only if it disappears from the ICC's Form M population and never returns through 1989. The authors assume that large carriers that exit the sample do so due to failure rather than merger, based on a check of one year's worth of one trade journal.
Number of large motor carriers (Class 1 and 2 firms, revenue at or above $1 million) operating in the United States at the end of year t. The square of large density, scaled by 1000, is also entered.

Number of small motor carriers (Class 3 firms, sales under $1 million) operating in the United States at the end of year t, taken from the ICC Annual Report to Congress; the square of small density is also entered.

An age clock that freezes in 1980, the year of deregulation; for the years 1981 through 1989 it retains its value from 1980, and it is set to 0 for carriers that were not born before 1980. It captures the effects of age at deregulation on a carrier's survival chances.

Age clocks for firms existing in 1980 and for firms born after 1980, respectively, each beginning with the first year of a carrier's existence after 1980. Separate clocks are constructed for incumbents and for entrants to test for different effects of age on the two types of firms.

The absolute value of the residual for each firm observation from a re-estimated two-sided Tobit model that predicts carriers' reliance on company drivers (miles driven by company drivers divided by all miles driven) from the proportion of revenue from LTL carriage, haul characteristics including average length of haul and average weight of haul, and control variables; the advertising variable was excluded because only a small subset of firms reported such expenditures, and the model was re-estimated for each year in the sample. Misalign ranges between 0, when the proportion of a firm's total miles driven by company drivers conforms perfectly to the prediction, and 1, when reliance on company drivers is diametrically opposite that predicted.

The authors employ debt and equity to construct the leverage variable in the form debt/(debt + equity) so that Leverage ranges from zero to one. Prior literature on the trucking industry has largely relied on debt divided by equity as the primary measure of motor carrier leverage.

The authors stress that LTL is not a category of carrier; rather, it measures the proportion of a carrier's traffic that is LTL carriage as opposed to TL carriage, varying across the continuum from 0 to 1. Many carriers haul a mix of LTL and TL traffic.
Return on sales, a measure of current profitability used as a second-best proxy for expected profitability. ROS has a significant negative effect on a firm's likelihood of failure.

Return on assets, a measure of current profitability used as a second-best proxy for expected profitability because most firms in the sample are private and Tobin's Q cannot be calculated. ROA is not significant in models that include ROS but is significant and negative in models that exclude ROS.
The total cash compensation received by the executive during the year. This variable includes salary, bonuses paid in cash, and the cash equivalent of benefits in kind where appropriate.

The value of long-term incentive awards made during the year, such as share option grants or shares allocated under long-term incentive plans (LTIPs). LTIP award valuations are the company share price multiplied by the maximum potential number of shares receivable, discounted by 20 percent to reflect the likelihood of full vesting; share option awards are valued using the Black-Scholes option valuation method adjusted for continuous dividends on the date the award is made.
The sum of cash compensation and incentive compensation, representing the full value of all awards, cash and noncash, made to an executive during the fiscal year.

Executives were allocated to three distinct organizational levels using information from the annual report and accounts. Level 1 is the Group CEO, the executive with highest authority in the firm; Level 2 is the Divisional CEO, an executive with highest authority within a division, including finance directors; Level 3 is other executives with mainly functional duties. In the regressions Level 1 and Level 2 are indicator variables with Other Executives as the excluded category.

variable_name: Log(CEO cash compensation) minus log(median non-CEO executive cash compensation)
description: The tournament prize measured on cash compensation: the log of CEO cash pay minus the log of median cash compensation received by the non-CEO executive team.

variable_name: Log(CEO incentive compensation) minus log(median non-CEO executive incentive compensation)
description: The tournament prize measured on incentive compensation: the log of CEO incentive pay minus the log of median incentive compensation received by the non-CEO executive team.

variable_name: Log(CEO total compensation) minus log(median non-CEO executive total compensation)
description: The tournament prize measured on total pay: the log of CEO total compensation minus the log of median total compensation received by the non-CEO executive team.

variable_name: Number of directors in the executive team
description: The number of executives in the company's executive team, used as the count of tournament contestants competing for the CEO position.

variable_name: Coefficient of variation of executive team compensation
description: The coefficient of variation of the board's executive compensation, constructed following Main et al. (1993) and Eriksson (1999), and used to capture wage variation within the executive team.

Annual total shareholder return, reflecting annual share price appreciation plus dividends on a continuously reinvested basis. It serves as a performance measure in the performance equation and as a control in the executive compensation equations.
Return on assets, used together with total shareholder return as a company performance measure in the performance determination equation.

Using data from Dataquest and ICE, the authors identified six broad product markets and subcategories within them, then gathered information on the size of the market, four-firm concentration ratio, and number of competitors in each market for each year from 1978 through 1987. Each firm in the sample was assigned to a market based on the first product shipped by the firm and the founding year. Each market was then typed as emergent, growth, or mature for each year in the study.

The four-firm concentration ratio obtained from market-research data. This figure is the ratio of sales of the four largest competitors in the market to the total sales in the market, gathered for each year from 1978 through 1987.

An objective measure, micron line width, which is a physical specification of the degree of miniaturization of the circuit designs created by semiconductor companies, referred to technically as the minimum feature size in microns. Smaller micron sizes represent more innovative technology, since increasing miniaturization to pack more circuits into a smaller area is the heart of semiconductor innovation.

Three questions answered by company respondents, each on a 0 to 10 scale: reliance on existing knowledge to build the first product, synthesis of existing knowledge to produce the first product, and difficulty of producing the first product. A three-item index was created by reverse coding the first question and computing the mean response to the three questions; the Cronbach alpha is .75.
scale: 0 to 10 for each question; index is the mean of the three

description: The number of founding executives who had worked with another founding executive for at least six months prior to founding the company, divided by the total number of founding executives. The variable ranges between 0, for teams in which none of the founders had previously worked together, and 1, for teams in which all of the founders had previous work relationships together.

The number of individuals who were designated by the company respondents as founders and who founded the firm and worked full time for the firm in executive positions at its inception. The number of founders ranged from one to seven.

The standard deviation of the number of years of semiconductor-industry experience for all executives on the founding team. Company respondents provided this information for each member of the founding team; these experience levels were averaged for a team score and the standard deviation was computed.
scale: standard deviation of years of industry experience

description: The team variables were collapsed into strong and weak team categories. Teams were typed as strong when they met three conditions: at least three founders, at least 50 percent joint experience, and at least three years of industry experience variation. At the fourth year of life there were 26 strong teams and 40 weak ones.

Growth was measured as the difference in sales in each year of life through 1988 relative to sales at founding; because sales at founding were 0 for all firms, the measure reduced to the sales in that year. Sales figures were obtained from firms and public sources and adjusted to 1988 dollars using the annual producer price index of the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Constructed from backward citations listed in patents assigned to a firm in a given year. The index equals 1 minus the sum, over each unique entity cited, of the squared share of the firm's backward citations accounted for by that entity; citations to the firm's own patents, to nonpatented materials, and to expired patents are excluded. Following Hall (2002), the index is adjusted for the downward bias of Herfindahl-based measures computed from few patents; the text presents the adjusted measure as the index multiplied by a factor built from the count of the firm's backward citations, a formula that is difficult to read as printed. The index ranges from 0 (all cited patents held by one entity) to 1 (cited patents assigned to many different entities).

The number of successful patent applications made by a firm in a given year, used as the dependent variable. The expected number of patents applied for during the year is modeled as an exponential function of the firm's R&D spending and other characteristics.

Measured on an annual basis as the deflated book value of a firm's property, plant, and equipment, normalized by number of employees (consistent with Hall and Ziedonis 2001). Financial data are converted to constant (1992) U.S. dollars; the variable enters the models in logged form.

The sample is split into years before and after the strengthened U.S. enforcement regime had been well demonstrated. Although the new appellate court was created in 1982, its significance was not widely felt until the mid-1980s, so the sample is divided into periods that predate and follow 1985, the latter corresponding to the era in which the 'new power of patents' was widely known.

Leadtime measured as the length of time the first-mover has a temporary monopoly versus a later entrant, i.e. the difference between the pioneer's entry year and the later entrant's entry year. One year was added to leadtime, following Urban et al., so that its logarithm could not equal zero.

Urban et al.'s leadtime measure, which is measured relative to the previous entrant rather than to the pioneer. For a category where the first entrant entered in 1950, the second in 1957 and the third in 1960, the lag between entry values are 7 years and 3 years.
Order of entry of the nth brand in category c (n = 1, 2, 3, ...), so that the market pioneer has a value of one.

The number of years the pioneer and the later entrant have both been in the market, measured by the difference between 1983 (when the Urban et al. market share data were gathered) and the later entrant's entry year. For example, a follower that entered in 1960 faced 23 years of competitive rivalry with the first entrant.
Ratio of the market share of the nth brand to enter category c to the market share of the first brand to enter the category.

Interaction-style terms that take the value of order of entry (1960E) or leadtime (1960LT) in markets that started from 1960 to 1974 and the value 1.0 otherwise. Because the log-linear model has no intercept, the logarithm yields the traditional dummy variable value of 0.0 for brands in markets pioneered in 1956 or earlier.

The market value of central processors (supercomputers, mainframes and minicomputers) reported in the IDG survey plus an estimate of the value of PCs and terminals, computed by multiplying a weighted average value for PCs and terminals by the number of PCs and terminals. The resulting value is converted to constant 1987 dollars using the computer systems deflator reported in Gordon (1993). The survey value is interpreted as a beginning of period capital stock value, matched to end of year Compustat data for the previous period.

Total capital computed from book value of capital stock, adjusted for inflation by assuming that all investment was made at a calculated average age (total depreciation divided by current depreciation) of the capital stock. The deflated value of COMPUTER CAPITAL is subtracted from this total, so that all capital of a firm is allocated to either COMPUTER CAPITAL or NON-COMPUTER CAPITAL.

The total central IS budget reported in the IDG survey multiplied by the percentage of the IS budget devoted to labor expenses, converted to constant 1987 dollars. It is a flow variable covering the labor portion of IS expenses only, so that capital expenditure is not double counted.

Total labor, materials and other noninterest expenses from Compustat converted to constant 1987 dollars, with deflated IS STAFF subtracted from this value. All the expenses of a firm are thereby allocated to either IS STAFF or NON-IS LABOR AND EXPENSE.

Total sales from Compustat converted to constant 1987 dollars with an appropriate government price deflator. The authors note that this approach will probably underestimate changes in product quality or variety since the deflators are imperfect.
Operationalized as the total number of incoming calls to the focal bank from all other banks in the 24-hour period. It is the dependent variable of the regressions.

Operationalized as the total number of different banks called by the focal bank in the 24-hour period. This measure is identical to Freeman's degree centrality as applied to out-ties; it is the number of banks called, not the number of conversations.

Operationalized as the multiplicative effect of two factors: the extensiveness of out-ties (the number of different banks called) and an index of concentration of the bank's outgoing conversations. The concentration index is the sum of squares of the outgoing conversation shares of each called bank, mathematically analogous to a Herfindahl index. A high value of the multiplicative term indicates an extensive network of out-ties with the bulk of information seeking concentrated with a few banks. The natural log of this term was used in the regression.

Operationalized as a count of the focal bank's ties with banks that have very few other ties to the network, that is, with relative isolates. Banks with five or fewer out-ties were considered relatively unconnected, and the number of ties the focal bank had with these relative isolates was counted. This approximates the probability of bridging structural holes.
Operationalized as the number of different countries the focal bank calls in the 24-hour period.

Operationalized as the speed with which banks respond to the hour-by-hour volatility in dollar-mark prices. The number of outgoing conversations for each focal bank for each of the 24 hours was correlated with market volatility for each hour, yielding a correlation coefficient for each bank that reflects its responsiveness to market volatility; this coefficient was used in the regression.
time_window: hourly over the 24-hour period of September 6, 1994

description: A three-item scale of design-manufacturing practices and actions: "We have people who are trained in DFA (Design for Assembly) or DFM (Design for Manufacture)"; "A Manufacturing representative is required to sign-off on design reviews for new products"; and "We have developed and implemented new structures in order to coordinate design and manufacturing." All items were coded as practices and actions, not attitudes, with "Yes" coded 3, "No" coded 1, and "in process" coded 2. The Cronbach alpha for this three item scale was 0.54 with an average inter item correlation of 0.28.

A two-item scale of design-manufacturing personnel mechanisms: "Job rotation between design and manufacturing engineering is practiced in the firm"; and "Personnel from design engineering are sometimes moved to manufacturing engineering or vice-versa." Items were scored as actions and practices with "Yes" coded 3, "No" coded 1, and "in process" coded 2. The Cronbach alpha for this scale was 0.67 with an average inter item correlation of 0.50.

A single "yes-no" question: "Do you benchmark (make visits to other firms and gauge their practices because of their known good reputation) in Design Approaches?" A total of 23 (55%) of these 43 firms said they benchmark on design practices. It is used as a dichotomous dependent variable in the discriminant analysis.

Respondents were asked to estimate the percentage of degreed manufacturing engineers in the firm or division. The sample mean was 60% with a standard deviation of 31%. This proportion is one of the two measures of concentration of specialists and enters the path model and the discriminant analysis.

Respondents were asked to estimate the percentage of degreed design engineers in the firm or division. The sample mean was 74% with a standard deviation of 29%. This proportion is the second of the two documented proportions used to measure concentration of specialists.

Sales per employee obtained from the Dun & Bradstreet Corporate Directory, which lists employees and sales for 1990, used as a proxy for overall performance. Average sales per employee for this sample was $172,000 (s.d. = $20,000). The authors note that the proportion of outsourcing, as well as subtle industry differences, is likely to have an important moderating influence on these labor productivity measures.

Development time for the last major product, estimated by respondents in years; it averaged three years (s.d. = 1.5). To test the hypothesis, development period in years was divided by the life-cycle of the major product of the firm or SBU in the sample, so development time is controlled by product life-cycle.
time_window: last major product introduced by the firm

description: Dichotomous questionnaire item classifying the exchange as either an internal profit center exchange or an external market exchange. The measure takes one value for a profit center supplier and the other for an external market supplier.

variable_name: Renegotiation costs (difficulty of and satisfaction with price adjustments)
description: Because renegotiation costs are not directly captured through standard accounting records, the degrees of difficulty in bargaining for and satisfaction with price adjustments are used as proxies; renegotiation costs increase with unsatisfactory or difficult adjustments since haggling with the supplier takes time. Three indicators are used: difficulty in agreeing on the allocation of costs due to engineering changes, difficulty in agreeing on the allocation of costs due to changes in material costs, and satisfaction with settlements over cost adjustments. The satisfaction item is entered as its negative (dissatisfaction) so that higher values indicate higher renegotiation costs.

Single questionnaire item asking how open the supplier has been about its manufacturing costs and cost structure. Managers are exposed to a standard list of manufacturing costs during training for cost reduction programs, and internal or external audits verify product cost disclosures.

Dichotomous questionnaire item asking whether the part is a new or a carryover part, measured by the firm's manufacturing policy of designing a part anew or carrying it over to the next model of the consumer good. A supplier of a new part anticipates a longer horizon of repeated exchanges than the supplier of a carryover part whose life cycle is near completion, so the new part represents a high probability of repeat business and the carryover part a lower probability.

Single questionnaire item asking how difficult it was to judge the competitiveness of the quotes or of the negotiated price for the part. When the manager does not experience difficulty in assessing price, the supplier's costs are known; greater difficulty indicates an asymmetric product cost information setting.

variable_name: UNIQUE LABOR, UNIQUE EQUIPMENT, PROPRIETARY TECHNOLOGY
description: Three single-item measures of unique assets: proprietary technology possessed by the supplier related to the part, technical labor skills required by the part that are relatively unique to the supplier, and manufacturing equipment required by the part that is relatively unique to the supplier. The items are not represented as a single construct because previous work shows that these indicators have independent effects on the dependent measures.

Project managers broke down the resources devoted to each project into project management, architecture design, development, and test; the ratio of architecture design resources to development and test resources was calculated. Because the size of products varies significantly, this ratio was modeled as a function of the lines of new code developed, and the residuals from this model are used as the measure, controlled for scale.

Project managers assessed the percentage of functionality that existed in the product at the first prototype and at the first beta release, assuming functionality at project start was 0% and functionality at launch was 100%. Each measure was adjusted for scale by predicting it with the logarithm of lines of new code and taking residuals; the composite measure was constructed by taking the first component from a principal component analysis of the two sets of residuals.

Project managers assessed the percentage of functionality that existed in the product at the first system integration, assuming functionality at project start was 0% and functionality at launch was 100%. This measure was adjusted for scale by modeling it as a function of the logarithm of lines of new code, and the residuals are used as the measure.

Project managers assessed the proportion of team members whose past experience with software development projects fell into each of four categories: no previous experience, one generation of experience, two generations of experience, and greater than two generations of experience. The proportion of team members with greater than two generations of experience is used as the indicator.

A panel of 14 industry observers rated the overall quality of each product relative to other competitive products targeting similar customer needs at launch, on a Likert scale from 1 to 7 with 4 indicating parity with competitive offerings. The second Delphi round, in which panelists were given the top competitive products and mean scores, produced convergence; the mean score provided by knowledgeable experts (those scoring 4 or higher on knowledge) is used as the dependent variable.
time_window: at the time the product was launched

description: The dependent variable was dichotomized into a franchised vs. wholly-owned unit; logistic analysis estimates the probability that the dependent variable takes on the value of one (i.e., franchising) rather than the value of zero (i.e., wholly-owned subsidiary). One firm included some joint venture arrangements, but due to the small number of outlets that involve such an agreement, those units were included in the category of corporate equity.
time_window: service outlet observations drawn mostly from 1989 annual reports

description: Monitoring difficulty is proxied by calculating the travel distance in terms of air travel time between corporate headquarters and the countries of the service unit operations. New York City was used as a standard point of travel origin for all firms and for most countries the nation's capital was used as the standard point of destination. The minimum flight time plus transfer time taking into consideration the change in time zones was used to operationalize the proxy.

The cultural distance index is patterned after research by Ronen and Shenkar (1985) and uses six cultural distance dummy variables for Latin Europe, Nordic/Germanic, Far East, Near East/Arabic, Latin American/Caribbean, and Independent country clusters. The Anglo grouping was used as the baseline because cross-cultural research findings indicated that this cluster is culturally closest to the United States. Dummy variables were used because continuous measures of cultural distance were not available.

This variable is proxied by measuring the cumulative number of years of the international service firm's overall foreign involvement beyond Canada and Mexico: the index equals 1989 minus the original year of international expansion, either through franchising or corporate equity, summed over all foreign operations. The year 1989 was used because most service outlet observations are drawn from 1989 annual reports.
time_window: 1989 minus original year of international expansion

description: This variable is proxied by estimating the level of advertising intensity for the industry at large. Advertising intensity was derived from the U.S. Census Bureau reports on the service and retail industries for 1982 and was measured as the percentage of advertising expenditures to overall sales for the specific subindustries of hotels, restaurants, retail merchandise and retail food sales operations.
scale: percentage of advertising expenditures to overall sales

variable_name: political risk (political turmoil, transfer of funds, investment of funds)
description: Political risk was proxied as the amount of political turmoil in the host country, the restrictiveness of host country policies towards the investment of funds, and the restrictiveness of host country policies toward the transfer and repatriation of dividends, fees, and royalties. The variables were derived from estimates by the Frost and Sullivan Country Risk service, which reported investment risk for 82 countries over January 1, 1988 to June 30, 1989. The transfer and investment forecasts were originally reported on a scale of A+ to D- and were converted to numerical grades using a 0 to 4.0 scale with the least restrictive countries receiving the lowest numerical scores; the political turmoil forecast was reported on a Low to Very High scale with Low defined as 1 and Very High as 4.
scale: 0 to 4.0 (least restrictive coded lowest); turmoil 1 = Low to 4 = Very High

description: Currency risk is proxied as the average fluctuation in the foreign exchange rate of each country's currency in the research sample. This measure was computed as the arithmetic average in exchange rate fluctuation based on the absolute value of the annual change in currency values over the period 1982-88, defined as the U.S. dollar price of one unit of foreign currency. Two data sources were used: the Price-Waterhouse annual report on exchange rates for 1985 to 1989, and the World Currency Yearbook reports on exchange rates for 1982 to 1984.

Host country environmental uncertainty was decomposed into political risk and currency risk. Political risk combines political turmoil, restrictions on investment of funds and restrictions on transfer of funds, from Frost and Sullivan country risk estimates for 82 countries converted to numeric scales. Currency risk is the average absolute annual change in the exchange rate over 1982-88.
scale: numeric country-level indices (0 to 4 scales; average percent change)

variable_name: Travel time and cultural distance dummies
description: Monitoring costs were proxied by geographical distance, measured as air travel time between New York and the host country's capital including transfer time, and by cultural distance, measured with six cultural cluster dummy variables based on Ronen and Shenkar with the Anglo cluster as baseline.
scale: hours of air travel; cultural cluster dummies

description: This composite measure uses an average of three parallel measures, each comprising 21 binary items. The first measure is a count of the number of areas monitored; the second is a count of the areas for which forecasts are produced; the third is a count of the number of areas about which assumptions are developed. Reported composite alpha is 0.90.

This composite measure averages the scores on six scales that measure the frequency of scanning. The scales gauge the frequency with which an organization gathers information on each of six environmental sectors. Reported composite alpha is 0.81.

This composite measure uses an average of two parallel measures each comprised of six binary items. The first measure is a count of the number of environmental sectors for which the CEO assumes responsibility for scanning; the second is a count of the number of environmental sectors for which the top management other than the CEO assumes responsibility for scanning. Reported composite alpha is 0.90.

Three scales form a composite measure of scanning system effectiveness using responses that indicate the extent to which the scanning system has contributed to awareness of problems, knowledge of strengths and weaknesses, and awareness of environmental conditions; the three scales are averaged. Organizations with average scores of greater than six are classified as having an effective scanning system, and those with average scores of six or less as having an ineffective scanning system. In the regressions it is a dummy variable with 0 = effective and 1 = ineffective.
scale: three scales each (1) highly negative contribution to (7) highly positive contribution, averaged

description: The measure uses two parallel measures, each composed of fifteen five-point scales. The first set gauges the impact of changes in task-environment conditions on demand in the organization's most important markets during the past three years; the second gauges the anticipated impact during the next three years. The composite measure is computed as the absolute value of the difference between the average scores of responses on the scales for the past three years and the next three years.
scale: (1) very adverse through (3) neutral to (5) very favorable
time_window: past three years and next three years

description: The measure uses two parallel measures each comprised of six five-point scales. The first set gauges the impact of changes in general-environment conditions on demand in the organization's most important markets during the past three years; the second gauges the anticipated impact during the next three years. The composite measure is computed as the absolute value of the difference between the average scores of responses on the scales for the past three years and the next three years.
scale: (1) very adverse through (3) neutral to (5) very favorable
time_window: past three years and next three years

description: Size here refers to the logarithm of the number of people employed.

A composite measure averages standardized scores on two scales used by Grinyer et al. (1986) as indicators of a core technology's degree of inflexibility. One scale assesses the investment-gestation period, measured as the number of months required to set up a new operating facility; the other assesses difficulty of adapting the organization's core technology to develop new but related products. Reported composite alpha is 0.55.

Dess and Davis's (1984) operationalization of Porter's (1980) low-cost generic strategy was adapted. Respondents indicated the extent of importance placed by their organization in the past three years on each of six competitive methods. The composite measure averages scores on the six items. Reported alpha is 0.73.

Citations index for the focal firm for 1990: the total number of citations by other firms in the electrical and electronics machinery sector to the patents the focal firm filed over the previous five years, divided by the citation count of an average firm in the sector, which is computed by averaging across the patent citation counts for all firms in the sector for the same time period. A ratio of 1.0 means that the company's patents were cited as often as the sector average. In the sample of 120 firms the citations index ranged from 0.22 to 2.02, with a mean of 0.933.
time_window: 1990, with a five-year look-back on patents filed

description: Count of the focal firm's agreements, with U.S. and foreign partners, coded as joint venture agreements from case descriptions compiled by Securities Data Company for 1990-1991. Cases whose description indicated a combination of two types were coded so as to indicate both types. Across the sample there were 278 joint venture agreements.

Count of the focal firm's agreements, with U.S. and foreign partners, coded as licensing agreements from case descriptions compiled by Securities Data Company for 1990-1991. Cases whose description indicated a combination of two types were coded so as to indicate both types. Across the sample there were 144 licensing agreements.

Count of the focal firm's agreements, with U.S. and foreign partners, coded as marketing agreements from case descriptions compiled by Securities Data Company for 1990-1991. Cases whose description indicated a combination of two types were coded so as to indicate both types. Across the sample there were 373 marketing agreements.

variable_name: number of research and development agreements
description: Count of the focal firm's agreements, with U.S. and foreign partners, coded as research and development agreements from case descriptions compiled by Securities Data Company for 1990-1991. Cases whose description indicated a combination of two types were coded so as to indicate both types. Across the sample there were 341 research and development agreements.

Proxies inventors' familiarity with components, based on the average degree to which the components have been recently and frequently used; components are proxied by patent subclasses. For each subclass of the focal patent, the indicator of occurrence in every prior patent since 1790 is multiplied by an exponentially decaying component representing the loss and forgetting of knowledge, with the time constant of knowledge loss set at five years; these occurrences are then summed and averaged across the focal patent's subclasses. Because the independent variables are highly skewed, the square root of the original value was taken.
time_window: 1790 to the focal patent application date

description: Proxies inventors' familiarity with the particular combination of subclasses, based on the degree to which the combination has been recently and frequently used. The authors look back at all other patents that used an identical combination of subclasses and multiply each indicator count by the exponential component reflecting loss and forgetting of experiential knowledge regarding the combination. The square root of the original value was taken because the variables are highly skewed.
time_window: 1790 to the focal patent application date

description: Measures how many times since 1790 a particular combination of subclasses has been used; for each previous patent that used an identical combination of subclasses, the cumulative combination usage is incremented. The square root of the original value was taken because the variables are highly skewed.
time_window: 1790 to the focal patent application date

description: An invention's usefulness is measured as the number of prior art citations that the focal patent receives from subsequent patents; prior art citations to the focal patent are measured for 6 years and 5 months after its granting, a period that should capture the bulk of citations to a patent. Bibliometric studies have repeatedly demonstrated that future prior art citations to a patent correlate with its technological importance and value.

Inventive uncertainty is operationalized by estimating the effects of the causal variables on the dispersion parameter of the negative binomial model; the dispersion parameter is the inverse of the gamma error parameter and is parameterized as an exponential function, and variables that decrease it decrease the variability and hence the uncertainty of inventive outcomes.

Dummy variable equal to 1 if the product development structure is concentrated and 0 otherwise, so that the subscript C refers to the concentrated structure and D to the distributed structure. The firms are classified by whether product development activities are concentrated in a single location in the United States (two firms) or split among three different manufacturing facilities (the third firm).

The time for a new product to progress from conception (marked by the entry date of an engineering file) to the time when the first customer-ready prototype is released. The dependent variable of the first-stage (prototyping) hazard model.
time_window: from conception to release of the first customer-ready prototype

description: The time from the date on which the first customer-ready prototype is released to the date on which accumulated shipments exceed 2000 units. The dependent variable of the second-stage (volume production) hazard model.
time_window: from first customer-ready prototype to accumulated shipments exceeding 2000 units

description: The number of individual customers who expressed intent to buy the product. Used as an explanatory variable in both stages of the model.

The number of concurrent projects being prototyped simultaneously in any quarter. Used as an explanatory variable in the time-to-prototype equation; the authors treat the number of competing prototypes as exogenous for a given product.

The number of concurrent projects going to volume production during the period of time when a particular new product is being taken to volume production. Used as an explanatory variable in the time-to-volume-production equation.

The engineering expenditures for new product development and process design, excluding engineering to maintain ongoing production. In some cases records were available to assign expenses to individual products; in others, managers determined engineering costs by individual products.

For the dependent variable the authors used the duration, or age, of the venture. An event is registered upon failure; a small number of terminations that represented the sell-off of the joint venture or its acquisition by a third party were categorized as failures. Terminations in which one partner acquired the assets of the operation were coded as censored outcomes.

A joint venture between direct competitors was assumed when the partners had the same four-digit SIC codes in their primary industries, as determined by the F&S Index. For the cases with more than two partners, the two largest equity holders were compared. The variable is dichotomous, coded one for competing partners.

To determine whether or not a joint venture was integrative in nature, the initial contractual terms, primary function of the venture, and the nature of the partners' contributions were reviewed. Where all partners' primary roles were the same and all partners contributed to a common pool of resources, the variable was coded 1; joint ventures such as those in which one partner manufactures and another markets a product were designated sequential and coded 0. If the distinction could not be determined from published sources, the partners were contacted directly.

Experience in interfirm collaboration was proxied by the average number of previous joint ventures per partner in the five years prior to the agreement, a duration consistent with data availability and resource constraints.
level: partner, averaged to the joint venture
time_window: five years prior to the agreement

description: A dichotomous variable for the presence of concurrent ties between partners, coded 1 if at least two of the partners had other interfirm agreements beyond the focal joint venture, and 0 otherwise.
scale: 1 = at least two partners have other interfirm agreements, 0 = otherwise

description: For the number of parties in a joint venture, a simple tally was used.

For each joint venture, the authors used the duration, or age, of the venture as the dependent variable, and the underlying distribution of duration times describes an underlying distribution that holds when all independent variables are set equal to zero. The estimated hazard rate as a function of venture age was used to assess the pattern of failures across time, comparing the log-normal and Weibull distributions.

States of balance or imbalance in each domain were inferred from historical sources rather than measured directly. The authors reconstruct the degree of consensus and work coordination among legislatures, professional associations, teacher-training institutions, and the state education agency at five-year intervals, and distinguish periods such as conditions in school health before and after 1950. They note that future studies might develop more precise questionnaire-based indices of ideological balance and work coordination.

variable_name: proportion of districts with administrative positions in a given domain
description: The percentage of districts in the sample with an administrative position in a domain (health officer, psychologist/psychometrist/psychiatrist, or curriculum supervisor/director), reported at five-year intervals for 1930-1970. Data were obtained by searching The Directory, which contains the names and job titles of personnel for all districts in the state. Adoption was inferred from administrative job titles relevant to the work of the domain.

Dependent variable in the LSDV regression, a dummy variable coded 1 if a district listed an officer in the domain and 0 if it did not. The data were analyzed separately for each of the three domains. The unit of analysis was the individual district, and the procedure pooled cross sections of the time series.

The proportion of instances in which a personnel-type position observed in any district was observed in that same district five and ten years later, computed for positions of each type over the period 1930-1970. The data on stability are for positions, not people, and districts sometimes listed positions even when no persons were currently occupying them.

A count of the total number of occupational titles listed by a district in a given time period. Because enrollment data were absent for 1930-1950, this variable was used as a proxy for organizational size, although the authors say it is more accurately a reflection of district complexity. The authors note that the absence of a specific size term probably inflated the autocorrelation terms.

Based on questionnaire data from registered nurses, who estimated the volume of patients in ten conditions, such as acute myocardial infarction, burns, and drug abuse cases, on a five-point scale. Responses of registered nurses were aggregated for each condition and an overall mean of the condition means was computed; the input uncertainty measure is the inverse of the variance of this overall mean, representing how homogeneous the volume estimates were across conditions.
scale: five-point scale for the volume estimates

description: Nurses and physicians assessed, on a five-point scale, the extent to which emergency units relied on rules to achieve coordination. The measure was negatively correlated with the use of flexibility in the units, providing evidence of validity.

Nurses and physicians assessed, on a five-point scale, the extent to which emergency units relied on scheduled meetings to achieve coordination. Evidence for the validity of this measure was mixed or nonexistent.

Nurses and physicians assessed, on a five-point scale, the extent to which emergency units relied on authority arrangements to achieve coordination. The measure was negatively correlated with the use of flexibility in the units.

Nurses and physicians assessed, on a five-point scale, the extent to which emergency units relied on autonomy of the staff to achieve coordination. The measure correlated positively with a measure of the use of clinical standards.

Nurses and physicians assessed, on a five-point scale, the extent to which emergency units relied on general policies of the unit to achieve coordination. The measure correlated positively with a measure of the use of clinical standards.

Nurses and physicians assessed, on a five-point scale, the extent to which emergency units relied on mutual adjustment among the staff to achieve coordination. Evidence for the validity of this measure was mixed or nonexistent.

Interview data from registered nurses and physicians provided the basis for this measure: nurses and physicians estimated the percentage of patients seen by a doctor within 15 minutes after their arrival at the units. The alpha coefficient for this measure was .73. It represents how efficiently units handle the input phase of their work cycle.

Constructed by summing three component measures. The first component weighted the quality of nursing care received by patients in specific conditions by the volume of patients in each condition. The second component used nurses' ratings of the quality of nursing care provided in their unit compared to other units. The third component included comparative assessments of the quality of nursing care, noncomparative assessments of the quality of nursing care, and ratings of the performance of the nursing staff, with an alpha coefficient of .67. It reflects how well units handle the transformation phase of their work cycle.

Constructed by summing three component measures. The first component weighted the quality of the medical management of patients in specific conditions by the volume of patients in each condition. The second component derived from ratings made by registered nurses of the quality of medical management patients receive. The third component used assessments of the quality of medical care in the emergency unit made by physicians working in the hospital but outside the emergency unit. It reflects how well units handle the transformation phase of their work cycle.
Placeholder for the second main test of the effectiveness relationships: the same three effectiveness measures were used in the median-split subgroup analyses of high and low input uncertainty.

Price volatility for each commodity and month, computed as the monthly standard deviation of daily prices. The average daily closing price for each commodity was calculated using the daily volume of transactions for different delivery months as weights, and these weighted daily closing prices were then used to calculate price volatility by computing monthly standard deviations. For the analysis of primary working rules, aggregate volatility was represented by the sum of monthly price variances in all commodities for which data were available.
level: commodity-month (aggregate exchange-month for primary working rules)

variable_name: changes in secondary rules and regulations
description: Changes in the primary and secondary rules and regulations were measured by counting the number of rules and regulations adopted or amended in each month; deleted rules or regulations were too few for analysis, and there was no attempt to evaluate the relative importance of specific rules or changes. Working rules were divided according to whether they were primary or secondary, then further classified as rules or regulations according to whether they were made by the membership or the board of directors. Rules and regulations related to specific commodities were classified as secondary; margin changes in each commodity constituted a separate category, and if more than one margin change occurred in a month, the average was used.

variable_name: changes in primary rules and regulations
description: Changes in the primary and secondary rules and regulations were measured by counting the number of rules and regulations adopted or amended in each month. Rules and regulations related to the general operations of the exchange, such as governance, membership, and floor operations, were classified as primary. For this analysis the market variables (volatility, volume, and open interest) were aggregated to include all commodities transacted at the CBT.

Volume is the total contracts traded in each month for each commodity. Data were obtained on volume in each of the commodities under study, as well as total monthly volume in all commodities traded at the CBT; the total volume of transactions used in the primary working-rule analysis is the total number of contracts traded in a given month.
level: commodity-month (aggregate exchange-month for primary working rules)

description: Sanctions and punishments of members by the CBT were measured in two categories: the number of reprimands and the number of suspension orders issued by the CBT in a given month. A third punishment, expulsion from membership, was not analyzed because there were too few cases in the study period, and because expulsion is a response to recurring illegal acts by a member rather than environmental conditions affecting the population of traders.

A single index generated from three highly intercorrelated county indicators that were theoretically and statistically independent of environmental volatility. Principal-component analysis of their correlations indicated that one factor was sufficient to account for most of their variance (77.27 percent), and this factor was used to generate the diversity values for each local environment; the measure was dichotomized at zero for the analysis.

The simple unstandardized regression coefficient for each county's yearly adjusted average unemployment regressed against the national seasonally adjusted unemployment levels for eleven years, following Gardner's volatility index. A slope greater than 1 indicates a relatively more volatile local environment; the measure was dichotomized at 1 for the analysis.

For each of seven hypothetical personal loan applications, the loan officer estimated the probability that the loan applicant would pay back the debt, on a scale running from 0 percent to 100 percent. The cases were constructed by varying information about the applicant to produce a full range of probability from .35 percent to .91.

For each of the seven hypothetical loan cases, respondents judged on a 7-point scale how certain or uncertain they were about their probability estimate that the loan would be repaid, with 1 labelled very certain and 7 labelled very uncertain. No interpretation of uncertainty was made beyond this.

A derived measure computed from the individual probability estimates for each case, using the entropy equation DE = (1 - P) log (1 - P) + (P) log (P), where P is the loan officer's probability estimate for a particular case and log10 was used.
The total number of items of information requested on the loan application form of the bank, reported by bank officers as a measure of the routine information collected for loan decisions.

The number of additional items of information a loan officer reported he or she would require before making a sound decision on a hypothetical loan application, other than the information requested on the application form. It was reported separately for each of the seven cases.

Bank officers reported general structural characteristics of loan decision making: the number of hierarchical levels needed for a final decision, the method of evaluating the credit application ranging from most informal to most formal and structured (e.g., computerized numerical evaluation), the amount of loans given without higher authorization (in dollars), the specifications contained in the bank's written loan policy, and the total number of items on loan application forms.

Reported amounts officers were authorized to grant without higher authorization, and, for the uncertain hypothetical case, the reported likelihood that the loan officer would seek the advice of superiors rather than of colleagues in deciding the case.

Environmental uncertainty was measured through two county-level characteristics of each bank's local environment. Diversity is a single factor score from population size, income level and the labor force split between industry and agriculture; volatility is the slope of the county's yearly adjusted unemployment regressed on national unemployment over eleven years. Both were dichotomized for analysis.
scale: factor score and regression slope, each dichotomized

description: An index developed from a sample of the operating room schedules compiled by each hospital's OR staff the evening before surgery and revised the next day to reflect the actual work performed, sampled every four days over eight and a half months. Two measures were developed: the proportion of operations cancelled (number cancelled divided by number originally scheduled) and the proportion of operations added (number added during the work day divided by number originally scheduled). The overall measure of change in the OR's workflow combines the two by adding the number of additions to and cancellations from the schedule and dividing by the number of operations originally scheduled.
time_window: sampled every four days over eight and a half months

description: Standardization of rules and procedures was measured by asking the OR staff nurses, by questionnaire, how explicit procedures were regarding the conditions under which staff may be requested to work overtime. The item was reverse-scored, so that a value of 1 indicated low destandardization and a value of 5 indicated high destandardization. The item was selected because preliminary field work showed it related specifically to the workflow of the OR and governed the conduct of the workers themselves.

A two-step procedure was used: influence scores for the position of staff nurse and for the position of the director of the OR were calculated, and then the centralization of influence was determined by subtracting the score of the staff nurses from the score of the director of the OR; the scale was then reversed to reflect decentralization. The measure combines two questions asked of both staff nurses and the OR director, who rated on a five-point scale the relative influence of several hospital positions with regard to two task-relevant decisions. The ratings of influence by staff nurses were averaged and then combined with those of the OR director, giving equal weight; the two questions were combined by taking a mean.

Professionalization of the workforce was measured by characteristics of the nursing staff of the OR. Two measures were used to distinguish initial level of training from the extent to which this training was supplemented and maintained by current professional activities. The first measure was based on the proportion of the OR's nursing staff with a B.S. degree or higher, obtained during interviews with the directors of each OR. The extent of current professional activity was measured by the number of articles in professional journals read per month, taken from the OR staff nurse questionnaire, where the actual measure was the mean frequency response. The two measures were significantly but modestly correlated (r = .57).

A risk-adjusted postsurgical death and complication rate averaged for all patients undergoing surgery in the operating room suite of a given hospital, described as an Indirect Standardized Adverse Event Ratio (ISAER): the ratio of observed adverse outcomes to expected adverse outcomes. The number of deaths within 40 days of surgery was added to severe complications assessed at the seventh day following surgery; if the patient was discharged before the seventh day, the information pertained to his or her condition at the time of discharge. Expected probabilities of an adverse outcome were estimated by fitting fifteen logistic regressions, one per surgical category, on patient condition variables (physical status, stage of surgical disease, age, sex, stress level, and insurance coverage). The standardized ratios were further adjusted for their relative reliability by weighting them back toward the mean with a Bayes adjustment of the ISAERs. Severe morbidity is expressed in positive numbers which are interpreted negatively: higher severe morbidity means lower effectiveness.
time_window: deaths within 40 days of surgery; complications assessed at the seventh day following surgery

description: The measure of resources was expressed as the average expenditures per patient-day, a standard of comparison used frequently among hospitals. It combined in a ratio the total expenses for 1973, the number of acute care beds, the occupancy rate for 1973, and the number 365, since the ratio is computed per patient-day; it was expressed as expenses for 1973 divided by (number of acute beds x 1973 occupancy x 365), using data from the hospital administrator questionnaire.

Informants were simply asked: 'In regard to your program generally, with which separate organizations in this community has your organization had the most cooperative relationships in the past 12 months?' Respondents were free to name as many organizations as they wished. A linkage between two organizations was recorded if organization i mentioned that it cooperated with organization j, thus retaining the asymmetry of the relation; organizations mentioned but not part of the sample were excluded. Four matrices were constructed, one for each of the four neighborhoods. Only one binary measure of cooperation was used.

Respondents were asked to list the organizations of which they were members. An N by N symmetric matrix was constructed for each community, where '1' indicated that two leaders had at least one organizational membership in common and '2' indicated that they had no common memberships.
scale: binary (1 = at least one common membership, 2 = no common memberships)

variable_name: racial and ethnic similarity of leaders
description: At the end of the interview respondents were asked about their racial and ethnic identity, and responses were recoded so that leaders were identified as either 'white', 'black', or 'Spanish-speaking'. A matrix was constructed for each neighborhood: if the leader of organization i had the same racial and ethnic identity as the leader of organization j then '1' was entered, and '2' if their identities were different. Respondents who could not be placed in these categories were given a missing data code.
scale: binary (1 = same racial and ethnic identity, 2 = different)

description: Respondents were asked about their religious preference, and responses were recoded so that leaders were identified as 'Protestant', 'Catholic', 'Jewish', 'agnostic', or 'fundamentalist'. A similar matrix was created for religious identities, with '1' for leaders of two organizations sharing a religious identity and '2' for different identities.

Respondents were asked about their education, and responses were recoded into a 'professional degree', 'college degree', or 'high school degree or less' category. A similar matrix was created for educational backgrounds, with '1' for leaders of two organizations having the same educational background and '2' for different backgrounds.

Demographic information from census data on the populations in the four neighborhoods, as well as the city of Chicago, was used to operationalize the degree of turbulence in the environment of the organizations studied. Three dimensions focused on clientele were analyzed: stability and instability (comparing the ethnic and income groups residing in a neighborhood in 1960 and 1970), homogeneity and heterogeneity (indices of dissimilarity for eleven occupational and eighteen ethnic-racial groups, based on differences in percentage distributions comparing each neighborhood with city-wide statistics), and richness and leanness (median family income and the percent of families with incomes under $3000). On this basis Little Village and Heart of Chicago were treated as the more turbulent neighborhoods and Pilsen and Near West Side as the less turbulent.
Residence was measured by whether the leader of the organization resided in the neighborhood or outside the neighborhood.
scale: binary (resides in the neighborhood vs. outside the neighborhood)

description: Each executive was asked to rate, on a scale from 1 to 7, the influence of each of the participating executives in the organization on four types of decisions determined a priori to be of major consequence. For each executive, an overall power score between 1 and 7 was generated by averaging all the scores he or she received for the four types of decisions; Cronbach alphas over .80 for the four-item measure were obtained in each industry sample.

Executives ranked up to three of eight standard functional areas as most similar to their own responsibilities; each area could take four ordinal values: 3 (most similar), 2 (second most similar), 1 (third most similar) or 0 (not ranked). In the strategy analysis, output function is a dummy variable representing all executives who indicated their primary function as marketing or product development.
scale: 0 to 3 ordinal per function; dummy in strategy analysis

description: Executives ranked up to three of eight standard functional areas as most similar to their own responsibilities, with values 3 (most similar), 2, 1 or 0 (not ranked). In the strategy analysis, throughput function represents all executives who indicated their primary function as accounting, process improvement, or operations.
scale: 0 to 3 ordinal per function; dummy in strategy analysis

description: Three methods measured scanning of the output sector: frequency of learning of events or trends in subsectors (7-point interval scale), interest in staying abreast (5-point ordinal scale), and percentage of scanning time aimed at each of the four environmental sectors. Scores on the three measures were converted to Z scores and averaged into a comprehensive scanning index for each sector; the practical range was about -2.00 to +2.00.

Scanning of the throughput sector was measured with the same three methods (frequency on a 7-point interval scale, interest on a 5-point ordinal scale, and percentage of scanning time) and combined by converting each measure to a Z score and averaging the three. The practical range of scanning scores for each sector was about -2.00 to +2.00.

Working from three homogeneous sets of organizations, two independent methods were used to assess strategies: quantifiable published data from annual industry source books on product/market additions over the previous four years, and assessments by expert panels. Only organizations whose strategies were rated at the extremes by both methods were selected; interviews with chief executives about concrete recent or planned product/service/market changes checked whether current strategic behaviors matched the external assessments.
time_window: previous four years for product/market additions

description: Births were determined by comparing entries from one year with those of the following year in Dun and Bradstreet's annual files; an entry that did not exist in the previous year's file was classified as a new firm only after it could be shown that the entry was not due to a change in name, legal status, location, or a file maintenance error. Pairwise inconsistencies were checked with alternative publications such as trade association volumes and telephone directories, and SMSAs with insufficiently accurate birth information were eliminated. New subsidiaries were excluded, so the birth information pertains to genuinely new ventures. Frequencies were computed for each of the three industries in each SMSA.

Urban centrality in the interurban network was measured with an index of three standardized, highly interrelated variables: the number of scheduled airline departures, the number of national headquarters in a city, and the location of a branch of the Federal Reserve Board. The authors describe this measure as somewhat analogous to 'urban dominance' as reported by Abrahamson and DuBick (1977).

The size of the SMSA was measured by the number of people in the areas, as indicated by the 1970 Census. In examining the curvilinearity of the relationship with birth frequencies, the authors also used the natural logarithm of urban size.

Occupational differentiation was based on the distribution of individuals among 20 occupational categories (e.g., professional, technical, health workers, teachers, managers, administrators, salaried employees), as reported by the 1970 Census. The measure was computed with a differentiation formula described by Gibbs and Poston (1975); the formula as printed in the text is not fully readable.

Industrial differentiation was measured by the distribution of value-added manufacture over 21 two-digit industry classes (SIC 19 to SIC 39), as reported by the U.S. Census of Manufacturers in 1967 and 1972, using the differentiation formula described by Gibbs and Poston (1975).
Domestic immigrants were the percentage of the 1970 SMSA population who resided in 1965 outside the 1970 SMSA, as reported by the 1970 Census.
Foreign immigrants were the percentage of SMSA individuals who had immigrated from abroad into the SMSA, as reported by the 1970 Census.

Economic volatility was determined by first regressing time on industrial employment over the period 1959-1972, so that actual and predicted values were obtained for every SMSA for each year. The variance in the difference between actual and predicted employment (i.e., mean square error) was then computed and treated as tapping economic volatility; a smooth trend yields differences close to zero, whereas major discrepancies indicate a volatile area.

Population size was measured by the number of production man-hours for 1967 and 1972 for the two pertinent industries, as reported by the 1967 and 1972 Census of Manufacturers. Because four-digit detail was often withheld, the corresponding two-digit industries were used: SIC 30 (Rubber and Plastics) for Plastic Products and SIC 36 (Electronics) for Telecommunication Equipment and Electronic Components.

Size distribution was determined by computing the concentration of employment in firms of different sizes as reported in County Business Patterns in 1967 and 1972, based on a Herfindahl index over the size categories of firms. The higher the index, the more concentrated is employment in small firms; all SMSAs showed a chi-square distribution with the volume of smaller firms much greater than that of the larger firms. Because information at the four-digit level was often withheld, the corresponding two-digit industries were used as the relevant populations.

The wage rate was computed by dividing the total industrial payroll by the number of employees for the two-digit industries Rubber and Plastic (SIC 30) and Electronics (SIC 36). This information was obtained from the 1967 and 1972 Census of Manufacturers.
The energy rate was the rate for electricity in 1967 and 1972, as reported by the Federal Power Commission.
Unemployment was measured by the percentage of unemployed persons in the SMSA in 1970, as reported by the 1970 Census.

Capital availability was determined with two standardized indices that were combined into a single index: the amount of savings capital in commercial banks during the period 1966-1974 and the number of income tax returns exceeding $100,000 in 1972. The FDIC information is recorded at the state level; when SMSAs cut across state boundaries, weighted averages were computed with weights proportional to the population of the SMSA within each state.

Venture capital sources was the number of venture capital firms in the main city or cities within the SMSA, as reported by Rubel (1972). The authors argue that the prevalence of such firms signals the entrepreneurial climate in the SMSA.

Bank concentration was the cumulative percentage of savings capital deposited in the four largest commercial banks in the SMSA, from the Federal Deposit Insurance Commission. The authors treat it as an indicator of risk-averse capital that might affect organizational birth frequencies negatively.
The number of scientists and engineers was obtained from the U.S. National Science Foundation and included the number of chemists, physicists, and engineers in the SMSA in 1970.

Academic influence was measured by summing the number of graduate students in chemical engineering (for Plastic Products) and electrical engineering (for Telecommunication Equipment and Electronic Components) departments. The number of graduate students was felt to approximate the potential influence of colleges and universities in diffusing scientific innovation.

Equals one if the 3-year lagged unit redundancy exceeds the sample mean and zero otherwise. Unit redundancy itself is the average of the pairwise cosine similarities between the text of the focal unit's patents (titles, abstracts and descriptions) and those of all other units of the same firm, computed from patents granted to each unit until the focal year. A discrete measure was used in the main analysis; a continuous measure was used only in robustness checks.
time_window: 3-year lag; patents until the focal year

description: Measured as the number of self-forward citations a patent received from its grant year until 2021, that is, citations from other patents originating from the same firm. Because the distribution of self-forward citations is skewed, the natural logarithm (1+) of this count is used as the dependent variable.

A binary variable that equals one when the firm failed to renew the focal patent within 4 years of its granting, and zero otherwise. About 14.3% of all patents in the sample were terminated within 4 years of their granting.

A dummy variable that depends on whether the unit that produced the focal patent was directly affiliated with the parent firm (proximate unit = 1) versus with one of the subsidiaries of the firm (proximate unit = 0), based on information in the DISCERN database on whether R&D units belonged to the ultimate parent or to a subsidiary.

Measured as the proportion of a firm's patents in the focal year that are assigned to the parent firm: the number of patents assigned to the parent until the focal year divided by the total number of patents assigned to that firm and all its subsidiaries until that year. A discrete measure is used that equals one if the share of patents assigned to the parent exceeds the sample mean, and zero otherwise; centralization varies only between firms and remains constant within a firm-year for all units.
time_window: patents until the focal year; 3-year lag
