description: Indicator variable capturing redeployment to an ethylene unit from any non-ethylene business unit. If an inventor who did not belong to ethylene units as of 2011 filed ethylene-related patents between 2012 and 2015, the variable is coded 1, and 0 otherwise. The 454 redeployed inventors exclude those who invented at a non-ethylene unit within 3 years of redeployment.

Inventor specialization was measured based on the patent classes (IPC codes) in all patents filed by the focal inventor between 2000 and 2011, using the Euclidean distance of IPC codes. The Euclidean distance is the square root of the Herfindahl index and has a value between 0 and 1; inventive breadth is 1 minus Euclidean distance, so the more the focal inventor filed patents in diverse fields, the higher her breadth.

Brokerage is measured based on effective network size, a well-known measure of structural holes, which conceptually captures the non-redundant elements of the focal inventor's network. The text reports the formula for effective size, where piq denotes the proportion of inventor i's ties with contact q, and mjq is the marginal strength of the relationship between contact j and contact q.

Inventors with an inventive breadth above the median value of all inventors in the industry were categorized as generalists, while others were categorized as specialists. Unit-level generalist slack is the proportion of generalists within each business unit.

Inventors were classified as brokers or non-brokers based on the median brokerage score of all inventors in the industry. Unit-level broker slack is the proportion of brokers within each business unit.

A unit-level knowledge network was created using knowledge components in patents (IPC codes) as nodes and patents containing other knowledge components as edges. The degree of knowledge interdependence was calculated with a clustering coefficient measure, the probability that the adjacent knowledge components of a focal knowledge component are connected; the clustering coefficient for a business unit is the average of the component-level values within the unit.

The dependent variable is the acquired patent's time-to-reassignment to the acquirer. Patents' exposure to reassignment risk begins at the time of the acquisition and is tracked monthly; risk spells end when the patent is centrally reassigned or when a censoring event occurs (end of term, expiration, divestment). Under the accelerated failure time setup, a shorter duration means a higher likelihood of centralized reassignment.
time_window: monthly spells from time of acquisition until reassignment or censoring

description: Measured by the originality index, computed as one minus the Herfindahl index of the patent's backward citations categorized by CPC subclasses, using Hall's (2005) bias correction for a small number of prior-art citations.

The count of the different medical specialties associated with the CPC subclasses of a patent, transformed using an IHS function. The CPC scheme is mapped to the FDA's 16 medical specialty panels by matching CPC subclass definitions to medical specialty descriptions.
scale: count transformed by an IHS function

description: Measured by the entropy index of the acquirer's pre-acquisition patent portfolio grouped by CPC subclasses.
Measured by the entropy index of the acquirer's pre-acquisition product listings with the FDA grouped by their medical specialties.

The number of workers hired via redeployment over all new hires in a mill. Redeployment is defined as the hiring of a worker who held a position at another mill belonging to the same business group within the previous year, limited to job movements that occur between consecutive years and between municipalities.

Indicator equal to one if the worker was redeployed to mill i in year t from an existing mill of the business group, and zero if the worker was hired in the external labor market. The unit of observation is a hired worker in the hiring year.

Labor market thickness in the mill's municipality, measured in the year 2000, which predates the expansion of sugar processing. Thickness in municipality m is computed as the sum across five-digit industries j of the municipality's employment share in industry j times the cosine similarity of industry j's occupation employment shares to those of sugar cultivation, milling, and refining; it represents the probability that a randomly selected worker has experience and skills relevant to sugar processing.
The mean labor market thickness in the municipalities of a firm's incumbent mills, measured in the year 2000.

A dummy for managers, used to capture occupations in which output is more sensitive to worker skill. The authors argue firm strategies are predominantly molded by managers, who wield greater influence on firm performance than other workers.

The 90th percentile of potential sugarcane yield within a 50 km radius of the mill, taken from the GAEZ database, which uses climate, temperature, and soil conditions to estimate potential crop yields under the assumption of high inputs.
When firms own multiple mills, initial market land quality is measured as the average across the firm's mills, using the same within-50-km 90th-percentile potential sugarcane yield from GAEZ.

variable_name: worker characteristics (log experience, college degree, log wage)
description: Regressions of worker attributes on an indicator for whether the worker was redeployed: log years of work experience including the current year, an indicator for whether the worker has a college degree, and the log of the worker's current monthly wage in Brazilian Reais. Wages are used as a proxy for skill, and the comparisons are also made within occupation, mill, and year.

The log number of workers in the mill, used as the dependent variable in regressions run separately for each of the first five years since the mill's opening, on a business group dummy and the log number of workers redeployed in the opening year.

Each coded attribution was classified as a favorable or unfavorable performance outcome. Explicit statements of improvement over past years or an absolute high level of performance in sales, profits, or costs were coded as favorable, and statements of the opposite sort as unfavorable. All 421 attributions were coded for outcome, with total agreement between coders; 232 (55 percent) were favorable and 189 (45 percent) were unfavorable.

An attribution was coded as internal if it referred to causal factors internal to the organization (e.g., strategy, R&D effort, workforce skill) and external if it referred to something outside of the company (e.g., market prices, inflation, the weather, competition). A total of 416 attributions could be coded for locus of causality, of which 187 (45 percent) were internal and 229 (55 percent) were external; coder agreement was 98 percent.

An attribution was coded as stable if the cause could be expected to persist over time and thus would predict the same outcome for the future (e.g., introduction of new technology that reduced production costs); unstable causes were those that could change in the future, such as high set-up costs. Only 287 of the 421 attributions could be coded, of which 184 (64 percent) were stable and 103 (36 percent) were unstable; agreement between coders was 93.7 percent.

A cause was coded as controllable if it could have been changed by the organization (e.g., strategy, marketing effort, acquisition decisions) and uncontrollable if the organization had no power to change it (e.g., market prices). A total of 407 attributions could be coded, of which 171 (42 percent) were controllable and 236 (58 percent) were uncontrollable; agreement between coders was 98 percent.

The context factor distinguishes the good year (1972, when GNP increased 6 percent in constant dollars and stock market indices increased roughly 11 percent) from the bad year (1974, when GNP decreased 2 percent in constant dollars and stock market indices decreased roughly 23 percent). Annual reports covering performance in each of the two years were collected.

Operating revenues were obtained for 1971, 1972, 1973, and 1974, with extraordinary one-time effects on revenue excluded and 'normal' revenues considered. The percentage change from 1971 to 1972 and from 1973 to 1974 was calculated for each company, and companies were ranked on this index within industry for each year and split into thirds. The lowest third was considered to have worse than expected performance, the middle third expected performance, and the top third better than expected performance.

variable_name: relative number of lines of attributions
description: The relative number of lines of attributions is the total number of lines of attributions divided by the total number of lines in the letter; the total number of lines of attributions in a letter was used as an alternative dependent variable. These measures are defined at the level of the company in a given year, so there is a single observation per company per year.

Degree centrality operationalizes structural embeddedness; the authors state that centrality can be defined for projects in the same manner as for project managers. For a project manager the measure is the number of projects in which the manager participates, and the analogous measure is used for projects.

Betweenness centrality operationalizes junctional embeddedness, the extent to which an entity connects other entities. The authors define it as the number of paths between other nodes on which the node lies and use centrality-based measures for projects in the same manner as for project managers.

Eigenvector centrality operationalizes positional embeddedness, the extent to which an entity is connected with other structurally embedded entities. The authors describe it as participation in important projects and define centrality for projects in the same manner as for project managers.

Degree centrality—the number of projects in which the manager participates—operationalizes the project manager's structural embeddedness. It captures the number of the manager's direct ties in the developer–project affiliation network.

Betweenness centrality—the number of paths between other nodes on which the manager lies—operationalizes the project manager's junctional embeddedness, that is, the extent to which the manager connects other entities.

Eigenvector centrality—the manager participates in important projects—operationalizes the project manager's positional embeddedness. It appraises the extent to which the manager is connected with other structurally embedded entities.

The number of CVS commits, treated as an indicator of successful technical refinement. A commit occurs when a developer uploads the altered source code file and the CVS tool updates the changed files automatically, so commits reflect meaningful changes to the source code. Because the count distribution is heavily skewed, the authors took the logarithm of the variable and approximated it as continuous.

The number of downloads over the life span of a project, used to assess commercial and economic success. The authors describe it as a market-based measure of popularity that should relate to product use when software is distributed through a single channel, and note that researchers have used downloads as a surrogate for sales when software is freely available. The log of the variable was taken and approximated as continuous.

The number of months since the inception of the project, used to control for the age of the project because the number of CVS commits and downloads are likely to increase with age. It also enters the latent class regression as a concomitant profiling variable.

The number of page views of the project, which directly signals the general interest level in the project and its market potential. It is used as a concomitant profiling variable in the latent class regression analysis.

A firm's AI capability combines AI-related job posts, original social media posts, and news reports about the firm into a single measure by taking the first principal component. A job post, social media post, or news report is identified as AI-related if it contains any of the AI keywords in the keyword dictionary in the summary texts. The underlying quantities are cumulative with a yearly depreciation rate of 15%, and the measure is standardized in the regressions.
time_window: Measured each year; cumulative quantity with a yearly depreciation rate of 15%

description: A job post, social media post, or news report is identified as discovery-AI related if it contains both AI and discovery keywords within the same sentence, and the first principal component of the resulting measures from the three data sources is used to measure a company's discovery-oriented AI. Discovery keywords such as search, explore, discover and insight were taken from the organizational learning literature and from a bag-of-words model trained on 1,000 randomly selected AI-related texts that the authors manually labeled as discovery or optimization oriented.

A job post, social media post, or news report is identified as optimization-AI related if it contains both AI and optimization keywords within the same sentence, and the first principal component of the resulting measures from the three data sources is used to measure a company's optimization-oriented AI. Optimization keywords such as refine, exploit, efficiency, optimize, automate, process and tune were taken from the organizational learning literature and from the same bag-of-words procedure used for discovery-oriented AI.

The authors count the number of job posts, social media articles, and news reports that contain keywords related to the lean startup method and take the first principal component of the factors derived from the three data sources as the firm's LSM level each year.
time_window: Measured each year; cumulative quantity with a yearly depreciation rate of 15%

description: The extent to which companies adopt the prototyping application of LSM is measured with keywords in job posts, social media articles and news reports. Prototyping keywords include minimum viable product, test product, validation, verification, trial and error, and customer/market demand and learning/response.

The extent to which companies adopt the controlled experimentation application of LSM is measured with keywords in job posts, social media articles and news reports. Its keywords include experimentation, laboratory (technician) and A/B testing.

variable_name: Number of Software Copyrights (software companies); Number of Product Trademarks (physical product companies)
description: For software companies the number of new products is the number of software copyrights the company applies for each year, and for physical product companies it is the number of product trademarks applied for each year. Software copyrights and product trademarks measure product development outcomes rather than the development process, and in China they are common practices for companies to protect intellectual property before launching new products. The dependent variable is led by one year.
time_window: Led by one year relative to the explanatory variables

variable_name: Number of First-Release Software Copyrights (software companies); Number of First-Release Product Trademarks (physical product companies)
description: For software, the registered software version is collected from the copyright certificate and all V1.0 software is treated as the first release of the firm. For physical products, the registered product subclasses are collected from the trademark certificates and a trademark is treated as a first release if it contains at least one new subclass relative to the company's existing trademarks. The dependent variable is led by one year.
time_window: Led by one year relative to the explanatory variables

variable_name: Number of Iterative-Release Software Copyrights (software companies); Number of Iterative-Release Product Trademarks (physical product companies)
description: Software version numbers subsequent to V1.0 are treated as iterative release versions of an existing product. A trademark is treated as an iterative release if it introduces no new product subclass relative to the company's existing trademarks. The dependent variable is led by one year.
time_window: Led by one year relative to the explanatory variables

variable_name: Average Completion Time (in Days) for First-Release Products and for Iterative-Release Products
description: For each company in each year the authors compute the average number of days between two first-release products as the average completion time for first-release products, and the average number of days between two versions of the same product as the average completion time for iterative-release products. Higher values indicate slower product development.
time_window: Led by one year when used as a dependent variable

description: The indicator of strong environmental performance is a positive environmental event, specifically the announcement by an independent third party of winning an environmental award. Events were identified by searching the NEXIS newswire database for the keyword "environment" within five words of "award" over the period from 1985 to 1991, with only publicly traded NYSE or AMEX firms (or wholly owned subsidiaries of such firms) retained. The first pass search identified 1,066 citations, yielding 140 observations (96 firms); after removing observations with contemporaneous financial and management announcements, the cleaned sample had 110 observations (82 firms).

The indicator of weak environmental performance is a negative environmental event, an environmental crisis identified from keywords such as "oil," "chemical," "gas leak," or "explosion" along with the words "spill" and "environment." Announcements about oil spills were included only if the amount of oil was significant, defined as more than 10,000 gallons by the U.S. Coast Guard. The sample period was limited to two years (1989-1990); 745 citations yielded only 22 observations (16 firms), and 18 observations remained after removing four with contemporaneous financial events.

Abnormal returns were estimated with the Market Model, which assumes a linear relationship between the expected return of an individual stock and the expected return of a broadly based market portfolio or index, with parameters estimated by ordinary least squares over a 200-day estimation period from Day -209 to Day -10. The event period of three days (Day -1 to Day +1) was used for calculating the cumulative abnormal return for each event, with Day 0 used as the first period for crises; standardized abnormal returns were used for the single period and cumulative test statistics.
time_window: 200-day estimation period (Day -209 to Day -10); three-day event period

description: The estimated change in market valuation of firm i over event period Ep is the cumulative abnormal return over the event period multiplied by the equity market valuation of the firm one period prior to the event period (shares outstanding times share price), using the formula given as Equation (4).
time_window: one period prior to the event period

variable_name: pollution abatement capital expenditures by industry
description: Annual pollution abatement capital expenditures were scaled as a percentage of total capital expenditures for each industry and then averaged over the seven-year period, using U.S. Bureau of the Census figures reported only for industries, not individual firms. Higher values indicate dirtier industries; because the figures are reported only for manufacturing industries, the sample size was reduced to 56.

For firm i in industry K, the emission ratio is the firm's total emissions as reported to the U.S. EPA Toxic Release Inventory divided by the firm's total revenue, scaled by the revenue-weighted average emission intensity of S&P 500 firms in the same industry. An emissions ratio equal to one indicates that the firm emits the same quantity of emissions per dollar of revenue as the industry, and a ratio less than one indicates better performance than the industry. The average IRRC indices were reported for a two-year period ending in 1989.
A ratio computed as the emissions ratio but with total compliance penalties (in dollars) replacing total emissions. The IRRC series was reported for a three-year period ending in 1989.

An overall rating computed from a simple average of the emissions ratio and the compliance ratio, reported as a ratio relative to the revenue-weighted industry average of S&P 500 firms in the same industry.

Time was entered as a covariate in the cross-sectional analysis of the 110 cleaned environmental award events, using a centered date variable to reduce collinearity. A nonsignificant coefficient indicates the market reaction to award events did not change over the 1985-1991 sample period.

Counts the environmentally consequential drilling accidents attributable to the driller in a given year. Reported accident types include drilling-fluid management failures, failures of surface containment, equipment and maintenance failures, breaches of well integrity during the active drilling phase, and losses of well control such as kicks and blowouts. An accident enters the count only if the DEP report records its environmental impact regardless of severity and assigns culpability to the driller. Project-level accidents are logged at the date of occurrence and aggregated to the firm-year level by summing the total drilling accidents committed by a driller in a given year.

Estimated by deriving the residual from a first-stage OLS regression of the firm's drilling rate at the project level on systematic determinants. The observed drilling rate is decomposed into systematic determinants captured by the explanatory variables and the residual, which reflects firm-specific deviations from expected drilling speed. For each driller, residuals for every well drilled are standardized, then averaged, and finally collapsed to the firm-year level. A positive value indicates the driller is intrinsically faster than the expected average, while a negative value indicates a slower intrinsic speed.

Measured as the proportion of the driller's fleet consisting of automated rigs rather than the traditional fully human-operated rigs. Automated rigs range from semi-automated to fully automated drilling machines that operate without on-site human crew. The authors note that the measure can only identify using available information whether a rig is automated but not its degree of automation.

Measured as a ratio of the number of estimated oil and gas job seekers divided by the number of oil and gas job openings in a given county and quarter. Local job seekers in the oil and gas industry for each county-quarter are estimated by multiplying the county's total unemployment in the quarter by that county's oil and gas employment share in that quarter; local job openings are estimated by multiplying the county's total job postings in the quarter by that county's oil and gas employment share in that quarter. Each driller's exposure depends on its focal county, assigned based on its primary field office. Values greater than 1 indicate a surplus of job seekers relative to available jobs.
level: county-quarter, assigned to the driller's focal county

description: Dummy variable taking a value of 1 if the firm was invited to participate in the RegRoom and 0 otherwise. Random assignment was blocked on firms' region of operation and their main owners' gender and resulted in 47 firms in Control and 43 in Treatment; the estimate reported is an intention-to-treat effect, since 79 percent of invited firms attended a session.

Response to the question 'How would you rate the quality of government agencies' consultative process?' on a five-point scale on which 'Needs major improvement' takes a value of 0 and 'Exceptional' takes the value of 4. Measured in both the pre-treatment and post-treatment surveys and used as one of the two dependent variables testing Hypothesis 1.

Response to the statement 'Government agencies have sufficient understanding of businesses like this one to effectively carry out their regulatory duties,' with responses ranging from 'Strongly disagree = 0' to 'Strongly agree = 4.' Measured in both the pre-treatment and post-treatment surveys and used as one of the two dependent variables testing Hypothesis 1.

Response to the question asking the respondent to rate their understanding of the draft; the table's footnote states that responses range from 'Not at all' = 0 to 'Fully understand' = 4, while the question text as printed says a scale from 1 to 5. Measured in the post-treatment survey only.

Response to the statement 'The Department of Provincial Administration fully understands the content of the comments that your firm submitted,' with responses ranging from 'Strongly disagree = 0' to 'Strongly agree = 4.' Measured in the post-treatment survey only.

Response to the statement 'The Department of Provincial Administration will use comments submitted by your firm to make changes to the draft regulation,' with responses ranging from 'Strongly disagree = 0' to 'Strongly agree = 4.' Measured in the post-treatment survey only.

variable_name: Submitting a comment to the online platform
description: Behavioral measure of whether the firm submitted a comment, taking a value of 1 if the firm submitted a comment and 0 if not. It is based on submissions to the Google-based form that replicated all key features of the state's Law Portal notice and comment system for the focal draft.
time_window: notice and comment window for the focal draft (February 2023)

description: Three external legal experts, each a commercial lawyer specializing in Thai business law, none otherwise associated with the project and with no knowledge of treatment status, read and rated each comment without knowing the firm's identity or treatment status. Each comment was rated on a five-point scale from 'strongly disagree' (1) to 'strongly agree' (5) on three criteria, and each criterion is analyzed as a separate outcome. In the all-sample models, comments not submitted were imputed the lowest score of 1.

Indicator variable equal to one if the firm has at least one subsidiary (multi-unit) in a given year and zero if the firm operates as a stand-alone entity without subsidiaries in that year. Stand-alone firms are operationalized as firms that lack separable business units with their own P&L accountability. The variable is lagged one year in the regressions.

Computed as the natural logarithm of one plus the prior-year number of base-level units directly controlled by the ultimate-parent firm. Base units are divisions and majority-owned subsidiaries with no subordinate divisions or subsidiaries, representing the lowest level of profit-center responsibility. The logarithm is taken because base-unit counts are right-skewed. A higher number indicates greater divisionalization.

Indicator variable for whether the manager is a woman manager. DCA does not directly report managers' gender, so gender is inferred from first names using the genderize.io API; the API-predicted gender is assigned when the associated probability is at least .90. Names below this threshold, names based only on initials, and names with insufficient information are reviewed manually using publicly available online sources. Cases that cannot be classified with sufficient confidence are coded as unclassified rather than assigned a gender, and 9.3% of managers could not be classified and are excluded from analyses involving manager gender.

Indicator variable denoting whether a manager has served as the head of a subsidiary in the previous seven years. The variable is set to one if the manager held such a position at any point from t-1 back to t-7 within the same parent company where the manager is employed at time t; if the individual has never been the head of a subsidiary within the same parent entity but has occupied a top-five senior role within the parent firm, the value is zero. The construction is limited to the subset of data in divisionalized firms with information on succession, head-of-subsidiary experience, and top positions, amounting to about 426,000 observations, within which 35.2% of managers have subsidiary-head experience.

Unit-level return on assets (ROA) is first standardized using z-scores computed within each two-digit SIC industry-year cell, then each unit's standardized performance is benchmarked against the leave-one-out mean of other units within the same firm-year. The measure uses the unit's lagged three-year average ROA. Higher values indicate that a unit performs better than its internal peers, net of industry-year conditions.

Indicator variable of whether a manager ascends to the CEO position of a parent company in a given year (year t), provided that in the preceding year (year t-1) the individual did not hold the CEO position at the parent company. A manager enters the promotion risk set in year t if observed in the DCA managerial records in year t-1 and not holding the parent-firm CEO position in year t-1; managers who become parent-firm CEO in year t are coded as promoted and exit the risk set thereafter. The risk set is further restricted to US-based ultimate parents with headquarters-state information and to managers ranked in the top 25 in the prior year.

Dummy variable indicating whether firms engaged in collaborations with advocacy groups in the 3 years prior to the survey year. It is built from an MIP survey question on firms' collaboration for innovation activities with a list of external partners, which the authors extended to include interest groups/non-profit organizations that they refer to as advocacy groups. The question requires respondents to think specifically about collaborations for innovation, not other forms of interaction.
time_window: 3 years prior to the survey year

description: Sales in the last year of the 3-year survey period (2018, 2020, 2022) of innovations introduced during that period, expressed in natural logarithmic terms. The variable is constructed by multiplying the proportion of sales of newly introduced products and services by total sales in Million Euros; zero observations were replaced with the minimum observed positive value of sales of new products and services in the sample. Higher sales indicate that an innovation has been more widely adopted by customers in the market.
time_window: last year of the 3-year survey period (2018, 2020, 2022)

description: Dummy variable equal to one if a firm was reported in the media for any product-centric corporate social irresponsibility incidents over the past 5 years (t - 4 to t). Product-centric incidents were identified in RepRisk by selecting categories of corporate social irresponsibility whose descriptions explicitly mention products, services, or product-related terms as the focal object of criticism. ZEW conducted a name-matching between all German firms covered in RepRisk and the entire MIP sample, with extensive manual cleaning.

variable_name: Industry-level variation in corporate social performance
description: Standard deviation of overall ESG scores across firms within each industry and year, using firms' industry-adjusted ESG score from the MSCI ESG Direct database, which ranges from 0 to 10. To ensure comparability across years, the industry-year standard deviation is normalized by the standard deviation of the same score across all firms in the same year, and a 3-year moving average is computed. Higher values correspond to industries characterized by greater variation in corporate social performance.
scale: 0 to 10 underlying ESG score; normalized dispersion index

description: The average perceived socio-cognitive distance between consecutive category sets along the VC's chronologically ordered category investment path during the five-year window from t-4 through t. The path is built by ordering the companies that received investments from the VC within the past five years by initial investment date and replacing each company with its affiliated industry category. Category similarity of categories I and J is the number of different VCs investing in both categories divided by the total number of VCs investing in category I in the previous five years; distance is one minus similarity. Distances between category sets are computed with the modified Hausdorff distance.
time_window: five-year window from t-4 through t

description: The magnitude of change in a VC's status over a 5-year forward interval, from year t to t + 5. Status is measured annually as standardized eigenvector centrality based on 5-year rolling windows of co-investment ties, and the 5-year forward interval ensures that status at t and status at t + 5 are based on non-overlapping investment histories.

The set of categories in which a VC invested during the previous 5 years (t-4 to t) and in which it invested again during the subsequent 5 years (t + 1 to t + 5) is first identified. The measure is then the share of total investment dollars allocated to these continuing categories during the prior 5-year window, relative to the VC's total investment across all categories during that same period.
time_window: t-4 to t, with continuation checked in t + 1 to t + 5

description: The proportion of unique portfolio companies in which the VC invested during t-4 to t that subsequently achieved a successful outcome during t + 1 to t + 5. Successful outcomes are defined as receiving a follow-on round of funding from a new VC, experiencing an IPO, or being acquired through an M&A transaction.
time_window: t-4 to t, outcomes observed in t + 1 to t + 5

description: Status is measured annually using the standardized eigenvector centrality measure based on 5-year rolling windows to aggregate network ties across years. The status of each VC is a function of the status of the other VCs with whom the VC formed a syndicate in the last 5 years. Each network's status is scaled with min-max standardization to a max of 1 and min of 0.
VC Experience in year t is the logged number of companies in which the VC invested until year t.

Measured as the number of separate flat packs a product is shipped in, based on product information from IKEA.com. IKEA's packaging is strongly motivated by minimizing inventory and transportation costs, so shipping components in separate packs suggests packs contain groups of components that are physically separable and functionally discrete enough to warrant separate packaging. The authors also control for product size and price to use the number of flat packs as a proxy for modularity.

Measured at the product level by how widely its constituent parts are used across different product contexts, adapting Mastrogiorgio and Gilsing's measure of knowledge component reuse in patents to physical components. The authors first collect IKEA product assembly manuals that list parts with unique part numbers, then measure each part's compatibility by counting the number of distinct fine-grained product function categories in which the same part number appears, and construct the product-level measure by averaging this part-level measure across all parts used in the product. When a manual is missing, UniqueComponents and ComponentCompatibility are set to 1.

An indicator variable based on a product-level field on IKEA's website that indicates whether a product is offered as a "single variant" or has other specific variant descriptors. The indicator takes the value of 0 when the product is described as a "single variant" and otherwise takes the value of 1; descriptors capture esthetic variations in color, size, material, or appearance.

Constructed from clean, centered images of each IKEA product on a white background, resized to a standard 200 x 200-pixel resolution. Three complementary indicators of visual complexity were computed: pixel standard deviation, image entropy, and edge density. These were reduced to a single underlying construct using factor analysis, with a single factor accounting for approximately 86% of the shared variance across the three measures; the negative of the factor scores is the composite measure of visual simplicity.

The dependent variable is categorical, distinguishing whether a hack resulted in the original product retaining its original function (adaptation), experiencing a new function only, or a new functionality. Two sets of MTurkers labeled the functionalities of the original IKEA product and of the hacked product; each product was labeled by at least two different MTurkers, who generated up to three action labels. Word Mover's Distance implemented with FastText embeddings measured the semantic distance between the action labels of the original and hacked products, and the same word modeling captured overlap in the original and hacked products' function sets to obtain a measure of whether the hack results in a change in its function.

The dependent variable is categorical, distinguishing whether a hack resulted in the original product retaining its original function (adaptation), experiencing a new function only, or a new functionality (which typically also comes with a new function). Two sets of MTurkers labeled the functionalities of the original IKEA product and of the hacked product; each product was labeled by at least two different MTurkers, who generated up to three action labels. A hack is classified as involving a change in functionality when the Word Mover's Distance between the action labels of the original and hacked products exceeds zero, indicating semantic divergence between subsets of the original and hacked action labels.

The average feet drilled per day for a well site, calculated by taking the total depth of the focal well site and dividing by the total number of drilling days needed to complete drilling there, using the drilling commencement and completion dates. The average measure is used to help smooth out daily variations during the drilling process. A higher value denotes faster speed.

A dummy variable constructed to be equal to 1 if the focal driller enters into a partnership with another driller for the given well project, and 0 if the focal driller goes it alone. The measurement of partnering is lagged relative to the subsequent speed performance realized in the project.
time_window: lagged relative to the subsequent speed performance realized in the project

description: A residual from a first-stage OLS regression of the well-level drilling rate (feet per day) on well type, project size, contract type, oil demand, and field and year fixed effects, capturing firm-specific deviations from the systematic expected drilling rate. The residuals are averaged for each firm-year and reverse coded so that higher values indicate slower drilling; the firm-year values are then mapped onto the firm-year panel as a three-year moving average lagged by one year, with a value of zero (neutral speed) assigned to years with no drilling information. A driller is classified as slow when its Slowness is above zero and as fast when its Slowness is below zero.
time_window: prior three years, lagged by one year

description: The number of partnerships in which the focal driller has previously engaged. In the interpretation of the interaction results, a standardized partnering experience value of 1 is used to represent a firm one standard deviation above the sample mean.
time_window: prior to the deal of interest

description: The types of interlocks composing a tie in 1962, coded as 'no directional interlocks' or 'at least one directional interlock.' Directional interlocks are those created by directors principally affiliated with one of the firms linked; nondirectional interlocks are created by directors not principally affiliated with either of the firms linked.
scale: binary (no directional interlocks / at least one directional interlock)

description: The number of interlocks composing a tie in 1962, coded as 1 or 2-or-more.
Coded dichotomously as 'directional' or 'nondirectional,' and cross-tabulated with reconstitution for only those ties that included at least one directional and one nondirectional interlock.

Single-interlock ties were coded 'broken' if the one interlock they consisted of was accidentally broken, and multiple-interlock ties were coded 'disrupted' if only one of their interlocks was accidentally broken and 'broken' if the rest were broken. A tie was coded 'reconstituted' if a new interlock linked two firms in 1964 or 1966 that were tied in 1962; to be considered new, an interlock must have been created by a director who did not link the same firms in 1962. The less ambiguous measure of continuity, rates of reconstitution, was used to evaluate the hypotheses; the more ambiguous measure of maintenance or reconstitution was used only to speculate about the percentage of ties that were vehicles of formal coordination.

For single-interlock ties, the direction of the tie was the direction of the interlock it consisted of; only directional interlocks possess a directional component. To increase the number of ties examined, the population of single-interlock ties was expanded to include ties accidentally disrupted between 1964 and 1966 that may or may not have been continued in 1966 and 1969.
If a broken tie was reconstituted with a directional interlock in the same direction as the original tie, directional continuity was coded 'preserved.'

Dummy variable for whether the company's operating structure is a worldwide functional division structure, in which the functional activities in a foreign subsidiary report directly to their respective functional divisions in the parent. Organizational structure was determined from company organization charts and extensive discussions with a senior international manager about formal reporting relationships and lines of authority, and represents the operating structure, which can be different from the legal structure. Coded 1 for companies with this structure.

Dummy variable for whether the company's operating structure is an international division structure, in which all foreign subsidiaries report to an international division separate from the domestic operations. Structure was determined from organization charts and discussions with a senior international manager about formal reporting relationships and lines of authority. Coded 1 for companies with this structure.

Dummy variable for whether the company's operating structure is a geographical region structure, which divides the world into regions, each with its own headquarters responsible for all of the company's products and business within its geographical area. Structure was determined from organization charts and discussions with a senior international manager about formal reporting relationships and lines of authority. Coded 1 for companies with this structure.

Dummy variable for whether the company's operating structure is a worldwide product division structure, which extends the responsibilities of the domestic product divisions to cover their product lines on a worldwide basis. Structure was determined from organization charts and discussions with a senior international manager about formal reporting relationships and lines of authority. Coded 1 for companies with this structure.

The number of broad product lines a company offered for sale in two designated foreign countries, one a major European country and the second Brazil. Because both were large, actively developed markets for most companies in the sample, the product offerings in these two markets were considered representative of the company's total foreign product offering. The correlation between the two measures was .87, and the highest of the two measures was used to represent the company's foreign product diversity.

Measured on a 5-point scale that the interviewer used to rate the MNC following a discussion with the respondent about product differences across subsidiaries. One on the scale indicates 'identical products, parts are interchangeable worldwide'; 3 indicates 'substantial cosmetic differences, but share same basic technology engineering'; and 5 indicates 'basic technology differences, require separate basic technology engineering'.
Measured by the percentage of company sales income spent on R&D, a measure also used by Stopford and Wells (1972). Financial data used to calculate this measure was for the year 1976.
Measured by the percentage of a company's sales occurring outside of the parent country. Financial data used to calculate this measure was for the year 1976.
Measured by the percentage of foreign sales accounted for by foreign manufacturing rather than exports from the parent country. Financial data used to calculate this measure was for the year 1976.

Measured by the number of foreign countries in which the company had either resident marketing or manufacturing operations. Financial data used to calculate this and subsequent measures was for the year 1976.

Measured by the percentage of a company's foreign sales accounted for by subsidiaries with greater than 30 percent outside ownership. The variable was measured by categories (e.g., 0-5 percent, 5-10 percent) with the final category open-ended (more than 20 percent), and was treated as an ordinal ranking of the six categories for purposes of analysis.

Measured by the percentage of a company's foreign sales accounted for by acquisitions made within the past 10 years. The variable was measured by categories (e.g., 0 percent, 0-5 percent) with the final category open-ended (more than 25 percent), and was treated as an ordinal ranking of four categories for purposes of analysis.

variable_name: Subcontracting expenditures as a proportion of construction receipts
description: Subcontracting expenditures are taken as a ratio of construction total receipts. Reported for firms of different types, sizes, and states, and computed for the statistical average firm in each state.

variable_name: Type of construction (specialization by type of construction)
description: General contractors of both types are divided into narrower types according to type of construction. The census does not report data that could be used as an independent indicator of complexity for each type of construction, but firms specializing in more complex projects do more subcontracting.

variable_name: Firm size (number of employees and total receipts)
description: Subcontracting expenditures are reported for firms in various size ranges, where size is measured both by number of employees and total receipts in dollars. The dollar measure is used on the assumption that large firms have large projects and that larger projects require more labor and materials and are more costly.

variable_name: Percentage of population living in a SMSA, April 1970
description: Market extent was taken to be indicated by urbanization, measured as percentage of population living in Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas (SMSAs) in 1970. Greater urban density concentrates construction activity around urban centers, resulting in more extensive markets, given the on-site, local nature of construction.

variable_name: Variability (month of highest employment / month of lowest employment)
description: The variability measure used was the month of greatest employment of construction workers divided by the month of lowest employment, with data reported for March, May, August, and November. It has a Pearson correlation coefficient of .694 (p = .001) with average annual inches of snow and sleet for selected cities in each state.
scale: ratio of highest to lowest monthly employment

description: Data on percentage of clerks in the labor force are not available, so the table gives the percentage of nonproduction employees; proportionate size of the administration is taken as the index of bureaucratization.

The dependent variable in each hypothesis is the relative number of projects (words) approved for each type of manager by the chief budget officer. Data from only the last ten cycles of each replication were used; during those ten cycles each simulated manager proposed 104 words to each chief budget officer, and on the average 42 percent of the proposed words were approved.
time_window: last ten cycles of each replication

description: One of the three attributes used to define the eight types of simulated managers, set at high or low. High profit managers were designed, on the average, to propose projects which were actually twice as profitable as those proposed by low profit managers.

One of the three attributes used to define the eight types of simulated managers, set at high or low, manipulated through comments placed at the bottom of the managers' project proposal forms. Low influence managers included comments to the budget officer on two of the ten trials used in the analysis, relatively innocuous messages about business conditions; high influence managers included comments on eight of the ten trials, all much more aggressive statements.
time_window: the ten trials used in the analysis

description: One of the three attributes used to define the eight types of simulated managers, set at accurate or biased. Accurate estimators were designed to estimate profitability within +5% of the true value, but biased estimators, on the average, overestimated actual profit by a factor of two.

A single questionnaire item asked which pay plan best described the compensation of the sales staff, with responses salary/hourly wage, commission only, base + commission, and other. The authors used a dichotomous measure, salary versus commission: commission plans were pay plans in which at least a portion of compensation was based on sales for which an employee was personally responsible, and in the stores studied all commission plans contained a commission component of at least 30 percent; salary pay plans were those in which pay was exclusively through a salary or an hourly rate.

Four questionnaire items measured the technology of the sales job and the amount of service in the selling process: the service offered to customers (1 = customer fills out warehouse requisition, check out only, to 5 = customer is assisted continuously), the minutes spent with the average customer who makes a purchase, how long it would take an average full-time salesperson to learn the basic duties of the job (1 = less than 3 days to 5 = more than 6 months), and how customers would describe the merchandise (1 = customer expends minimal effort to 3 = customer expends much effort to understand product features and brand differences). Responses of all informants in a store were averaged item by item, and the four item means were combined into a single scale using the factor-loading scores of the first factor.

Three items were used: the size of the store (square footage), the number of salespeople who work at the store, and the number of managers and assistant managers at the store. Store size, number of salespeople, and number of salespeople per manager were the three measures of span of control, combined into a single measure using the factor-loading scores of the first factor.

Stores were typed according to their designated line of merchandise in the shopping center directory, and outcome uncertainty was then measured with failure rates reported in Dun and Bradstreet's Survey of Retail Store Failures for 1975 and 1979 and with Census Bureau figures for the number of competitors in the San Francisco Standard Metropolitan Statistical Area for the same period for a given line of merchandise. The two measures were combined using factor-loading scores of the first factor; the first measure captures downside variation and the second general instability in industries like retailing.
level: store, typed by line of merchandise

description: One item asked managers when the chain was founded, and age was computed by subtracting the year given from 1981, the last year the data were collected. Age was measured as the number of years of age of the store chain, or of the store for single stores, because type of compensation is a decision made at the chain level in retailing businesses like those studied.
level: store chain (or store, for single stores)

description: A dummy variable indicating whether the store was a shoe store, determined by its designation in the shopping center directory.
scale: dummy: 0 = not a shoe store, 1 = shoe store

description: The store manager's response to a questionnaire item: 'What is the average purchase size ($'s) in this store?'

Each group was randomly assigned to one of three decision-making approaches using the manipulations developed by Schweiger and colleagues (1986): dialectical inquiry, devil's advocacy, or consensus. Groups remained intact and used the same approach for both cases, and orientation sessions were not repeated. Two items per approach on the post-decision questionnaire served as manipulation checks, and judges classified tape recordings of the sessions.

variable_name: group performance (number, validity, and importance of assumptions; quality of recommendations)
description: Three judges independently rated each group's final recommendations and supporting assumptions on four dimensions. Judges counted the assumptions each group provided, rated the validity of each assumption on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (low confidence in its validity) to 5 (high confidence), and rated the importance of each assumption on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (not important) to 5 (very important). Each group's validity score was its summed validity ratings divided by the number of assumptions it provided, and its importance score was computed in the same way; the overall quality of each group's recommendations was rated on a 5-point scale from 1 (low quality) to 5 (high quality).

variable_name: member satisfaction and desire to continue working with their group
description: Two items on the 12-item post-decision questionnaire assessed participants' satisfaction and desire to continue working with their group, administered immediately upon completion of the group's work on each case (alphas of .63 and .64 for the first and second sessions).

variable_name: acceptance of the group's assumptions and recommendations
description: Two items on the post-decision questionnaire assessed the extent of participants' acceptance of the group's assumptions and recommendations (alphas of .73 and .75 for the first and second sessions).

variable_name: critical evaluation (reevaluation of own assumptions and recommendations)
description: Two items on the post-decision questionnaire assessed the extent to which group conditions had led participants to reevaluate their own assumptions and recommendations (alphas of .67 and .71 for the first and second sessions).

Measured as the number of minutes elapsed from the moment the experimenter left a group's workroom until the experimenter received the group's final assumptions and recommendations. The experimenter had announced that elapsed time would break any ties in the competition for the group prize.

Experience was operationalized through the two work sessions of the longitudinal design: each group solved the Leitch case in the first session and the lengthier and more complex Hudepohl case in the second, using the same decision-making approach. No feedback was provided on the first case, and orientation sessions were not repeated.

Organizational effectiveness was assessed along five distinct dimensions adapted from Quinn and Rohrbaugh's (1983) model: resource acquisition, efficiency, human relations, quality, and costs. Each effectiveness dimension was measured with two to four Likert-type items. The mean Cronbach's alpha for the set of effectiveness measures was .77 at time 1 and .80 at time 2.

Ideal types fit was measured by the additive inverse of the deviation between an organization's design and the most similar of Mintzberg's ideal-type configurations. Deviations were computed with a weighted Euclidean distance formula applied to standardized measures, with scales weighted so that each design and contextual factor had equal theoretical importance.

The appropriate design was determined by finding the minimum deviation between the organization's contextual configuration and the five ideal-type contextual configurations. The contingent ideal types fit score was then computed as the additive inverse of the deviation between the organization's design and context and the indicated ideal-type design and context.

The appropriate hybrid type for each organization was identified by calculating the deviation of the organization's context from each of the ideal contexts; the deviations were used to determine the hybrid type with a context most similar to the organization's context. The contingent hybrid types fit score was then computed as the additive inverse of the organization's deviation from the appropriate hybrid type.

The organization's design was classified as the design of the ideal type with the smallest deviation score, and the context of each organization was classified as the ideal context that was most similar to the organization's context. Organizations were then classified into two groups, one for organizations with the appropriate designs and one for organizations with the inappropriate designs.
time_window: time 1 and time 2 (and context at time 1 with design at time 2)

description: Design was assessed with questionnaire measures of the key coordinating mechanisms, the dominance of each of the five organizational parts, and vertical and selective decentralization, plus secondary bureaucratic characteristics. Each organization's design was classified as the design of the ideal type with the smallest deviation score, following standardization of all measures.

Contextual factors included age and size (log-transformed), environmental turbulence and complexity, and technology measured as analyzability and the number of exceptions, used as proxies of regulation and sophistication. Each organization's context was classified as the ideal context that was most similar to the organization's context.

The effectiveness measures used in this study were identical to those in study 1. The interitem reliability of each of the effectiveness measures is .65 or higher, and the mean across the set of effectiveness measures is .80.

One of the four measures of fit formulated with the continuum-of-types interpretation of Miles and Snow's ideal types. Under this interpretation, the profile for the analyzer was specified as the arithmetic means of the values for the prospector and the defender, and fit measures were calculated for all organizations in the time 2 sample.

One of the four measures of fit formulated with the continuum-of-types interpretation of Miles and Snow's ideal types, calculated in parallel with study 1's contingent ideal types fit measure. In the stepwise canonical analysis this measure was eliminated at the second step without loss of predicted variation.

One of the four measures of fit formulated with the continuum-of-types interpretation of Miles and Snow's ideal types. In the stepwise canonical analysis this measure was eliminated at the third step with an insignificant decline in predicted variation.

The hybrid types model measure of fit, which does not bound the set of effective organizational forms with contingency factors so that an organization is free to adopt any hybrid type and remain effective. When used alone, the hybrid types measure of fit explained only 7 percent (p < .05) of the variance in effectiveness.

variable_name: Set of fit measures in canonical correlation
description: Composite configurational fit was tested by using the set of fit measures together as predictors of the set of five effectiveness measures in canonical correlation analysis. Study 1 uses ideal types, contingent ideal types and contingent hybrid types fit; study 2 adds hybrid types fit and runs step-down hierarchical canonical correlations.

Calculated as the ratio of the number of employees in a year to the number of employees in the prior year, with subscripts denoting the year, 0 for the event year and -1 for the prior year. If employment data were unavailable for the year of analysis and the prior year, the company was excluded from the sample for that year.
time_window: event year relative to the prior year (year -1 to year 0)

description: Each firm was classified in each period into one of seven mutually exclusive categories. Employment downsizers: the decline in employment was greater than 5 percent and the decline in plant and equipment was less than 5 percent. Asset downsizers: a decline in employment of more than 5 percent and a decline in plant and equipment that exceeded the change in employment by at least 5 percent. Combination downsizers: reduced the number of employees by more than 5 percent but did not fit into either of the two other downsizing categories. Stable employers: changes in employment between plus or minus 5 percent. Asset upsizers: an increase in employment of 5 percent or more and an increase in plant and equipment that exceeded the change in employment by at least 5 percent. Employment upsizers: an increase in employment greater than 5 percent and an increase in plant and equipment less than 5 percent. Combination upsizers: increased employment more than 5 percent but did not fit into either of the other upsizing categories.
time_window: event year, relative to the prior year

variable_name: return on assets (ROA) and industry-adjusted change in ROA
description: Operating income before depreciation, interest, and taxes divided by total assets; OIBDP/AT. To measure the improvement or decline in profitability, the authors calculated differences in ROA between the base period, t = -1, and the periods t = 0, 1, and 2. Industry-adjusted measures were generated by subtracting the corresponding industry ratio from the company ratio, also relative to performance in time period -1.
time_window: base year -1; event year 0; years 1 and 2

description: Stock return = [price of common stock, end-of-year close, in period t minus price of common stock, end-of-year close, in period t-1 plus dividends on common stock in period t] divided by price of common stock, end-of-year close, in period t-1, for each one-year period, time periods 0, 1, and 2. Industry-adjusted returns were computed by subtracting the industry-average stock return from the company return; the authors note this implicitly factors out the return on stocks with the same level of systematic market risk.

The percentage of equity owned by investment managers (mutual funds plus investment banks), taken from the Spectrum ownership database. Mutual fund owners were identified as those listed in the Investment Company Institute's Directory of Mutual Funds, which lists the 3,700 largest mutual funds. Investment banks were identified by comparing investor firm names from Compact Disclosure with those listed on the COMPUSTAT tapes within SIC codes 60 and 62. Investors with less than 1 percent equity were eliminated.

The percentage of equity owned by pension funds, taken from the Spectrum ownership database (part of Compact Disclosure). Pension fund investments were identified using the Pensions & Investments list of the 1,000 largest pension funds and money managers, compared with the list of institutional investors in Compact Disclosure. Investors with less than 1 percent equity were eliminated.
The percentage of firm equity owned by a firm's top management team, obtained from 1991 proxy statements.
The number of directors with no personal or professional relationship to a firm, other than their membership on its board, divided by board size. Data were obtained from 1991 proxy statements.

A latent factor formed from three KLD ratings: community relations, treatment of women and minorities, and employee relations. Each firm's score on each of the five KLD dimensions was adjusted by subtracting the industry average for that dimension calculated at the two-digit Standard Industrial Classification code level. The three industry-adjusted ratings load on the people factor, which was used as an endogenous factor.

A latent factor formed from two KLD ratings: product quality and response to the natural environment. Each firm's score on each of the five KLD dimensions was adjusted by subtracting the industry average for that dimension calculated at the two-digit Standard Industrial Classification code level. The two industry-adjusted ratings load on the product quality factor, which was used as an endogenous factor.

The dependent variable was merger frequency, defined as the proportion of the total number of mergers and acquisitions formed by business units in industry i that involved business units in industry j. Business units in industry i and industry j were, respectively, M&A acquirers and targets. In the grouped logistic specification, n_ijt is the number of mergers formed between industry i and industry j, N_it is the total number of mergers formed by industry i with any industry, and p_ijt is the proportion of those mergers that industry i formed with industry j.

variable_name: constraint of industry i over industry j (normalized)
description: Constructed in a three-step process. The authors began with measures of interindustry flows, z_ij, expressed as the total dollar value of goods and services sold by industry i to industry j. They then derived dependence of industry i on industry j, which is high to the extent that industry i sells a significant proportion of its goods and services to industry j, S_ij, or it buys a significant proportion of its goods and services from industry j, P_ij. To convert this to dependence of business units in industry i on business units in industry j, the dependence measure was multiplied by four-firm concentration ratios in industry j, O_j. The paper presents the formal definition of this measure in displayed equations that are not readable in the text; because the measure is not distributed normally the authors used Stata's lnskew0 function to obtain a zero-skewness transformed variable.
time_window: time-invariant over five-year periods (input-output data for 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997)

description: Based on the directional measures of constraint, the authors constructed a dyadic measure of power imbalance between business units in industry i and business units in industry j. They used the absolute value of the constraint difference because, according to their model, the direction of power imbalance is theoretically inconsequential for the hypothesized effect of power imbalance on the likelihood of mergers. Because the measure of constraint is not distributed normally, they used Stata's lnskew0 function to obtain a zero-skewness transformed variable. The formal expression is given in a displayed equation that is not readable in the text; an alternative ratio measure was precluded by the many cases in which one of the directional constraints equaled zero.
time_window: time-invariant over five-year periods (input-output data for 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997)

description: Business units in industries i and j are mutually dependent to the extent that the constraint of business units in industry i on business units in industry j is high and simultaneously the constraint of business units in industry j on business units in industry i is high. Formally, mutual dependence is measured as the sum of the two directional constraint measures. Because the measure is not distributed normally, the authors again used Stata's lnskew0 function to obtain a zero-skewness transformed variable. As an alternative they also constructed mutual dependence as the product of the two directional constraint measures, and results were not affected.
time_window: time-invariant over five-year periods (input-output data for 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997)

description: Binary variable coded for whether the firm's CEO changed. CEO succession occurred in 122 of the 921 firm-year observations.

Overall change in the executive team taken as the sum of the number of entering executives and the number of exiting executives for the given year. The measure was standardized by the size of the team in that year. The executive team was defined as all individuals that reported directly to the CEO, with an average team size of 5.3 members.
Count, in each year and for each firm, of the number of executives reporting to the CEO who were not on the team in the previous year, standardized by the size of the team in that year.
Count, in each year and for each firm, of the number of executives who were listed the prior year but not in the current year, standardized by the size of the team in that year.

Reorientations were defined as having occurred when both strategy (adding cement types and brands, adding cement plants, and/or distribution centers) and structure (divisionalizing, adding functions, adding level, and/or consolidating senior positions) changed over a maximum of two years. Three independent coders compiled a preliminary identification of reorientations and agreed on over 90 percent of them; inductively derived criteria were then used to rereview the data and generate a final set of reorientations.
time_window: change over a maximum of two years

description: Relative change in return on assets from the time of organizational change until two years later, adjusted by industry change in ROA to control for year effects. The dependent variable is represented by an equation of the form Performance change = [r(t + 2) - r(t)] involving r(t), ROA at time t, and i(t), average industry ROA at time t; the equation as printed is partly unreadable. The variable ranged from -0.66 to 0.42 with a mean of -0.01 and a standard deviation of 0.06.
time_window: from the time of organizational change until two years later

description: Binary variable where 1 indicates turbulence during and subsequent to a turbulence event. Two discontinuous technological changes were identified, the introduction of computerized long kilns in 1960 and suspension preheating in 1972, with all years from the discontinuities through the emergence of their respective dominant designs in 1965 and 1979 coded as turbulent. Regulatory changes included the banning of information sharing in 1923 and its reversal in 1925, the abolition of base-point pricing in 1947, the Federal Highway Act of 1956, and the Clean Air Act in 1969, with the year of the regulation and the two subsequent years coded as turbulent; 1941-1945 was coded as turbulent due to World War II.
time_window: year of event and subsequent period

description: Dummy variable coded as 1 if the firm's ROA decreased two years in succession, determined by examining the firm's ROA level over three successive years; a performance crisis occurs in year t when r(t) < r(t - 1) and r(t) < r(t - 2). Thirty percent of the firm-year observations were so defined as performance crises.

variable_name: Sample membership (Sample A vs Sample B)
description: Sample A consists of 114 patents filed between 1980 and 1990 belonging to the U.S. subsidiaries of 22 foreign (non-U.S.) semiconductor firms; up to three design and three fabrication patents were randomly selected for each foreign subsidiary. Sample B consists of 114 matched patents belonging to U.S. firms, matched to Sample A patents by technology subclass, time, geographic region and firm size. Membership in Sample A identifies a patent belonging to a foreign firm; membership in Sample B identifies a matched patent belonging to a domestic firm.

The percentage of patents cited by a major sample patent that belong to the same geographic location (U.S. region, or country) as the major patent; self-citations are not used in the statistical tests. Because the observed frequency of geographic coincidence may reflect the existing distribution of patenting activity, the same frequency was computed for control patents matched to the cited patents on technology class and application date, giving the 'Control matching %' baseline. The t-statistic tests the equality of the cited and control proportions, with a positive significant value indicating that knowledge flows are geographically more localized than expected.

The percentage of patents citing a major sample patent (Sample A) that belong to the same geographic location (U.S. region, or country) as the major patent, compared with the corresponding percentage for matched control patents. The same t-statistic construction as in the learning study is used, a positive significant value indicating that foreign firms' patents are cited locally more than expected given the spatial distribution of patenting activity.

RTA of Country A in Technology i is computed as X divided by Y, where X is Country A's share of total patents granted in Technology i in a given year and Y is Country A's share of total patents granted in all semiconductor technologies in the same year. Technology i is the technological subclass assigned by the U.S. Patent Office to each patent in the sample. An RTA greater than 1 indicates relative strength in the technology and less than 1 indicates relative weakness; the indicator was calculated for the home country of the firm owning the patent and for the U.S.A. for each of the 114 patents in the study.

Eigenvector centrality of the firm in the media-reported stakeholder network. Status is computed as λ_t e_it = Σ_k G_ikt e_kt, where G_ikt is the matrix of the number of interactions between firm i and other stakeholders k at time t, e_it is the eigenvector centrality of firm i at time t, and λ_t is a time-varying eigenvalue. Network matrices are aggregated into annual units of observation.

Status of each stakeholder j at time t computed in the same manner as firm status using eigenvector centrality: Stakeholder Status_jt = λ_t e_jt = Σ_k G_jkt e_kt. To compare firm and stakeholder status, the authors measure a given stakeholder’s status as their percentile rank in status among all the stakeholders for that mine, and interact this percentile rank with firm status.

Monthly average of Goldstein scores for all events initiated by a given stakeholder toward the firm that are cooperative, coded as ≥10 on the conflict-cooperation scale. The scale ranges across 20 categories from extremely conflictual events valued at one to highly cooperative events valued at 20; neutral events are valued at 10.

Monthly average of Goldstein scores for all events initiated by a given stakeholder toward the firm that are conflictual, coded as <10 on the conflict-cooperation scale. The scale ranges across 20 categories from extremely conflictual events valued at one to highly cooperative events valued at 20; neutral events are valued at 10.

Structural holes constraint measure multiplied by −1 to capture the firm’s access to structural holes and diverse information. Formula: Firm Structural Holes_it = Σ_{j=1}^n (g_ijt + Σ_{q=1}^{n-1} g_iqt g_qjt)^2 * −1, where g_ijt are direct interactions between firm i and stakeholders j at time t and g_iqt g_qjt is the sum of indirect interactions. Smaller constraint values indicate greater access to structural holes.
Simple count of media reports in which the firm appears in a given year. Entered directly and interacted with firm access to structural holes.
Simple count of media reports in which a stakeholder appears in a given year. Entered directly and interacted with firm access to structural holes.

Subjective rating from the World Bank Institute’s World Governance Indicators of the extent to which citizens have confidence in and abide by the rules of society. Used to divide the sample into subsamples of relatively high and low rule of law: the first excludes country-years in the bottom quartile and the second excludes country-years in the top quartile.

variable_name: ever adopted disruptive technology / firm adopted disruptive technology in this year
description: A firm is flagged as a pioneer if it adopts any of the potentially disruptive ASR technologies (software-only, word-spotting, grammar-free recognition, introduced in 1990, 1992 and 2001 respectively) within three years of the technology's initial introduction into the market. In firm-level analyses a non-time-varying indicator records whether the firm ever adopted a potentially disruptive technology. In longitudinal firm-month (collapsed to firm-year) analyses a time-varying variable is set to 1 only in the year the firm adopted the technology, and is nonzero for 3% of observations. Results are robust to two- and four-year windows and to a decaying coding of 1/n in subsequent years.
time_window: firm level; firm-year for the longitudinal models

description: Commercialization strategy was coded from the trade journals: firms selling end-user products, building custom solutions or providing an advertising-supported service were coded as compete, while firms licensing technology or development tools were coded as cooperate, with firms doing both coded as a mixed mode. A shift of strategy was coded as having taken place in the month it was reported, and the variable switched TCS was set to 1 for a firm-year observation if the firm had previously changed from its initial TCS and 0 otherwise. Subcategorizations were noted for cooperate -> compete and compete -> cooperate switches; in the default analysis a firm that started by competing and was then acquired (or began licensing) is treated as having switched to cooperate, counting only acquisitions classified as attractive.
scale: 0/1 indicator (with multiple unordered outcome categories in the multinomial logit)

description: Firm-level indicator of whether the firm ever changed from its initial technology commercialization strategy; approximately one-fifth of firms ever switched.

variable_name: instantaneous transition rate for employee resignation
description: The dependent variable is the instantaneous transition rate for employee resignation, the product of the hazard rate and the probability that an individual moves from one state to another at a particular time. It is calculated as the number of individuals who exit in a period divided by the number of individuals who were employed at the start of the period. The rate is modeled as r(t) = exp(bX) and estimated with the RATE event-history package; because changes in the transition rate capture hazard shifts, the models compare transition rates across time periods. Resignations are distinguished from terminations and placements, and employees who moved to another public accounting firm are treated as right-censored.
scale: theoretically has a lower bound of zero and no upper bound
time_window: first five years of each employee's firm tenure, using semiannual intervals and a three-month interval after the 24th month

description: Indicator variable contrasting auditors in a two-year jurisdiction with auditors in a one-year jurisdiction, both with similar breadths of focus. The two-year jurisdiction takes a value of 1, and the one-year jurisdiction takes a value of 0. The sign of the indicator shows whether the two-year jurisdiction has a higher or lower transition rate than the one-year jurisdiction.
time_window: time periods within the first three years of tenure

description: Indicator variable capturing the narrowly focused effect, contrasting a narrowly focused, two-year experience requirement with a broadly focused, two-year experience requirement.
