Company A uses a seven-category rating scheme, in which the highest two categories (1, 2) were reserved for the top 12.5 percent and the lowest two categories (5, 6) for the bottom 2.5 percent, while the remaining 85 percent of employees were rated within the two central categories (3, 4). No engineers with the company at the time of the survey were rated in the lowest performance category (7). Lower category numbers indicate higher assessed performance.

Company B used three separate rating schemes at the time of the survey. Scheme I was an A-through-E categorization scheme, recoded as 1 through 5, with 71 percent of respondents categorized in category 2 alone. Scheme II was a 1 through 7 rating scheme, with 72 percent of respondents evenly distributed between categories 2 and 3. Scheme III was a 1-100 evaluation scheme; employees governed by this scheme were not included in subsequent analyses. Lower category numbers indicate higher assessed performance.
scale: rating categories (1-5 in Scheme I; 1-7 in Scheme II)

description: Respondents were asked to indicate the number of years they intended to remain at Company A (0-1 year, 1-2 years, etc.) and to indicate the likelihood (very likely, likely, 50/50 chance, unlikely, very unlikely) that they would depart within two years. For Company A, those indicating intentions of remaining two years or less and responding with "very likely" or "likely" to the likelihood assessment were categorized as intending to leave (22.5 percent).

Respondents were asked to indicate the number of years they intended to remain at Company B (0-1 year, 1-2 years, etc.) and to indicate the likelihood (very likely, likely, 50/50 chance, unlikely, very unlikely) that they would depart within two years. For Company B, only those indicating intentions of remaining one year or less and responding with "very likely" on the likelihood assessment were categorized as intending to leave (11.5 percent).

Respondents were asked to assess their overall job performance relative to peers within the firm, with response categories of top 1 percent, 5 percent, 10 percent, 25 percent, 50 percent, and bottom 50 percent. The perceived difference score was computed by subtracting the standardized performance rating score from the standardized perceptual score (both reverse-scored).

Respondents were asked to assess their overall job performance relative to peers within the firm, with response categories of top 1 percent, 5 percent, 10 percent, 25 percent, 50 percent, and bottom 50 percent. The perceived difference score was computed by subtracting the standardized performance rating score from the standardized perceptual score (both reverse-scored).

Yearly salary increases from personnel records, annualized because increases did not necessarily occur on an annual basis. If the latest increase occurred more than 300 days prior to the survey, the percentage increase was annualized by adjusting for the number of months since the date of the increase; if it occurred within the last 300 days, the annualized increase reflected in the last two pay increases was used. The models control for performance ratings, salary range, promotion, hierarchical level, and time since the last increase.
time_window: yearly increase, latest increase as of June 1987

description: Salary increases reported in the Company B questionnaire. Data on salary range and time since an individual's last increase were not available for Company B, so individual tenure in the company and overall experience, along with corresponding quadratic terms, were substituted as control variables.

Promotion between June 1, 1986 and June 1, 1987, taken from Company A personnel records and modelled with a maximum likelihood logistic regression on tenure, experience, hierarchical level, education, and performance. Only categorization as an extremely high performer (category 2) significantly enhanced the probability of subsequent or contemporaneous promotion; the estimated effect of the promotion dummy on yearly salary increase is a 2.8 percentage-point rise.

For each job spell, the number of temporary workers hired from outside into the job's mobility cluster during the spell divided by the total number of workers hired from outside into that mobility cluster. The measure therefore ranges from 0 to 1 and is not affected by the duration of the job spell or by growth of the mobility cluster. A value of .5, for instance, means that half of the outside hires into the cluster during the spell were temporaries.

The operational dependent variable is the duration of each job spell in days. Each spell was designated as ending in vacancy promotion, upgrade promotion, lateral change, demotion, layoff, quit, retirement, or censoring, where the sample period ended before the end of the job spell. The models estimate the effects of the covariates on the waiting time until the focal promotion event, conditional on a spell not being censored or ending from another kind of job change.

Company records labelled each job change, and these labels were used to define each event. Vacancy promotions occurred when a person was promoted into an open job; upgrade promotions occurred when a person received a higher rank without being placed in a vacant job. To test hypothesis 3, upgrade and vacancy promotions were treated as events with competing risks, so each waiting time is modeled conditional on the competing event not having occurred.

The clerical workforce was divided into a lower segment and an advanced segment, and a separate rate-dependent mobility model was estimated for each. The advanced segment was considerably less permeable: advanced-segment jobs were 42 percent less likely to be filled by outsiders than were lower-segment jobs during the study period, while lower-segment jobs were subject to practically limitless competition from outside.

Three-item scale adapted from an effectiveness measure based on the multiple-constituency approach (Tsui, 1984), asking the extent to which the constituent is satisfied with the performance of the HR subunit, whether the department has met the constituent's expectations in its human resource management roles and responsibilities, and the extent to which the constituent would change the manner in which the department does its job (scale reversed). A 7-point scale was used, ranging from 1, "not at all," to 7, "entirely." Responses were obtained independently from each constituent; a constituency-level score was created by averaging the responses of all individuals in that constituency in the operating unit (alpha coefficients .90, .91, and .89 for the executive, manager, and nonmanagement constituencies).
level: operating unit (constituency-level aggregate of individual respondents)

description: Three hierarchically defined constituencies: top executives of operating units (plant managers in Organization A, executive directors in Organization B, and divisional general managers in Organization C), managers (or supervisory staff) of other functional subunits, and nonmanagement employees. Constituents were drawn randomly from the employee population in each operating unit, with 100 percent of executives, 5 percent of managers (minimum eight), and 2 percent of nonmanagement employees (minimum 12) sampled, and each constituent rated the HR subunit's effectiveness.
level: individual (constituent), aggregated to constituency within operating unit

description: Resource munificence was measured by both financial resources and other support from the corporate HR groups. Financial resources was measured by the personnel ratio, operationalized as the number of employees in the operating unit relative to each HR subunit staff member, so that a low ratio indicates a munificent environment. Frequency of corporate new programs was measured by three items on a 7-point scale ranging from 1, "seldom (once every several years)," to 7, "frequently (once a month)." Hours of corporate assistance was measured in actual number of hours per month that the various corporate, company, or regional HR groups provided to the HR subunit, adjusted for the size of the operating unit (per 100 employees). Data on the munificence measures were requested from the HR subunits.

Measured by the distributions of the manager and employee constituents on age, education, company tenure, gender, and race, obtained directly from the constituents. The variance in age, the variance in education, and the variance in company tenure, all in years, were calculated for each operating unit. Gender composition was measured by the absolute difference of 50 and the percentage of constituents in the operating unit who were female, so that a score of 0 (50 percent female and 50 percent male) is the highest degree of heterogeneity and a score of 50 reflects the highest degree of homogeneity; the same procedure produced a race-composition score.

Co-optation was measured by the number of human resource committees per 100 employees in the operating unit that existed in the operating unit; these committees co-opt constituencies by involving them in managing the subunit's affairs. Data on this measure were obtained from the HR subunits.

Responsiveness was measured by the average number of days the HR subunit took to fill vacant positions (days to fill jobs) and the average number of days the subunit took to answer inquiries or questions from constituents (days to answer questions); longer times denote lower responsiveness. Data on these measures were obtained from the HR subunits.

Respondents were asked to report the number of unexcused absences that they personally had incurred within a recent 12-month period; data were obtained directly from the manager and employee constituents because absence records in general are incomplete and noncomparable across organizations and most companies do not keep absence data on managerial employees. A unit-level aggregate absence score was created by taking the average of absences reported by the sample of managers and employees in each operating unit, with the individual scores that make up the aggregate equally weighted.

The HR subunits reported the number of grievances within the most recent 12-month period, adjusted for the size of the operating unit (i.e., per 100 employees in the operating unit). Data were obtained from the HR subunits.

The HR subunits reported the numbers of female promotions and minority promotions within the most recent 12-month period, adjusted for the size of the operating unit (i.e., per 100 employees in the operating unit). Only female and minority promotions were measured because the HR subunit usually is expected to play a larger role in the career development of these employees than of white male employees.

The adaptive responses were seven variables: number of HR committees per 100 employees (co-optation), days to fill jobs and days to answer questions (responsiveness), employee absences, grievances, and female and minority promotions. They were taken from HR subunit reports and employee surveys at the operating-unit level.

Indicator for whether a job spell was in contracting versus regular employment. A spell was defined as contracting when the job was on a temporary contractual basis (179 job spells), or when the job was acquired through a temporary agency (7 job spells), or when a job was described as self-employment taking place at a site with more than two other individuals where the respondent did not have anybody reporting to them (4 job spells). All other job spells were assigned regular employment status.

The survey asked whether respondents had a spouse living with them at home, whether they had children, and how old these children were; children's ages were used to estimate birth years, and for each job spell the number of children born during or before the year the job started was calculated. Marital status was coded from responses at the time of the survey because the data did not allow a time-varying measure for marriage. Separate dummies were created for the eight possible combinations of gender, marital status, and having children, with single men without children as the omitted category; job spells for single men and women with children were dropped from the logit analyses because none of these 21 job spells involved contracting.

variable_name: involuntary separation from the most recent job
description: Involuntary separation from the most recent job is used as a measure of negative cues about worker behaviors and attitudes. Research on hiring indicates that reasons for past job separations are an important signal of workers' behaviors and attitudes, although involuntary separations may also reflect economic troubles at a previous employer or a poor fit for the worker.

Dummy variables at the individual level for whether respondents had bachelor's degrees, master's, and Ph.D.s, built from university records of degrees awarded and from respondents' reports of degrees subsequently awarded. Because data on degrees awarded prior to enrollment at the sampled universities were lacking, the authors assumed that workers with master's degrees also had bachelor's and that those with Ph.D.s also had master's, so these educational categories are not mutually exclusive.

Dummy variable for a previous job in high technology, created from open-ended questions that asked which industry the company housing the previous job was in. Thirteen word forms related to technology, such as 'computing,' 'dotcom,' and 'web,' were used to assign job spells to high technology. Industry data were missing for around half of the job spells and these were coded as not in the technology industry, which the authors say should bias their estimates downward but not create spurious results.

Job-level variable based on the previous job title, classifying jobs into three skill levels, low, middle, and high (coded -1, 0, and 1). The terms used to classify jobs were based on a scheme developed in conjunction with three senior subject matter experts, received complete agreement among them, and were validated using the O*Net online dictionary of occupations. The title of the respondent's previous job rather than the current one was coded, to avoid contracting jobs receiving systematically different titles.

Experience is the difference between the date that a worker's focal job began and the date that his or her first job began, minus any time the worker spent out of the labor market, reported in years. Nonlinearity was tested with a two-part spline split at the median value of experience (3.89 years): the first variable takes the value of experience for observations below the median and 3.89 above it, while the second takes the value 0 below the median and experience minus 3.89 above it. The authors chose the spline over a squared experience term to test nonmonotonicity more precisely.

Contiguous contracting job spells were combined and a spell was defined as long-term if it was equal to or over one year in duration, following the U.S. Census Bureau's definition of a temporary 'contingent' job as one expected to last for less than a year. This definition produced 25 spells of short-term contracting and 24 spells of long-term contracting. In the multinomial logit analyses the dependent variable was either short-term contracting or long-term contracting, and spells that began less than a year before the survey date were dropped to avoid erroneously assigning spells to short-term contracting because of right censoring.
scale: short-term (less than one year) / long-term (one year or more)
time_window: one year threshold; spells beginning less than a year before the survey dropped

description: Job duration of each job spell, used to compare the stability of contracting and regular employment spells. The authors note that the measure does not provide a true gauge of protection against dismissal but indicates whether contracting spells are less stable than regular employment in practice.

Two questions asked for each job spell about workers' ability to learn skills in their jobs. Workers were much less likely to answer yes to either question for job spells in contracting than for regular employment spells.

Questions about employer-sponsored degree programs, where employers fully or partially paid tuition incurred in study for a formal degree. Such sponsorship was more common in regular employment, and the authors note that the one individual who reported sponsorship in a contracting spell may have received it before entering contracting.

The time of establishment of a country's first stock exchange; the date of establishment was the first trading day reported in the Handbook of World Stock Derivatives and Commodity Exchanges, cross-referenced with exchange web pages and regional associations. Subsequent additional exchanges and commodity exchanges were ignored; countries with an exchange existing on their territory prior to independence were excluded from the risk set. Time to adoption was measured from January 1, 1980, or from the point at which a country first became independent if this was after 1980.

variable_name: number of domestic companies listed on an exchange
description: The number of domestic companies listed on an exchange, taken from the 2007 World Development Indicator published by the World Bank. The authors state that the number of traded companies indicates the attractiveness of listing shares on the exchange for companies as well as the investment choices available to investors, and is an apt indicator of vibrancy if the goal of market creation is to stimulate indigenous entrepreneurship and promote market governance of economic assets. Estimated with a logarithmic link function (negative binomial family) in the GEE models.

variable_name: market capitalization as a percentage of country GDP
description: The share price of all listed firms times the number of their shares outstanding, expressed as a percentage of country GDP, from the 2007 World Development Indicator. The authors state that it captures what overall portion of a country's economy is governed by financial markets and is the most commonly used metric in studies following La Porta et al. Estimated with a logarithmic link function (family Gaussian) in the GEE models.

variable_name: percentage of a country's population of Protestant religionists in 1980
description: The percentage of a country's population of Protestant religionists in 1980, taken from La Porta et al. (1999b). Protestantism is argued to be associated with the viability of capital markets because the relatively less hierarchical Protestant tradition facilitates the horizontal ties useful for market transactions.

A dummy variable for countries that were French colonies or protectorates prior to independence, coded from the World Factbook. Former French colonies are expected to be less inclined to create stock market-based economic systems and more likely to pursue more statist paths to development.
scale: dummy (1 = former French colony or protectorate)

description: A country's level of political democracy, with data from the Polity IV database. More democratic and less left-leaning regimes are expected to support the transparency and potential dispersion of economic participation of public trading.

Whether the ideology of a country's government was left-leaning, with data from the Polity IV database. Rulers whose ideology is founded on authoritarian or socialist ideas are expected to be suspicious of uncontrolled flows of capital in private hands and to use their power to create different governance structures.

Concessional aid a country had received from the IMF and World Bank divided by the country's GDP, from the WDI database. Concessional aid is disbursed at a discounted interest rate but is tied to the implementation of specific development programs and policies stipulated by the IMF or World Bank, and is treated as a proximate channel of influence for global policy making communities located in international financial institutions.
scale: aid as a share of GDP

description: Measured on the basis of a country pair's similarities in patterns of trade and calculated as the normalized correlation between the import and export shares of two countries across trade partners, as used by Lee and Strang (2006). The variable served as the weight for the influence that a prior adoption event in the other country exerted on a focal country. Annual trade data came from the United Nations COMTRADE database; the measure was updated every five years and prior adoption events annually.

variable_name: number of recent adoption events in a country's region
description: The number of recent adoption events in a country's region, with regions as defined by the World Bank; these groupings approximate regional reference groups, data reporting and geographic proximity. The authors focused on recent adopters because recent events have been shown to be most salient and relevant in diffusion processes, and they controlled for the cumulative percentage of prior adopters in a region and the total size of the regional risk set.

Following the 'cohesion in trade' measure developed by Guille n and colleagues (Guler et al., 2002; Polillo & Guille n, 2005), bilateral trade data were used to measure the ratio of imports and exports from the influencing country to all imports and exports received by the influenced country annually; this measure weighted previous adoptions of a stock exchange by trade ties with adopters. Annual trade data were from COMTRADE.

variable_name: home to headquarters of international professional financial associations
description: A binary variable for a country being home to the headquarters of one or more international professional financial associations, which are associations of public and private finance professionals and organizations, as listed in the Yearbook of International Associations. Headquarters located in one of the generally more peripheral countries in the risk set suggested that this country had greater exposure to international financial expert communities and their normative discourse.

variable_name: position in the world system in 1993
description: A country's overall position in the world system in 1993, as reported by van Rossem (1996), who used a block-modeling approach to collapse five types of intercountry ties (imports, exports, diplomatic, arms trade, troops) into four categories: core, semiperiphery, periphery 1, and periphery 2. The authors used core as the base category and collapsed both periphery clusters into one because many periphery 2 members were dependent territories excluded from the analysis.

variable_name: closeness centrality in the world trade system
description: A country's 'closeness centrality' in the world trade system, calculated from annual input-output matrices of imports and exports. Closeness centrality reflects an established pattern whereby countries closer to the core are connected more directly to more others; following van Rossem (1996), bilateral trade was counted as a tie if either exports to or imports from the other country amounted to at least 1 percent of a focal country's GDP, and annually standardized centrality measures were used to control for changes in the number of countries participating in global trade.

Eight items from Eisenberger, Huntington, Hutchison, and Sowa's (1986) 36-item survey of perceived organizational support, with the referent changed to 'my supervisor'; a sample item is 'My supervisor is willing to help me if I need a special favor.' Measured on a 1 ('completely disagree') to 7 ('completely agree') scale at time 1. Cronbach's alpha was .91 in this sample.

Nine items adapted from the social undermining scale (Duffy et al., 2002), the abusive supervision scale (Tepper, 2000), and a measure of dispositional verbal aggression (Infante & Wigley, 1986), adapted to refer to 'my supervisor.' Measured at time 1 on the same 1-to-7 agreement scale; Cronbach's alpha was .94.

Eight items written for the pleasant and high-activation quadrant of Russell's (1980) circumplex model of emotions to measure newcomers' accumulated experiences of positive affect triggered by their supervisors. Measured at time 2 on the 1-to-7 agreement scale. For this sample the Cronbach's alpha reliability coefficient was .94.

Eight items written for the unpleasant and high-activation quadrant of Russell's (1980) circumplex model of emotions to measure newcomers' accumulated experiences of negative affect triggered by their supervisors. Measured at time 2 on the 1-to-7 agreement scale. For this sample the Cronbach's alpha reliability coefficient was .95.

Measured using VandeWalle, Ganesan, Challagalla, and Brown's (2000) five-item feedback seeking behavior scale, plus one item added because interviews with newcomers suggested future success was a major concern. Response scale ran from 1 ('almost never') to 7 ('very frequently'); a sample item is 'How frequently do you ask your supervisor for feedback about your overall job performance?' Measured at time 3; alpha was .89.

Eight items adapted from the Personal Report of Communication Apprehension (PRCA; McCroskey, 1982) and modified to assess avoidance behavior directed at a supervisor, thus converting the trait scale into a state measure. Measured at time 3 on the 1-to-7 agreement scale; Cronbach's alpha was .87.

Operationalized by three measures: role clarity (Rizzo, House, and Lirtzman's (1970) six-item role ambiguity scale, alpha = .94), social adjustment (the six-item 'people' scale from Chao et al. (1994), alpha = .85), and task mastery (Chao et al.'s (1994) five-item 'performance proficiency' scale, alpha = .93). All measured at time 4. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated a second-order factor on which role clarity, social adjustment, and task mastery loaded (all standardized loadings greater than .60), so newcomer adjustment was included as a latent construct with these three manifest variables.
Supervisor-rated in-role performance of the newcomer, measured with the seven-item scale of Williams and Anderson (1991). Sample item: meets formal performance requirements of the job (alpha = .97).
Supervisor-rated helping behavior of the newcomer, measured with the five altruism items from Podsakoff et al. (1990). Sample item: helps others who have heavy workloads (alpha = .96).

Reputation of the violator was manipulated by describing the restaurant as either 'Zagalin cuisine rating 28. Comments: creative, innovative, unique style' (high reputation) or 'Zagalin cuisine rating 20. Comments: lacks imagination, unoriginal, ordinary style' (low reputation). 'Zagalin' (a portmanteau of Zagat and Michelin) was explained as equivalent to a Zagat rating and ranging from 0 to 30. As a manipulation check, respondents evaluated on a seven-point Likert scale the extent to which the chef described in the scenario was likely to be considered highly reputed by colleagues; the manipulation was successful.

Public scrutiny was manipulated using frequency of review. The restaurant was described as either 'frequently reviewed by local media and customers (among restaurants with more reviews)' (high frequency of review) or 'rarely reviewed by local media and customers (among restaurants with fewer reviews)' (low frequency of review). No reference point such as 'among the top 5% of reviewed restaurants' was inserted, and because the treatment was a statement of fact no manipulation check was needed.

Competition was measured based on two manipulated treatments, one of which was physical proximity. The restaurant was described as either 'physically very close to your restaurant' (high physical proximity) or 'physically very distant from your restaurant' (low physical proximity). No reference point (such as five miles away or within the same block) was inserted since effective distance may be a function of geography, traffic, and so on; because the treatment was a concrete statement of fact, no manipulation check was needed.

The second manipulated treatment used to measure competition was similarity of positioning. The restaurant was described as having either a 'cuisine style and ambience similar to your restaurant' (high similarity of positioning) or a 'cuisine style and ambience very different from your restaurant' (low similarity of positioning). The manipulation was checked by asking respondents to evaluate on a seven-point Likert scale the extent to which the restaurant in the scenario was comparable to their own restaurant in terms of positioning; the manipulation was successful.

Severity of the violation was captured through the type of knowledge that was misused. Each respondent was asked separately about the propensity to sanction violations of norms regulating the transfer of three types of knowledge: the recipe of a dish, the recipe of a signature dish, and information about a cooking technique. The three knowledge types are marked with dummy variables (recipe, signature, and technique), and the authors look at the effect of the dummies recipe and signature compared with the case of technique to capture the effect of severity.
level: observation (chef x scenario x knowledge type)

description: Propensity to sanction is a scaled measure of the respondent's propensity to sanction the violation described in the scenario. After each of the two scenarios, chefs were asked on a seven-point Likert scale how likely it was that they would: (a) provide NO more information; (b) provide NO more help (e.g., missing ingredients, emergency labor); (c) reveal what happened to other chefs. The authors averaged the three measures into a single measure, since Cronbach's alpha supported the reliability of a single scale (a = 0.77), and also ran an analysis using each of the three measures separately.
level: observation (chef x scenario x knowledge type)

description: Propensity to transfer knowledge is measured as the likelihood that a respondent would transfer culinary knowledge to the chef described in the scenario. Specifically, after each of the two scenarios chefs were asked: 'If the chef in the scenario asked you for it, how likely is it that you would provide: the recipe for a dish/the recipe for one of your signature dishes/information about a cooking technique?' As with the propensity to sanction, each respondent was asked about transferring three types of knowledge: recipe, signature, and technique.
scale: 1-7 (the highest value, 7, is referred to in the text)
level: observation (chef x scenario x knowledge type)

description: Dummy variable coded '1' for players who participate in the ASG in the focal season (treatment group, the players who experienced ritual enactment) and '0' for those players who are part of the control group (Almost All-Stars). It is interacted with Post ASG, a dummy taking the value '1' for games played after the ASG and '0' for games played before it; the interaction equals '1' when a player is in the treatment group and the game occurs after the ASG.
time_window: focal season (10 games before and 10 games after the ASG)

description: Productivity operationalized as a ratio of overall performance to the level of input received, computed as the NBA Efficiency Rating divided by minutes played. The NBA Efficiency Rating is a composite measure officially used by the NBA to assess a player's overall performance for each game.
An alternative measure of productivity, computed as the ratio of the NBA Efficiency Rating to Usage Rate, i.e. overall performance relative to the offensive plays that involve the focal player.

Used as a measure of inputs received from coaches, on the argument that coaches might deploy players for longer periods of time if they have recently received a prestigious award. Playing time is determined by the head coach, who decides when and for how long to deploy players on the court.

Touches is an official NBA statistic measuring the number of times a player touches the ball on the floor, by aggregating the various actions he can do while possessing the ball (e.g., pass, shoot, draw a foul, or commit a turnover). It is used as an approximation of passes received from teammates, and is computed per minute to keep inputs received by teammates orthogonal to those received by the coach; it is used to test Hypothesis 2.

The percentage of offensive plays that involve the focal player, employed as an additional measure of inputs received by teammates; the higher the Usage Rate, the more the focal player becomes central in the team's offense.

A composite measure officially used by the NBA to assess a player's overall performance for each game, incorporating information on failed attempts to score, turning over the ball, or possessions by the opposing team that a player stopped, blocked, or retrieved. It is used to test Hypotheses 3a and 3b.

One unit of time corresponds to one game; Progressive Game Number corresponds to each game number in a season and is included as fixed effects to account for time-variant effects. To test whether the performance effect declines over time, the continuous variable Progressive Game Number is split by a spline regression into two continuous variables, Progressive Game Number pre ASG and Progressive Game Number post ASG, each interacted with the treatment variable.

Dichotomous variable indicating whether the star and nonstar scientists were in the same geographic cluster, as assigned by a city clustering algorithm using the location data in their most recent patent application. A star and a nonstar were considered colocated if they belonged to the same geographic cluster; the median distance of colocated dyads was 12 miles versus 725 miles for non-colocated dyads.

Dichotomous variable for the presence of third-party ties, set to 1 when a star and a nonstar scientist had at least one connection within the firm in common. Third-party ties were identified by considering all star and nonstar scientists' collaborators on patent applications filed during the five years before the current year.
time_window: five years before the current year

description: Dyadic dichotomous variable set to 1 if the star and nonstar scientist collaborated for the first time in the current year, as observed by coauthoring a patent application. Copatenting ties are used as indicators of collaboration ties because patent coauthorships require intense collaboration and knowledge exchange.

Dummy variable for the gender of the nonstar scientists, built from U.S. Social Security Administration first-name gender data for 96% of scientists, with the rest collected manually from LinkedIn, public profiles, and Google searches, yielding gender for 99.5% of scientists. The 0.5% of scientists without a known gender were classified as male.

variable_name: Male star–male nonstar / Male star–female nonstar / Female star–male nonstar / Female star–female nonstar
description: Set of dummy variables combining the gender of the star and the gender of the nonstar scientist, created to test whether the effects differ by the star's gender. Male star–male nonstar is the reference category in the models.

The amount of time it takes for a surgical team to complete a total joint replacement, taken from the surgical note. In the sample, procedure completion time has a mean of 3.6 hours with a standard deviation of 1.3; the minimum is 28 minutes and the maximum is 11.5 hours. Because the distribution is skewed, the authors take the natural log of completion times as the dependent variable.

For each person involved in a procedure, the authors calculate the number of times that he or she has performed the procedure, not including the current procedure (IKi). They sum across these individual values and divide by team size to define the level of individual knowledge on the team, the sum of IKi divided by N. The variable indicates the amount of individual knowledge available to the team.

The cumulative number of times that a kind of procedure has been performed at the hospital prior to the focal operation; the variable is procedure specific (for a TKR, the number of times a TKR has been performed at the hospital prior to the current procedure). To capture knowledge accumulated by people outside the focal team, the authors subtract the cumulative experience of individuals inside the focal team from cumulative organizational experience.

For each pair of individuals on a team, the authors calculate the number of times that the pair has performed the procedure with each other in the past, not including the current procedure (RKij). They sum across pairs on the team and divide by the possible number of pairs, N(N-1)/2, where N is team size. The variable indicates the average amount of experience that team members have working with each other.

A nine-item scale measured respondents' perceptions of new product success in four dimensions: the company's relative success level in the industry; its NPD success level relative to its objective; its NPD success level in terms of cycle time, quality, product line width, and market share relative to competitors; and the timing of new product introductions. Item ratings were summed and divided by the number of items, and the variable was mean-centered.

A modified four-item scale based on Dyer and Song (1997). Item ratings were summed and divided by the number of items and mean-centered; the regression model includes the linear and squared terms. The item wording is not given in the text.
Measured by the extent to which functions refrain from arguments and avoid the issues. The authors describe the conflict resolution measures as single-item measures.
Measured by the extent to which the conflicting functions sacrifice their own wishes to those of others. Single-item measure.
Measured by the extent to which functions use the power of their position to win acceptance. Single-item measure.
Measured by the extent to which functions exchange complete information to resolve conflicts. Single-item measure.
Measured by the effort functions make in finding an intermediate position. Single-item measure.
Measured by the frequency with which functions refer the problem to top management for resolution. Single-item measure.

National culture is represented by the country of the sample: Japan, Hong Kong, the United States and Great Britain. The same regression model is estimated separately for each country and the country results are compared; the countries are characterized by Hofstede (1994) scores on individualism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance and long-term orientation cited in the text.

Built from four resource indicators of the retailer: sales revenue deflated by the CPI, dollar value of retail inventories adjusted by the CPI, number of retail stores, and employees divided by the number of stores. Following Dess and Beard, each indicator is regressed on time and the standard error of the regression is divided by the indicator's average, once over each product's life cycle and once year by year. Principal components analysis reduces each pair of volatility measures to one factor per indicator and then the four factors to one composite index, operationalized as regression-method factor scores that vary by year and by product.
time_window: varies by year and by product; entered one month before the development decision in Stage 1

description: Ratio of the count of standard components to the total number of components in the product in each month. A standard component is a module the firm developed or purchased from an external vendor that is used many times in the firm or in many other firms; whether a component is standard or custom comes from the software change control system, where standard components have different naming conventions.

For every product and month, the number of components in the product that were created using CASE tools divided by the total number of components in the product. Based on information in the software change control system about the technology used to create each component.

Counts how often updates to the software product are accomplished by a team member other than the one who completed the previous software change, using the developer identities in the change event logs. The number of changes in developer-component assignments is summed for each product each month.

Frequency: the average time since the previous enhancement for each enhancement event for each component in the product during the month, reverse scored by subtracting it from the number of months the product has existed, so that a higher value indicates greater volatility; a month with no enhancements scores zero. Magnitude: the number of the product's components enhanced or added during the month.

Frequency: the average time since the previous correction for each repair event for each component in the product during the month, reverse scored by subtracting it from the number of months the product has existed, so that a higher value indicates greater volatility; a month with no corrections scores zero. Magnitude: the total number of components corrected for the product during the month.

Experimental condition induced by instructions given before the first practice trial. Division-of-labor teams (twelve) were told they were like division vice presidents in a decentralized organization, with one member in charge of attendance, one of beer and coffee, and one of hot dogs and ice cream, positions assigned by the flip of a coin. Committee teams (thirteen) were told to agree as an executive decision-making committee on attendance and each product decision, with no decision-making structure provided. Hierarchical teams (eleven) had a president with complete decision power who reviewed and revised the two vice presidents' estimates.

The ratio of actual profit to potential profit was calculated for each trial and multiplied by 100, so the criterion on each trial was 100 per cent relative profit rather than an absolute dollar amount. Initial and final levels of relative profit were compared across structures. The number of teams reaching a complete solution (100 per cent profit) was also compared.
time_window: per trial; initial and final levels

variable_name: b parameter of the power function learning curve
description: Each group's learning curve was fitted by the logarithmic transform of the power function y = ax^b, where y is the percentage of performance and x the trial number. The a parameter is an index of a group's initial performance level and the b parameter an index of the rate of improvement in performance. A parameter model relating b to log a was fitted for each organization structure, and b values were compared across structures at assumed a values.

Multiple-item questionnaire scale built by factor analysis; the variety questions asked about such things as variety and dissimilarity of work activities. The scale has 5 items with coefficient alpha of .77. Work-unit scores were computed by averaging the scores of respondents in each work unit, with equal weight for each individual.

Multiple-item questionnaire scale built by factor analysis; the analyzability questions asked about the extent to which work activities were understood and about the availability of standard practices, to reflect Perrow's definition. The scale has 6 items with coefficient alpha of .86. Work-unit scores were computed by averaging respondents' scores in each work unit; aggregated scores correlated highly with Van de Ven and Delbecq's measures, external judges and supervisor responses in a separate validation study.

Multiple-item questionnaire scale built by factor analysis; the information amount questions asked about the extent to which data were gathered and interpreted in problem solving and decision making. The scale has 4 items with coefficient alpha of .71. Work-unit scores were computed by averaging respondents' scores in each work unit.

Multiple-item questionnaire scale built by factor analysis; the equivocality questions asked about the clarity of the data inputs gathered for problem solving and decision making. The scale has 3 items with coefficient alpha of .73. Work-unit scores were computed by averaging respondents' scores in each work unit.

Professionals reported the years and months they had been associated with their specific project group. Group longevity was calculated by averaging the individual project tenures of all project members. Groups were included only when tenure and age scores were obtained from over 75 percent of members. For the category comparisons the 50 groups were divided into five longevity categories (0 to 1.5, 1.5 to 2.5, 2.5 to 3.5, 3.5 to 5.0, and 5 or more years); the regressions use mean project tenure and its square.

variable_name: departmental, laboratory, organizational, professional and operational communication
description: From the 15-week sociometric logs, communication reported by project members with people outside the project group was captured in five mutually exclusive domain measures: departmental, laboratory, organizational, professional and operational communication. Each was calculated by summing the relevant interactions reported during the 15 weeks, normalized for the number of project team members and for missing weeks, as average technical communication per person per project. The authors examined each domain separately across longevity categories; the text gives no single combined score.

Professionals logged the people they talked with and how many times on one randomly chosen day each week for 15 weeks. Intraproject communication is the communication reported among all members of the project group, summed over the 15 weeks and normalized for the number of project members and for missing weeks. Because scores were adjusted for the number of possible interactions they cannot be linked to an absolute scale; for presentation they were standardized to an overall sample mean of 100.

The first four of the six communication domains: intraproject, departmental, laboratory and organizational communication. Each domain measure sums the interactions reported during the 15 weeks, normalized for the number of project team members; data of respondents with missing weeks were proportionately normalized. The regressions and partial correlations control for these domain measures separately.

The last two of the six communication domains: professional communication with professionals outside the parent organization (universities, consulting firms, professional societies) and operational communication with external operational areas such as vendors and suppliers. Each sums the interactions reported during the 15 weeks, normalized for the number of project team members and for missing weeks.

Each department manager and laboratory director was separately interviewed and asked to evaluate the overall technical performance of all projects with which he was technically familiar; if he could not make an informed judgment he was asked not to rate the project. Each project was independently rated by an average of five managers on a seven-point scale from very low to very high. Because ratings across the nine judges were highly intercorrelated (Spearman-Brown reliability .81), individual ratings were averaged to yield overall project performance scores.
scale: seven-point scale from very low to very high, averaged across raters

description: Respondents selected the category (basic research, applied research, development, technical service) that best characterized their project's objectives and indicated on a three-point scale how completely it represented them; the twelve possible answers were scored on a single scale from completely basic research to completely technical service. Respondents also indicated the percentage of work in each category and a weighted average was calculated; the two scored responses were averaged (Spearman-Brown reliability .91). Pooled member responses classified each project as research (basic and applied combined), development, or technical service, with analysis of variance used to check the appropriateness of pooling.
scale: single scale from completely basic research to completely technical service

description: Unit heads indicated, in percentage terms, the extent to which the unit's choice of research themes was determined by guidelines and/or instructions from national science policymaking bodies. The question was asked in interviews together with five other questions on influence from other sources, and the six percentages summed to 100.

Composite index of three types of scientific output the unit produced during the previous three years, collected from project records provided by unit heads. Skewed output scores were transformed to lognormal scores using the Pelz and Andrews procedure. Books were weighted 3, journal articles published outside the country 2, and journal articles published within the country 1, based on judgments of an international panel; the weighted, transformed scores were summed.

Assessed by the unit's scientific field: physics and chemistry units form the highly developed-paradigm group, biology units the moderately developed group, and geology units the less developed group, based on combined rankings from two prior studies. In the hierarchical regression it is coded 1 for high, 0 for medium, and -1 for low.
level: scientific field of the research unit

description: The authority structure was a set of n vectors, one per member, each containing only 0, 1 entries, 1 denoting a direct supervisory or subordinate relationship with the other party and 0 otherwise. The elements in each vector were normalized before comparison; the printed formula reads as each entry divided by the sum of the entries of the vector, but the OCR of the formula is partly illegible. An individual's similarity to his communication pattern is the sum of absolute differences between the normalized entries.

The task structure was represented like the authority structure: either a direct task relationship existed (1) or it did not (0). The task network was developed with the cooperation of the personnel department, indicating who must relate to whom as part of his job. Vector elements were normalized before comparison (formula partly illegible in the text).

Distance between the work stations of the two members of a dyad, calculated from office layout drawings locating the position of every individual in the sample. Distances were divided into classes and the rank ordering of distances was compared with the rank ordering of average traffic per dyad channel in each class. Since the distance from i to j equals the distance from j to i, only entries above the diagonal of the organizational matrix were considered. Higher values mean less proximity.

From the communication tally, each entry is the number of written communications received by i from j over the tally period, forming a vector per individual with n-1 elements that was normalized before comparison. The individual's similarity to a formal structure is the sum of absolute differences between the normalized communication and structure entries. For the distance analysis, dyad traffic was combined in both directions and averaged per dyad channel within each distance class.
level: individual role vector; dyad for the distance analysis

description: From the communication tally, each entry is the number of telephone calls received by i from j over the tally period, forming a vector per individual with n-1 elements that was normalized before comparison. The individual's similarity to a formal structure is the sum of absolute differences between the normalized communication and structure entries. For the distance analysis, dyad traffic was combined in both directions and averaged per dyad channel within each distance class.
level: individual role vector; dyad for the distance analysis

description: From the communication tally, each entry is the number of face-to-face interactions (personal visits) received by i from j over the tally period, forming a vector per individual with n-1 elements that was normalized before comparison. The individual's similarity to a formal structure is the sum of absolute differences between the normalized communication and structure entries. For the proximity analysis, dyad traffic was combined in both directions and averaged per dyad channel within each distance class.
level: individual role vector; dyad for the distance analysis

description: Formal hierarchical position, taken from organization records, was scored from 1 to 6; the lower the score, the higher the formal rank. Scores 1 to 3 correspond to the laboratory director, his assistants and departmental heads; 4 to project supervisors; 5 and 6 to project members without administrative status, ranked on seniority and to some extent technical skill.
scale: 1 to 6, lower score means higher rank

variable_name: Influence in personnel, budgetary and technical decisions
description: Each respondent was asked to nominate the most influential people in the laboratory whom he or she had personally tried to influence during the previous year, separately for technical, budgetary and personnel decisions. The number of times each individual was nominated was counted. Because the distributions were highly skewed, the three influence variables were transformed into ordinal scales with three categories when used in multivariate analysis. The data were gathered on a separate instrument three weeks after the communication data.
scale: count of nominations; ordinal scale with three categories in multivariate analysis

description: Individuals reported their actual work related oral communication by writing names on survey forms. Boundary spanning individuals were defined as those individuals who were both internal and external communication stars. Using these methods 34 boundary spanning individuals were identified.
time_window: once a week for five weeks

description: Internal communication stars were identified for each department as those individuals who engaged in more than one standard deviation above the mean number of intra-departmental communications, as reported by their peers. Using these methods 18 internal stars were identified.
time_window: once a week for five weeks

description: Two external areas were identified: one within the organization but outside the department, and the other outside the organization. External stars for each area were defined as those individuals in the top fifth of the extra-department communication distribution. Using these methods 53 external stars were identified.
time_window: once a week for five weeks

variable_name: Project task score (research to technical service)
description: Respondents selected the category (basic research, applied research, development, technical service) that best characterized their project's objectives and indicated approximately what percentage of their work fell in each category; a weighted average of the percentages was calculated. Respondents also described their project's objectives on a 7-point scale from basic research to technical service; the scored responses to the two questions were averaged (Cronbach's alpha = 0.71). Project measures were calculated by averaging individual members' scores; the distribution of project task scores split projects into applied research and development (N = 11) and technical service (N = 12).
scale: task dimension from basic research to technical service; 7-point scale item

description: A firm's average annual after-tax net income, including extraordinary items, divided by the book value of its stockholders' equity, averaged over the study period (calculation in Appendix A). The logarithm of RETURN was used to bring symmetry to its distribution.

Variability of annual returns on equity, adapted from Fisher and Hall (1969): deviations of annual returns around a trend line estimated with an autoregressive time series model, so that trends are removed. Estimated with ten years of information for each firm. The text says the sine of RISK was used as a transformation for symmetry.

The debt ratio of the firm, the proportion of its assets supported by borrowed funds. It is an endogenous variable and, unlike the other business strategy variables, is not calculated as a ratio to the industry value. The appendix lists total liabilities (TL) of the firm among its inputs; the formula is not readable in the text.
Industry sales growth calculated as described in Appendix C; the formula is not readable in the text.
Variability of industry sales growth calculated as described in Appendix C; the appendix refers to a root mean square for error (RMS), but the formula is not readable in the text.

The average rating on a ten-point scale of two academic industry experts for each industry studied. A delphi-like procedure was used: the experts independently rated the height of entry barriers and received feedback on each other's ratings until ratings were no more than two scale points apart, which took two rounds.

Four-firm sales concentration of the industry, the mean of two points, one near the beginning and one near the end of the 1970s. Only the four-firm ratio was used because it was highly intercorrelated with the 8-, 20- and 50-firm ratios.
Number of firms in the industry, the mean of two points, one near the beginning and one near the end of the 1970s.

Business sales growth calculated as a ratio of the firm value to the corresponding industry value (Appendix D); the appendix refers to a firm-level equivalent (b) of the industry measure, but the formula is not readable in the text.

Variability of business sales growth calculated as a ratio of the firm value to the corresponding industry value (Appendix D); the appendix refers to a firm-level root mean square for error (RMS), but the formula is not readable in the text.
The natural logarithm of business size, calculated as a ratio of the firm value to the corresponding industry value.
Capital intensity calculated as a ratio of the firm value to the corresponding industry value (Appendix D); the formula is not readable in the text.
Worker productivity calculated as a ratio of the firm value to the corresponding industry value (Appendix D); the formula is not readable in the text.

Industry structure was represented by five industry-level variables: industry sales growth, variability of industry sales growth, entry barriers rated by two academic experts on a ten-point scale, four-firm sales concentration, and number of firms. Concentration and number of firms were means of two points near the start and end of the 1970s.

variable_name: GROWTH, GROWVAR, ASSETS, CAPINT, PROD (plus DEBT)
description: Business strategy was represented by a set of business-level variables: sales growth, variability of sales growth, size (log assets), capital intensity and worker productivity, each calculated as a ratio of the firm value to the corresponding industry value, plus the debt ratio as an endogenous variable.

Multiteam groups working on the same target area, with a subject matter expert, reviewed the medical literature for each potentially better practice and assigned each article a Muir Gray score, from 1 (meta-analysis of randomized control trials, highest evidence) to 5 (expert opinion, lowest evidence). Each practice received a score equal to the highest MG score among its articles. For each NICU the MG ratings of the practices it chose to implement were averaged. Lower scores reflect higher levels of evidence.
scale: 1 (highest level of evidence) to 5 (lowest level of evidence)

description: Project respondents rated how frequently their project team used each of 12 learning activities during their project. Principal axis factoring with an oblique promax rotation produced two factors; the five activities loading on the second factor form learn-what. Responses were aggregated to the NICU level.
scale: 1 = did not use the practice at all, 5 = used the practice to a very great extent
time_window: during the course of the project

description: Project respondents rated how frequently their project team used each of 12 learning activities during their project. Principal axis factoring with an oblique promax rotation produced two factors; the seven internally focused activities loading on the first factor form learn-how. Responses were aggregated to the NICU level.
scale: 1 = did not use the practice at all, 5 = used the practice to a very great extent
time_window: during the course of the project

description: Three items modified from Edmondson's (1999) scale, answered by nonproject respondents and aggregated to the NICU level. For the mediation test, psychological safety was calculated from one random half of nonproject respondents.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Three survey items drawn from Baker et al. (2003) measured the extent to which nonproject staff perceived that new practices improved NICU care. Responses were aggregated to the NICU level. For the mediation test, implementation success was calculated from the other random half of nonproject respondents.
scale: seven-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree)

description: Following Horn et al. (1996), drug availability is the number of drugs available on the hospital formulary for specified therapeutic categories divided by the total number of drugs in those categories, and drug standardization is 1 minus drug availability. The total number of drugs was counted from the 2001 AHFS Drug Information for ace inhibitors, beta blockers, nitrates, and calcium channel blockers (coronary artery diseases) and for miscellaneous beta-lactam antibiotics, macrolides, tetracyclines, quinolones, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, and penicillins (pneumonia). A separate measure is computed for each diagnostic category.

Total pharmacy charge divided by the length of stay for each patient hospitalized with coronary artery diseases or pneumonia, used as a proxy for pharmacy cost. A logarithmic transformation was used to normalize the variable. Higher charges indicate lower cost effectiveness.

Survey scale measuring the extent to which formulary decisions were made according to objective standards rather than the personal preferences of pharmacy and therapeutic committee members. Three items with five response options from one (to a small extent) to five (to a large extent), averaged into an index. Scale developed by the author and checked with confirmatory factor analysis.

Survey scale measuring the extent to which pharmacy and therapeutic committee members received input from prescribers. Five items with five response options from one (to a small extent) to five (to a large extent), averaged into an index.

Single survey item on whether the hospital has an internal appeals process if a request for a nonformulary drug is denied, measuring the presence of an appeal mechanism by which decisions could be reconsidered by a higher authority. Coded 1 for presence and 0 for absence of due process.

Survey scale measuring the extent to which exceptions to the standardized drug formulary were made. Two items with five response options from one (to a small extent) to five (to a large extent), averaged into an index.

Variance, within team-year, of the predicted values of individual pay level from a league-wide individual-level regression of logged, CPI-adjusted pay on individual performance inputs from year t-1 and its square, with year dummies.
Variance, within team-year, of the residuals from the league-wide individual-level pay regression, i.e., pay independent of productivity-relevant player observables.
Variance of pay in each team-year observation. Variance does not explicitly factor out the mean.

Sum of seven on-ice performance components of a player value measure approved by the NHLPA for fantasy hockey, each standardized within year, using a two-year average from years t-1 and t-2 where available. Team-year inputs are the within-team-year mean of individual inputs.
time_window: two-year average of t-1 and t-2

variable_name: movement of high-input players to high-DEP teams
description: Players continuing in the league were classified as stayers or movers, and as high, moderate or low input players in year t-1; the DEP level of the team they flowed to was measured in year t, with high-DEP teams above the median.
High-input stayers (those who remained with the prior year's team) compared across high-DEP and low-DEP teams, with high-DEP teams above the median.
Calculated by the NHL by summing two points for each regular season win, one point for each tie, and one point for each overtime loss.
Each team's final position in the play-off tournament bracket, coded 0 for non-play-off teams through 5 for the championship team.
Average salary of individual players within each team-year, adjusted for the CPI, with all salaries in 1998 dollars.
Within each team-year, the correlation of individual inputs from year t-1 with logged individual pay from year t.

Binary dependent variable: whether contrada i is involved in at least one incident related to Palio j. Incidents were drawn from historical sources reporting violent altercations before, during or after the race.
Count of formally declared alliances of each contrada for each year.
Count of formally declared rivalries of each contrada for each year.
Number of previous affiliations of the jockey with allies of the current employer, reconstructed from jockey careers.
Number of previous affiliations of the jockey with rivals of the current employer, reconstructed from jockey careers.
1962 annual sales in billions of dollars, grouped into four categories (0.6-1.0, 1.1-1.5, 1.6-2.0, 2.1 and up).
Number of employees in thousands, grouped into three categories (0-49, 50-99, 100 and up).
Number of plants of the corporation. The grouping used in the test is not stated in the text.

variable_name: existence of an IR research program
description: Whether the company reported engaging in IR research (yes or no) in the questionnaire. Forty-three companies reported they do and twenty reported they do not.
Established scale of items on knowledge, experience and familiarity with the supply chain, rated 1 to 7 by each node and standardized then averaged to the supply chain level.

Multi-item scale adapted from established scales, rated 1 to 5 by each node and standardized then averaged to the supply chain level. The text does not separate which listed items belong to this scale rather than information distribution.

Multi-item scale adapted from established scales, rated 1 to 5 by each node and standardized then averaged to the supply chain level. The text does not separate which listed items belong to this scale rather than knowledge acquisition.
Scale based on Huber (1991), averaged across nodes to the supply chain level.
scale: 1 to 5 strongly disagree to strongly agree

description: Perceptual items about the speed and length of the order fulfillment process, rated 1 to 7. It was reverse-coded to correspond to the direction of objective cycle time. One item was omitted after testing.
The cycle time of the supply chain (order fulfillment) process in number of days.
Amount of funds requested from Congress, in millions of dollars.
Amount of funds appropriated by Congress, in millions of dollars; the previous fiscal year's value is used in equation 1.
Number of applications for complaint, treated as exogenous.
Number of investigations filed, lagged one year.
Number of investigations that remain uncompleted.
Output of each of four workflow stages divided by the number of employees.
Index A: the number of formal complaints divided by funds received.
Index B: the number of cases litigated divided by funds received.
Number of investigations completed by the bureaus.
Number of FTC employees.
Average salary in dollars.
Number of formal complaints.
Dummy variable coded 0 for 1954-1964 and 1 for 1965-1971.
Number of cease and desist orders.
Throughput measure of cases handled by the hearing examiners.
Number of cases litigated.
Cases handled by the Office of General Counsel.
Number of orders contested by business respondents, reported from 1959.
Ratio of contested orders to total orders.

Coefficient of variation of faculty salaries within a department, computed from respondents' salary reports using the midpoints of reported income categories. Departments needed at least five respondents.
Coefficient of variation across departmental members of a productivity scale that sums standardized scores of articles published, books published and articles published within the previous two years.
Coefficient of variation across departmental members of college teaching experience.
Faculty members' estimates of the number of regular members, coded as the midpoint of the response range and averaged within the department.
Percentage of department members indicating they were essentially working alone on their current major piece of research or scholarship.
Mean of members' responses to how many of the people they saw socially were members of their department, from almost all through about half to almost none.
Colleges and universities coded by the Carnegie Commission by form of control; private institutions were those coded as privately controlled.
Departments were coded as having a long-term chairperson if the majority of respondents indicated appointment for a long or indefinite period rather than a fixed short term of three years or less.
Proportion of departmental members answering yes to whether decisions other than personnel matters are normally made by vote of the whole department, including junior members.
Mean departmental response on whether the administration was very autocratic, somewhat autocratic, somewhat democratic or very democratic, with very autocratic coded 4.

variable_name: proportion of women in the firm and in occupational categories
description: Computed from the personnel manager's questionnaire on the distribution of male and female employees across occupations. The authors computed the proportion of women in the firm's total work force and in nine occupational categories, and indexes of occupational dissimilarity between men and women.

variable_name: return on assets, return on equity and growth in sales
description: Three indicators of firm performance collected from the managing director, each measured over the fiscal year prior to the interview.
time_window: fiscal year prior to the interview

description: The sample was stratified by the nationality of the home-country firm: American, Japanese and Thai firms.

variable_name: organizational commitment, job satisfaction and quality of vertical bonds
description: Organizational commitment was measured with six items selected from the Porter Organizational Commitment Scale, each coded as a Likert scale from 1 to 7. Job satisfaction and the quality of vertical bonds within the organization were measured using indicators suggested by Lincoln and Kalleberg (1990).

The index of dissimilarity summed over the eight non-managerial occupations within each establishment, with D ranging between 0 and 100. Gender-homogeneous establishments were assigned a dissimilarity score of 100. Negative coefficients in the regression models indicate integration effects.

variable_name: percentage of female officials and managers
description: The percentage of female officials and managers in each establishment, with a squared term included for a non-linear effect. A one-year lag was used for these gender composition variables.

variable_name: natural logarithm of total number of workers
description: Establishment size was measured with the natural logarithm of the total number of workers.

The mean annualized growth rate of each establishment's total employment over the previous four-year period, calculated by ln[N(T)/N(0)]/T, where N(T) is size in the final year, N(0) is size in the first year and T is the years elapsed.
A variable indicating the calendar year, from which 1975 was subtracted so that the intercept represents establishments in the first year of the dataset.

Average shipments per plant in a size category divided by the capacity utilization for the industry in that year. Capacity utilization is assumed to be the same for each category of plants in an industry.
level: plant size category within four-digit industry

variable_name: P2/P1 (ratio of output per worker in 1982 to 1972)
description: Total shipments divided by payroll expense, used as output per worker, with the dependent variable being the ratio of this measure in 1982 to 1972.
level: plant size category within four-digit industry

description: The Census specialization ratio for a plant, equal to its shipments in its primary industry divided by its total shipments. The Census reports only an industry-wide average, so the authors assume it is the same for all plant categories in an industry. The authors call this measure rather poor.
level: industry average applied to plant size categories

description: Vertical integration is measured as the ratio of value added to shipments, where value added is total shipments minus the cost of materials, energy and outside services.
level: plant size category within four-digit industry

description: Supervisory overhead at the plant level is the ratio of all employees to production workers, where the Census defines production workers to include workers up through the line-supervisor level.
level: plant size category within four-digit industry

variable_name: Census year (1972 versus 1982) and change in coefficients
description: Time is operationalized by estimating the productivity model with 1972 and 1982 Census data and comparing the parameters across the two years. Equation (4) is estimated with 1982 coefficients plus change terms for 1972 to 1982, so that the change in the plant size elasticity and in the vertical integration elasticity shows whether the effect strengthened or weakened over the decade.
scale: two census years; coefficient change terms

variable_name: industry rank by research and development spending
description: Research and development spending was used to create a ranking of 18 industry groups, from leather goods at the bottom to aerospace at the top, using data presented by Tybout. The authors rely on Mueller's finding that spending relates strongly to patents granted when a proper time lag is allowed.
Coded as no college = 1, some college = 2, Bachelor's degree = 3, Master's degree = 4 and Doctorate = 5. Educational background was drawn from Dun's Reference Book of Corporate Managements.

variable_name: technical level of undergraduate degree, Master's degree and Doctorate
description: Three variables for the technical level of the executive's undergraduate, Master's and Doctoral education, drawn from educational background in Dun's Reference Book. The coding scheme for these variables is not described in the text.
Length of service in the firm was used as a proxy for job mobility, since mobility was not measured directly. Shorter service indicates higher mobility.
Age of the top executives, drawn from their date of birth in Dun's Reference Book of Corporate Managements.

variable_name: relative size of the 1935-1944 faculty cohort
description: The range of years faculty entered the department was divided into 10-year spans, and the proportion of the department represented by faculty who entered in 1935-1944 was used. The authors say it indexes both the clustering of the department and the extent to which older members dominated numerically. It pertains to the distribution in the 1974-1975 academic year.

variable_name: number of five to eight year gaps among entrants
description: The number of years between entry dates for adjacent hires was calculated, and the number of five to eight year long gaps among entrants in each department was used. The authors treat five to eight years as a consequential period because tenure is typically granted after six or seven years.

variable_name: departmental turnover by category and total
description: Turnover figures for five years were summed for each department. Categories were voluntary resignations by assistant, associate and full professors, early retirements of full professors, and involuntary expired appointments of assistant professors, plus a total across all categories. Deaths and mandatory retirements were excluded.

The average of 33 standardized items coded from the Vault and MCAA diversity surveys, for example diversity priorities (already completed or currently addressing coded 1, not a current priority coded 0) and recruitment from historically black colleges (coded 1 if any colleges were listed, 0 otherwise). The authors view the measures as formative.
time_window: as reported in April-May of each year

description: Four practices coded as dummy variables (0 for absence, 1 for presence), such as diversity training, which were standardized and averaged. The authors treat them as formative measures.
time_window: as reported in April-May of each year

description: Eight items, such as appointing a chief diversity officer or having a diversity committee, each standardized and then averaged as a formative measure.
time_window: as reported in April-May of each year

variable_name: turnover rate among women and racialized non-leaders
description: The number of women and racialized associates who departed during a year divided by the firm's total women and racialized associates at the beginning of that year. The year's turnover comes from the following year's survey and is predicted by practices reported in the year before.

variable_name: turnover rate among women and racialized leaders
description: The number of women and racialized partners who left the firm during a year divided by the firm's total women and racialized partners at the start of that year.
High and low conditions in which the fictional company offered (coded 1) or did not offer (coded 0) specific resources to aid the career success of women and racialized employees.
Practices manipulated by providing (coded 1) or not providing (coded 0) equal opportunity and access for all employees.
Practices varied by the presence (coded 1) or absence (coded 0) of formalized diversity plans and committees with defined actions and management accountability.

Three items adapted from Dover et al. (2016), such as worrying that one's gender, race or ethnicity would put one at a disadvantage, with a reverse-coded item on whether the diversity practices make the company a good place to work. Responses were on a 7-point Likert scale with higher values representing greater concerns.

Five items adapted from Ford and Noe (1987) and Ng and Burke (2005), such as whether the diversity practices would be useful to me or worthwhile to me. All were on a 7-point Likert scale with a higher value representing more personal relevance.

The three-item measure from Landau and Hammer (1986) of intention to leave the fictional company, such as likelihood of actively looking for a job outside of Ascentira. A 7-point Likert scale was used.

Number of full-time government employees within a county, from the 1972 Census of Governments. Variants scaled the count by population (GOVSIZE PER CAPITA) and by the number of administrative units (GOVSIZBADM).
Number of local government units with property tax power in a county, from the 1972 Census of Governments. A second measure, ADM PER CAPITA, is the ratio of administrative units to population.
